main_predictor: reward scheme type (discriminating = 345COM vs. symmetrical = 444COM)
sample_definition: Complementarity production function treatments only: 345COM (12 matching groups, 36 subjects) and 444COM (11 matching groups, 33 subjects), all 6 periods included
model_specification: Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U) with normal approximation and tie correction, comparing group-level average effort rates between 345COM and 444COM
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's approach in Table 2, the analysis uses matching-group-level averages as the unit of observation to account for within-group dependence, and compares the two complementarity treatments that differ only in reward scheme (discriminating vs. symmetrical). The rank-sum test with tie correction exactly reproduces the paper's reported p-value of 0.0649 (two-sided); the one-sided p-value of 0.0324 is reported here because the claim is explicitly directional.
reasoning: Under complementarity, the discriminating reward scheme (345COM, mean effort = 91.7%) elicits significantly higher effort than the symmetrical scheme (444COM, mean effort = 72.2%), with a difference of about 19 percentage points. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test yields z = 1.846, one-sided p = 0.032, supporting the claim that symmetrical reward schemes elicit lower efforts under complementarity.

dependent_variable: Anti-minus-Pro compensating action measure (1 = anti-immigration action mentioned without pro-immigration action; -1 = pro without anti; 0 = both or neither)
main_predictor: Constituent letter type (pro-immigration vs. anti-immigration letter), within-subjects
sample_definition: 56 U.S. senators who responded to both the pro-immigration and anti-immigration constituent letters
model_specification: McNemar chi-square test for within-subjects comparison of paired binary outcomes
controls: none (within-subjects design where each senator serves as their own control)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 2 analysis, the 'Anti - Pro' measure captures whether senators differentially mention compensating anti- vs. pro-immigration actions depending on constituent letter type. The McNemar test is the standard chi-squared equivalent of the exact within-subjects sign test described in the paper, appropriate for comparing paired binary outcomes. The 13 positive discordant pairs (more anti-immigration mentions in response to anti-immigration letters) vs. 1 negative discordant pair yield χ² = 10.29, consistent with the paper's reported p < 0.01.
reasoning: A McNemar chi-square test (the large-sample equivalent of the within-subjects sign test used in the paper) on the 56 senators who responded to both pro- and anti-immigration constituent letters yields χ²(1) = 10.29, p = 0.001. Senators were significantly more likely to mention anti-immigration actions relative to pro-immigration actions when responding to anti-immigration constituents (42.9% net anti-minus-pro rate) compared to pro-immigration constituents (19.6%), a 23.2 percentage point difference-in-difference. This supports the claim that senators tailor their explanations to their audiences.

dependent_variable: Percentage of free-association responses connoting the learned negative meaning of the cue (combined across homograph and nonhomograph cue types)
main_predictor: Cue status (baseline vs. suppressed) within the nonruminator group
sample_definition: 27 nonruminators (Group 1, lower RRS quartile) from Experiment 2 of the study
model_specification: Repeated-measures ANOVA with within-subjects factor of condition (baseline vs. suppressed) and between-subjects factor of counterbalancing (3 levels), restricted to nonruminators; F test for the condition main effect with error df = N - 3 = 24
controls: Counterbalancing factor (3 levels for rotating word-pair sets across conditions)
operationalization_notes: The claim that nonruminators' transfer-task responses show suppression practice is beneficial maps directly onto testing the SIF effect (baseline > suppressed) within nonruminators. The data file contains Experiment 2 (free association) data. Following the paper's method, cue types (homograph/nonhomograph) were combined, and the counterbalancing factor was included as a between-subjects blocking variable. The F(1, 24) test replicates the paper's reported simple-effects analysis for nonruminators.
reasoning: For nonruminators in Experiment 2, a repeated-measures ANOVA (with counterbalancing as a between-subjects factor) testing the simple effect of condition (baseline vs. suppressed) on the percentage of learned-meaning responses yielded F(1, 24) = 10.94, p = .003, ηp² = .31. Nonruminators produced more learned-meaning responses to baseline cues (M = 45.68%) than to suppressed cues (M = 29.63%), confirming suppression-induced forgetting on the indirect free-association test. This supports the claim that suppression practice can be beneficial for nonruminators.

dependent_variable: Psychological well-being (CES-D 8 scale, reverse coded, range 0-3, higher = better well-being)
main_predictor: Cross-level interaction between parental status (living with children vs. childless) and country-level percentage disapproving of childlessness
sample_definition: Respondents aged over 40 from 24 European countries in ESS round 3 (2006), excluding cases with missing data on any analysis variable (N=24,203)
model_specification: Two-level linear mixed model (individuals nested in countries) with random intercepts for country and random slopes for parental status indicators (live_child, empty_nest), estimated via REML
controls: Age (centered at 41), age squared, marital status (separated/divorced, widowed, never married vs. married/cohabiting ref.), education (lower secondary, upper secondary, tertiary vs. primary ref.), parental education (lower secondary, upper secondary, tertiary, missing vs. primary ref.), religious attendance, paid employment, born in country, gender, country-level disapproval percentage (main effect)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 2a specification, the key test is the cross-level interaction between the individual-level parental status dummy (living with children vs. childless reference) and the country-level percentage of respondents who (strongly) disapprove of childlessness. The country-level disapproval variable was computed from the individual-level childless_disapp variable (≥3 = disapprove/strongly disapprove). The full sample (both genders) was used to test the general claim stated in the abstract, with gender added as a control.
reasoning: The cross-level interaction between living with children (vs. childless) and country-level disapproval of childlessness is positive and significant (z = 3.18, p = 0.0015), indicating that the well-being disadvantage of childless people is smaller in countries with more tolerant norms towards childlessness. This directly supports the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: DSM5_Total (total psychopathology score)
main_predictor: MiniK_Total (Mini-K life history strategy score; higher = slower strategy)
sample_definition: All 138 participants with complete data (46 men, 92 women; ages 16-69)
model_specification: OLS regression of DSM5_Total on MiniK_Total, controlling for Age and Sex (equivalent to partial correlation)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 4, I computed the partial correlation between the Mini-K (the primary life history strategy measure) and total psychopathology, controlling for age and sex. The Mini-K was chosen over the HKSS as the paper describes it as more superior for assessing behavioral traits of life history strategy. The negative partial correlation indicates that faster life strategies (lower Mini-K) predict greater psychopathology, consistent with the claimed directional effect.
reasoning: The partial correlation between MiniK_Total (life history strategy) and DSM5_Total (psychopathology), controlling for Age and Sex, is r = -0.51 (t(134) = -6.90, p < .001). The negative association confirms that lower Mini-K scores (faster life strategy) are associated with higher psychopathology scores, supporting the original claim.

dependent_variable: PolWis_score (political knowledge test score, sum of correct answers)
main_predictor: Stereotypaktivierung (stereotype activation condition: not activated vs activated by gender difference statement)
sample_definition: Female participants (gender_alle=1, 'weiblich') with Filter=1 (meeting inclusion criteria: gender_alle<3, honesty=1, citizen=1), in stereotype-not-activated (condition 0) or stereotype-activated-by-gender-difference-statement (condition 2) conditions
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (pooled variance), two-tailed
operationalization_notes: Used gender_alle variable (gender regardless of experimental condition) rather than gender variable, since gender was not asked in all experimental conditions. The Filter variable was applied as specified in the dataset to exclude participants who failed honesty/citizenship checks. The comparison follows the paper's specific contrast: condition 1 (stereotype not activated) vs condition 3 (stereotype activated by gender difference statement) for female participants only, on the political knowledge total score.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing political knowledge scores of female participants in the stereotype-not-activated condition (M=8.90, SD=4.60, n=73) versus the stereotype-activated-by-gender-difference-statement condition (M=7.03, SD=4.11, n=70) yielded t(141)=2.57, p=.011. This supports the original study's claim that female participants performed better when the stereotype was not activated compared to when it was activated by a gender difference statement.

dependent_variable: GDP growth index at t+2 (f2gdpidx), measured as GDP index with previous year = 100
main_predictor: Binary indicator = 1 if either the city party secretary or the mayor has a patronage tie to the incumbent provincial secretary (msec2currentsec | mayor2currentsec)
sample_definition: All prefecture-level and subprovincial cities in mainland China excluding Tibet and centrally administered municipalities, years 2000-2011, with non-missing values on all model variables
model_specification: OLS with city fixed effects and province-year fixed effects (implemented via alternating within-group demeaning), cluster-robust standard errors at the city level
controls: City economic controls: net fiscal transfer (dep), predecessor's GDP growth, log GDP, log population, and log investment (for both city secretary and mayor predecessors). City leader controls: age, education, gender, and tenure duration dummies (<1yr, 1-3yr, 3-5yr; >5yr reference) for both city secretary and mayor.
operationalization_notes: Replicates Table 1 Model 3 from the paper—the full specification with both economic and leader controls. The connection variable follows the paper's definition: the city is 'connected' if either the municipal party secretary (msec) or the mayor was promoted while the current provincial secretary was in a supervisory position. Tibet is excluded per the paper's sample definition. Two-way demeaning (city + province-year) is used to absorb high-dimensional fixed effects.
reasoning: In a two-way fixed effects OLS regression (city FE + province-year FE) of GDP growth at t+2 on a binary indicator for patronage ties to the provincial secretary, with city economic and leader controls and cluster-robust SEs at city level, the coefficient on 'connected' is 0.372 (SE = 0.120, t = 3.086, p = 0.002). This confirms the paper's claim that city leaders with informal ties to incumbent provincial leaders deliver significantly faster economic growth than those without.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for top-quality player (selected for senior national team, level A)
main_predictor: Denmark × Post-1991 reform interaction (difference-in-differences estimator)
sample_definition: All foreign players (those playing in a country different from their nationality) in the top leagues of 14 European countries from 1985 to 2008, excluding domestic players
model_specification: Linear probability model (OLS) with country fixed effects, year fixed effects, and the Denmark × Post-reform interaction; cluster-robust standard errors at the country level (14 clusters)
controls: Country fixed effects and year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: The paper's Danish case study (Table 1, Panel B2) tests the effect of the 1991 Danish foreigners' tax scheme on the ability composition of foreign players. I operationalize this as a DD comparing the share of top-quality (national team A-level) foreign players in Denmark versus other countries, before (1985-1990) vs after (1991-2008) the reform. Top-quality is defined as having been selected for the senior national team, consistent with the paper's definition. The sample is restricted to foreign players only, as the claim specifically concerns the composition of foreigners.
reasoning: A difference-in-differences analysis on foreign players across 14 European countries (1985-2008) finds that the 1991 Danish tax scheme for foreigners increased the probability that a foreign player in Denmark is top-quality (national team A-level) by 40.1 percentage points relative to other countries (t = 14.77, p < 0.001, cluster-robust SE at country level). The share of top-quality foreign players in Denmark rose from 20.0% pre-reform to 57.3% post-reform, while other countries saw virtually no change (58.0% to 58.2%). This strongly supports the claim that the tax cut changed the ability composition of foreigners in favor of higher-ability players.

dependent_variable: Willingness to Pay (WTP) scale score
main_predictor: Intrinsic relative to Extrinsic values (I/E) score
sample_definition: All 155 university students from Study 1 with complete data on I/E and WTP variables
model_specification: Pearson correlation testing the bivariate association between I/E and WTP, converted to t-statistic
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the directional relationship between I/E and WTP. The most direct test is the Pearson correlation, which the paper itself reports in Table 1 (r = .42***). I computed this directly from the data. The I/E score was calculated by the original authors by centering values around each individual's overall mean, reversing extrinsic values, and averaging intrinsic and reversed-extrinsic scales. The WTP scale was the mean of three items.
reasoning: The Pearson correlation between intrinsic relative to extrinsic values (I/E) and willingness to pay (WTP) was r = 0.426, t(153) = 5.83, p < .001, confirming that higher endorsement of intrinsic relative to extrinsic values is significantly associated with higher willingness to pay to protect the environment, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: ln_imports (logged imports of disputed products into defendant country from each trade partner)
main_predictor: Complainant (binary indicator = 1 if partner is complainant in the dispute)
sample_definition: Early settlement disputes only (observations where _est_re=1), covering 45 disputes with 6,027 partner-year observations
model_specification: OLS with dispute fixed effects (LSDV with dispute_combined dummies), standard errors clustered by dispute
controls: Defendant GDP (ln_gdp_resp), Partner GDP (ln_gdp_part), Democratic Pair (dempair), Disputed Imports t-1 (imports_tminus1), Total Imports (ln_total_imports)
operationalization_notes: Replicated the paper's Model 2 from Table 0 (Early Settlements/Privacy), which directly tests whether complainant countries gain disproportionately more than non-participants in private settlements. The model includes dispute fixed effects and clustered standard errors, matching the paper's specification. The coefficient and standard error (0.430, SE=0.180) match the paper's reported values exactly.
reasoning: The coefficient on Complainant in the early settlement (privacy) model is 0.430 (clustered SE = 0.180, t = 2.384, p = 0.017), indicating that complainant countries gain significantly more in terms of disputed-product imports into defendant markets compared to non-participants. This confirms the paper's claim that private (early) settlements lead to discriminatory trade outcomes favoring complainants.

dependent_variable: Entrepreneurship rate (early-stage, pays wages)
main_predictor: Median age of population aged 20-64
sample_definition: All country-year observations in the GEM dataset (82 countries, years 2001-2010, N=393)
model_specification: Weighted Least Squares (WLS) with year fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors at the country level
controls: Year dummies (2001 as reference); weights = number of GEM survey respondents per country-year cell
operationalization_notes: This replicates Table 2 Column 3 from the paper, which is the specification most directly testing the claim about median age and entrepreneurship. The claim on p. S140 references this specification, noting 'a one standard deviation decrease in median age...results in a 2.5 percentage point increase in the entrepreneurship rate.' Using median age rather than the estimated shrinkage parameter r makes the result more interpretable and directly tests the stated claim.
reasoning: A WLS regression of country-year entrepreneurship rate on median age (with year dummies, weighted by survey sample size, and clustered SEs by country) yields a coefficient of -0.0073 (t = -5.71, df = 81, p < 0.001), confirming that a decrease in a country's median age is associated with significantly higher new business formation. A one standard deviation (~3.0 year) decrease in median age corresponds to a ~2.2 percentage point increase in the entrepreneurship rate, consistent with the paper's claimed 2.5 percentage point effect.

dependent_variable: Ratio of perceived arm length to actual arm length
main_predictor: Arm side (right vs. left), within right-handed participants
sample_definition: 15 right-handed participants (Handedness = 2) from Experiment 1
model_specification: One-tailed paired-samples t-test comparing right arm ratio vs. left arm ratio
controls: Actual arm length is controlled for by using the ratio (perceived/actual) as the dependent variable
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, the ratio of perceived to actual arm length was used as the dependent variable, and a one-tailed paired t-test was conducted for right-handed participants only, matching the paper's reported analysis approach for this directional hypothesis.
reasoning: A one-tailed paired-samples t-test on the ratio of perceived to actual arm length for right-handed participants yielded t(14) = 2.12, p = .026 (one-tailed), with right arm ratios (M = 0.970) exceeding left arm ratios (M = 0.920). This replicates the paper's reported t(14) = 2.12 and supports the claim that right-handed participants perceived their right arms as longer than their left arms. Note that the two-tailed p = .052 is borderline, but the directional hypothesis justifies the one-tailed test used in the original paper.

dependent_variable: Appreciation index (average of three items: how appreciated, how valued, how satisfied with acknowledgment)
main_predictor: Acknowledgment condition (verbal acknowledgment vs. financial acknowledgment with $.05)
sample_definition: 49 hotel guests who completed the study (2 excluded participants who left before answering DV questions, per exclude variable)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA comparing two groups
controls: None (random assignment; paper verified review word count did not differ across conditions)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's reported analysis for Study 1a, used the pre-computed dv_index3 as the DV (averaged from dv1, dv2, dv3 with Cronbach's alpha = .96), excluded participants flagged with exclude=1, and ran a one-way ANOVA with condition as the grouping variable. The paper reports F(1,47) = 8.50, p = .005; my independent analysis reproduces this result exactly.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA on the appreciation index (averaged from three items) comparing the verbal acknowledgment condition (M = 5.57, SD = 1.27, n = 18) and the financial acknowledgment condition (M = 4.38, SD = 1.45, n = 31) yielded F(1, 47) = 8.50, p = .005. Participants who received the financial acknowledgment with $.05 felt significantly less appreciated than those who received the verbal acknowledgment, supporting the trivialization effect claimed in the paper.

dependent_variable: s_tot (mean standardized midterm and final exam scores)
main_predictor: avg5_girl (share of females among the 5 surrounding students)
sample_definition: Female students (girl==1), excluding favored students with nonrandom seat assignments (special1==0), with non-missing data on all covariates
model_specification: OLS regression with block (classroom×row-group) fixed effects and classroom-clustered standard errors
controls: Baseline test score, desk mate favored status, share favored among neighbor 4, height, age, birth order, father's education, mother's education, baseline interest in Chinese/English/math
operationalization_notes: Following Table 4 Panel B specification from the paper: female-only subsample, neighbor-5 female share as the key regressor, with the full set of controls and block fixed effects as described in the paper's equation (2). This directly tests the claim that surrounding gender composition affects female test scores.
reasoning: In the female subsample (N=245), the coefficient on share female in neighbor 5 is 0.215 (SE=0.078), yielding t=2.77, p=0.006. This indicates that being surrounded by five females rather than five males increases a female's test scores by approximately 0.2 standard deviations, consistent with the paper's claim of a 0.2–0.3 SD effect.

dependent_variable: Attitude instability (absolute difference between mean attitude at Time 1 and Time 2)
main_predictor: Certainty × Objective Ambivalence interaction
sample_definition: Study 1 participants who completed both Time 1 and Time 2 attitude measures (N = 174)
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression: Step 1 entered extremity, certainty, and objective ambivalence; Step 2 added the certainty × ambivalence product term. The key test is the t-test for the interaction term in Step 2.
controls: Attitude extremity (|mean T1 attitude - scale midpoint|)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods: objective ambivalence was computed using the similarity-intensity model [(pos+neg)/2 - |pos-neg|]; certainty was the mean of 7 items; extremity was covaried to isolate unique effects of certainty and ambivalence. Study 1 was chosen as the primary analysis because it is the first study, has the largest complete-case sample, and the analysis specification is clearest in the paper.
reasoning: A hierarchical OLS regression predicting attitude instability (|mean attitude T1 - mean attitude T2|) from certainty, objective ambivalence, extremity (covariate), and their interaction revealed a significant certainty × ambivalence interaction (B = 0.037, t(169) = 2.28, p = .024). At low ambivalence (-1 SD), greater certainty was associated with less attitude instability (more stability; simple slope = -0.033), whereas at high ambivalence (+1 SD), greater certainty was associated with more instability (simple slope = 0.105). This supports the claim that greater certainty is associated with greater stability as ambivalence decreases.

dependent_variable: Number of complaints filed with the Better Business Bureau (complaints_2008)
main_predictor: Indicator for firm name begins with A or a number (first_A)
sample_definition: All 2,293 plumbing firms operating in Illinois from the 2008 BBB data
model_specification: Poisson regression with log(employees) offset (coefficient constrained to 1) and robust standard errors (HC1)
controls: Ad spending in $000s (ad_spend_k), firm age, metro Chicago indicator
operationalization_notes: Replicated specification 2 from Table 5 of the paper, which is the most direct test of the claim that A-name firms receive more complaints while controlling for basic firm characteristics. The multiple_names control is excluded as it may be a mediator rather than a confounder.
reasoning: A Poisson regression of BBB complaints on an indicator for A-name firms, controlling for ad spending, firm age, metro Chicago, and log(employees) as offset (with robust SEs), yields a coefficient of 1.138 (IRR = 3.12) with z = 3.946 (p < 0.001). Firms whose names begin with A or a number receive approximately 3 times more complaints than other firms, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Cooperative Strategy (dv), ordinal: 0=concession-extracting, 1=refuse concessions, 2=offer concessions, 3=offer significant concessions
main_predictor: Issue-linkage structure (issue_linkage_structure), continuous measure of how differently valued the bargaining issues are
sample_definition: All 588 state-bargaining phase observations from 23 EU negotiations
model_specification: Generalized ordered logit (partial proportional odds model) with clustered standard errors by negotiation phase (23 clusters). Issue-linkage structure and five other variables constrained to proportional odds; five variables allowed to vary across thresholds.
controls: lnGDP, security and defense policy, Euro state, new member state, agreement importance, parliamentary scrutiny, majority voting, publicity, presidency, lagged dependent variable
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 1 specification, I estimated a generalized ordered logit (partial proportional odds) model where issue_linkage_structure satisfies the proportional odds assumption (same coefficient across all DV thresholds). Standard errors clustered by negotiation phase to account for within-phase dependence. The coefficient (1.219) and clustered SE (0.188) closely replicate the paper's reported values (1.219 and 0.192 respectively).
reasoning: The generalized ordered logit model (partial proportional odds) with clustered standard errors yields a coefficient of 1.219 for issue_linkage_structure (SE = 0.188, z = 6.49, p < 0.001), indicating that more differently valued issues are associated with significantly more cooperative (concession-offering) bargaining strategies. This strongly supports the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Dispute (MID initiation: binary indicator of whether a country initiated a militarized interstate dispute in a given year)
main_predictor: Coup events (lcoupsum: log of weighted coup events, instrumented via control function approach)
sample_definition: All 798 country-year observations from 22 Latin American countries, 1960-1999
model_specification: Rivers-Vuong control function probit: (1) First-stage OLS of coup events on all exogenous variables (instruments + controls); (2) Second-stage probit of dispute on coup events, first-stage residual, and control variables, with cluster-robust standard errors by country
controls: Previous dispute (lagdisp), ethnic fractionalization (ethfrac), relative power (cinc), number of borders (nborder), number of allies log (lnumber), regional conflict (regconf), polity lagged (polity2l), real GDP log lagged (llrgdpch), and first-stage residual (for endogeneity correction)
operationalization_notes: The paper uses the cdsimeq procedure in Stata (Maddala 1983 simultaneous equations). I implement the Rivers-Vuong (1988) control function approach, which is the standard econometric method for handling endogenous continuous regressors in probit models. Excluded instruments for the coup events equation are: previous coup (rcoupbin), recent war (rwar), and conflict ends (lagconfendparts). This approach provides both a consistent estimate of the coup risk effect and an endogeneity test. The positive and significant coefficient on coup events (z=2.24, p=0.025) replicates the paper's key finding, though the magnitude differs somewhat (1.93 vs. paper's 2.96) due to differences in estimation procedure.
reasoning: Using the Rivers-Vuong control function probit to correct for endogeneity between coup events and conflict involvement, the coefficient on coup events is positive (1.93) and statistically significant (z = 2.24, p = 0.025) in the dispute model. This supports the paper's claim that as threats to political survival (measured by coup risk) increase, the likelihood of conflict involvement increases. The endogeneity test (residual coefficient z = -2.16, p = 0.031) confirms that correcting for endogeneity is necessary, consistent with the paper's argument that standard probit without correction yields a null finding.

dependent_variable: d12outgroup (amount sent to out-group recipient in dictator game, 0-5 euros)
main_predictor: albregion (dummy for primarily Albanian region, highest out-group exposure; reference = primarily Serb region)
sample_definition: All 158 ethnic Serb participants across three regions in Kosovo (40 in primarily Albanian region, 40 in border region, 78 in primarily Serb region)
model_specification: OLS linear regression with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
controls: borderregion, female, age, education, employed, village, alphaviolence, alphadamaged, displaced
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 2 specification, the dependent variable is out-group dictator giving and the key predictor is the Albanian region dummy (highest vs. lowest exposure contrast). OLS was used rather than the paper's Tobit model for simplicity and transparency, but both yield the same directional conclusion. The positive coefficient on albregion directly tests the claim that out-group bridging norms increase with exposure.
reasoning: An OLS regression of out-group dictator giving on region dummies (with Serb region as reference) and extended controls yields a positive and significant coefficient for the Albanian region dummy (b = 1.31, t = 3.54, p = 0.0005, df = 147, n = 158), indicating that ethnic Serbs in the primarily Albanian region (highest out-group exposure) give significantly more to out-group recipients than those in the primarily Serb region (lowest exposure). This supports the claim that out-group bridging norms increase with exposure to the out-group.

dependent_variable: enjoyrelativ (relative enjoyment/preference rating of the target clip on a 7-point scale)
main_predictor: condition (interrupted with commercial vs. no interruption/continuous)
sample_definition: All participants with valid condition and enjoyment data (N = 102 out of 105 rows); 3 rows with missing condition excluded
model_specification: Independent samples t-test with equal variances assumed
operationalization_notes: Study 2 used a between-subjects design where participants watched either a continuous animated sword fight clip or one interrupted by a 30-second commercial. The key DV is the enjoyment rating of the target clip (enjoyrelativ). The paper's analysis for Study 2 was an independent samples t-test, which I replicated here. The condition labeled 'good' corresponds to the interrupted condition and 'no' to the continuous condition.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test on enjoyment ratings (enjoyrelativ) comparing the interrupted condition (M = 5.38, n = 53) to the continuous/no-interruption condition (M = 4.47, n = 49) yielded t(100) = 2.45, p = .016, indicating that commercial disruption significantly increased enjoyment of the program. This replicates the original study's reported finding of t(100) = 2.43, p = .016.

dependent_variable: acceptedbribes (belief that politician accepted bribes or engaged in illegal practices, 1-5 scale)
main_predictor: Causal correction condition vs. Denial condition (tested as difference between regression coefficients for causal_d and denial_d dummies)
sample_definition: All respondents with non-missing acceptedbribes (N=986 out of 1000), across all four experimental conditions
model_specification: WLS regression with inverse probability weights (IPW), regressing acceptedbribes on dummies for Innuendo, Denial, and Causal conditions (Control as reference); linear hypothesis test of causal_d = denial_d
controls: None (treatment dummies only; block randomization handled via IPW weights)
operationalization_notes: The claim compares causal correction to denial on misperception reduction. I used the 'acceptedbribes' DV as it directly measures acceptance of the misperception about illegal activity and was available for all conditions. IPW weights (1/assignment probability) account for the block randomization. The test of coefficient equality in the full model (all four conditions) is the most direct test of whether the causal correction outperforms the denial, consistent with the paper's Table 2 Model 3 approach.
reasoning: Testing whether the causal correction reduces misperceptions more than the denial, I estimated a WLS regression with inverse probability weights on all four conditions (Control reference) with 'acceptedbribes' as the DV. A linear hypothesis test comparing the causal and denial coefficients yielded t = -5.07, p < 0.001, indicating the causal correction significantly reduced belief in misperceptions by 0.48 points more than the denial (causal coefficient = 0.07 vs. denial coefficient = 0.55, on a 1-5 scale). This supports the paper's claim that an alternate causal explanation is more effective in limiting acceptance of misperceptions than providing evidence against the innuendo.

dependent_variable: Intimacy score (composite of 4 items: understanding, validation, caring, and reversed caring, rated on 7-point scale)
main_predictor: Attention condition (1=attention/80% monitoring vs. 2=no attention/0% monitoring)
sample_definition: All 30 participants from Study 2a dataset (15 per condition); the original paper excluded 1 participant for suspected deception (N=29), but the specific excluded participant could not be independently verified, so all available data was used
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed; Levene's test p=.698)
controls: None, consistent with the paper's reported analysis for Study 2a
operationalization_notes: Used the pre-computed Intimacy score from the original dataset (Sheet3 of the Excel file), which was calculated by the original authors from the 4 intimacy questionnaire items. The paper describes these as: understanding, validation, caring, and a reversed caring item, aggregated into a single score. All 30 available participants were included as the specific excluded participant could not be verified.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test on the pre-computed Intimacy scores from Study 2a revealed that intimacy was significantly higher in the attention condition (M=4.58, SD=0.82) than in the no attention condition (M=2.78, SD=0.77), t(28)=6.20, p<.001, Cohen's d=2.26. dependent_variable: q147_learnmore_apbd_REC2 (willing to monitor/learn more about the budget, binary 0/1)

dependent_variable: Number of givers per 23-minute session (total across doors 1 and 2)
main_predictor: Ask1 treatment dummy (verbal ask at door 1 vs. silent opportunity at door 1)
sample_definition: All 64 session-level observations from the 2009 Salvation Army field experiment (4 days × 4 blocks × 4 sessions per block)

controls: Date fixed effects (day 2, 3, 4 dummies) and session fixed effects (session 2, 3, 4 dummies)
operationalization_notes: The Ask1 vs. Opp1 comparison is the cleanest test of whether the verbal ask increased giving, as both conditions have one solicitor at door 1 and differ only in verbal ask vs. silent bell ringing. This matches the paper's Table 2, Column 1 specification.
reasoning: An OLS regression of the number of givers per 23-minute session on treatment dummies (with Opp1 as the omitted category) and date/time fixed effects yields a coefficient on Ask1 of 4.06 (SE = 1.22), t(54) = 3.34, p = .002. This means the verbal ask at one door increased the number of givers from 7.44 (silent opportunity) to 11.50, a 55% increase, strongly confirming the claim that the verbal ask increased giving.

dependent_variable: zakaibag (Bagrut certification status, 0/1)

operationalization_notes: Follows the paper's Table 2 Panel A column 5 specification for girls, which is the primary cross-sectional result. The model controls for school-level covariates, individual lagged score quartiles, and micro covariates as in the paper's equation (1). Cluster-robust SEs account for the group-randomized design with 34 school clusters. Degrees of freedom use G-1=33 per BRL convention.
reasoning: The OLS estimate of the treatment effect on girls' Bagrut certification rates is 0.102 (SE=0.044, t=2.31, p=0.028), indicating a statistically significant increase of about 10 percentage points. dependent_variable: Intrafirm import share (share of related-party imports in total U.S. imports by industry-year)
main_predictor: DownMeasure × 1(Buyer-industry demand elasticity > median)
sample_definition: 253 IO2002 manufacturing industries, years 2000-2010 (2783 industry-year observations)
model_specification: OLS regression following equation (32): S_it = β₁ D_i × 1(ρ<med) + β₂ D_i × 1(ρ>med) + β₃ 1(ρ>med) + controls + year FE, with standard errors clustered by industry (253 clusters)
controls: Buyer-industry weighted: skill intensity (log s/l), equipment capital intensity (log equipment k/l), plant capital intensity (log plant k/l), materials intensity (log m/l), R&D intensity (log(0.001+R&D/Sales)), dispersion; plus year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's empirical specification (eq. 32), we use the DownMeasure downstreamness variable interacted with an indicator for above-median buyer-industry demand elasticity (w1sigma). The buyer-industry weighted variables (w1 prefix) are used for both the elasticity measure and the control variables, consistent with the paper's approach of weighting by IO usage shares. The key test is whether β₂ (the high-elasticity interaction) is positive, directly testing the claim that downstreamness positively relates to intrafirm import share only for high demand elasticity (sequential complements case).
reasoning: The coefficient on DownMeasure × 1(Demand elasticity > median) is positive and highly significant (β₂ = 0.292, t = 3.75, p = 0.0002), confirming a positive relationship between downstreamness and intrafirm import share for high-elasticity industries. In contrast, the coefficient for low-elasticity industries is near zero and insignificant (β₁ = 0.017, p = 0.79), and the difference β₂ − β₁ is significant (t = 2.77, p = 0.006), supporting the claim that the positive relationship emerges only for high demand elasticity values.

dependent_variable: Whether PAP applied for child (binary: bid_on_d)
main_predictor: Non-African American girl indicator (nonaa_girl)

model_specification: Logit regression with PAP-clustered robust standard errors
controls: Other race-gender dummies (nonaa_boy, black_girl, black_boy, black_unknown), already born, months to birth, finalization cost, Hispanic indicator, PAP type dummies (gay, lesbian, single vs. straight reference), year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: The paper uses a conditional logit at the PAP-child-day level with a 10-day activity window; I collapsed to PAP-child level and used a standard logit, which tests the same directional hypothesis about preference for non-AA girls. The sample is restricted to eligible PAP-child pairs with determinate race-gender classifications (binary dummies summing to 0 or 1).
reasoning: A logit regression of whether a PAP applies for a child on race-gender dummies (with non-African American unknown gender as the reference) and controls yields a positive and highly significant coefficient on the non-African American girl indicator (coef = 0.478, z = 4.56, p < 0.001 with PAP-clustered standard errors). The application rate for non-AA girls is 9.0% versus 6.0% for the reference category, confirming PAPs have a positive preference for non-African American girls as claimed.

dependent_variable: a-insensitivity index (a) — computed as a = 3 × (1/3 − (m̄_c − m̄_s)), where m̄_s and m̄_c are the average matching probabilities for single and composite events respectively
main_predictor: Part1 × TP treatment dummy (1 if observation is from Part 1 in the time pressure treatment, 0 otherwise)
sample_definition: 99 subjects (42 control, 57 TP) after excluding 5 TP subjects who did not submit matching probabilities on time in Part 1; each subject contributes two observations (Part 1 and Part 2)
model_specification: OLS regression with standard errors clustered at the individual level: a = intercept + β₁(Part1×TP) + β₂(Part2×Control) + β₃(Part2×TP) + ε, with reference group = Part 1, control treatment
controls: Part2×Control and Part2×TP dummies (Model 1, no demographic controls)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's analysis: computed a-insensitivity from matching probabilities of single (E1, E2, E3) and composite (E12, E13, E23) AEX events for Parts 1 and 2, excluded the 5 TP subjects with missing Part 1 data, and used the same OLS regression with clustered SEs as specified in the paper's Methods section. The Part1×TP coefficient directly tests whether time pressure increases insensitivity.
reasoning: OLS regression with clustered standard errors on the a-insensitivity index (N=99 subjects, 198 observations) shows that the Part1 × TP treatment coefficient is 0.19 (SE=0.089), z=2.12, p=0.034, indicating that a-insensitivity is significantly higher under time pressure (mean a=0.34) compared to the control condition (mean a=0.15). This confirms the paper's claim that people become more insensitive (perceive more ambiguity) under time pressure.

dependent_variable: Conflict duration (months)
main_predictor: Technology of rebellion (Irregular vs Conventional/SNC)
sample_definition: All 147 civil wars in the Technology of Rebellion (TR) dataset, including 11 right-censored ongoing conflicts
model_specification: Weibull accelerated failure time (AFT) model with irregular and SNC dummies (conventional as base category), right-censoring for ongoing conflicts
controls: none (baseline Model 1 specification, matching paper's simplest model)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 0 Model 1, I use the TR conflict-level dataset with a Weibull AFT duration model. The irregular dummy coefficient (positive = longer duration) directly tests whether irregular wars last longer than conventional wars (base category). A second model with irregular as base confirms the comparison with SNC. Duration in months was computed from start/end dates; 5 missing durations were imputed from available date components or censoring times (mid-2008 for ongoing conflicts).
reasoning: In a Weibull AFT model predicting conflict duration with technology of rebellion dummies (conventional as base), the coefficient for Irregular is 1.22 (SE = 0.22), yielding z = 5.57 (p < 0.001). The time ratio of 3.40 indicates irregular wars last about 3.4 times longer than conventional wars. A separate model with irregular as the base confirms irregular wars also last significantly longer than SNC wars (z = 2.35, p = 0.019). Both comparisons support the claim that irregular conflicts last longer than all other types of conflict.

dependent_variable: log monthly mortality rate (lndrate)
main_predictor: Number of days with mean temperature >90°F, interacted with post-1960 indicator (both current and lagged month effects)
sample_definition: All available state-year-month observations for the continental US from 1931-2004, excluding observations with missing mortality rates or lagged temperature variables
model_specification: Weighted OLS with 3-bin temperature model (current and lagged) interacted with post-1960 indicator; year×month fixed effects, state×month fixed effects, state-month-specific linear and quadratic time trends; clustered standard errors at the state level (49 clusters)
controls: Precipitation indicators (devp25, devp75), age share variables (sh_0000, sh_4564, sh_6599) interacted with month dummies, log real per capita income (lri) interacted with month dummies, state×month quadratic time trends, year×month fixed effects, state×month fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 5 Row 1 specification, I estimate a pooled model for 1931-2004 with temperature bins (<40°F, 80-89°F, >90°F) for both the current and previous month, interacted with a post-1960 indicator. The F-test for the >90°F × post-1960 interactions directly tests whether the temperature-mortality relationship for extremely hot days declined after 1960, which is the central claim. The residualization approach (FWL theorem) was used to absorb high-dimensional fixed effects before estimating the key temperature coefficients.
reasoning: An F-test of the joint significance of the >90°F temperature × post-1960 interaction terms (current and lagged) yields F(2,48)=30.54, p<0.001, strongly rejecting the null that the temperature-mortality relationship for very hot days remained unchanged. The cumulative effect of >90°F days on log mortality declined from 0.0404 (pre-1960) to 0.0116 (post-1960), a 71% decline, confirming the paper's claim of a sizable decline in the temperature-mortality relationship across decades.

dependent_variable: DVD purchase decision (1 = buy, 0 = not buy)
main_predictor: interaction between opportunity cost cue and connectedness to future self
sample_definition: All 88 adult participants from Study 1A with complete data on connectedness, opportunity cost condition, and purchase decision
model_specification: Logistic regression: purchase ~ connectedness + opportunity_cost_cue + connectedness × opportunity_cost_cue
controls: none beyond the constituent main effects of connectedness and opportunity cost cue
operationalization_notes: Connectedness was measured as the standardized average of two measures (self-rating and Euler circle overlap), each coded 0–100, as described in the paper's methods. The interaction term in the logistic regression directly tests the claim that opportunity cost cues reduce spending primarily when future self-connectedness is high. A negative interaction coefficient means the cue's spending-reducing effect is stronger at higher levels of connectedness.
reasoning: A logistic regression predicting DVD purchase from connectedness (ZFINAL), opportunity cost cue (0=no cue, 1=cue), and their interaction revealed a significant negative interaction (z = -2.10, p = .036). This indicates that the opportunity cost cue reduces spending primarily among those more connected to their future selves, consistent with the paper's claim. The cue decreased purchase rates from 71% to 51% overall, but the connectedness-spending relationship was strong in the cue condition (r = -.41, p < .01) and absent without the cue (r = .04, NS).

dependent_variable: Whether the referral is female (binary)

operationalization_notes: The either-gender treatment is the key condition for this claim because it captures unrestricted referral choices. The paper's Table 1, Panel C presents this exact comparison (p = 0.002 in the original). The z-test for two proportions directly tests the directional claim that men are less likely to refer women than women are.
reasoning: In the either-gender treatment condition, male CAs referred women 22.6% of the time (30/133) while female CAs referred women 42.5% of the time (37/87), a difference of 19.97 percentage points. A two-proportion z-test yields z = -3.15 with a one-tailed p-value of 0.0008, strongly supporting the claim that CA men are less likely to refer women than CA women. This replicates the original paper's finding (Table 1, Panel C, p = 0.002).

dependent_variable: log continuously compounded interest rate (interval-censored from intertemporal choices)

controls: 1 Week vs. 2 Weeks dummy, Larger Stakes dummy, Larger Stakes × (1 Week vs. 2 Weeks) interaction

reasoning: An interval regression of log continuously compounded interest rate on an ethnicity-salience treatment dummy (with controls for delay length, stake size, and their interaction, and standard errors clustered by subject) yields a coefficient of -1.4165 (SE = 0.3756) for the Asian-American subsample (N=71 subjects, 284 choices). dependent_variable: average cooperation rate (fraction of time a subject spends cooperating, averaged across all 23 supergames per subject)
main_predictor: termination rule (deterministic vs stochastic horizon)
sample_definition: Subjects in Short-Deterministic (n=48) and Short-Stochastic (n=48) treatments only; Variable-Deterministic and Long treatments excluded
model_specification: Welch's t-test (two-sample t-test assuming unequal variances) on subject-level average cooperation rates
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's definition, cooperation rate is the fraction of time a subject spends cooperating within a supergame, averaged by subject across all supergames. The paper's Table III regression uses all four main treatments with controls and cluster-robust SEs; here I directly compare the two short-duration treatments using a Welch's t-test, which is the most direct and transparent test of the specific claim about short duration treatments.
reasoning: A Welch's t-test comparing average cooperation rates between Short-Deterministic (M=63.28%, SD=11.65%) and Short-Stochastic (M=52.32%, SD=18.51%) treatments yields t(79.19)=3.44, p<.001, confirming that cooperation rates are significantly higher with a deterministic horizon than with a stochastic horizon in short duration treatments. dependent_variable: pldist1 (plurality party distance from median voter)

Comparing pldist1 between the two electoral systems is the most direct test of this directional claim.

Green targets were perceived as more feminine (M = 2.64) than nongreen targets (M = 1.82), confirming the claim that consumers who engaged in green behavior were perceived as more feminine than those who engaged in nongreen behavior.

dependent_variable: Error rate in the LV (lottery variation) format — proportion of dominated lottery choices out of 10 decisions
main_predictor: Average number of safe choices across PV and RV formats (risk aversion measure)
sample_definition: 79 risk-averse subjects (out of 106 total, after removing 2 experimenter entries with age=99) who averaged 5 or more safe choices across the PV and RV MPL formats
model_specification: Pearson correlation (equivalent to OLS linear regression) testing the relationship between error rate and risk aversion; t-test for H0: ρ = 0
operationalization_notes: Risk aversion is measured as the average number of safe choices in PV and RV MPL formats. Decision error is the proportion of non-dominant choices in the LV format, where for decisions 1–4 the RV lottery dominates (Risk3i=1 = chose B/RV = dominant) and for decisions 6–10 the PV lottery dominates (Risk3i=0 = chose A/PV = dominant); decision 5 has identical lotteries and is always counted as dominant. The coding Risk3i=1=chose B(RV), 0=chose A(PV) was verified by confirming that ~32% of risk-averse subjects chose all 10 dominant lotteries, matching the paper's description.
reasoning: A t-test of the Pearson correlation between decision error rate (proportion of dominated lottery choices in the LV format) and risk aversion (average safe choices across PV and RV formats) among 79 risk-averse subjects yields r = -0.4625, t(77) = -4.577, p = 0.000018. The significant negative correlation confirms that decision error decreases with risk aversion, consistent with the paper's claim.
