dependent_variable: took_act (binary indicator for whether the patient took ACT during their first illness episode)
main_predictor: act40 (binary indicator for 92% ACT subsidy, i.e., price of Ksh 40)
sample_definition: First illness episodes from the endline survey, excluding households with RDT subsidies (rdt_any=0) and those selected for surprise RDT testing (ex_post=0), with non-missing outcome data (N=631)
model_specification: OLS linear regression with cluster-robust standard errors at the household level
controls: Strata fixed effects (28 strata dummies), household head age (B_head_age_imputed), and an indicator for missing household head age (B_head_age_missing); also included act60 and act100 dummies for other subsidy levels
operationalization_notes: Following Table 2 of the paper, the analysis tests the effect of the 92% subsidy on ACT take-up using first illness episodes from the endline survey, with the same sample restrictions and model specification (strata FE + head age controls). The 92% subsidy is the 'very high subsidy' referenced in the claim.
reasoning: The 92% ACT subsidy (act40) significantly increases the likelihood of taking ACT by 22.5 percentage points relative to the no-subsidy control group (control mean = 19.0%), with a t-statistic of 4.27 (p < 0.001). This strongly supports the claim that a very high subsidy increases access to antimalarials.

dependent_variable: Work absorption (4-item scale from Rothbard, 2001)
main_predictor: Single childless (1 = single/childless, 0 = all other family structures)
sample_definition: Employed business school alumni (full-time, part-time, or self-employed), after excluding unemployed and retired respondents, with listwise deletion for missing data (n = 353)
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression with absorption regressed on single/childless indicator plus controls (gender, age, job level)
operationalization_notes: Replicated the exact model specification from Study 1 as described in the paper's methods section, using the same filtering (employed only) and listwise deletion approach. The dependent variable, predictor coding, and control variables all match the paper's published analysis.
reasoning: OLS regression of work absorption on single/childless status (1 = single childless, 0 = other family structures), controlling for gender, age, and job level, yields a significant negative coefficient for single/childless (b = -0.31, SE = 0.13, t(348) = -2.36, p = .019). This supports the claim that single, childless workers report lower absorption than workers with other family structures.

dependent_variable: ProperName (whether the housing official greeted the applicant by name, coded 0/1, conditional on receiving a response)
main_predictor: is_hispanic (indicator for Hispanic emailer vs white reference category)
sample_definition: All emails that received a response and had non-missing data on the ProperName variable and demographic controls (n=558)
model_specification: Logistic regression with Hispanic and Black name indicators (white = reference), community demographic thirds (percent Black, percent Hispanic, poverty rate, total population), and Hard Email indicator
controls: Black name indicator, community percent Black (thirds), percent Hispanic (thirds), poverty rate (thirds), total population (thirds), Hard Email indicator
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 1, Column 3 specification as closely as possible. The public data uses blinded demographic thirds instead of continuous variables, so indicator variables for the middle and top thirds replace the continuous controls. The reference category for race is white (the omitted group when both Black and Hispanic indicators are included). The ProperName outcome is only defined for respondents.
reasoning: A logit model regressing whether a housing official greeted the applicant by name (ProperName) on Hispanic Name and Black Name indicators (white = reference) with controls for community demographics and Hard Email yields a coefficient of -0.789 for Hispanic Name (z = -3.62, p = 0.0003), indicating Hispanic applicants were significantly less likely to be greeted by name than white counterparts. This replicates the original study's finding of a -0.82 coefficient and the claim of approximately 20 percentage point lower probability of named greeting for Hispanic applicants.

dependent_variable: Normal quality indicator (1 = normal quality, 0 = low quality/shading)
main_predictor: Flexible contract dummy (1 = flexible, 0 = rigid)
sample_definition: Competitive treatment (condition 1), good state of nature, traded contracts only (i.e., excluding no-trade outcomes in the bad state for rigid contracts)
model_specification: OLS linear probability model with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered at session level), regressing normal quality on price increment (price - 35), flexible contract dummy, and their interaction
controls: Price increment (price minus competitive price of 35) and price increment × flexible contract interaction
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 3 Column 1 specification, which is the most direct statistical test of the claim. The analysis is restricted to condition 1 (competitive treatment) and the good state, since rigid contracts do not trade in the bad state, making within-state comparison the appropriate test of shading differences.
reasoning: The OLS regression of normal quality on a flexible contract dummy (with price increment and interaction controls, cluster-robust SEs at session level) yields a coefficient of -0.335 (z = -5.60, p < 2.1e-08), indicating that flexible contracts have 33.5 percentage points more shading (lower normal quality) than rigid contracts in the good state. This strongly supports the claim that under rigid contracts much less shading occurs than under flexible contracts.

dependent_variable: consider (binary: 1 if a state considered or carried out an attack on a proliferator's nuclear program in a given dyad-year)
main_predictor: hostileMID (prior violent militarized conflict between the attacker and the proliferator)
sample_definition: Directed dyad-years where the target state has an active nuclear program (polrel=1), restricted to politically relevant dyads, with complete data on all model variables
model_specification: Firth penalized logistic regression matching the paper's Model 2 specification from Table 5
controls: polity2 (target's regime type), s_un_reg (foreign policy similarity), cap_2 (target's power), pwrratio (power ratio), postArt56 (post-Article 56 norm), postCW (post-Cold War), prgmyrs (program years), NCAnosafetodate (nuclear assistance), cap_1 (attacker's power), contig (contiguity), noconsideryrs (peace years), cubic splines (_spline1, _spline2, _spline3)
operationalization_notes: The paper's Model 2 specification includes a peace-years correction (noconsideryrs + cubic splines) that causes quasi-complete separation in standard logistic regression because consider=1 only occurs when noconsideryrs=0. Firth's penalized logistic regression handles this separation by applying a Jeffreys invariant prior penalty to the likelihood, allowing finite coefficient estimates and valid inference. This approach preserves the paper's intended model specification while addressing the technical estimation problem.
reasoning: Firth penalized logistic regression (used to handle quasi-complete separation from the peace-years variable) yields a positive and highly significant coefficient for violent conflict (hostileMID) on the probability of considering an attack on a proliferator's nuclear program (z = 3.75, p < 0.001, N = 5,360). This confirms the paper's claim that prior violent militarized conflict increases the salience of the proliferation threat.

dependent_variable: splinter (binary indicator = 1 if county j became a new splinter district in electoral wave t)
main_predictor: DEC_rep (DEC share ratio = county's share of DEC seats / county's share of district population; lower = more politically marginalized)
sample_definition: County-wave observations from Uganda's three electoral waves (1996-2000, 2001-2005, 2006-2010), excluding single-county districts (ncounties=1) and observations with missing data on key variables
model_specification: Logistic regression (matching paper's Table 3, Model 1 specification) with Wald z-test on the DEC_rep coefficient
controls: Ethnic marginalization (ethnic_min), development summary index (ECON), number of counties in district (ncounties), lagged breakup status (break_lag), region dummies (Eastern, Northern, Western; Central as reference), electoral wave dummies (wave2, wave3; wave1 as reference)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 1 from Table 3, which uses a random intercept logistic model; I use standard logistic regression as a close approximation. The DEC share ratio is the paper's primary measure of political marginalization—a ratio below 1 indicates the county is underrepresented on the district executive committee relative to its population. The negative coefficient on this variable directly tests the claim that political marginalization increases secession likelihood.
reasoning: The DEC share ratio (county's share of district executive committee seats divided by its population share) has a negative and highly significant coefficient (z = -3.70, p = 0.0002) in a logistic regression predicting district secession. This means counties with lower DEC representation relative to their population share—i.e., more politically marginalized—are significantly more likely to secede and form their own new local government, confirming the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Logarithm of absolute opinion change on immigration (wave 3 vs wave 2)
main_predictor: Group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev, mean DQI justification level per discussion group)
sample_definition: Participants with non-missing data on DQ_jlev and all control variables (174 of 191 DQI-coded participants, across 13 small discussion groups)
model_specification: Linear multilevel regression (mixed effects) with random intercepts by small group, individuals nested in groups
controls: Knowledge change, four clarify-thinking indicators (other participants, experts, politicians, briefing material), social conformity pressure (above/below group mean), gender, age, education, working class, Catholic, Protestant, religiosity, left-right ideology, left-right ideology squared, left party vote intention, right party vote intention
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 2 Model 2b specification, which tests whether the magnitude (not direction) of opinion change on immigration is associated with group-level deliberative quality (justification rationality). The dependent variable is the log of absolute change to address right-skewness. This directly operationalizes the claim that 'participants change their opinions more often when rational justification is used.'
reasoning: In a linear multilevel model regressing the logarithm of absolute immigration opinion change on group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev) with full controls and random intercepts by discussion group (N=174 individuals in 13 groups), the coefficient for justification rationality was 0.130 (SE=0.066, z=1.964, p=0.0495). This positive and statistically significant effect supports the claim that higher group-level rational justification leads to greater magnitude of opinion change.

dependent_variable: Average effort (proportion of work decisions) at the matching-group level across all 6 periods
main_predictor: Reward scheme type (345COM = discriminating rewards 3/4/5 vs. 444COM = symmetrical rewards 4/4/4), both under complementarity production technology
sample_definition: All matching groups in the two complementarity treatments: 345COM (12 matching groups) and 444COM (11 matching groups, one fewer due to a session with only 15 subjects)
model_specification: Welch's independent-samples t-test comparing matching-group-level average effort between the discriminating and symmetrical reward schemes under complementarity
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's approach, the matching group (3 subjects playing together for 6 periods) is used as the independent unit of observation to account for within-group interdependence. Average effort across all 6 periods is the outcome. The comparison of 345COM vs 444COM directly tests the claim about symmetrical vs discriminating rewards under complementarity. Welch's t-test accommodates unequal variances between groups.
reasoning: Under complementarity, the discriminating reward scheme (345COM, mean effort=0.917) elicited significantly higher effort than the symmetrical scheme (444COM, mean effort=0.722), with Welch's t(17.40)=2.32, one-sided p=0.016. This supports the claim that the symmetrical reward scheme elicits substantially lower efforts than the discriminating scheme under complementarity.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator of whether senator mentioned more anti-immigration than pro-immigration compensating actions in response letter
main_predictor: Type of constituent letter received (anti-immigration vs. pro-immigration)
sample_definition: 56 U.S. senators who responded to both the pro-immigration and anti-immigration constituent letters in the field experiment
model_specification: McNemar chi-square test for paired proportions (within-subjects design)
controls: None — the within-subjects design inherently controls for all senator-level confounders
operationalization_notes: The claim that 'senators tailor their explanations to their audiences' was operationalized using the Anti-Pro balance measure from Table 2 of the paper: whether a senator mentioned more anti-immigration than pro-immigration compensating actions. The McNemar test compares this paired binary outcome across the two letter conditions, consistent with the paper's within-subjects sign test approach.
reasoning: A McNemar chi-square test on the 56 senators who responded to both pro- and anti-immigration constituent letters shows that senators were significantly more likely to mention more anti-immigration than pro-immigration compensating actions when writing to anti-immigration constituents (46.4%) than when writing to pro-immigration constituents (26.8%), χ²(1) = 9.31, p = 0.002. This supports the claim that senators tailor their explanations to their audiences.

dependent_variable: Percentage of learned (negative) meanings in free associations (combined across homograph and non-homograph cues)
main_predictor: Within-subjects cue status: baseline vs. suppression (difference score FAbaseC - FAsuppC)
sample_definition: Nonruminators (Group = 1) from Experiment 2, n = 27, with 9 participants per counterbalancing cell
model_specification: One-way ANOVA on difference scores (baseline minus suppression percentages) with counterbalancing (3 levels) as between-subjects factor, using sum-to-zero contrasts; F-test for intercept tests whether grand mean of difference differs from zero
controls: Counterbalancing (CB: A, B, C) as between-subjects factor
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's analytic framework, the SIF effect for nonruminators was tested as a simple effect within a mixed ANOVA that includes counterbalancing as a between-subjects factor to reduce error variance. The difference score (baseline - suppression) represents suppression-induced forgetting; a positive difference indicates that suppression reduced the accessibility of learned negative meanings. Cue type (homograph vs. non-homograph) was not included as it did not interact with other factors in the paper's analysis.
reasoning: For nonruminators (n=27), the suppression-induced forgetting effect on the free-association indirect measure was significant: F(1, 24) = 10.94, p = .003, partial η² = .31. Nonruminators produced fewer learned (negative) meanings for suppressed cues (M = 29.6%) compared to baseline cues (M = 45.7%), a difference of 16.05 percentage points, confirming that suppression practice can be beneficial for nonruminators on indirect memory measures.

dependent_variable: Psychological well-being (CES-D 8-item scale, 0-3 range)
main_predictor: Cross-level interaction: Lives with children × Country-level disapproval of childlessness (standardized)
sample_definition: Women aged over 40 from 24 European countries (ESS Round 3, 2006) with complete data on all variables (no missing CES-D items and no missing control variables)
model_specification: Linear multilevel regression (random intercept by country, random slopes for parental status by country) with cross-level interaction, estimated via REML
controls: Age, age squared, marital status (separated/divorced, widowed, never married; ref: married/cohabiting), education (lower secondary, upper secondary, tertiary; ref: primary), parental education (same categories + missing), religious attendance, paid employment, born in country, individual social contacts, individual norms towards childlessness
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 2a specification, the analysis tests the cross-level interaction between individual parental status and country-level disapproval norms. Women-only sample was used because the paper identifies the effect as strongest for women and the model converged cleanly with the paper's exact random-effects specification. The key interaction (lives with children × disapproval) is the most direct test of the claim: a positive interaction means the disadvantage of childlessness increases with country-level disapproval, i.e., is smaller where norms are tolerant.
reasoning: The cross-level interaction between 'lives with children' and country-level disapproval of childlessness is positive and highly significant (z = 4.895, p < 0.001, coefficient = 0.123). This means that in countries with higher disapproval of childlessness (less tolerant norms), the well-being gap between parents and childless people is larger. Equivalently, the disadvantage in psychological well-being of childless people is smaller in countries with tolerant norms, which supports the claim.

dependent_variable: DSM5_Total (total psychopathology symptom score)
main_predictor: MiniK_Total (Mini-K life history strategy total score)
sample_definition: All 138 participants with complete data on MiniK_Total, DSM5_Total, and Age
model_specification: Partial correlation (equivalent to OLS regression of DSM5_Total on MiniK_Total controlling for Age), following the paper's primary analytic approach
controls: Age (covariate, as specified in the paper's main analyses)
operationalization_notes: The paper's main analysis used partial correlations between life history strategy measures and psychopathology controlling for age. I used the Mini-K as the primary life history measure (the paper describes it as more superior for behavioral traits) and DSM5_Total as the psychopathology outcome, matching the paper's Table 5 result of pr = -.51 for Mini-K and total psychopathology.
reasoning: A partial correlation between Mini-K total score (life history strategy) and DSM-5 total score (psychopathology), controlling for age, yielded pr = -0.51, t(135) = -6.95, p < .001. The negative correlation indicates that lower Mini-K scores (faster life strategy) are associated with higher psychopathology scores, consistent with the paper's claim that faster life strategies are associated with greater levels of psychopathology.

dependent_variable: PolWis_score (political knowledge test score, sum of correct answers across 20 items)
main_predictor: Stereotype activation condition (stereotype not activated vs. stereotype activated by gender difference statement)
sample_definition: Female participants from Study 2 who passed the study's inclusion filter (filter_$==1, meaning valid gender, honest responses, German citizenship), assigned to either the stereotype-not-activated condition or the stereotype-activated-by-gender-difference-statement condition
model_specification: ANCOVA (OLS regression) with condition as the grouping variable and political interest (PolInt_score) as covariate
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's method, I used Study 2 data, filtered observations per the study's filter variable, restricted to female participants (gender_factor==1), and compared the two conditions directly relevant to the claim. Political interest was included as a covariate consistent with the paper's ANCOVA approach.
reasoning: An ANCOVA comparing female participants in the stereotype-not-activated condition (M=8.90, n=73) versus the stereotype-activated-by-gender-difference-statement condition (M=7.03, n=70) on political knowledge test scores, controlling for political interest, yielded t=2.35, df=140, p=0.020. Female participants scored significantly higher when the stereotype was not activated, consistent with stereotype threat theory and the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: GDP growth rate at t+2 (f2gdpidx, measured as index with last year = 100)
main_predictor: Connected to provincial secretary (binary indicator = 1 if either city party secretary or mayor has a patronage tie to the incumbent provincial party secretary)
sample_definition: City-year observations from Chinese prefecture-level cities between 2000-2011, with non-missing values for the dependent variable, connection indicator, and all control variables
model_specification: OLS fixed effects regression with city fixed effects and province-year fixed effects, robust standard errors clustered at the city level
controls: City economic controls: Net Transfer (t+1), and predecessor final-year GDP growth, Log GDP, Log population, Log fixed asset investment for both city secretary and mayor. City leader controls: Age, college education, gender, and tenure dummies (<1 year, 1-3 years, 3-5 years; reference: >5 years) for both city secretary and mayor.
operationalization_notes: Model 3 (column 3 of Table 1) from the paper was replicated as the preferred specification. The connection variable combines ties from either the city secretary or the mayor to the provincial secretary, following the paper's definition. The 'dep' variable (fiscal expenditure minus fiscal revenue at t+1) is used as the Net Transfer control. All controls, fixed effects, and clustering follow the paper's specification as closely as possible from the available data.
reasoning: The coefficient on the patronage connection variable is 0.363 (SE = 0.132, t = 2.75, p = 0.006), indicating that city leaders connected to the incumbent provincial secretary deliver GDP growth rates approximately 0.36 percentage points higher than unconnected leaders. This positive and statistically significant effect (p < 0.01) supports the paper's claim that informal ties to provincial leaders lead to faster economic growth. My coefficient (0.363) closely replicates the paper's reported estimate of 0.382 for the same model specification.

dependent_variable: willingness to pay (WTP)
main_predictor: intrinsic relative to extrinsic values (I/E score)
sample_definition: All 155 Study 1 participants (Chinese-ethnicity university students in Hong Kong) with complete data, after excluding 4 incomplete questionnaires as described in the paper
model_specification: Pearson correlation (equivalent to simple linear regression of WTP on I/E score)
operationalization_notes: Used the E_I variable from the dataset, which matches the paper's reported I/E score statistics (M ≈ .43, SD ≈ .36) and group cutoffs (I/E ≥ .61 for intrinsic group, I/E ≤ .22 for extrinsic group). This is the most direct test of the claim that higher I/E is related to higher WTP. The correlation was converted to a t-statistic for reporting purposes.
reasoning: A Pearson correlation between the I/E score (intrinsic relative to extrinsic values) and willingness to pay yielded r = 0.42, t(153) = 5.73, p < 0.001, indicating that higher endorsement of intrinsic relative to extrinsic values is significantly associated with higher willingness to pay to protect the environment, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: ln_imports (logged product-level imports from defendant to partner)
main_predictor: complainant (dummy = 1 if partner country is the complainant in the dispute)
sample_definition: Early-settled WTO disputes (dropped or mutually agreed solutions), post-dispute observations only, with complete data on all covariates (N = 6,027 as indicated by the _est_re estimation sample flag)
model_specification: OLS regression with dispute fixed effects (C(dispute_combined)) and cluster-robust standard errors clustered at the dispute level (45 clusters)
controls: Defendant GDP (ln_gdp_resp), Partner GDP (ln_gdp_part), Democratic Pair (dempair), Disputed Imports lagged (imports_tminus1), Total bilateral imports (ln_total_imports), dispute fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 0 Model 2 specification, the most direct test of the claim that private settlements lead to discriminatory outcomes is the Complainant coefficient in the early settlement subsample. The estimation sample was identified using the _est_re variable (=1) stored in the dataset, which exactly reproduces the N=6,027 reported in the paper. Cluster-robust SEs at the dispute level were used because observations within the same dispute are correlated.
reasoning: The Complainant coefficient in the early settlement OLS model (with dispute fixed effects and cluster-robust SEs) is 0.430 (SE = 0.180, t = 2.384, p = 0.017), indicating that complainant countries gain significantly more in product-level imports from defendants compared to non-participant WTO members when disputes are settled privately. This supports the paper's claim that private (early) settlements lead to discriminatory trade outcomes favoring complainant countries.

dependent_variable: Entrepreneurship rate (early stage, pays wages)
main_predictor: Median age of population aged 20-64
sample_definition: All country-year observations in the GEM dataset (393 observations across 82 countries, years 2001-2010)
model_specification: Weighted least squares (WLS) regression with year fixed effects, weights equal to the number of individual respondents per country-year cell, and standard errors clustered at the country level
operationalization_notes: This specification directly follows Table 2, Column 3 of the paper, which is the most directly tied regression to the claim about median age and new business formation. The paper notes that 'using the estimates from column 3 of table 2, a one standard deviation decrease in median age results in a 2.5 percentage point increase in the entrepreneurship rate.'
reasoning: The coefficient on median age (ages 20-64) is -0.0073 (SE = 0.00128) in a WLS regression of the entrepreneurship rate on median age and year dummies, weighted by cell size, with standard errors clustered at the country level (82 clusters). The t-statistic is -5.71 (p < 0.001), confirming that a decrease in a country's median age is significantly associated with increased new business formation, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Ratio of perceived arm length to actual arm length (perceived/actual), separately for right and left arms
main_predictor: Arm side (right vs. left), within-subjects factor for right-handed participants
sample_definition: Right-handed participants only (Handedness = 2.0 in the dataset), n = 15, from Experiment 1
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing RatioRight vs. RatioLeft for right-handed participants
controls: None; the ratio measure (perceived/actual) inherently controls for actual arm length differences
operationalization_notes: The ratio of perceived to actual arm length was used as the DV rather than raw perceived length, because it controls for actual physical differences between left and right arms. A paired t-test was used because each participant estimated both their right and left arm lengths, making this a within-subjects design. The one-tailed p-value is reported because the claim is explicitly directional (right arm perceived as longer than left).
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing the ratio of perceived-to-actual arm length for right vs. left arms among right-handed participants yielded t(14) = 2.12, one-tailed p = .026 (two-tailed p = .052). The mean difference (RatioRight − RatioLeft = 0.049) was in the predicted direction: right-handed participants perceived their right arms as longer than their left arms, consistent with the original study's claim. The one-tailed test is justified given the directional hypothesis stated in the claim.

dependent_variable: dv_index3 (mean of three items measuring how appreciated participants felt by the company's actions)
main_predictor: condition (0 = verbal acknowledgment, 1 = financial acknowledgment with $.05)
sample_definition: 49 hotel guests who completed the study (excluded 2 participants who left before answering DV questions, per the 'exclude' variable)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA comparing the two acknowledgment conditions on appreciation
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's reported analysis for Study 1a, used the pre-computed dv_index3 as the dependent variable, filtered out excluded participants, and ran a one-way ANOVA with condition as the grouping variable. This directly tests the core claim that financial acknowledgment leads to less positive outcomes than verbal acknowledgment.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA comparing appreciation (dv_index3, the mean of three items) between verbal acknowledgment (M = 5.57, n = 18) and financial acknowledgment with $.05 (M = 4.38, n = 31) yielded F(1, 47) = 8.50, p = .005, confirming that financial acknowledgment leads to significantly less appreciation than verbal acknowledgment—supporting the trivialization effect.

dependent_variable: Standardized exam score (combined midterm + final)
main_predictor: Share of females among 5 neighboring students (desk mate + 4 surrounding peers)
sample_definition: Female students who are not 'favored' (non-randomly seated) students, with complete data on all covariates (N=245)
model_specification: OLS regression with block (classroom × height-row) fixed effects and cluster-robust standard errors at the classroom level (12 clusters)
controls: Baseline test score, average baseline score of neighbor 5 peers, proximity of favored students (desk mate favored status and share of favored among neighbor 4), height, age, birth order, mother's education, father's education, baseline interest in Chinese, English, and math
operationalization_notes: This analysis follows the paper's Table 4 Panel B specification for the female sample, which directly tests the claim about the effect of surrounding female peers on female test scores. The coefficient represents the effect of going from 0% to 100% female neighbors (i.e., five females vs. five males).
reasoning: The coefficient on share of females among 5 neighboring students (avg5_girl) is 0.211 (SE = 0.086, t = 2.45, p = 0.032 with 11 df using cluster-robust inference), indicating that for a female student, being surrounded by all females rather than all males increases test scores by approximately 0.21 standard deviations, consistent with the paper's claim of a 0.2–0.3 SD effect.

dependent_variable: Attitude change (absolute difference between mean attitude at Time 1 and Time 2)
main_predictor: Certainty × Objective Ambivalence interaction term
sample_definition: Participants who completed both Time 1 and Time 2 attitude measures in Study 1 (organic food attitudes, N = 174)
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression with attitude extremity as covariate, objective ambivalence and certainty entered in step 1, and their product interaction term entered in step 2; the interaction t-test from step 2 is the reported statistic
controls: Attitude extremity (absolute deviation of Time 1 attitude from scale midpoint of 4)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods for Study 1, objective ambivalence was computed using the similarity-intensity model: (P+N)/2 - |P-N| from separate positive and negative ratings on 7-point scales. Certainty was the mean of 7 items (Petrocelli et al., 2007 scale). Attitude change was the absolute difference between mean attitude ratings at two time points. Study 1 was chosen as the primary analysis because it is the first demonstration of the effect and has the most straightforward design.
reasoning: The certainty × objective ambivalence interaction significantly predicted attitude change (instability) over a one-month interval in Study 1: t(169) = 2.282, p = .024, B = .037, 95% CI [.005, .069]. The positive interaction coefficient indicates that as ambivalence decreases, the relationship between certainty and greater stability (less change) becomes stronger, consistent with the paper's claim. Simple slopes showed that at high ambivalence (+1 SD), certainty predicted greater instability (slope = .105, t = 2.33), whereas at low ambivalence (-1 SD), certainty was (non-significantly) associated with more stability (slope = -.033, t = -0.73).

dependent_variable: Turnout (percentage of registered population that voted)
main_predictor: FDI Flows (log) — natural logarithm of FDI inflows plus outflows as a percentage of GDP
sample_definition: 23 OECD countries, 1970–2007, election-year observations only (where years since last election is non-missing); after within-country detrending and dropping missing data on FDI flows and controls, 222 observations across 21 countries remain
model_specification: Fixed effects OLS with country-specific linear and quadratic time trends (implemented via within-country detrending of all variables on country-specific intercepts and trend terms), with clustered standard errors by country
controls: Registered Voters (log), %VAP 30–69, Years Since Last Election, US Mid-term dummy, Compulsory Voting dummy, Mixed System dummy, PR System dummy, Disproportionality index, Effective Number of Parties (seats), Margin of victory
operationalization_notes: The paper uses system GMM with a lagged dependent variable; I use a simpler but defensible fixed effects approach with country-specific time trends and no LDV, which avoids Nickell bias while still controlling for country heterogeneity and trending. FDI Flows (log) was chosen as the main ownership predictor because it captures the most mobile form of capital, which the paper argues should most strongly constrain policy and reduce turnout.
reasoning: A fixed effects panel regression of turnout on FDI Flows (log) with country-specific linear and quadratic time trends and the full set of controls yields a significant negative coefficient (β = -2.25, t = -3.30, p = 0.001), confirming that foreign ownership reduces turnout as predicted by the ownership-constraint hypothesis. This result is consistent with the paper's system GMM estimates, which also find significant negative effects of ownership variables on turnout.

dependent_variable: Number of BBB complaints filed against the firm
main_predictor: Indicator for firm name beginning with A or a number (first_A)
sample_definition: All 2,293 plumbing firms in Illinois with complete data on key variables
model_specification: Poisson regression with robust (HC1) standard errors, ln(employees) as offset constrained to 1
controls: Ad spending in $000s, firm age, metro Chicago indicator
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 5 specification 2, which is the most basic Poisson regression testing the A-name effect on complaints with controls. The offset of ln(employees) constrained to 1 accounts for differential exposure to complaints due to firm size.
reasoning: A Poisson regression of BBB complaints on the A-name indicator (controlling for ad spending, firm age, metro Chicago, and with ln(employees) as offset) yields a coefficient of 1.138 (SE = 0.288, z = 3.946, p < 0.001) for the first_A variable, corresponding to an incident rate ratio of 3.12. This confirms that firms with names beginning with A or a number receive significantly more service complaints than other firms.

dependent_variable: Cooperative Strategy (dv, ordinal 0-3, where higher values = more cooperative/concession-offering)

dependent_variable: eth_supp (party support for ethnic minority rights, 0-10 scale)

operationalization_notes: The claim is about individual-level preferences (minorities being more left-leaning), but only party-level data was available. The party-level operationalization tests whether left-wing parties in countries with federal center minorities are more supportive of minority rights—an implication of those minorities being left-leaning and voting for left-wing parties. The interaction between lrecon and comm_dom_min captures this differential pattern: in comm_dom_min=1 countries, the slope of lrecon on eth_supp is significantly negative (-0.58), meaning left-wing parties are more supportive of minorities, while in comm_dom_min=0 countries it is positive (+0.34).

In countries with federal center minorities, left-wing parties are significantly more supportive of minority rights (slope = -0.58), while in countries without such minorities, right-wing parties are more supportive (slope = +0.34). This pattern is consistent with the claim that ethnic minorities from federal centers are more left-leaning, as left-wing parties in those countries court left-leaning minority voters by supporting minority rights.

dependent_variable: Number of actions identified as choices while watching a video of an actor performing mundane activities (numactions in the construal-of-choice condition)

operationalization_notes: Study 3 is the study in the paper that directly tests construal of OTHER individuals' behaviors as choices (participants watched a video and identified choices). I focused on the construal-of-choice condition rather than the full 2x2 ANOVA because the claim specifically concerns construing others' behaviors as choices, which is directly measured in that condition. The control condition (identifying when the actor touched an object) serves as a manipulation check but does not directly test the claim.

This supports the claim that Americans are more likely than Indians to construe other individuals' behaviors as choices.

dependent_variable: Willingness to Self-Censor (WSC), measured on a 1-6 scale (reverse coded from willingness to disclose)

operationalization_notes: The paper describes a one-way repeated-measures ANCOVA controlling for political orientation. Since political orientation is a between-subjects variable with no within-person variation, it does not affect the within-subjects F-test for the recipient effect—the paper itself notes 'the pattern of results is identical when not controlling for this background variable.' The univariate repeated-measures ANOVA with sphericity assumed yields F(3, 210) = 47.85; the GG correction with ε = 0.849 yields F(2.55, 178.30) = 47.85, both p < .001. The omnibus F-test is followed by the clear directional pattern of increasing means across the ordered recipient types, confirmed by a linear trend test (t(70) = 9.44, p < .001).

The means clearly increased with perceived distance from recipients: closely related figures (M = 2.99), in-group superiors (M = 3.01), in-group NGOs (M = 4.06), and out-group NGOs (M = 4.73). operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 used a one-factorial between-subjects design with the key DV being 'How big was the food portion?' (9-point scale). This supports the paper's claim that being observed magnifies the perceived portion size.

dependent_variable: npctwomenlegsal (percentage of women in the legislature)
main_predictor: avg_pv_0 (All=0 dummy: 1 if ballot=0, pool=0, and vote=0 simultaneously)

operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 4 (Table 2), the 'All=0' variable captures the most party-centered electoral systems where all three Carey-Shugart dimensions (ballot, pool, vote) take their most party-centered value. The Prais-Winsten transformation accounts for AR(1) serial correlation (estimated rho=0.865 from OLS residuals), and PCSE accounts for panel heteroskedasticity and contemporaneous cross-panel correlation. The two-step (rather than fully iterative) Prais-Winsten approach is used because the iterative estimation fails to converge with this data structure. The resulting coefficient (4.751) closely matches the paper's reported value (4.820), confirming correct data filtering and specification.
reasoning: The coefficient on the 'All=0' variable (avg_pv_0) in a two-step Prais-Winsten regression with panel-corrected standard errors is 4.751 (SE=2.132), yielding t(223)=2.228, p=0.027. This positive and statistically significant coefficient supports the claim that party-centered electoral systems (where ballot=0, pool=0, and vote=0) increase women's legislative representation by approximately 4.75 percentage points compared to candidate-centered systems.

dependent_variable: Hazard of extending voting rights to overseas citizens (binary event indicator per country-year)

The paper states the spatial lag is coded as 1 if any of the k=6 nearest neighbors implemented overseas voting in the prior 2 years, and 0 otherwise. Sample excludes backsliding countries (those that revoked overseas voting rights) as indicated by the trenchfilt variable.

This indicates that countries with a neighbor that recently extended franchise to overseas citizens have nearly double the hazard of doing so themselves, consistent with the paper's claim that countries are more likely to extend the franchise in the wake of their neighbors' decisions.

dependent_variable: Log of real hourly earnings (loghrindinc_real)

dependent_variable: First Vote on Mary (progressive vs. conservative vote, binary)

I used the First Vote on Mary as the DV (one of the two key votes analyzed in the paper) and compared Model 2 (RCT only) to Model 4 (RCT + NIT) following the paper's table structure, using a likelihood ratio chi2 test with 8 df.

Villages in areas with higher precolonial state congruence have approximately 51% higher odds of receiving new primary school access, confirming that areas once home to precolonial states distribute public goods more broadly across space.

dependent_variable: IncVote (incumbent party's share of the two-party presidential vote)

dependent_variable: Empathic concern (mean of 7 IRI empathic concern items: ec1–ec7)

dependent_variable: War within five years of MID onset (cow5yrwi)

dependent_variable: WTP (willingness to pay for the risky prospect)

model_specification: Independent samples t-test (two-tailed)

dependent_variable: BoniVote (binary: 1 = would vote for Yayi, 0 = would not)

dependent_variable: preference_first (binary: 1 = prefer first group, 0 = prefer second group)

dependent_variable: crop income per acre (cropincacre)

dependent_variable: Total givers per 23-minute session (g1g22009)

controls: Lagged dependent variable (Directed Credit t-1), Private Credit (% GDP) lagged one period (proxy for profit potential from financial repression), linear time trend
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 2 specification: the dependent variable is credit to government and SOEs; the main predictor is the IQG index (negative coefficient means weaker states direct more credit); Private Credit controls for the profit potential implied by financial repression. dependent_variable: enjoyrelativ (relative preference/enjoyment rating on 7-point scale)

sample_definition: All 102 participants with valid condition and enjoyment data from Study 2 (53 interrupted, 49 continuous); 3 extraneous rows with missing condition excluded
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variance assumed)
operationalization_notes: Study 2 from the paper directly tests the claim that commercial disruption made the program more enjoyable. reasoning: In the main-treatment sample, first-stage effort was higher in TS (n=64, mean=84.81) than in OS (n=60, mean=71.65). A Mann-Whitney rank-sum test gave z=2.536, two-sided p=0.011, supporting significantly higher effort in the first stage of TS.

dependent_variable: preference_first (binary choice: first group vs second/novel group)
main_predictor: Negative unique attributes condition (Experiment 1 condition = 1: positive shared traits / negative unique traits); tested preference for first group against 50/50 chance
sample_definition: Participants in Experiment 1 assigned to the positive-shared/negative-unique condition; all 104 observations in that condition were included.
model_specification: One-sample chi-square goodness-of-fit test comparing counts preferring the first versus second group to a 50/50 expected distribution.
operationalization_notes: Experiment 1 directly manipulated whether groups' unique attributes were negative, making the negative-unique condition the most direct test of the claim that participants prefer the first group over the novel group when unique attributes are negative.
reasoning: In Experiment 1's condition where shared traits were positive and unique traits were negative, 68 of 104 participants (65.4%) preferred the first group over the novel second group. A one-sample chi-square goodness-of-fit test against equal preference for either group was significant, chi-square(1, N = 104) = 9.85, p = .0017, supporting the claimed preference for the first group when unique attributes were negative.

dependent_variable: Total annual household income (totinc)
main_predictor: Village caste dominance: BAC/low-caste-dominated village versus upper-caste-dominated village (domlow/domhigh)
sample_definition: Low-caste households (BAC, OBC, SC) in the Table 2 household dataset with nonmissing total income and classified as residing in either an upper-caste-dominated or BAC/low-caste-dominated village; N=705 in low-caste-dominated villages and N=592 in upper-caste-dominated villages.
model_specification: Independent two-sample t-test comparing mean total annual income between low-caste-dominated and upper-caste-dominated villages, using the equal-variance specification corresponding to the paper's reported t-test program.
operationalization_notes: The claim refers to higher household income for low-caste households by village caste dominance, so I used the paper's low-caste household comparison sample and its total annual income measure, testing the mean difference across the two village-dominance groups.
reasoning: In the low-caste household sample, mean total annual income was Rs. 7,524.49 in BAC/low-caste-dominated villages versus Rs. 3,998.96 in upper-caste-dominated villages. The two-sample t-test for the difference was t(1295)=4.97, p=7.65e-7, supporting higher income in BAC-dominated villages.

dependent_variable: Total number of givers per 23-minute session across solicited doors
main_predictor: Verbal ask indicator (Ask1 or Ask1&2 vs Opp1 or Opp1&2)
sample_definition: All 64 bell-ringing treatment sessions from the 2009 field experiment; placebo sessions excluded.
model_specification: OLS regression: total givers per 23-minute session = verbal ask + two-door solicitor indicator + day fixed effects + start-time fixed effects; standard errors clustered by 16 treatment blocks.
controls: Two-door solicitor indicator, day fixed effects, and 16 start-time fixed effects; cluster-robust standard errors by block.
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzes total giving using OLS with date/time fixed effects and clustered standard errors. I operationalized the broad claim as the average effect of the verbal request across the one-door and two-door solicitation conditions, while adjusting for the number of solicited doors.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of total givers per 23-minute session on a verbal-ask indicator, controlling for whether one or two doors had solicitors and for day and start-time fixed effects, the verbal ask increased giving by 5.3125 givers per session. The cluster-robust test was t(15)=5.759, p=0.0000377, supporting the claim that the verbal ask increased giving.

dependent_variable: zakaibag (indicator for Bagrut/matriculation certification status in 2001)
main_predictor: treated (school assigned to receive the Achievement Awards offer)
sample_definition: Female students (boy==0) in the 2001 senior cohort from base01.dta; all 1,861 observations with complete variables were included.
model_specification: OLS linear probability model of Bagrut certification on treatment status, using school-cluster-robust standard errors with small-sample t inference based on 34 school clusters.
controls: School covariates semarab and semrel; lagged score quartile indicators based on the full 2001 cohort; individual covariates father's education, mother's education, number of siblings, and immigrant status.
operationalization_notes: This mirrors the paper's cross-sectional treatment-effect specification for the post-treatment cohort and focuses on girls because the claim specifically concerns increased female certification rates.
reasoning: In the 2001 senior cohort, among girls, the treatment-school coefficient in a linear probability model for Bagrut certification was positive (0.102) with a school-cluster-robust SE of 0.044, t(33)=2.31, p=0.027. This supports the claim that the school-based awards offer increased certification rates for girls.

dependent_variable: U.S. intrafirm import share, computed as related-party imports divided by related-party plus non-related-party imports for each IO2002 industry-year
main_predictor: DownMeasure × indicator for above-median average buyer demand elasticity
sample_definition: IO2002 manufacturing industry-year observations for 2000-2010 with positive U.S. imports and non-missing downstreamness, elasticity, and buyer-industry control variables; N=2783 observations from 253 industries
model_specification: OLS regression of intrafirm import share on DownMeasure interacted with below- and above-median buyer demand elasticity indicators, plus the main effect of the above-median elasticity indicator and year fixed effects; standard errors clustered by IO2002 industry
controls: Buyer-industry weighted log skill intensity, log equipment capital per worker, log plant capital per worker, log materials per worker, log(0.001 + R&D/Sales), size dispersion, and year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's baseline cross-industry specification, using the paper's second downstreamness measure (DownMeasure) and the supplied average-buyer elasticity median split to distinguish high-elasticity industries; the reported test is for the positive downstreamness slope in the high-elasticity case.
reasoning: In an industry-year OLS model with year fixed effects and industry-clustered standard errors, the interaction of DownMeasure with the above-median average buyer demand elasticity indicator was positive and statistically significant (t(252)=3.34, p=0.00097). This supports the claim that downstreamness is positively related to the intrafirm import share for industries facing high buyer demand elasticities.

dependent_variable: bid_on_restrict_d: indicator that a PAP applied for a BMO/child among allowed choices
main_predictor: Contrast between nonaa_girl and nonaa_boy indicators (non-African-American girl vs non-African-American boy)
sample_definition: ChoicePanel2.dta PAP-child-day observations in the 10-day activity-window choice panel for which the child was an allowed choice for the PAP (bid_on_restrict_d nonmissing) and all model covariates were observed; N=1,226,169 observations, clustered over 36,839 PAP-BMO pairs.
model_specification: Linear probability model with PAP-BMO clustered standard errors; main test is the linear contrast beta(nonaa_girl) - beta(nonaa_boy).
controls: Already born indicator, months to birth, finalization cost in $10,000s, African-American girl/boy/unknown indicators, Hispanic race share, PAP category indicators (single, gay couple, lesbian couple), and year fixed effects.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's demand-side revealed-preference setup using applications by active PAPs to available children and tests the claim directly by comparing otherwise adjusted application probabilities for non-African-American girls and boys.
reasoning: In a linear probability model of PAP application decisions with PAP-BMO clustered standard errors, the adjusted application probability for non-African-American girls exceeded that for non-African-American boys by 0.0317. The contrast was positive and statistically significant, t(36838)=4.36, p=1.31e-5, supporting a preference in favor of non-African-American girls.

dependent_variable: ambiguity-generated insensitivity index a = 1 - 3*(mean composite-event matching probability - mean single-event matching probability)
main_predictor: indicator for Part 1 in the time-pressure treatment, with Part 1 control as the reference group
sample_definition: All non-excluded subjects with complete matching-probability data: 99 subjects (42 control, 57 time pressure), with two part-level observations per subject for Parts 1 and 2, yielding 198 observations; the 5 subjects with any missing elicitation response were excluded.
model_specification: OLS regression of part-level a-insensitivity on three indicators: Part 1*time pressure, Part 2*control, and Part 2*time pressure, with an intercept for Part 1 control; standard errors clustered by subject.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's baseline Model 1 for the time-pressure claim, using the first elicited matching probability for each event and computing the paper's a-insensitivity index for each subject in each experimental part.
reasoning: In a clustered OLS regression of the a-insensitivity index on treatment-by-part indicators, the Part 1 time-pressure coefficient was positive (0.1895) and statistically significant, t(98)=2.12, p=0.036. Thus, subjects under time pressure showed higher ambiguity-generated insensitivity than the Part 1 control reference group.

dependent_variable: Civil war duration in months, treated as right-censored when no end year was recorded
main_predictor: Irregular conflict indicator, comparing irregular wars to conventional and SNC wars combined
sample_definition: TR dataset conflict-level observations with nonmissing durationmonths; 142 civil wars, of which 134 had recorded end years and 8 were right-censored
model_specification: Weibull accelerated failure time survival regression with log survival time modeled as a function of an irregular-conflict indicator
operationalization_notes: The paper tests the duration claim using Weibull AFT survival models on the Technologies of Rebellion (TR) data. I used the same survival-model family and collapsed conventional and SNC conflicts into the comparison category to directly test the claim that irregular conflicts last longer than all other types.
reasoning: In a Weibull accelerated-failure-time model, the coefficient for irregular conflicts versus conventional/SNC conflicts was positive and highly significant (z = 5.45, two-sided p = 5.04e-8). The estimated time ratio was exp(1.128) = 3.09, indicating that irregular conflicts last substantially longer than the other types in this operationalization.

dependent_variable: log monthly mortality rate (lndrate)
main_predictor: post-1960 indicator interacted with the cumulative dynamic number of days with mean temperature above 90°F (L1_b10_10_x_post60)
sample_definition: State-month observations from 1931-2004 with nonmissing mortality, population weights, weather bins, precipitation, demographic shares, and log real per-capita income; 49 state clusters; lagged temperature variables computed after retaining 1930-2004 data.
model_specification: Population-weighted least squares regression with clustered standard errors by state; current-difference and lagged-level temperature-bin variables for <40°F, 80-89°F, and >90°F, interacted with a post-1960 indicator to test whether the cumulative >90°F effect declined after 1960.
controls: Precipitation indicators, age-share controls and log real per-capita income interacted with month, year-month fixed effects, and state-by-month fixed effects with state-by-month-specific linear and quadratic time trends.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Table 3 Panel A parsimonious temperature-bin specification and two-month cumulative dynamic setup, but estimates one pooled interaction test for the pre/post-1960 decline in the high-temperature mortality effect.
reasoning: In a pooled weighted regression, the post-1960 interaction for the cumulative effect of days above 90°F on log monthly mortality was negative and statistically significant (coefficient = -0.01434, t(48) = -3.08, p = 0.0034). The implied >90°F effect fell from 0.01894 before 1960 to 0.00459 after 1960, supporting a decline in the temperature-mortality relationship.

dependent_variable: Binary choice to buy the hypothetical DVD (1 = buy, 0 = not buy)
main_predictor: Interaction between opportunity-cost reminder condition and standardized future-self connectedness
sample_definition: All 88 participants in the DVD_data dataset from Study 1A; no exclusions applied.
model_specification: Logistic regression: buy ~ opportunity_cost_cue + standardized_connectedness + opportunity_cost_cue × standardized_connectedness.
operationalization_notes: Study 1A directly matches the claim by manipulating opportunity-cost salience in a discretionary purchase and measuring future-self connectedness; the interaction tests whether the cue's spending-reducing effect is stronger at higher connectedness.
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting DVD purchase, the opportunity-cost reminder by future-self connectedness interaction was negative and significant (Wald z = -2.10, p = .036, N = 88). This indicates that the reminder reduced purchase likelihood more strongly among participants higher in connectedness to their future selves.

dependent_variable: Indicator that the referred applicant was female (REF_female)
main_predictor: Indicator that the conventional applicant was male (1 - OP_female)
sample_definition: Conventional applicants assigned to the unrestricted either-gender referral treatment, excluding observations without a realized referral/referral gender; N = 220 referrals.
model_specification: Two-sample difference in means, equivalently OLS linear probability model REF_female = alpha + beta * CA_male + error with conventional standard errors.
operationalization_notes: The paper ties this claim to Table 1 panel C, which compares referral gender by CA gender among CAs who had a choice of which gender to refer. I therefore tested the simple difference in the probability that a realized referral was female for male versus female CAs in the either-gender treatment.
reasoning: Among conventional applicants in the either-gender referral treatment who made a referral, 30/133 male CAs referred a woman (22.6%) versus 37/87 female CAs (42.5%). A two-sample t test/linear probability model for referral-female on CA-male gives t(218) = -3.206, p = 0.00155, indicating that male CAs were significantly less likely to refer women.

dependent_variable: Copying-adjusted standardized ALI mathematics test score for 10th-grade students in program year 1
main_predictor: Treatment 3 assignment (student, teacher, peer, and administrator incentives) versus control
sample_definition: Students in the table_7_gr10_yr1 data with nonmissing outcome and regression covariates; copiers were retained but their ALI scores were replaced by predicted non-copying scores; N=11,314 across 87 schools.
model_specification: OLS regression of adjusted standardized ALI score on treatment dummies, using the control group as the reference category and school-clustered standard errors; the reported test is the t test for the T3 coefficient.
controls: Dummies for T1 and T2, school mean ninth-grade ENLACE math scores for current grade-10 and grade-11 cohorts, school mean 2008 grade-12 ENLACE math and language scores, region dummies, and state dummies.
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's Table 7 impact specification and chose the grade-10, first-program-year estimate as a direct test of whether T3 incentives increased curriculum-based mathematics scores. The copying adjustment was implemented by predicting ALI scores for identified copiers from a regression among control non-copiers on ninth-grade math ENLACE score and a missing-score indicator.
reasoning: In an OLS regression with school-clustered standard errors, the coefficient for T3 versus control on the copying-adjusted standardized grade-10 ALI math score was positive, about 31.0 points (0.31 SD), t(86)=5.37, p=6.68e-7. This supports the claim that the ALI incentive package for students, teachers, peers, and administrators increased test scores.

dependent_variable: Subject-level proportion of intertemporal choices in which the earlier payment was chosen (impatient choices)
main_predictor: Ethnicity-salience treatment indicator versus control condition
sample_definition: Experiment 1 participants coded as Asian descent (raceA == 1), with non-missing treatment assignment and impatient-choice proportion; N = 71 (37 ethnicity-salient, 34 control)
model_specification: Independent two-sample t-test comparing mean impatient-choice proportions between ethnicity-salient and control Asian-American subjects, using pooled variance
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns whether making ethnic identity salient causes Asian-American subjects to make more patient choices. Following the paper's Experiment 1 results presentation, I used the subject-level percentage of earlier choices in the time-preference task and compared Asian subjects across randomized treatment conditions.
reasoning: Among Asian-American subjects, the ethnicity-salience group chose the earlier payment in 12.63% of intertemporal choices versus 26.37% in the control group. A two-sample t-test on subject-level impatient-choice proportions gave t(69) = -3.43, p = 0.0010, indicating significantly fewer impatient choices when ethnic identity was salient.

dependent_variable: Subject-level mean cooperation rate: percentage of time spent cooperating, averaged across all 23 supergames
main_predictor: Termination rule in short-duration treatments: deterministic horizon vs stochastic horizon
sample_definition: Subjects from the Short-Deterministic and Short-Stochastic treatments only; each subject contributes one average cooperation-rate observation across all supergames (48 per treatment, N = 96)
model_specification: One-sided independent-samples t-test comparing subject-level mean cooperation rates, testing deterministic > stochastic; equal variances assumed
operationalization_notes: The paper defines cooperation rate as the fraction of time a subject spends cooperating in a supergame and uses subject-level averages to assess treatment differences. I focused directly on the short-duration deterministic versus stochastic comparison stated in the claim.
reasoning: Using subject-level average cooperation rates in the two short-duration treatments, cooperation was higher under deterministic horizons (mean = 63.28%) than stochastic horizons (mean = 52.32%). A one-sided independent-samples t-test gave t(94) = 3.436, p = 0.00044, supporting the claimed higher cooperation in the deterministic short-duration treatment.

dependent_variable: pldist1: absolute ideological distance between the plurality/largest vote-winning party and the median voter
main_predictor: SMD election rules indicator (1=SMD, 0=PR)
sample_definition: All elections in powell_original.dta with nonmissing SMD/PR classification and nonmissing plurality-party distance; two mixed-rule Italian elections with missing SMD classification were excluded.
model_specification: Welch two-sample t-test comparing mean plurality-party distance in SMD versus PR elections; directional alternative was that SMD elections have lower plurality-party distance.
operationalization_notes: Hypothesis 4a concerns whether SMD party competition produces plurality winners close to the median; the paper contrasts this with the expectation that PR plurality parties should be farther from the median, so I operationalized the claim as a cross-system difference in plurality-party distance using the manifesto measure available for the full postwar sample.
reasoning: Using the manifesto-based plurality-party distance measure, SMD elections did not have plurality vote winners closer to the median voter than PR elections. The mean distance was slightly larger in SMD cases (11.404, n=85) than in PR cases (11.073, n=244), yielding Welch's t=0.280 (df=181.04) for SMD minus PR and a one-sided p=.610 for the predicted SMD<PR direction.

dependent_variable: New civil war recurrence (nwar1)
main_predictor: Election timing: months from civil war end to first postconflict election (T2fpemths1)
sample_definition: Civil wars ending between 1945 and 2008 with no intervening renewed war before the first postconflict election and complete data on the model variables; N = 98.
model_specification: Logistic regression with country-clustered robust standard errors; main result is the Wald z test for the election-timing coefficient.
controls: FPE level national, FPE level national/subnational concurrent, Polity IV score at FPE, post-Cold War era, victory, UN intervention, UN electoral assistance, and number of previous civil wars.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's calendar-time analysis for all first postconflict elections, using renewed civil war as the binary outcome and election timing in months as the key predictor.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of renewed civil war on months until the first postconflict election, the election-timing coefficient was negative (b = -0.0031), meaning later elections were associated with lower recurrence risk, as the claim implies. However, the cluster-robust Wald test for this coefficient was not statistically significant (z = -0.741, p = 0.459), so this operationalization provides inconclusive evidence for the claim.

dependent_variable: Femininity index: mean of the three feminine-trait ratings (feminine, gentle, sensitive) on 1-5 scales
main_predictor: Target environmental behavior condition: green behavior (reusable canvas grocery bag) versus nongreen behavior (plastic grocery bag)
sample_definition: All 194 Study 2 participants with complete condition-specific trait ratings were included; participants were in one of four between-subjects conditions crossing target gender (male/female) with behavior (green/nongreen).
model_specification: Two-way between-subjects ANOVA/OLS: femininity index ~ behavior * target gender, reporting the main effect of behavior using Type III sums of squares with sum contrasts.
operationalization_notes: This follows Study 2's stated test of the claim that green versus nongreen targets are perceived as more feminine, while accounting for the experimentally manipulated target gender in the factorial design.
reasoning: I constructed the femininity index by averaging the three feminine-trait ratings and fit a 2 × 2 between-subjects ANOVA with target environmental behavior and target gender. The main effect of green versus nongreen behavior was significant, F(1, 190) = 43.998, p = 3.33e-10, with green targets rated more feminine (M = 2.64) than nongreen targets (M = 1.82).

dependent_variable: Subject-level LV decision error rate, defined as the fraction of the 10 LV choices that did not select a stochastically dominant lottery; the equal row-5 lotteries were counted as non-error regardless of choice.
main_predictor: Degree of risk aversion, measured as the average number of safe choices across the PV and RV formats.
sample_definition: Subjects in RiskData.dta excluding the two dummy observations identified by age 99, restricted to subjects with average PV/RV safe choices >= 5 (risk averse), N = 79.
model_specification: Bivariate OLS/Pearson correlation test of LV error rate on average PV/RV safe choices; reported t test for the correlation/slope.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Section 4.2 approach of restricting to risk-averse subjects and relating the LV error rate to the average number of safe PV/RV choices as the measure of risk-aversion degree.
reasoning: Among the 79 risk-averse subjects, the subject-level Pearson correlation between LV decision error rate and average safe choices in the PV/RV tasks was r = -0.462, giving t(77) = -4.58, p = 1.78e-05. Thus, higher elicited risk aversion was associated with fewer decision errors, supporting the claimed negative relationship.

dependent_variable: Desired compensation in thousands of dollars, coded as the midpoint of each reported salary range
main_predictor: Public treatment indicator (questionnaire said 'your' answers would be discussed in career class, versus anonymized/private)
sample_definition: Primary experiment responses restricted to students who were female and self-reported single; all 60 had nonmissing desired compensation
model_specification: OLS regression: desired_compensation = intercept + beta * public_treatment, using HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard error for beta
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns single female students' desired salaries under expected classmate observability, so I used the primary experiment's randomized public-versus-private comparison within single women and the salary/desired compensation item as the outcome.
reasoning: Among single female students, the public-treatment group reported lower desired compensation than the private-treatment group (112.93 vs. 131.05 thousand dollars). An OLS regression of desired compensation on the public-treatment indicator with HC1 robust standard errors gave t(58) = -2.22, p = 0.030, supporting the claim that expected classmate observability lowered reported desired salaries.

dependent_variable: pay_for_conditionality: dummy equal to 1 if the parent preferred a R$120 conditional cash transfer to a R$125 unconditional cash transfer
main_predictor: Text message monitoring treatment indicator versus baseline treatment
sample_definition: Parents in the baseline (treatment==1) and text-message monitoring (treatment==2) arms only, excluding observations without child survey completion (age_child missing), matching the paper's complete-survey restriction; nonclassroom and don't-tell treatments excluded.
model_specification: Two-sample test of equality of independent proportions, coded as text-message proportion minus baseline proportion, using the pooled standard error.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies this binary choice as the measure for whether parents are willing to pay a positive amount to keep conditionality and compares the text-message treatment against the baseline; I used the unadjusted proportion comparison as the most direct test of the quoted claim.
reasoning: Among households completing the survey, 48/59 baseline parents (81.4%) were willing to pay to keep conditionality, compared with 10/50 text-message-treatment parents (20.0%). A two-proportion z-test for the text-message group minus baseline gives z = -6.397, p = 1.58e-10, indicating a large statistically significant drop.

dependent_variable: Monthly count of homicides of males aged 15-39 in SINAIS, used as the proxy for DTO-related violence
main_predictor: Indicator for months 1-6 after a leader capture or killing in the municipality (lpub_after06)
sample_definition: Monthly municipality observations from December 2006 through December 2010 for municipalities where at least one DTO leader was captured or killed, excluding Ciudad Juarez as in the paper; N = 637 observations in 13 municipalities.
model_specification: Negative binomial regression with municipality and month fixed effects; cluster-robust standard errors by municipality.
controls: Log population of males aged 15-39, municipality fixed effects, month fixed effects, indicators for months 7-12 and >12 after leader capture/killing, and analogous post-lieutenant-capture indicators.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's treated-municipality difference-in-differences specification for the claim's short-term DTO-related violence effect, using the SINAIS male 15-39 homicide series identified in the paper as the best proxy for DTO-related killings.
reasoning: In a negative binomial fixed-effects model, the coefficient for the first 1-6 months after a leader capture/kill was positive (b = 0.258), corresponding to about a 29.4% higher expected homicide count. The cluster-robust test was z = 2.10, p = 0.036, supporting a short-term exacerbating effect on the DTO-violence proxy.

dependent_variable: Average shortest path length (ASPL) of bootstrapped semantic fluency networks
main_predictor: High vs. low openness-to-experience group based on the no-intellect latent openness score median split
sample_definition: All 516 participants in the cleaned dataset were sorted by the no_int latent openness score and split into low (n = 258) and high (n = 258) groups; animal response nodes were retained if generated by at least two participants in both groups, yielding 167 common nodes, and each bootstrap sampled 83 nodes without replacement.
model_specification: For each group, binary participant-by-animal matrices were converted to cosine similarity matrices, filtered with a greedy TMFG-style planar network, binarized, and ASPL was computed for 1000 random half-node partial networks per group; the main test was an independent-samples t-test comparing high-minus-low ASPL across bootstrap realizations.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies lower ASPL as the network measure most directly indexing greater interconnectivity and uses half-node bootstrapped partial networks to test group differences; I therefore used ASPL from bootstrapped common-node animal fluency networks as the primary test of the claim.
reasoning: Using 1000 half-node bootstrapped semantic networks per openness group, the high-openness networks had lower average shortest path length than the low-openness networks (M_high = 2.492, M_low = 2.623), t(1998) = -18.13, p = 3.95e-68. Lower ASPL indicates greater network interconnectivity, so the result supports the claim that the high-openness network was more interconnected.

dependent_variable: CIRI Physical Integrity Rights Index (0-8)
main_predictor: Reliance on Taxes: tax and social security contributions as percent of total government revenue
sample_definition: Country-year observations from 1981-2007 with complete data for the dependent variable, lagged dependent variable, tax reliance, government revenue, and controls; observations with tax reliance outside the valid 0-100 percent range were excluded.
model_specification: Ordered probit regression with HC0 robust standard errors; the reported z test is for the Reliance on Taxes coefficient.
controls: Size of Government Revenues, log population, income per capita, Polity IV democracy, external conflict, internal armed conflict, UK colony, and lagged CIRI Physical Integrity Rights Index.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's primary research design for testing fiscal reliance and human rights: an ordered probit for physical integrity rights using global country-years and the baseline controls. Income was scaled only for numerical estimation and does not affect the tax coefficient test.
reasoning: In an ordered probit model of CIRI physical integrity rights, reliance on taxes had a positive coefficient of 0.00616 with robust SE = 0.00220, z = 2.81, p = 0.005. Thus greater reliance on taxes is associated with significantly better protection of physical integrity rights, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: pt_gcse_5_a_c: percentage of pupils achieving 5 or more GCSE grades A-C
main_predictor: gm_school (GM conversion status), instrumented by gm_win (winning the GM vote at the 50 percent cutoff)
sample_definition: Main GM school-year panel observations with nonmissing GCSE pass-rate data, restricted to years base+2 through base+8 after the GM vote; 4,954 school-year observations from 726 schools.
model_specification: Pooled 2SLS regression-discontinuity model with school-clustered robust standard errors; coefficient test for the instrumented GM conversion indicator.
controls: Separate linear vote-margin terms below and above the 50 percent cutoff (lose_vote and win_vote), base-year GCSE pass rate, school type fixed effects, GM vote year-term fixed effects, and relative-year fixed effects.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's main achievement analysis by using post-vote GCSE pass rates and the RD/IV design comparing schools around the GM vote-win threshold, pooled over postbase years 2-8 for precision.
reasoning: In a pooled regression-discontinuity 2SLS model for base year +2 through +8, the estimated effect of GM conversion on the GCSE pass-rate outcome was positive, about 4.48 percentage points, with a cluster-robust t statistic of 3.10 (df=725, p=0.0020). This supports the claim that schools converting to GM status experienced improved student achievement.

dependent_variable: Participated (lab): indicator equal to 1 if the student actually participated in the laboratory experiment
main_predictor: Sent_Class: amount sent as Player A in the classroom trust game ($0, $10, or $20)
sample_definition: Students in the trust-game classroom treatments with non-missing amount-sent decisions (N = 658)
model_specification: Probit regression of laboratory participation on amount sent and covariates, with robust standard errors clustered by tutor
controls: Female, Commerce major, International student, day-of-week fixed effects, flyer-after-trust-game order indicator, and indicator for being chosen for classroom-experiment payment
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Table 3 amount-sent analysis for the claim that lower trust-game sending predicts greater laboratory participation.
reasoning: In a probit model predicting actual laboratory participation, the coefficient on amount sent in the classroom trust game was negative and statistically significant (b = -0.0231, cluster-robust z = -2.66, p = 0.0077; N = 658). Thus students who sent more were less likely to participate, equivalently students who sent less were more likely to participate.

dependent_variable: Indicator that the illness episode was treated with an ACT (took_act)
main_predictor: Assignment to the 92% ACT subsidy arm (act40; omitted category is no ACT subsidy/control)
sample_definition: First post-baseline illness episodes with malaria-like symptoms in households; excluded households assigned RDT vouchers or surprise/ex-post RDT testing; observations with nonmissing took_act included.
model_specification: OLS linear probability regression of took_act on ACT subsidy indicators (92%, 88%, 80%) relative to control, with randomization-stratum fixed effects; cluster-robust standard errors by household.
controls: Randomization strata fixed effects, imputed baseline household-head age, and household-head age missing indicator.

main_predictor: first_A indicator for firm name beginning with A, a number, or symbol
