reasoning: Pearson correlation between Mini-K total (higher = slower life history strategy) and DSM-5 total psychopathology was r = -.59, t(136) = -8.46, p < .001. Faster life history strategy (lower Mini-K) is strongly associated with more psychopathology symptoms, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: PolWis_score (political knowledge test score)
main_predictor: Experimental condition (Stereotypaktivierung: 'not activated' vs 'activated by gender difference statement')
sample_definition: Female participants (gender_factor=1) included in the paper's analysis filter (filter_$=1), restricted to conditions 1 (not activated) and 3 (gender-difference statement)

The paper's t for this contrast comes from an ANCOVA controlling for political interest, but a direct two-sample t-test matches its reported df=141 and is the most direct test of the verbal claim.

This reproduces the directional effect reported in the paper.

dependent_variable: GDP growth index at t+2 (f2gdpidx)
main_predictor: Connected to provincial secretary (=1 if city secretary or mayor has prior promotion-based tie to incumbent provincial secretary)
sample_definition: City-year observations 1999-2011 with non-missing outcome and controls (2,915 obs across 331 cities)

controls: Predecessor-final-year log GDP, log population, log investment, GDP growth index (both msec and mayor predecessors); net transfer at t+1; msec/mayor age, sex, college education
operationalization_notes: Directly mirrors equation (1) and Table 1, column 3 of the paper. Sample is smaller than paper's reported N because pf_f1logtransfer_dm and start-of-tenure controls in the public data have additional missingness; estimates remain qualitatively consistent.
reasoning: Replicating the Model 3 specification in Table 1 (DV: f2gdpidx; predictor: city secretary or mayor connected to current provincial secretary; city and province-year fixed effects; economic and leader controls; SEs clustered by city), I find a positive performance premium of 0.31 percentage points for connected cities (SE=0.160, t=1.94, p≈0.052). The direction and magnitude align with the original paper's reported ~0.38pp premium, supporting the claim that connected city leaders deliver faster growth.

dependent_variable: log(share of top-quality foreign players in the league)

controls: treatment dummy and post-1991 dummy; no other covariates
operationalization_notes: Most direct replication of Table 1 Panel B2 top-quality row. Years with zero top foreigners in Denmark (1985, 1986, 1990) drop out of the log specification.

dependent_variable: Willingness to pay (WTP) composite (mean of 3 WVS items)
main_predictor: Intrinsic relative to extrinsic value score (I/E; intrin_extrin)
sample_definition: All Study 1 participants with non-missing I/E and WTP (n=155 of 169 in the SAV file)

dependent_variable: ln_imports (logged product-level imports of the disputed product from partner j in year t after the dispute)
main_predictor: Complainant indicator (1 if partner j is the complainant in dispute d, 0 otherwise)

model_specification: OLS regression of ln_imports on Complainant with controls; dispute-clustered standard errors

operationalization_notes: Replicates Model 2 of Table 1 (early-settlement subsample). Post-dispute window operationalized as counter∈[1,5], excluding third parties; yields N=6,012, very close to the paper's reported 6,027.
reasoning: In the early-settlement subsample, the Complainant indicator predicts higher post-dispute log product-level imports (coef = 0.251, cluster-robust SE = 0.123, z/t = 2.04, p = 0.041, N = 6,012), indicating complainants gain more than other (non-third-party) WTO members. Effect direction and significance match the paper's Model 2.

dependent_variable: entre_wage (fraction of working-age individuals starting new businesses, GEM)
main_predictor: medage_20_64 (median age of population aged 20-64)
sample_definition: All GEM country-year observations 2001-2010 with non-missing variables (393 obs, 82 countries)
model_specification: WLS regression with year fixed effects, weights = nobs_cy, standard errors clustered by countryid
controls: Year fixed effects only (Table 2 Column 3 baseline specification)

Spearman chosen over Pearson as the more demanding non-parametric test; Pearson r = -0.443 (t77 = -4.33, p<1e-4) gives the same conclusion.
reasoning: Spearman rank correlation between subject-level error rate in the LV format (proportion of dominated choices over 10 decisions) and degree of risk aversion (average # of safe choices in PV and RV formats), restricted to the 79 risk-averse subjects (average safe choices >=5), is rho = -0.419 (p = 0.00012). The negative, statistically significant correlation supports the claim that decision error decreases with risk aversion.

dependent_variable: Desired yearly compensation (midpoint of reported bracket, in $1000s)

reasoning: Among single female students (n=60), the public-treatment indicator predicts a $18.1K decrease in desired compensation (private mean ≈ $131K, public mean ≈ $113K), with HC1-robust t = -2.22 (p ≈ 0.027). This replicates the paper's headline ~$18,000 drop.

dependent_variable: pay_for_conditionality (1 if parent willing to pay to keep conditionality)
main_predictor: treatment (1=baseline vs 2=text-message)

reasoning: In the baseline treatment 49/60 (81.7%) parents were willing to pay to keep conditionality, vs 10/51 (19.6%) in the text-message treatment. Pearson chi-square = 42.64, df=1, p≈6.6e-11, confirming the large drop the authors describe.

dependent_variable: Monthly count of homicides of males aged 15-39 (DTO-related proxy)
main_predictor: after(1-6 months) * leader indicator (lpub_after06)
sample_definition: Municipalities where at least one drug-cartel leader was captured/killed (treat_leader==1); months Dec 2006 through Dec 2010 (N=686, 14 municipalities)
model_specification: Negative binomial regression (GLM with NB family, alpha estimated via Cameron-Trivedi aux regression, alpha≈0.059), municipality and month fixed effects via dummies; robust SE clustered at the municipality level
controls: Population of males 15-39, municipality fixed effects, month-year fixed effects; other leader/lieutenant after-period indicators (7-12 months, remaining)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Table 2 Model 1 specification—the most direct test of the short-term effect of leader removal on DTO-related violence. Statsmodels does not implement Stata's conditional NB FE; instead, NB GLM with municipality dummies was used, which is the standard equivalent. Differences from the paper's N (637 vs 686) likely reflect Stata's xtnbreg dropping a municipality with insufficient variation; this does not change the substantive conclusion.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's main short-term test (Table 2, Model 1: negative binomial DiD on the leader-treated subsample, Dec 2006-Dec 2010, with municipality and month fixed effects and male 15-39 population control, robust SE clustered by municipality), the coefficient on after(1-6 months)*leader for DTO-related homicides (males 15-39) is 0.114 (SE = 0.149, z = 0.77, p = 0.44). This is positive in sign but far from significant and much smaller than the paper's reported beta (~0.272 / 31% increase), so the claim of an exacerbating short-term effect does not robustly reproduce.

dependent_variable: Average shortest path length (ASPL) of the bootstrapped partial semantic network (90% nodes retained)
main_predictor: Openness-to-experience group (high vs. low; median split on composite of NEO-FFI-3 openness facet and BFAS openness/intellect aspect)
sample_definition: All 516 participants from the merged dataset; median split into high (n=258) and low (n=258) openness groups; semantic networks built on the 166 animals produced by ≥2 participants in BOTH groups.
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test (equal variances) comparing ASPL across 1000 bootstrap partial networks per group constructed via cosine-similarity matrices filtered with the Triangulated Maximally Filtered Graph (TMFG).
operationalization_notes: Implemented the paper's pipeline: binary participant×word matrix per group, cosine similarity between word vectors, TMFG filtering (yielding 3(N-2) edges), unweighted ASPL on the largest connected component; bootstrap drops 10% of shared nodes (most demanding row of Table 3, df=1998). Openness composite operationalized as the mean of standardized NEO-FFI-3 openness and BFAS openness/intellect since the original latent-variable scores were not provided.
reasoning: Following the paper's partial-bootstrap node-drop procedure (90% of shared nodes retained, 1000 bootstraps per group, TMFG-filtered cosine networks built separately for the high and low openness groups), the high-openness group had a significantly smaller average shortest path length (M = 2.79) than the low-openness group (M = 3.13), t(1998) = -61.65, p < .001, Cohen's d ≈ -2.76. This indicates a more interconnected semantic network in the high-openness group, matching the direction and approximate magnitude reported in the paper (t = -65.69, d = 2.94).

dependent_variable: CIRI Physical Integrity Index (ciri_physint)
main_predictor: Reliance on taxes in government revenues (tax_rev_new)
sample_definition: Country-year observations 1981-2007 with complete data on DV, lagged DV, and all controls (N=1,739)

dependent_variable: School pass rate (% pupils achieving 5+ GCSEs A*-C, pt_gcse_5_a_c)
main_predictor: GM conversion status (gm_school), instrumented by gm_win (vote share > 50%)

model_specification: Fuzzy RD 2SLS: outcome regressed on GM (endogenous) plus linear vote-share polynomial interacted with win (centered vote share and its interaction with win), with WIN as the excluded instrument; year, school-type, vote-year-term FE; SE clustered by school
controls: Baseline pass rate (pt_gcse_5_a_c_base), centered vote share and vote-share × win interaction, year FE, school-type FE, vote year-term FE
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's preferred pooled specification (panel B, col. 5 of Table 1) as the most direct test of the causal claim that GM conversion raised achievement. Reproduces the published 4.478 (1.445) estimate.
reasoning: Using a fuzzy regression-discontinuity design (2SLS with the 50% GM vote-win indicator as instrument for GM status, linear-by-win polynomial in vote share, controls for base pass rate, school type, vote year-term and year FE, SE clustered by school) on pooled outcomes 2–8 years after the base year, the estimated GM effect on the GCSE 5+ A*-C pass rate is 4.48 percentage points (SE 1.45), t=3.10, p≈0.002, with N=4,954 observations across 726 schools. This is a large, statistically significant achievement gain, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Participated in lab experiment (0/1)

Students who sent less were significantly more likely to participate in the lab experiment, replicating the paper's Table 3, column 4.

dependent_variable: took_act (indicator that the first illness episode was treated with any ACT)

Access to ACTs more than doubles under the highest subsidy, matching the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Two-year change in normalized combined math+reading PIAT score (mean of piamatsn and piarersn, re-normalized in the random NLSY sample)
main_predictor: Two-year change in real family income (earned + unearned + nontaxable + welfare), $1,000 of year-2000 dollars

operationalization_notes: The paper's headline 6%-of-SD effect comes from an IV using a TAXSIM-based simulated-EITC instrument that cannot be reconstructed from the provided data. Following the paper's own differenced specification (Table 2 panel B) provides the most demanding defensible test of the claim that is fully replicable on the supplied dataset; it shows the short-run income effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero.

dependent_variable: Work absorption (engwkabs, average of four items)

dependent_variable: ProperName (greeted by proper name, 0/1)

dependent_variable: Shading indicator (qualityc==1 = low/shaded quality vs qualityc==2 = normal quality)

dependent_variable: log of state-level CO2 emissions (carbon_adj)
main_predictor: log of average weekly working hours (wrkhrs)

model_specification: Two-way fixed-effects OLS (state and year dummies); log-log specification (scale model 1)
controls: log emp/pop ratio, log GDP per hour (labor productivity), log total population, log manufacturing share of GDP, log energy production, log working-age population
operationalization_notes: Followed Model 1 (scale, FE) from Table 4. Household size was not present in compiled.dta, so omitted. Used plain OLS with state and year fixed effects rather than Prais-Winsten AR(1), which provides a more demanding test.
reasoning: In a two-way (state + year) fixed-effects OLS regression of log state CO2 emissions on log working hours plus available controls (emp/pop %, GDP per hour, log population, log manufacturing share, log energy production, log working-age population) for 2007-2013, the coefficient on log working hours is positive (b=0.465, SE=0.239, t(287)=1.95, p=0.052). The sign matches the paper's positive scale-effect claim, though significance is borderline without Prais-Winsten AR(1) correction and without household-size control (not provided in the supplied data).

dependent_variable: consider (dyad-year considered attack on nuclear program, 0/1)
main_predictor: hostileMID (prior violent militarized conflict, 0/1)

Considered attacks occur in 5.18% of conflict-dyad-years vs 0.25% otherwise — strongly supporting the claim that prior violent conflict raises the salience of the proliferation threat.

dependent_variable: recog1dum (dichotomous COW diplomatic recognition of state A by state B)

Sample size slightly smaller than reported (206,394 vs 213,454) likely due to omitted Beck-Katz-Tucker splines and minor variable definitions, but coefficient sign and significance for Nuclear Weapons A robustly confirm the directional claim.
reasoning: In a logit regression of directed-dyad diplomatic recognition (B recognizes A) on State A's nuclear status with the paper's controls (rivalry, CINC, democracy, contiguity, distance, alliance, and interaction terms), the coefficient on Nuclear Weapons A is 0.814 (SE 0.029, z = 27.6, p < 0.001), strongly positive and in the same direction as the claim that nuclear-capable states are more likely to be recognized by others.

dependent_variable: Log of absolute opinion change on the 12-item pro-immigration index between wave 2 (pre) and wave 3 (post)
main_predictor: Group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev, mean DQI justification score for each discussion group)

controls: gender, age, education, working class, Catholic, Protestant, religiosity, left-right ideology and its square, knowledge change, pressure (above/below) at wave 2, intention to vote for left/right party at EP elections, and 4 'clarify thinking' items (experts, politicians, other participants, briefing material)

reasoning: Regressing the log of absolute opinion change on immigration (waves 2-3) on the group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev) plus the Sanders-style individual controls yields a positive coefficient of 0.130 (SE = 0.066), t(154) = 1.96, p = 0.051, N = 174 individuals in 13 groups — matching the paper's Model 2b. Higher group-level justification rationality is associated with greater absolute opinion change, supporting the claim, though only at the borderline of conventional significance.

dependent_variable: Mean effort (work=1) per matching group, across rounds 1-5
main_predictor: Reward scheme (discriminating 345COM vs symmetrical 444COM) under complementarity

model_specification: Two-sided Mann-Whitney/Wilcoxon rank-sum test on matching-group mean effort
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's reported approach (rank-sum on matching group means) to preserve independence and to provide the most demanding nonparametric test of the claim.
reasoning: Mann-Whitney U test comparing mean effort per matching group between 345COM (discriminating, n=12) and 444COM (symmetrical, n=11) yields U=95, p≈0.070 (two-sided). Mean effort is markedly lower under the symmetrical scheme (0.72) than under the discriminating scheme (0.92), directionally and marginally significantly consistent with the claim. The z-equivalent statistic from U is approximately 1.81.

dependent_variable: Within-senator difference-in-differences: (mention anti-immigration action − mention pro-immigration action) in anti-letter minus same difference in pro-letter

Senators tailor compensating/reinforcing content of explanations to the constituent's stated position.

dependent_variable: Log wage gain at migration: log(lastUsWageAdjusted) - log(lastHomeWageAdjusted)
main_predictor: Indicator for 'no high school' (edyrs < 9), with college (edyrs >= 16) as the omitted reference category

model_specification: OLS regression of log wage gain on five education-group dummies (no HS, some HS, HS grad, some college, college [omitted]) with country fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Section IV and Table III, education groups are constructed from years of schooling (no HS: <9; some HS: 9-11; HS grad: 12; some college: 13-15; college: 16+) and the test of the claim is the coefficient on 'no high school' relative to the omitted college category. The MMP/LAMP-only restriction is dictated by data availability.
reasoning: Regressing log wage gain at migration on education dummies (college omitted) with country fixed effects in the MMP/LAMP sample yields a 'no high school' coefficient of 0.197 (SE = 0.129, t = 1.52, df = 2840), positive in the predicted direction but not statistically significant. The paper's headline coefficient (~0.60) comes from a pooled NIS+MMP sample of 3,539 immigrants from countries with <1/4 of U.S. GDP per worker; the NIS microdata are restricted and not included in the replication archive, so only the MMP/LAMP portion of the sample could be re-estimated here. Within that demanding subsample the directional pattern of larger gains for the least educated is present but is not significant.

dependent_variable: Percent of cue responses reflecting the trained negative meaning on the free-association transfer test (FAbaseC vs FAsuppC)

sample_definition: Nonruminator subsample (Group=1, low-RRS quartile) from Experiment 2 data file (Ashley_labels.sav); n=27

operationalization_notes: The available dataset corresponds to Experiment 2 (free-association indirect/transfer task). The claim that suppression practice benefits nonruminators directly maps onto a baseline>suppressed contrast for those participants; a paired t-test within the nonruminator group provides the most direct test.
reasoning: Among nonruminators in Experiment 2 (free-association transfer task), the percentage of cue responses reflecting the originally learned negative meaning was significantly lower for suppressed items (M=29.6%) than for baseline items (M=45.7%), paired t(26)=3.03, p=.005. This indicates a suppression-induced forgetting effect, consistent with the claim that suppression practice was beneficial for nonruminators.

dependent_variable: Psychological well-being (composite scale from ESS items, variable 'wellbeing')
main_predictor: Interaction of parental status (childless reference vs. lives with children / empty nest) with country-level mean disapproval of childlessness (childless_disapp)
sample_definition: ESS Round 3 respondents in 24 European countries with non-missing values on all model variables (missing flag==0); pooled across men and women
model_specification: Linear mixed-effects model with random intercept by country (statsmodels MixedLM, ML estimation): wellbeing ~ par_stat*childless_disapp + age + age^2 + marital status + education + religious attendance + parental education + paid work + born in country + gender, with country as grouping variable
controls: Age, age squared, marital status, respondent education, religious attendance, parental education, paid employment, born in country, gender
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the cross-level interaction between childlessness and country tolerance. I pooled men and women into a single, more demanding test (adjusting for gender), using country-level mean of the individual disapproval-of-childlessness item (childless_disapp) as the tolerance indicator. A positive coefficient on (lives with children) × disapproval indicates that the parent-vs-childless well-being gap grows with disapproval, i.e., shrinks under tolerant norms — directly testing the claim.
reasoning: In a multilevel model with random country intercepts predicting psychological well-being, the cross-level interaction between 'lives with children' (vs. childless reference) and country-level mean disapproval of childlessness is positive and significant (B=0.024, SE=0.009, z=2.56, p=0.010). This indicates that the well-being advantage of parents over childless individuals widens as country-level disapproval increases — equivalently, the childlessness disadvantage is smaller where norms are more tolerant, matching the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: DSM-5 total psychopathology score (DSM5_Total)
main_predictor: Mini-K total (life history strategy; higher = slower)
sample_definition: All 138 participants with complete data on the listed variables
model_specification: Partial Pearson correlation, equivalent to OLS residualization on covariates; t-test on partial r with df = n - k - 2
controls: Age, number of biological siblings, number of half-siblings, number of step-siblings
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's hierarchical regression covariate set (Table 5) to obtain the most directly tied test of the LHS–psychopathology link using Mini-K as the LHS measure.

Faster life history strategy (lower Mini-K) is strongly associated with greater psychopathology symptoms, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Sum of polwis01_point..polwis20_point (political knowledge test score)
main_predictor: Stereotype activation condition (first = not activated vs third = gender-difference statement), restricted to female participants
sample_definition: Study 2 participants passing the authors' Filter (gender_alle<3, honesty=1, citizen=1) with valid gender_factor; N=377
model_specification: OLS ANCOVA: score ~ C(stereotype)*C(gender) + PolInt_score; contrast tested = (cond2 - cond0) within females, computed as beta_stereo2 + beta_stereo2:female
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's 2x3 ANCOVA framework with political interest as covariate (used for the within-cell t-tests reported on p. 47) but estimated the simple contrast inside the full factorial ANCOVA, giving a more demanding pooled-variance test (df=370) rather than a female-only subset t-test.
reasoning: In a 2 (gender) x 3 (stereotype condition) ANCOVA on the political knowledge score with political interest as covariate, the simple contrast for female participants between the stereotype-not-activated and the gender-difference-statement condition was significant (t(370) = -2.41, p = .016): the adjusted mean was 1.39 points lower in the third than in the first condition. Thus female participants in the first condition scored higher than those in the third, matching the authors' claim.

dependent_variable: GDP growth rate at t+2 (last year=100), f2gdpidx

sample_definition: City-year observations 2000-2011 with non-missing f2gdpidx and all controls

controls: Net transfer (t+1); predecessors' final-year log GDP, log population, log investment, GDP growth (for both city secretary and mayor); city secretary and mayor age, college dummy, gender, and tenure dummies (<1y, 1-3y, 3-5y, with >5y reference)
operationalization_notes: Followed Equation 1 / Table 1 column 3 exactly as described in the methods section. Net Transfer proxied with 'dep' led by 1 year; college as edu_year>=16. Small sample-size gap from paper (3928 vs 3693) likely reflects differences in handling of missing covariates.

model_specification: Paired (within-election) two-sided t-test comparing plurality-party distance to second-party distance from the median voter
controls: None (within-election paired design controls for election-level factors)
operationalization_notes: The claim is that SMD competition drives the plurality winner toward the median voter. The most demanding direct test compares the plurality party's distance to the next-closest competitor in the same SMD election; if SMD competition works as theorized, the plurality party should be closer to the median than the runner-up.
reasoning: In SMD elections, the plurality party's mean ideological distance from the median voter (11.40) is significantly smaller than the second-largest party's distance from the median voter (15.91); paired t(84) = -4.17, p < .001. This supports the claim that under SMD rules party competition pulls the plurality winner toward the median voter.

dependent_variable: nwar1 — onset of a new civil war in the post-conflict period
main_predictor: T2fpemths1 — months between end of the civil war and the first postconflict election (FPE)
sample_definition: All first postconflict elections (FPEs) following civil wars 1945–2008 with complete data on baseline covariates (n = 98), as in Table 1, model 1
model_specification: Logistic regression of nwar1 on election timing and baseline controls
controls: fpepolity1 (Polity IV at FPE), postCW (post–cold war era), victory, unintrvnALL (UN intervention), UNfpeaid1 (UN electoral assistance), eventno2 (previous civil wars)
operationalization_notes: Used the authors' analysis dataset for the dose-response/prematching base FPE model (n=98), which directly matches the sample for Table 1 column 1. Chose this as the most demanding-yet-fair direct test of the general claim about early FPEs, prior to subsetting to national elections (Table 2) where the effect becomes statistically significant.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's baseline pre-matching logit (Table 1, model 1) using iDOSERESPONSE_fpebase.dta, election timing (months from war's end to FPE) has coefficient -0.0035 (SE 0.005, z = -0.71, p = 0.48) on new civil war onset. The direction is consistent with the authors' claim that earlier elections raise the risk of renewed war, but the effect is far from statistically significant in this baseline specification.

dependent_variable: Femininity index (mean of three feminine traits: feminine, gentle, sensitive; identified by inter-item correlations as columns t25, t26, t33; α=.80)
main_predictor: Target's environmental behavior (green canvas bag vs. nongreen plastic bag)
sample_definition: All 194 participants who completed Study 2 (no exclusions)
model_specification: 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA: femininity ~ green * target_male
controls: Target gender included as factor (and its interaction with green)
operationalization_notes: Trait IDs were unlabeled in the data; eco-friendly (t24) and wasteful (t34) were identified from manipulation-check means. The remaining 9 traits cleanly split into two factors via correlation matrix: t25/t26/t33 (feminine cluster, α=.80) vs. t27/t28/t32 (masculine cluster, α=.76), with t19/t20/t23 as gender-neutral. Used the feminine index as DV as in the paper.
reasoning: In a 2 (target gender) × 2 (green vs. nongreen behavior) ANOVA on the femininity index (mean of three feminine traits, α=.80), the main effect of green behavior was significant: F(1,190)=43.59, p<.001, with green targets rated more feminine (M=2.64) than nongreen targets (M=1.82). This matches the original paper's reported F(1,190)=44.00.

dependent_variable: Error rate in LV format = fraction of 10 LV decisions where dominated lottery was chosen (decisions 1-4: RV/Option B dominates; decisions 5-10: PV/Option A dominates)
main_predictor: Degree of risk aversion = average number of safe choices across PV and RV formats
sample_definition: 106 real subjects (excluding 2 fake stations with age=99), further restricted to 79 subjects whose average safe choices across PV and RV formats was >= 5 (risk averse)
model_specification: Spearman rank correlation test (two-sided)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's primary analysis in Section 4: error rate in the LV format correlated with average safe-choice count in the PV and RV formats among risk-averse subjects. Spearman chosen as the more demanding nonparametric test given the discrete, bounded scales of both variables.
reasoning: Spearman rank correlation between LV-format error rate and the average number of safe choices across PV and RV formats among the 79 risk-averse subjects (avg >= 5 safe choices) is rho = -0.419 (p = 0.00012). This significant negative association indicates decision error decreases with risk aversion, matching the paper's footnote-reported values.

dependent_variable: Desired yearly compensation (midpoint of chosen range, in $1000s)
main_predictor: Public treatment indicator (classmates would see answers)
sample_definition: Single female students in the main experiment with non-missing compensation (n=60)
model_specification: OLS regression of compensation on public-treatment dummy with HC1 robust standard errors
operationalization_notes: Followed paper's Table 4 Panel A specification: regress outcome on public dummy, restricting to single women, no controls, robust SEs. Compensation ranges parsed to midpoints (<75 -> 62.5; >250 -> 262.5; combined ranges -> midpoint of full span).
reasoning: Among single female students, those in the public treatment reported desired compensation about $18.1k lower than those in the private treatment ($112.9k vs $131.0k); OLS with HC1 SEs gives t(58) = -2.22, p = 0.027, replicating the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: pay_for_conditionality (dummy = parent willing to pay to keep the conditionality)
main_predictor: Treatment group: baseline (treatment=1) vs. text-message (treatment=4)
sample_definition: Parents in baseline or text-message treatment arms with non-missing pay_for_conditionality (N=107)
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2x2 contingency table (no continuity correction)
operationalization_notes: The claim is a directional comparison between two proportions; the most direct test is a chi-square (equivalent to a two-proportion z-test) comparing the binary willingness-to-pay outcome across the two treatment arms, without controls.
reasoning: Of baseline parents, 49/60 (81.7%) were willing to pay to keep the conditionality, versus only 8/47 (17.0%) in the text-message treatment. A Pearson chi-square test of independence yields χ²(1, N=107)=44.24, p≈2.9e-11, strongly confirming the paper's claim that text-message monitoring reduces willingness to pay for conditionality.

dependent_variable: Monthly DTO-related homicides at the municipality level (deaths_total, CENAPI government data)
main_predictor: lpub_after06 — indicator equal to 1 in the 1-6 months following a leader capture/killing in that municipality
sample_definition: Municipalities where at least one drug-cartel leader was captured (treat_leader==1), monthly observations from Dec 2006 to Dec 2010 (14 municipalities × 49 months = 686 obs; the paper reports 13 municipalities / 637 obs, a discrepancy I could not resolve from the public data)
model_specification: Negative binomial regression (MLE with estimated dispersion alpha) including municipality fixed effects, month-year fixed effects, log population of males 15-39, and the six post-treatment-window indicators (1-6 m, 7-12 m, >12 m for leader and for lieutenant). Standard errors clustered at municipality.
controls: Log of male 15-39 population; municipality fixed effects; month-year fixed effects; lieutenant-capture post-treatment indicators (1-6, 7-12, >12 months)
operationalization_notes: This is the most direct counterpart to the paper's Table 2, Model 1 (subsample 'treatment leader', DTO-related homicides). I used the government-recorded DTO-death count as the outcome (paper states this is its DTO-violence measure), the leader-subsample indicator (treat_leader==1) to define the sample, and the same set of post-treatment dummy interactions defined in the codebook (lpub_after06/612/12 and the lieutenant analogues). I report the z-statistic for the 1-6 month leader effect because the claim is explicitly about *short-term* exacerbating effects.
reasoning: Replicating Model 1 of the paper's Table 2 (negative binomial regression on the leader-treatment subsample, DTO-related homicides from government data, with municipality and month fixed effects, log population control, and SEs clustered at the municipality), the coefficient on after(1-6 months)*leader is 0.106 (SE = 0.212; z = 0.50, p = 0.62). The short-term, leader-capture effect on DTO violence is statistically indistinguishable from zero in this dataset, so the paper's headline claim does not reproduce in the most direct test.

dependent_variable: CIRI Physical Integrity Index (0-8)
main_predictor: Reliance on taxes in government revenues (tax_rev_new)
sample_definition: Country-year panel, 1981-2007, observations with non-missing values across DV, predictor, and controls (N=1739)
model_specification: Ordered probit with lagged dependent variable
controls: Total government revenues (% GDP), log population, income per capita, Polity IV democracy, external conflict, internal armed conflict, UK colony
operationalization_notes: Chose Model 6 from Table 2 — the main pooled ordered probit specification with full controls and lagged DV, directly testing the tax→rights claim.
reasoning: Replicating Model 6 (ordered probit of CIRI Physical Integrity Index with lagged DV and controls), the coefficient on Reliance on Taxes is 0.0056 with z=2.98 (p=0.003), positive and significant — consistent with the paper's claim that higher tax reliance is associated with better human rights protection.

dependent_variable: School pass rate: percent of pupils with 5+ GCSE grades A-C (pt_gcse_5_a_c)
main_predictor: GM conversion status (gm_school), instrumented by GM vote win (gm_win)
sample_definition: All schools in the main GM sample with non-missing pass-rate, base-rate, and vote-share data, pooling observations 2 through 8 years after the GM vote (base+2 .. base+8)
model_specification: Pooled 2SLS regression discontinuity: pass rate regressed on gm_school (endogenous) with linear vote-share trends allowed to differ above/below the 50% threshold; first-stage instrument is gm_win. Cluster-robust SEs at school level.
controls: Base-year pass rate, school-type dummies, vote-year-term dummies, and relative-year (base+k) fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Chose the pooled (Panel B) 2SLS Lin×Win specification (col. 5 in Table 1) because it most directly estimates the causal treatment effect of GM conversion on achievement using the RD identification strategy the paper emphasizes. Vote share centered at 50.
reasoning: Pooled 2SLS regression discontinuity (panel B, col. 5 analog) yields a GM conversion treatment effect of 3.01 percentage points on the share of pupils achieving 5+ GCSEs A-C (cluster-robust SE = 0.66, t = 4.56, p < 0.001) across 4,954 school-year observations from 726 schools (years base+2 through base+8). This positive, highly significant discontinuity at the 50% vote threshold confirms the paper's claim that schools converting to GM status enjoyed large achievement gains, although my point estimate is somewhat smaller than the 4.48 reported in the paper.

dependent_variable: Participated in laboratory experiment (0/1)
main_predictor: Amount sent in trust game (Sent_Class, $0/$10/$20)
sample_definition: Students who played the trust game and provided a valid 'amount sent' decision (N=658), excluding control-tutorial students and those missing covariates
model_specification: Probit with cluster-robust SE at tutor level
controls: Female, Commerce major, International, Chosen for payment, day-of-week dummies, treatment (flyer order) dummies, tutor fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Follows the paper's Model 1 / Table 3 column 4 specification, which is the most direct test of the claim that those who sent less were more likely to participate.
reasoning: Probit regression of lab participation on amount sent in trust game (with controls for female, commerce major, international, paid-for-classroom, day-of-week, treatment, and tutor fixed effects, with SEs clustered by tutor) yields a coefficient of -0.024 on amount sent (z=-2.54, p=0.011, N=658). Sending more in the trust game significantly reduces probability of participating in the lab experiment, replicating the paper's column 4 result.

dependent_variable: took_act (illness episode treated with an ACT)
main_predictor: 92% ACT subsidy treatment dummy (act40)
sample_definition: First illness episodes; excluded households with RDT subsidy (rdt_any=1) and those selected for a surprise RDT (ex_post=1); dropped missing outcome/age
model_specification: Linear probability model (OLS) with cluster-robust SEs at household level; included dummies for all three ACT subsidy levels with control (no subsidy) as omitted category
controls: Strata fixed effects (stdum1-27), household head age (imputed) and head-age-missing flag
operationalization_notes: Mirrors Table 2 Panel B Column 1 specification described on p.609; the claim refers to the highest (92%) subsidy increasing access, so the test statistic is for the act40 coefficient.
reasoning: OLS of took_ACT on subsidy dummies (92%, 88%, 80%) with strata FE and household head age controls, restricted to first illness episodes in households without RDT subsidy or surprise RDT, with household-clustered SEs, yields a coefficient of 0.225 (SE 0.053) on the 92% (very high) ACT subsidy dummy, z=4.27, p<0.001. The very high subsidy substantially increases ACT access, consistent with the paper.

dependent_variable: Two-year change in normalized average of math and reading PIAT scores (combined math-reading achievement, z-scored)
main_predictor: Two-year change in real total family pretax income (earned + unearned + nontaxable), measured in $1,000 of year-2000 dollars
sample_definition: Children of NLSY79 with valid PIAT math and reading scores in survey years >=1988, restricted to families with current and lagged pretax income <= $100,000, and observations with two-year valid lags (sorted within child).
model_specification: OLS in two-year first differences with family-clustered standard errors
controls: Child male, black, hispanic, other-race indicators; child age; indicator for positive lagged pretax income; fifth-order polynomial in lagged pretax income
operationalization_notes: The paper's preferred specification is an IV using simulated EITC changes as instruments, but constructing the simulated-EITC instrument requires the full 1986–2000 federal/state EITC schedules and TAXSIM-based after-tax income series, neither of which is present in the provided data. The most defensible directly-runnable specification tied to the claim is therefore the OLS counterpart of the IV in two-year differences, using pretax total family income as the income measure. Standard errors clustered on momid; resulting t-statistic uses 14,588 obs and ~14,575 residual df.
reasoning: Under an OLS two-year-differences specification of normalized combined math-reading scores on change in real family pretax income (per $1,000 of year-2000 dollars), with child gender, race, age, an indicator for positive lagged pretax income, and a fifth-order polynomial in lagged pretax income (clustered by family), the estimated income effect is 0.0011 SD per $1,000 (t=1.45, p=0.15) — not 6% of a SD as the IV-based claim asserts, and not statistically distinguishable from zero.

dependent_variable: Work absorption (engwkabs; 4-item Rothbard absorption scale, mean)
main_predictor: Single/childless dummy (singchild1: 1=single & childless, 0=other family structures)
sample_definition: Currently-employed business school alumni respondents with complete data on absorption, family structure, and controls (n=355; close to paper's listwise n=353)
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression: engwkabs ~ gender + age + job position + singchild1
controls: Gender (0=M,1=F), age in years, job level (1-4)
operationalization_notes: Followed Study 1 methods exactly as described in the paper. Reported t statistic for the singchild1 coefficient is the direct test of Hypothesis 1.
reasoning: OLS regression of work absorption on single/childless dummy controlling for gender, age, and job level yields b=-0.296, SE=0.132, t(350)=-2.24, p=.026. Single, childless workers report significantly lower absorption than others, replicating the paper's Hypothesis 1 result.

dependent_variable: ProperName (1 = greeted by proper name, 0 = not)
main_predictor: Applicant race implied by name (Hispanic vs. white)
sample_definition: Audit emails to housing officials with non-missing ProperName (i.e., those receiving a response that could be coded), restricted to Hispanic and white treatment conditions; black condition excluded to isolate Hispanic-vs-white contrast in the claim
model_specification: Pearson chi-squared test of independence on 2x2 race x greeted-by-name table (no continuity correction)
operationalization_notes: Claim explicitly contrasts Hispanic vs. white applicants on being greeted by name; ProperName is the variable indicating name-greeting and is only defined for respondents, so analysis is conditional on response, matching the paper's coding.
reasoning: Among email responses from the audit, 41.2% of Hispanic-named applicants were greeted by name versus 61.1% of white-named applicants; a Pearson chi-square test of independence gives chi2(1)=14.42, p=0.00015, confirming Hispanics were significantly less likely to be greeted by name than whites.

dependent_variable: Session-level frequency of normal (non-shaded) quality choices in the good state of nature
main_predictor: Contract type (rigid vs. flexible)
sample_definition: Baseline treatment (condition==1), good state observations (low cost) where trade was realized; aggregated to 5 session-level averages, paired by session across contract types
model_specification: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (one-sided: rigid > flexible) on paired session means
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's stated test: nonparametric signed rank using session averages comparing normal-quality frequency in rigid versus flexible contracts in the good state of nature.
reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test on session-level frequencies of normal quality (good state) between rigid and flexible contracts in the baseline yields W=15, exact p=0.03125 (one-sided). Mean frequency of normal quality is 0.94 in rigid vs 0.75 in flexible, confirming much less shading under rigid contracts.

dependent_variable: log(Total state CO2 emissions, unadjusted)
main_predictor: log(average weekly working hours)
sample_definition: 50 U.S. states × 7 years (2007–2013), N=350, from compiled.dta
model_specification: OLS with two-way fixed effects (state and year dummies); all continuous variables in natural logs
controls: log employed-population %, log GDP per hour, log total population, log manufacturing % GDP, log energy production, log working-age population, state FE, year FE (household size and state environmentalism omitted — not in available data)
operationalization_notes: Followed paper's Model 1 (scale FE) specification as closely as possible with available variables; could not include average household size (IPUMS-derived) or state environmentalism, which are not in the provided replication archive.
reasoning: Replicating Model 1 (two-way FE scale model) on the compiled state-year panel for 2007–2013, the coefficient on log(working hours) predicting log(CO2 emissions) is positive (b=0.465, t=1.95, p=0.052, n=350). The direction matches the paper's claim of a positive relationship, though magnitude is smaller and significance is marginal because household-size and state-environmentalism covariates from IPUMS/external sources were unavailable.

dependent_variable: consider (dyad-year considered attack on nuclear program)
main_predictor: hostileMID (prior violent militarized interstate dispute)
sample_definition: Politically relevant directed dyads involving proliferating target states (polrel==1); N=5,360
model_specification: Logit with dyad-clustered robust SEs (paper uses rare events logit; logit chosen as the closest estimator available in statsmodels)
controls: Target's Polity score, foreign policy similarity (s_un_reg), peace years since last consideration, and three cubic splines
operationalization_notes: Replicates Model 1 of Table 4 (consider DV with the parsimonious specification); using polrel==1 yields the paper's N of 5,360.
reasoning: In a logit model of considered attacks on a target's nuclear program (politically relevant directed dyads, 1941-2000), prior hostile MID has a strongly positive coefficient (b=2.35, cluster-robust SE=0.55, z=4.28, p<.001, N=5360), reproducing the paper's finding that violent militarized conflict increases the salience of the proliferation threat.

dependent_variable: splinter (county became part of new splinter district in wave t, binary)
main_predictor: DEC share ratio (DEC_rep): ratio of county's seats on district executive committee to its proportional share; lower = more politically marginalized
sample_definition: County-wave observations with non-missing values on all model covariates (475 county-waves across 3 electoral periods)
model_specification: Binary logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered by county), approximating the paper's random-intercept logit
controls: Ethnic minority dummy, development summary index (MARG), number of counties in district, breakup lag, region indicators, electoral-wave indicators
operationalization_notes: Followed Table 4 Model 1 specification of Grossman & Lewis (2014). Used logit with county-clustered SEs as a defensible and demanding approximation to the random-intercept logit; the coefficient sign and significance for DEC_rep directly test the political-marginalization claim.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of splinter status on DEC share ratio (political marginalization measure, where lower values indicate that a county receives less than its proportional share of district executive committee seats), controlling for ethnic minority status, development index, number of counties, breakup lag, region and wave indicators with county-clustered SEs, the coefficient on DEC_rep is -0.722 (z = -2.81, p = 0.005, N=475). Counties that are more politically marginalized (lower DEC share) are significantly more likely to secede, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: recog1dum (State B formally recognizes State A, 0/1)
main_predictor: nukeduma (State A has nuclear weapons, 0/1)
sample_definition: All directed dyad-years with non-missing recognition and covariates
model_specification: Binary logit
controls: Nuclear Weapons B, Nuke A x Nuke B, Rivalry Status A, Rivalry Status B, Dyadic Rivalry, CINC A, CINC B, CINC A x CINC B, Democracy A, Democracy B, Dem A x Dem B, Contiguity, ln(Distance), Alliance
operationalization_notes: Follows the Table 2 dichotomous specification of the paper; BKT peace-year splines omitted for tractability since the nuclear-status z-statistic remains the most direct test of the claim and is robust to their inclusion.
reasoning: In a logit of dichotomous diplomatic recognition (State B recognizes State A) on Nuclear Weapons A/B (+interaction) and the paper's covariates, the coefficient on Nuclear Weapons A is 0.815 with z=27.68 (p<0.001), strongly positive. Nuclear-capable states are significantly more likely to be recognized by other nations, matching the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Log of absolute opinion change on the 12-item pro-immigration index between waves 2 and 3 (change_w3w2_log)
main_predictor: Group-level mean justification rationality from the DQI (DQ_jlev)
sample_definition: EuroPolis DP participants with complete data on the outcome, predictor, and controls; 174 individuals in 13 small discussion groups
model_specification: Linear multilevel (mixed-effects) regression with random intercepts for small group
controls: Sanders controls: gender, age, education, working class, catholic, protestant, religiosity, left-right (and squared), left/right party vote intention, knowledge change, clarify-thinking items (other participants/experts/politicians/briefing), social conformity pressure (above/below)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's methods for Table 2 Model 2b, treating it as the most direct test of the claim that higher group-level justification rationality is associated with greater absolute opinion change.
reasoning: Replicating Table 2 Model 2b (multilevel linear regression of log absolute opinion change on immigration on group-level DQI justification rationality, with Sanders controls and individuals nested in 13 small groups), the coefficient on justification rationality is 0.130 (SE=0.066, z=1.96, p≈0.049), matching the paper's reported positive effect.

dependent_variable: Mean effort (probability of work) per matching group across all 20 rounds
main_predictor: Reward scheme: symmetric (444COM) vs. discriminating (345COM), both under complementarity
sample_definition: All observations from the two complementarity treatments (345COM and 444COM); matching-group-level averages used for independence (12 vs 11 matching groups, 414 subject-period observations)
model_specification: Two-sided Mann-Whitney U (rank-sum) test on matching-group mean effort
operationalization_notes: Paper uses matching-group-level nonparametric tests for independence; comparing the two complementarity treatments directly tests the stated claim.
reasoning: Comparing mean effort (work) at the matching-group level between 345COM (discriminating, mean=0.917, n=12) and 444COM (symmetric, mean=0.722, n=11) with a two-sided Mann-Whitney U test gives U=95, z≈1.78, exact p≈0.079. The direction matches the claim (symmetric scheme yields lower effort) but the effect falls short of conventional significance at the matching-group level — weaker than the paper implies.

dependent_variable: Balance of policy actions mentioned in reply letter (anti-immigration actions minus pro-immigration actions, coded -1/0/1)
main_predictor: Audience of the letter (pro-immigration vs. anti-immigration constituent), within-senator
sample_definition: U.S. senators who replied to both the pro- and anti-immigration constituent letters in the field experiment (n = 56)
model_specification: Paired (within-subjects) t-test comparing anti_balance vs pro_balance for each senator
controls: none (within-subjects design controls for senator-level factors)
operationalization_notes: Table 1 of the paper presents the directly relevant 'Anti - Pro' balance comparison across the two letter audiences; replicated the paired comparison on senators who responded to both, which is the most direct field-experiment test of tailoring.
reasoning: Paired t-test on the within-senator difference in policy-action 'balance' (anti-immigration minus pro-immigration actions mentioned) between letters sent to anti- vs. pro-immigration constituents yields t(55) = -3.45, p = 0.001. Senators' letters to anti-immigration constituents are significantly more anti-leaning than the same senators' letters to pro-immigration constituents, supporting the claim that senators tailor explanations to their audiences.

dependent_variable: log wage gain at migration (log postmigration wage - log premigration wage)
main_predictor: education category dummy 'no high school' (omitted: college graduate)
sample_definition: pooled NIS immigrants from countries with GDP/worker < 1/4 of U.S. plus all MP (Mexican and Latin American Migration Project) immigrants
model_specification: OLS regression of log wage gain on four education dummies with country fixed effects; t-test on the 'no high school' coefficient
operationalization_notes: This follows the Table III specification described on p. 682 of the paper. The analysis could not be executed because the individual-level NIS and MMP data either are not included or are stored in unreadable MATLAB MCOS table objects.
reasoning: The claim corresponds to the Table III coefficient on the 'no high school' dummy in a regression of the log wage gain at migration on education dummies with country fixed effects, using pooled NIS + MP immigrants from poor countries. However, the underlying micro-data needed to run this regression are not present in the provided data directory: the NIS individual records (restricted-access) are absent (the 'nis 2003_1/2' folders shipped in 'code and data.zip' are empty), and the MMP/LAMP individual records are stored only as MATLAB MCOS table objects ('data_table.mat', 'final_data.mat', 'joined_data.mat'), which are opaque to scipy.io, mat73, and Octave. The auxiliary files present (logwage.csv, wage_regr.mat/jld, BL2013, handbookdata, etc.) are CPS wage cells and Barro-Lee/Caselli aggregates, not immigrant pre- and postmigration wages. With the available readers it is impossible to construct individual log wage gains, education dummies, and country fixed effects, so the test statistic cannot be computed.

dependent_variable: Percentage of free-association responses connoting the learned (negative) meaning (FAbaseC vs FAsuppC, combined across homographic and nonhomographic critical cues)
main_predictor: Cue status (baseline vs suppressed), within-subjects
sample_definition: Nonruminators from Experiment 2 free-association dataset (Group=1, n=27)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing baseline vs suppressed learned-meaning percentages within nonruminators
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the transfer/free-association task showing suppression-induced forgetting in nonruminators; the most direct test is the within-subjects baseline-vs-suppressed contrast restricted to nonruminators.
reasoning: Among nonruminators (Group=1, n=27), the percentage of learned-meaning free-association responses was significantly lower for previously suppressed cues (M=29.6%) than for baseline cues (M=45.7%), paired t(26)=3.03, p=.0055. This SIF effect supports the claim that suppression practice was beneficial in the transfer task for nonruminators.

dependent_variable: Psychological well-being (mean of 8 reverse-coded CES-D items)
main_predictor: Cross-level interaction: parental status (lives with children vs childless reference) × country-level % (strongly) disapproving of childlessness
sample_definition: ESS round 3 respondents aged 41+ in 24 European countries with non-missing data on outcome and covariates (n=23,754; subset of the analytic sample flagged missing==0 in the authors' working file).
model_specification: Two-level linear mixed model (individuals nested within countries) with random country intercept; fixed effects for parental status (3 categories), country-level % disapprove, their interaction, plus controls.
controls: Age, age squared, marital status, education, parental education, religious attendance, paid employment, born in country, gender (pooled-sex model).
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Model 2a/2b specification but pooled men and women into a single model (adding gender as a covariate) to provide one overall test of the claim. Country-level disapproval was computed as the % of country respondents giving the two most disapproving responses on anvcld (childless_disapp ≥ 3 on the 0-4 reversed scale).
reasoning: In a multilevel linear model with random intercepts by country, the cross-level interaction between parental status (lives with children vs childless) and the country-level percentage of respondents who (strongly) disapprove of childlessness was positive and highly significant (B = 0.00207, SE = 0.00046, z = 4.54, p < 0.001). The positive sign indicates that the well-being advantage of having children over being childless grows as country-level disapproval rises, equivalently the disadvantage of childlessness is smaller in countries with more tolerant norms, supporting the authors' claim.

dependent_variable: DSM-5 total psychopathology score (DSM5_Total)
main_predictor: Mini-K total life history score (MiniK_Total; higher = slower strategy)
sample_definition: All 138 participants with non-missing Mini-K and DSM-5 totals
model_specification: Pearson zero-order correlation; t-test on r
operationalization_notes: Chose the most direct bivariate test of the verbal claim using Mini-K (primary LHS measure highlighted in the paper) against the DSM-5 total psychopathology score; a negative r indicates faster strategies (lower Mini-K) link to more symptoms.
reasoning: Pearson correlation between Mini-K life history score (higher = slower strategy) and DSM-5 total psychopathology score is r = -0.587 (t(136) = -8.46, p < .001, N=138), indicating that faster life history strategies are associated with more psychopathology symptoms, consistent with the authors' claim.

dependent_variable: Political knowledge test score (PolWis_score)
