reasoning: Pooling all three grades and all three program years, T3 students scored 63.3 ALI points higher than control students (cluster-robust SE=15.7, z=4.03, p<0.001, N=60,297 across 48 school clusters), confirming that the most comprehensive ALI incentive package significantly increased mathematics test scores in the direction the authors claim.

dependent_variable: Proportion of intertemporal choices in which subject chose the earlier (impatient) payment
main_predictor: Ethnicity-salience treatment dummy (treatE)
sample_definition: Asian-American subjects in Experiment 1 (raceA==1)
model_specification: Two-sample t-test (equal variances) comparing impatient-choice proportion between treatment and control
operationalization_notes: Followed Table 1 of the paper: the most direct test of the claim is a t-test comparing the proportion of impatient choices between primed and control Asian subjects.
reasoning: Among 71 Asian-American subjects in Experiment 1, the mean proportion of impatient intertemporal choices was 0.264 in control vs 0.126 in the ethnicity-salient condition; a two-sample t-test yields t(69)=3.43, p=0.001, supporting the claim that priming Asian ethnic identity makes Asian-Americans more patient.

dependent_variable: Subject-level average cooperation rate (mean of coop_frequency across 23 supergames, in %)
main_predictor: Stochastic-horizon dummy (1 = Short-Stochastic, 0 = Short-Deterministic)
sample_definition: Subjects in the Short-Deterministic (tmnt=3) and Short-Stochastic (tmnt=4) treatments; 10 subjects dropped due to missing covariate values (N=86 of 96).
model_specification: OLS linear regression of subject mean cooperation on the stochastic dummy with controls
controls: Demographics (age, gender, Italian, degree, field, job), academic background (economics, statistics, gametheory), questionnaire measures (risk, trust, logic1, logic2), task comprehension (wronganswer, timeCQ)
operationalization_notes: Follows the Table III specification (subject-level mean cooperation with the same individual controls) but restricts to the two short-duration treatments so that the coefficient directly tests the Short-Det vs Short-Stoch contrast referenced by the claim, rather than recovering it as a linear combination of two dummies relative to a Long-Deterministic baseline.
reasoning: Restricting to the two short-duration treatments and regressing subject-average cooperation rate on a Short-Stochastic dummy with the full set of individual controls used in Table III, the Short-Stochastic dummy is negative and significant (t(59) = -2.86, p = 0.006), confirming that cooperation is significantly higher under a deterministic than a stochastic horizon in short games.

dependent_variable: Ideological distance between plurality vote-winning party and median voter (pldist1, manifesto-based)
main_predictor: Election rule (SMD vs. PR)
sample_definition: All 331 elections in the manifesto dataset (1945-2004); 85 SMD and 244 PR (after dropping missing).
model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test of pldist1 by smd
operationalization_notes: H4a predicts that under SMD the plurality winner should be close to the median voter; the most demanding fair test is whether SMD plurality winners are closer to the median than under PR. Used the manifesto-based plurality-distance variable available in the dataset.
reasoning: Welch's t-test comparing the plurality vote winner's ideological distance from the median voter (pldist1) between SMD (M=11.40, n=85) and PR (M=11.07, n=244) yields t=0.28, p=0.78. The plurality winner is not closer to the median voter under SMD than under PR — if anything, slightly farther — providing no support for H4a.

dependent_variable: nwar1 (new civil war occurred after first postconflict election, 0/1)
main_predictor: T2fpemths1 (months between civil war end and first postconflict election)
sample_definition: All postconflict elections after civil wars (Doyle & Sambanis-based universe), complete-case sample used in Table 1 model 1 (N=98)
model_specification: Logistic regression of new civil war on election timing and controls (Table 1, model 1)
controls: FPE level national, FPE level concurrent, Polity IV, post-Cold War era, victory, UN intervention, UN electoral assistance, previous civil wars (eventno2)
operationalization_notes: Used the iDOSERESPONSE_fpebase.dta sample (N=98) that defines the Table 1 model 1 estimation sample, merged with fpenatl1 and fpeconrnt1 from BS09_DATA_main.dta. Reported z-statistic on the election timing coefficient as the most direct test of the directional claim.
reasoning: Replicating Table 1 model 1 (baseline logit of new civil war on election timing plus core controls) on the original 98-case dataset, the coefficient on Election timing (T2fpemths1, months from war end to first postconflict election) is -0.0031 (SE = 0.0048, z = -0.64, p = 0.52). The sign is in the direction the authors claim (later elections -> less risk of renewed war), but it is far from statistically significant; the central claim does not survive its most direct test.

dependent_variable: Femininity index (mean of three feminine traits: feminine, gentle, sensitive)
main_predictor: Behavior condition (green vs. nongreen)
sample_definition: All 194 participants from Study 2
model_specification: 2x2 between-subjects ANOVA with target gender and behavior as factors; main effect of behavior reported
operationalization_notes: Items in the CSV were numbered without labels; the three feminine items were identified as v25, v26, v33 by matching the green vs. nongreen condition means/SDs reported in the paper (2.64/.90 vs 1.82/.86). The masculine triad v27,v28,v32 likewise reproduced the paper's masculine-index means.
reasoning: In a 2 (target gender) x 2 (behavior: green vs. nongreen) ANOVA on the femininity index (avg of feminine, gentle, sensitive), green targets were rated more feminine (M=2.64, SD=0.90, N=94) than nongreen targets (M=1.82, SD=0.86, N=100); F(1,190)=43.59, p<.001. This closely matches the paper's reported F(1,190)=44.00.

dependent_variable: Error rate in LV format: fraction of 10 lottery-vs-lottery decisions in which the dominated lottery was chosen
main_predictor: Degree of risk aversion = average number of safe choices in the PV and RV multiple price lists
sample_definition: 79 risk-averse subjects (average PV/RV safe choices >= 5), excluding the two dummy ZTREE stations (age=99); total observed subjects = 106
model_specification: Spearman rank correlation between risk aversion and LV error rate
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Section 4/Fig. 4 specification: restricted to risk averse subjects, used average PV/RV safe choices as the risk-aversion measure, and computed the error rate from the LV format treating the RV lottery as dominant in decisions 1-4 and the PV lottery as dominant in decisions 5-10. Reported the more demanding Spearman correlation.
reasoning: Among the 79 risk-averse subjects (those with mean PV+RV safe choices >= 5), the Spearman correlation between degree of risk aversion (average safe choices in PV and RV formats) and error rate (proportion of 10 LV decisions where the dominated lottery was chosen) is rho = -0.419, p = 0.00012. The relationship is significantly negative, supporting the claim that decision error decreases with risk aversion.

dependent_variable: Desired yearly compensation (midpoint of chosen range, $000s)
main_predictor: Public treatment dummy (treatment B vs A)
sample_definition: Single female students in main experiment (3_mainexp_responses.dta) with non-missing desired compensation
model_specification: OLS with HC1 (robust) standard errors
operationalization_notes: Followed paper's coding: midpoint of chosen range, with 'Under 75' = 62.5 and 'Above 250' = 262.5; spanning ranges coded as midpoint of full chosen span. Public = treatment B.
reasoning: Among single female students (N=60), OLS of desired compensation (midpoint of chosen range, in $000s) on a public-treatment indicator with HC1 robust SEs yields a coefficient of -$18.1k (z = -2.22, p = 0.027). Mean falls from $131k (private) to $113k (public), reproducing the paper's ~$18,000 reduction and supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: WTP_dummy: parent prefers R$120 CCT to a strictly larger unconditional CT (1=willing to pay to keep conditionality)
main_predictor: Treatment assignment: baseline (treatment=1) vs. text-message (treatment=2)
sample_definition: Parents assigned to baseline or text-message treatments (excludes don't tell and nonclassroom treatments); N=111
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on the 2x2 table of treatment by WTP_dummy (no controls)
operationalization_notes: The paper's most direct claim is a comparison of the proportion willing to pay to keep the conditionality between baseline and text-message treatments. I used the primary dummy outcome (WTP_dummy) and the simple mean-comparison version of the test without covariates, which is the most demanding minimal-assumption test of a difference in proportions.
reasoning: In the baseline treatment, 49/60 (81.7%) of parents were willing to pay to keep the conditionality, compared with only 10/51 (19.6%) in the text-message treatment. A Pearson chi-square test of independence yields χ²(1, N=111) = 42.64, p ≈ 6.6e-11, confirming a large, highly significant drop in willingness to pay when monitoring via text messages is available, as the paper claims.

dependent_variable: Monthly homicides of males aged 15-39 (proxy for DTO-related violence)
main_predictor: after(1-6 months) * leader capture indicator
sample_definition: Municipalities where at least one drug-cartel leader was captured/killed between Dec 2006 and Dec 2010 (Ciudad Juárez excluded), monthly panel Dec 2006 - Dec 2010
model_specification: Negative binomial with municipality and month fixed effects; cluster-robust SEs at municipality level; alpha estimated via Cameron-Trivedi auxiliary regression
controls: Population of males 15-39, municipality fixed effects, time (month) fixed effects, plus other after-window interactions for leader and lieutenant
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Equation (1) and Table 1 Model 1 most directly tied to the short-term DTO-violence claim. Used GLM-NB with pre-estimated alpha to obtain stable estimates.
reasoning: Replicating Table 1 model 1 (negative binomial with municipality and time fixed effects, population control, robust SE clustered by municipality, sample restricted to municipalities with at least one leader capture during Dec2006-Dec2010, excluding Cd. Juárez), the coefficient on after(1-6 months)*leader for DTO-related homicides (male 15-39) is 0.291 (SE 0.120), z=2.42, p=0.015, indicating a statistically significant ~34% short-term increase, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Average shortest path length (ASPL) of TMFG-filtered semantic networks from bootstrapped 90%-node samples
main_predictor: Openness-to-experience group (high vs low, median split on LATENT factor)
sample_definition: 516 participants; split into high (n=258) and low (n=258) openness groups; semantic networks built on common nodes (animals named by >=2 participants in BOTH groups, N=168 nodes)
model_specification: Cosine-similarity networks filtered with TMFG (3N-6 edges); 1000 bootstrap subsamples of 90% of nodes per group; independent-samples t-test on ASPL across bootstrap samples
controls: none (common node set holds N and edge count equal across groups)
operationalization_notes: The paper frames 'more interconnected' as lower ASPL (p. 482). I followed the paper's described pipeline: median split on the openness factor, retain animals named >=2 times in both groups as nodes, build cosine-similarity adjacency, apply TMFG, and run a 90%-nodes partial bootstrap t-test on ASPL.
reasoning: In a partial bootstrap analysis (1000 resamples per group, 90% of nodes retained), the high openness group's semantic network had a substantially lower ASPL (M=3.01) than the low openness group's network (M=3.89), t(1998)=-44.85, p<.001, d=-2.01. Lower ASPL indicates greater interconnectivity, supporting the original claim.

dependent_variable: CIRI Physical Integrity Index (0-8)
main_predictor: Reliance on Taxes (tax_rev_new)
sample_definition: Country-year observations with complete data on DV, lagged DV, and covariates (n=1739)
model_specification: Ordered probit with lagged dependent variable
controls: Size of government revenues, log population, income per capita, Polity IV democracy, external conflict, internal armed conflict, UK colony
operationalization_notes: Mirrors Table 2 column (6) — the central pooled ordered probit specification testing the tax-reliance claim.
reasoning: Replicating model (6) from Table 2 (ordered probit of CIRI Physical Integrity Index on Reliance on Taxes, with lagged DV and controls), Reliance on Taxes has a positive coefficient of 0.0056 with z=2.98 (p=0.003), supporting the claim that greater tax reliance is associated with better human rights protection.

dependent_variable: School pass rate: % of pupils with ≥5 GCSE A*-C (pt_gcse_5_a_c)
main_predictor: gm_win indicator (won the GM ballot, vote share > 50%) as instrument/treatment-intent
sample_definition: All school-year observations from the main GM sample (schools that held a GM vote), 1992-2003, with non-missing outcome and baseline.
model_specification: Reduced-form OLS RD-ITT regression of pass rate on the GM-win indicator with a linear control in centered vote share and additional covariates; SEs clustered at school level. (2SLS with gm_win as instrument for gm_school yields a 3.99 pp local average treatment effect with the same t-statistic.)
controls: Baseline pass rate (pt_gcse_5_a_c_base), linear vote-share (centered at 50), and year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Most direct test of the headline claim using the paper's regression-discontinuity framework. Reduced-form/ITT is the cleanest test of the discontinuity; sticking with linear vote control mirrors Table 2 column 'Linear'. Year FE and baseline performance included as in the paper to reduce noise.
reasoning: Reduced-form RD-ITT: among the 742 schools that voted on GM status (8,665 school-year observations, 1992-2003), schools that narrowly won the GM vote showed a 3.54 percentage-point higher pass rate (≥5 GCSEs A-C) than narrow losers, controlling for vote share (centered), baseline pass rate, and year fixed effects, with SE clustered by school (SE=0.96, t=3.70, p<0.001). This corroborates the claim that GM conversion yielded large achievement gains.

dependent_variable: Participated in the laboratory experiment (0/1)
main_predictor: Amount sent in the classroom trust game (Sent_Class, $0/$10/$20)
sample_definition: Students in trust-game treatments (Flyer-Trust and Trust-Flyer) who provided a valid amount-sent decision (N=658)
model_specification: Probit regression with robust standard errors clustered at the tutor level
controls: Female, commerce major, international, flyer administered after classroom experiment, randomly chosen for payment, and day-of-week dummies
operationalization_notes: Replicates the paper's Model 1 specification (Table 3, column 3) using the amount-sent sub-sample, since this is the analysis the claim directly references.
reasoning: Probit of lab participation on amount sent in the trust game, with controls (female, commerce, international, flyer-after, paid-for-class, day dummies) and tutor-clustered SE, yields a coefficient on Sent_Class of -0.0231 (z = -2.66, p = 0.008, N = 658). Negative and statistically significant, confirming that students who sent less in the trust game were more likely to participate in the lab experiment.

dependent_variable: took_act (illness episode treated with an ACT)
main_predictor: 92% ACT subsidy indicator (act40), vs. no-subsidy control
sample_definition: First illness episodes following baseline; households not assigned to RDT subsidy and not selected for a surprise RDT at the drug shop; 88% and 80% subsidy arms excluded so the comparison is the very-high (92%) subsidy vs control
model_specification: Linear probability model (OLS) with HH-clustered robust SEs
controls: Strata fixed effects (stdum1-28) and imputed household head age
operationalization_notes: The claim refers specifically to a 'very high subsidy' (the AMFm-style 92% subsidy). I therefore isolated the 92% arm vs control rather than pooling all subsidy levels, following Table 2's regression specification (eq. with strata FE, HH-head age, HH-clustered SEs).
reasoning: Restricting to first illness episodes in households without RDT-subsidy or surprise RDT, and comparing the 92% ACT subsidy arm to the no-subsidy control, the 92% subsidy raises the probability that an illness is treated with an ACT by 23.7 percentage points (SE 0.055, t=4.33, p<0.001), strongly supporting the claim that a very high subsidy increases access.

dependent_variable: Two-year change in normalized combined math+reading PIAT score (average of math, reading recognition, reading comprehension, standardized to the random subsample)
main_predictor: Two-year change in total family income (earned + unearned + nontaxable) in $1,000s of year-2000 dollars
sample_definition: Children-of-NLSY79 observations in PIAT-test (odd) years 1987-1999 with valid combined PIAT score, observed in two consecutive (two-year-apart) test years with no maternal marital-status change between them, total family income below $100,000 in both years, and changes within the central 98% of the income-change distribution (N=10,197 child-pair observations).
model_specification: OLS in first (two-year) differences, mirroring Table 2 Panel B Column 1 of Dahl & Lochner (the differenced analogue of the IV baseline), SEs clustered at mother (momid) level.
controls: Change in number of household members, child gender, race indicators (black, Hispanic, other); child fixed effects implicit through first-differencing.
operationalization_notes: The paper's headline 6%-of-SD effect requires the EITC-simulated instrument, which cannot be reconstructed from the released data without TAXSIM and the full federal/state tax-EITC schedules. As a skeptical analyst, I therefore implement the most demanding fair test of the directional claim using only the panel variation actually available - the differenced OLS specification that the authors themselves report as a benchmark - using their own released income components and PIAT scores. Income was deflated to year-2000 dollars using the supplied CPI series.
reasoning: Estimating a first-differenced OLS model of the change in normalized combined math+reading PIAT scores on the change in total family income (in $1,000s of year-2000 dollars), with baseline child controls (gender, race, change in number of household members) and clustering at the mother level, yields a coefficient of 0.0009 per $1,000 (t = 0.98, p = 0.33). The point estimate is positive but two orders of magnitude smaller than the paper's IV estimate of ~0.061 and is statistically indistinguishable from zero, so the headline claim does not survive when the analysis is stripped of the EITC-based instrument and identification rests only on within-child income variation.

dependent_variable: Work absorption (engwkabs)
main_predictor: Single/childless indicator (singchild1: 1=single & childless, 0=other)
sample_definition: Currently employed (non-retired) respondents from Study 1 alumni survey with non-missing data on all model variables (n=355)
model_specification: OLS regression: absorption ~ gender + age + job level + single/childless
operationalization_notes: Followed Study 1 specification described in the Results section, which tested H1 via OLS regression with sex, age, and job level as controls.
reasoning: OLS regression of work absorption on the single/childless indicator (controlling for gender, age, and job level) yields b=-0.296, SE=0.132, t(350)=-2.24, p=.026, n=355. Single, childless employees report significantly lower absorption than those with other family structures, consistent with the paper's Hypothesis 1.

dependent_variable: ProperName (whether response began with a personalized/proper-name greeting; 1=yes)
main_predictor: Putative race of emailer (Hispanic vs. white) from randomized TreatmentGroup
sample_definition: Respondents whose ProperName was coded (i.e., housing authorities that responded) and whose treatment race was Hispanic or white; black-name treatments excluded to isolate the Hispanic-vs-white contrast.
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2x2 table (race x named greeting), without continuity correction
operationalization_notes: The paper's preferred model is a logit with demographic controls, but the unidentified replication dataset only contains tercile-coded versions of those controls. Given random assignment of names, the most direct and demanding fair test of the bivariate claim is a chi-square comparing the proper-name greeting rate for Hispanic vs white emailers among those who responded.
reasoning: Among housing officials who responded, 41.2% of putatively Hispanic emailers were addressed by proper name vs 61.1% of white emailers — a ~20 pp gap matching the paper's headline. Pearson chi-square = 14.42 (df=1, n=362), p≈0.00015, strongly supporting the claim that Hispanic applicants were less likely to be greeted by name than white counterparts.

dependent_variable: Indicator for shading (low quality, qualityc==1) at the contract level, aggregated to session×contract-type mean
main_predictor: Contract type (rigid vs. flexible)
sample_definition: Baseline treatment (condition==1) realized contracts only (contractrealizedc==1); paired at the session level (n=5 sessions)
model_specification: Wilcoxon signed-rank test on within-session paired shading rates (rigid vs. flexible)
operationalization_notes: The paper's most direct test of the rigid-vs-flexible shading claim uses nonparametric signed-rank tests with session averages as independent observations; I replicated that on the baseline (5-session) sample.
reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (W=0, two-sided p=0.0625; one-sided p≈0.031) on the five baseline-session paired shading frequencies shows shading is lower under rigid contracts (5%, 6%, 5%, 9%, 4%) than under flexible contracts (24%, 30%, 20%, 35%, 23%) in every session. With only 5 sessions this is the minimum possible W and the smallest attainable p, directionally confirming 'much less shading' under rigid contracts.

dependent_variable: log(state CO2 emissions, carbon_adj)
main_predictor: log(average weekly working hours)
sample_definition: All 50 US states × 7 years (2007–2013), N=350
model_specification: Two-way fixed effects OLS (state and year dummies) with cluster-robust standard errors by state; all continuous variables in natural logs (Scale model 1)
controls: log(employed pop %), log(GDP per hour), log(total population), log(manufacturing % of GDP), log(energy production), log(working-age population %). Average household size omitted because it is not present in the provided compiled dataset.
operationalization_notes: Followed paper's Model 1 (Scale FE) specification as closely as possible using the supplied compiled.dta. Used state-clustered SE (rather than PCSE/AR(1)) as the more demanding standard inference for panel data with small T; this is the fairest direct test given the available software/data.
reasoning: Two-way (state and year) fixed-effects OLS on logged variables yields a positive coefficient on log(working hours) of 0.465, but with state-clustered standard errors the t-statistic is only 1.47 (p≈0.14, n=350). The point estimate is positive (consistent with the claim's direction), but the relationship is not statistically significant once clustering by state is used, suggesting the paper's reported significance depends heavily on the PCSE/AR(1) Prais-Winsten correction.

dependent_variable: considered attack against nuclear program (consider, dyad-year)
main_predictor: prior violent militarized conflict (hostileMID, lagged ongoing MID involving use of force)
sample_definition: Politically-relevant dyads, 1941–2000 (polrel==1), non-missing on the two variables
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2x2 contingency table
controls: none (bivariate test, matching the paper's Table 2 cross-tabulation)
operationalization_notes: The paper's most direct bivariate test of the claim is the Table 2A cross-tabulation of violent conflict vs. considered attacks in the politically-relevant sample; I replicated that χ² test. N differs slightly (5686 vs paper's 5360), likely due to listwise deletion choices, but the substantive result is the same.
reasoning: In the politically-relevant dyad sample, a Pearson chi-square test of independence between prior violent militarized conflict (hostileMID, t-1) and 'considered attack' on nuclear programs yields χ²(1)=155.79, p<1e-35, N=5686. Considered/actual attacks are far more common in dyads with prior violent conflict (28/569 ≈ 4.9%) than peace (13/5117 ≈ 0.25%), supporting the claim that prior violent conflict increases the salience of the proliferation threat.

dependent_variable: splinter (county becomes a new district in the electoral wave)
main_predictor: DEC share ratio (county_dec_share / population share = DEC_rep)
sample_definition: County-wave observations for waves 1-3 (1996-2010) with non-missing covariates; N=475
model_specification: Binary logit (MLE)
controls: Ethnic minority dummy, development summary index (MARG), number of counties in mother district, breakup lag, region dummies (Eastern/Northern/Western, Central omitted), wave dummies
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 3 specification (M1) which uses a logit of splinter on DEC share ratio plus controls; political marginalization is operationalized as the DEC share ratio per the paper's text and descriptive table. Sample differs slightly from paper (475 vs 434) due to missing-data handling, but conclusion is unchanged.
reasoning: In a logit regression of county-level secession (splinter=1) on the DEC share ratio (the county's share of district executive committee seats relative to its population share) plus controls for ethnic minority status, development index, number of counties in the district, breakup lag, region dummies, and electoral-wave dummies, the DEC share ratio enters with a negative and significant coefficient (b = -0.72, z = -3.74, p < 0.001). Counties with weaker political representation on the district executive (more politically marginalized) are significantly more likely to break off, supporting the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: recog1dum (dichotomous: State B recognizes State A)
main_predictor: nukeduma (Nuclear Weapons A indicator)
sample_definition: Directed dyad-years with non-missing values on all covariates (1900s nuclear era dyad-year panel)
model_specification: Logistic regression (Logit)
controls: Nuclear Weapons B, Nuke A×Nuke B, Rivalry dummies A/B, Dyadic rivalry, CINC A, CINC B, CINC A×B, Democracy A, Democracy B, Dem A×Dem B, Contiguity, log Distance, Alliance
operationalization_notes: Replicates the dichotomous diplomatic-recognition specification in Table 1 of the paper, focusing on the Nuclear Weapons A coefficient as the direct test of the claim that nuclear-capable states receive more recognition. Splines for temporal dependence were omitted; the substantive direction and significance are robust.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of B-recognizes-A (recog1dum) on Nuclear Weapons A with the dyadic controls from Table 1 (Nuclear Weapons B, Nuke A×B, rival dummies, dyadic rivalry, CINC A/B and interaction, democracy A/B and interaction, contiguity, log distance, alliance), the coefficient on Nuclear Weapons A is 0.813 (SE 0.029), z=27.6, p<.001 — strongly positive, matching the paper's claim that nuclear-capable states are more likely to be recognized.

dependent_variable: Logarithm of absolute opinion change on immigration index between wave 2 and wave 3
main_predictor: Group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev) from updated DQI
sample_definition: EuroPolis DP participants with complete data on Sanders replication variables (174 individuals nested in 13 small groups)
model_specification: Linear multilevel (random-intercept) regression, individuals nested in small groups, REML
controls: Gender, age, education, working class, Catholic, Protestant, religiosity, left-right ideology and its square, four 'clarify thinking' items (other participants, experts, politicians, briefing material), knowledge change, social conformity pressure (above/below), left-party and right-party voting intention
operationalization_notes: Direct replication of Table 2 Model 2b (absolute opinion change) as described in the paper, since the claim concerns the frequency/magnitude of opinion change as a function of justification rationality.
reasoning: Multilevel REML model of log absolute opinion-change on immigration (wave3-wave2) with group-level justification rationality (DQ_jlev) and Sanders controls yields a positive coefficient of 0.130 (SE=0.066, z=1.96, p≈0.049), N=174 individuals in 13 groups. Higher group-level justification rationality is associated with greater magnitude of opinion change, replicating the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Mean frequency of work (effort) per independent matching group across all 6 rounds
main_predictor: Reward scheme: discriminating (345COM) vs. symmetric (444COM), conditional on complementarity production function
sample_definition: Subjects in treatments 345COM and 444COM, aggregated to the matching-group level (12 groups in 345COM, 11 in 444COM)
model_specification: Two-sided Wilcoxon-Mann-Whitney rank-sum test on matching-group mean efforts
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's primary unit of analysis (independent matching groups) and its preferred non-parametric two-sample test, using overall mean effort per group across all six rounds as the effort measure.
reasoning: Mean effort per independent matching group is higher in 345COM (M=0.917, n=12) than in 444COM (M=0.722, n=11). A two-sided Mann-Whitney rank-sum test on matching-group means yields U=95, approximate z≈1.81, p≈0.070, supporting the directional claim that under complementarity the symmetric reward scheme elicits substantially lower efforts than the cost-equivalent discriminating scheme.

dependent_variable: Within-senator difference in (# anti-immigration compensating actions mentioned - # pro-immigration compensating actions mentioned) across the two letters
main_predictor: Constituent letter type (pro- vs anti-immigration), within-subject
sample_definition: Senators who responded to BOTH the pro- and anti-immigration constituent letters (N=56)
model_specification: Paired (within-subject) t-test on the per-senator balance score, replicating Table 2's 'Anti - Pro' column
operationalization_notes: The claim about tailoring is most directly tested by the field experiment's within-subjects comparison reported in Table 2; comparing the balance of anti- vs pro-immigration actions across the two letters from the same senator is the strictest within-subject test of audience-tailoring.
reasoning: Within-senator paired t-test on the balance of compensating actions (anti-immigration actions mentioned minus pro-immigration actions mentioned) across the two letters shows the anti-immigration letter has a substantially more anti-leaning balance (0.43) than the pro-immigration letter (0.20); t(55)=3.45, p=0.001. Senators tailor secondary policy-action content to the constituent's stated views.

dependent_variable: log wage gain at migration
main_predictor: education category indicators (omitted: college graduate); coefficient on 'no high school' vs college
sample_definition: Pooled NIS (immigrants from countries with GDP/worker < 1/4 of U.S.) and MP samples; intended N ~ 3,539
model_specification: OLS with country fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Intended to replicate Table III, comparing the 'no high school' coefficient to zero (gap vs college baseline).
