sample_definition: All 320 participants with complete data on the 4 within-subject prospect rounds
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test on per-participant mean contributions in losses-and-gains rounds vs. mean contributions in no-variance & gains-only rounds (equivalent to within-subject contrast / repeated-measures F = t^2)
operationalization_notes: Paper tests H2 with a repeated-measures contrast across the within-subject outcome-prospect levels. Each participant in the dataset played four rounds with bonuses (0,1200), (200,1000), (400,800), and 600. Following the paper's classification (required contribution = 75; bonus distributions whose minimum/4 < 75 contain loss prospects), (0,1200) and (200,1000) are losses-and-gains, (400,800) is gains-only, and 600 is no variance. I averaged each participant's contributions within each category and ran a paired t-test.
reasoning: Paired t-test comparing each participant's mean contribution in the two losses-and-gains rounds ((0,1200) and (200,1000)) vs. the no-variance (600) and gains-only ((400,800)) rounds yielded t(319) = -0.58, p = .56. Mean contributions were nearly identical (losses-and-gains M = 73.20 vs. no-variance/gains-only M = 73.75), so the claimed reduction in contributions under loss prospects did not replicate in this dataset.

dependent_variable: HP-filtered cyclical component of interstate (intercounty) migration rate (HPmigration)
main_predictor: Cross-state standard deviation of state employment gaps (StateEmploymentGapSD)
sample_definition: Annual U.S. observations 1948-2009 from MigrationRateMerged.dta (54 non-missing years; CPS migration data are missing for 1972-75 and 1977-80)
model_specification: OLS time-series regression: HPmigration_t = a + b*(HP-filtered national employment gap_t) + c*(StateEmploymentGapSD_t) + e_t
controls: HP-filtered national employment gap (aggregate business-cycle measure)
operationalization_notes: Mirrors Table 1 col. 2 of the paper (Saks-Wozniak style): aggregate migration regressed on a national cyclical indicator and a cross-state dispersion measure, employment-gap version, 1948-2009 sample. The t-statistic on the dispersion term is the test of the claim.
reasoning: Regressing HP-filtered (cyclical) interstate migration on the HP-filtered national log-employment gap and the cross-state standard deviation of state employment gaps over 1948-2009 yields a coefficient on dispersion of 0.91 with SE 1.27 (t = 0.72, p = 0.48, n = 54). The dispersion measure is statistically indistinguishable from zero, matching the paper's conclusion that geographic dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to aggregate migration.

dependent_variable: Mean response latency (s) to indicate the first emotion had disappeared, on the angry-to-happy transition
main_predictor: Target age (old vs. young) — within-subjects, restricted to White targets
sample_definition: All 60 participants in the reaction-time file; trials with latency >17 s (movie length) excluded as impossible/no-response; 57 had usable data in both old- and young-White angry-to-happy cells
model_specification: Paired-samples (within-subject) t-test on subject-mean latencies, old-White vs. young-White, angry-to-happy transition
operationalization_notes: The claim couples 'anger lasting longer' and 'anger appearing sooner' on old vs. young White faces. I chose the angry-to-happy transition because its offset-latency directly indexes how long anger lingers — the clearest single quantitative operationalization of 'lasting longer.' Sample restricted to White targets per the claim. Latencies above the 17-s movie duration treated as missing.
reasoning: Paired-samples t-test on White-face trials in the angry-to-happy transition (the offset measure capturing 'anger lasting longer') showed participants judged anger as persisting significantly longer on old White faces (M=11.76 s) than on young White faces (M=10.48 s), t(56)=5.07, p<.001, d=0.67. The other anger transitions for White faces also showed the same pattern (e.g., neutral-to-angry: t(55)=-4.93, p<.001, anger appearing sooner on old), consistent with the original study.

dependent_variable: Not adhering to social distancing (keep_distance < 5 on 7-pt agreement scale = 1, else 0)
main_predictor: Male (sex==0)
sample_definition: All respondents in replication data with non-missing sex, keep_distance, and covariates (n=3264 after listwise deletion).
model_specification: Binary logistic regression of 'not adhering to social distancing' on male, with controls.
controls: Age (continuous), unmarried, education, household income, smoking habit, Big Five traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness).
operationalization_notes: Paper's Table 4 uses a logit of 'not conducting social distancing' on male plus demographic, lifestyle, and personality controls. The available replication dataset (April/May 2020 follow-up rounds, N=3892) differs from the paper's March 2020 survey (N=11,342) and uses a 7-pt scale instead of 5-pt, so social distancing was dichotomized at <5 (below 'agree a little') to mirror the paper's 'not following' construction. Covariates approximate those in Table 4.
reasoning: In a multivariate logit predicting 'not adhering to social distancing' (keep_distance < 5 on 7-pt scale), the coefficient on male was +0.864 (z = 6.79, p < .001), corresponding to an odds ratio of ~2.37. Men are significantly more likely than women to NOT follow social distancing, i.e. lower likelihood of following it, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Criticality of part-time work as a future-employment characteristic (Prefs_1, 1-5 Likert)
main_predictor: Cluster membership (satisficer / free agent / maximizer) derived from 24 work-desire items
sample_definition: Respondents who self-reported age ≥40, were active job seekers (Seek=1, A40=1), finished the survey, and had at least one non-missing desire item (N=767 for clustering; same N with non-missing Prefs_1).
model_specification: Two-step cluster analysis (Ward's hierarchical linkage giving initial centroids, then K-means with k=3) on 24 desire items; one-way ANOVA of Prefs_1 by cluster.
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's stated procedure: Ward's method to choose/initialize three clusters, K-means for final assignment, then one-way ANOVA on Prefs_1 (the part-time characteristic). Missing desire values imputed with item means (simple alternative to the paper's NORM multiple-imputation, which is not feasible here). No cluster-label variable was present in the data.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's two-step Ward-then-K-means cluster analysis on the 24 desire items in the provided dataset yielded three clusters (n = 172/235/360). A one-way ANOVA on the criticality rating of part-time work (Prefs_1) across these clusters gave F(2, 764) = 0.03, p = .97. The cluster means on the part-time preference item were essentially identical (~2.74-2.77), so the claim that satisficers, free agents, and maximizers differ in their part-time work preference does not reproduce in these data.

dependent_variable: Death (fecha_def != '9999-99-99')
main_predictor: Sex (male = sexo==2 vs female)

model_specification: Multivariable logistic regression: death ~ male + age group (25-49 ref, 50-74, 75+) + diabetes + hypertension + obesity + COPD + CKD + immunosuppression + pneumonia + hospitalized + intubated + ICU
controls: age group, diabetes, hypertension, obesity, COPD, CKD, immunosuppression, pneumonia, hospitalization, intubation, ICU
operationalization_notes: Followed Table 4 of the paper (mortality model). Used Wald z for the male coefficient as the test statistic most directly tied to the claim.
reasoning: In a multivariable logistic regression of death on sex adjusting for age group, comorbidities, pneumonia, hospitalisation, intubation, and ICU admission among positive SARS-CoV-2 cases aged ≥25 in the original-paper sample, being male was associated with significantly higher mortality (β=0.451, z=8.86, p<0.001, OR≈1.57), replicating the paper's finding (reported OR=1.53).

dependent_variable: Perceived stress (T2)
main_predictor: Dispositional optimism (LOT-R, T1)

operationalization_notes: The claim is a bivariate directional statement; a Pearson correlation pooling both partners is the most direct test (paper's main APIM analysis embeds this same association). Non-independence of dyad members is not adjusted for in this simple test.
reasoning: Pooling both partners' data, optimism (LOT-R) correlated r = -0.56 with perceived stress, t(200) = -9.47, p < .001, indicating more optimistic individuals reported substantially lower stress, consistent with the paper's claim.

controls: Symbolic threat at T1 included as a simultaneous predictor (per paper's SEM)

reasoning: In a latent-variable SEM with realistic and symbolic threat (T1) jointly predicting latent negative affect (T2), realistic threat had a significant positive standardized path coefficient (z = 2.23, p = .026, N = 239), supporting the claim that T1 realistic threat is positively associated with negative affect over the following week.

dependent_variable: Cooperate (1 = attempted risky coordination, 0 = work alone)
main_predictor: Knowledge condition (private, secondary, tertiary, common)

operationalization_notes: The paper's key DV is the binary choice to attempt risky coordination; the predictor is the 4-level knowledge manipulation. A chi-square test is the natural omnibus test of differences across conditions described in the paper.
reasoning: A chi-square test of independence comparing the proportion choosing risky coordination (Cooperate=1) across the four knowledge conditions yields χ²(3, N=588)=27.70, p<.001. Cooperation rates rise monotonically from private (53%), secondary (57%), tertiary (66%), to common knowledge (80%), supporting the claim that common knowledge produced the most risky coordination.

dependent_variable: Intention to support the nonprofit (mean of ITS1_1, ITS2_1, ITS3_1)

controls: Fit and similarity main effects included in mediator and outcome models (no demographic controls).
operationalization_notes: The paper operationalizes the 'joint effect' of fit and similarity on intention to support as the indirect effect of the fit x similarity interaction via clarity of positioning (Sobel-tested). I reproduce that exact test in the replication data using composite scales as in the original measurement model.
reasoning: The Sobel test of the joint indirect effect of the fit x similarity interaction on intention to support the nonprofit via clarity of positioning (path a from OLS regression of COP on FITc*SIMc: a=.058, SE=.022; path b from OLS of ITS on COP controlling for FITc*SIMc: b=.348, SE=.040) yields indirect effect = .020, SE=.0079, z=2.55, p=.011. This replicates the original finding that fit and similarity jointly affect intention to support the nonprofit.

reasoning: Pearson correlation between the empathy composite (emp; items b1-b3) and the social distancing composite (sodi; items b7-b11) is r=.51, t(61)=4.68, p<.001, n=63. Empathy is positively and strongly associated with motivation for physical distancing, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Monthly arrest indicator (1 = arrested that month; 0 otherwise)
main_predictor: Group-mean-centered (within-individual) divorce indicator; reference status = married
sample_definition: Respondents who were ever married AND ever arrested between 1997 and 2009 (ages 12-28); person-month observations with non-missing marital and arrest data.
model_specification: Logistic regression with within-between (Mundlak) decomposition: time-varying single/married/separated/divorced indicators decomposed into group-mean (between) and group-mean-centered (within) components; cluster-robust standard errors clustered on person.
controls: Age (centered) and age-squared, monthly incarceration indicator, ever-incarcerated, male, and between-person means of single/separated/divorced.
operationalization_notes: Mirrors the paper's HLM specification (Table 3, Model 2) by decomposing time-varying relationship states into within- and between-person components. Used pooled logit with cluster-robust SEs as a feasible approximation to the multilevel Bernoulli model, since the paper's central inferential test is the within-individual coefficient on divorce.
reasoning: Within-individual logistic regression on the ever-married & ever-arrested subsample (774 persons, 116,577 person-months) yielded a positive coefficient for group-mean-centered divorce on monthly arrest of 0.425 (cluster-robust SE = 0.211, z = 2.02, p = .044). The effect is positive and statistically significant, replicating the paper's substantive finding that divorce raises the likelihood of arrest (paper reported coef = .418, SE = .093).

model_specification: Pearson chi-square test on a 2 (state) x 2 (autism / not-autism) contingency table; odds ratio = 0.95 (z = -6.82)
operationalization_notes: The paper compared each state's identification odds to California using logistic regression on count data. reasoning: A 2x2 chi-square comparing autism identification (autism count vs. remaining enrolled students) in Ohio vs. California yielded chi2(1)=46.49, p<.001, with an odds ratio of 0.95 (Ohio vs CA), indicating that students in Ohio were significantly less likely to be identified with autism than students in California, consistent with the paper.

dependent_variable: Group made the correct decision (group_jar == true_jar)

A chi-square test of independence between voting institution and group-correct decision yields chi2(2,N=352)=30.73, p<0.001. Far from being diminished, institutional differences are large and highly significant in this deliberation dataset, contradicting the claim.

dependent_variable: Group-level average market price in uniform-price auction (proxy for seller revenue, given near-full subscription)

Excluding bankrupt/dropout groups follows the original paper's exclusion logic.
reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of group-level average uniform auction prices against the BF-prescribed fixed price benchmark of 1.94 (the FIXED treatment's predetermined price) yields V=286.5, n=32, p=0.337 (one-sided, greater). Mean uniform price = 1.957, virtually identical to the fixed-price benchmark. The replication data do not support the original claim that uniform price auctions raise higher revenues than fixed price offerings.

reasoning: One-way ANOVA on perceived stress (PSS-10 mean) across three agreement-with-containment-measures groups (agreement, no agreement, no agreement at all) yielded F(2,1076)=17.99, p<.001. controls: Malice and Greed experimental condition dummies (vs. Control)

dependent_variable: Academic achievement composite (mean of X7RSCALK5 reading IRT scale and X7MSCALK5 math IRT scale)

operationalization_notes: The released dataset contains only 5th-grade wave (X7) achievement and teacher-reported social-emotional measures rather than the 3rd-grade child self-report SDQ variables specified in the paper, and lacks the OLDS-based ELL flag. I therefore operationalized the claim as a single bivariate correlation in the closest available ELL proxy subsample using the available achievement and social-emotional indicators, averaged across reading/math and externalizing/internalizing respectively.
reasoning: Among children from non-English home-language households (a proxy for ELL status, since the OLDS-based ELL flag used in the paper is not in this dataset), the Pearson correlation between teacher-reported social-emotional problems (mean of externalizing and internalizing, X7TCHEXT/X7TCHINT) and academic achievement (mean of IRT reading and math scale scores, X7RSCALK5/X7MSCALK5) is r = -0.256, t(2080) = -12.08, p ≈ 1.6e-32. Fewer social-emotional problems are linked to higher achievement, matching the paper's claim direction.

dependent_variable: Perceived societal good (mean of SocGood ratings across the four organizations: Artisan, Green, Food, MedTech)

operationalization_notes: The claim is the focal pairwise contrast from Study 3 between profit and non-profit motives on perceived societal good. Condition 3 was identified as For-Profit (lowest societal good) and condition 2 as Non-Profit based on means matching the paper's reported pattern (Non-Profit > For-Profit). The DV was averaged across the four scenarios as in the paper's combined analysis.
reasoning: An independent-samples t-test comparing perceived societal good (mean of the four SocGood items across scenarios) between the For-Profit condition (cond3, M=3.75, SD=0.58, n=123) and the Non-Profit condition (cond2, M=4.09, SD=0.52, n=121) yielded t(242)=4.80, p<.001. The For-Profit condition was rated significantly lower in societal good, reproducing the directional effect reported in Study 3.

dependent_variable: Sharing intention for each headline (6-point Likert, rescaled to 0-1)
main_predictor: Headline veracity (true real headline vs. false fake headline; within-subject)

model_specification: OLS regression of sharing intention on a true/false indicator, with cluster-robust standard errors clustered at the participant level (mixed-effects model with random participant intercepts gave essentially the same z = -1.04, p = 0.30)
operationalization_notes: The paper tests the within-treatment contrast of true vs. false headlines using a linear mixed model on headline-level sharing intentions (Figure S1 uses the [0,1]-rescaled continuous scale). I followed this operationalization, restricting to treatment-condition participants and regressing the [0,1]-rescaled sharing intention on the true-vs-false indicator with participant-cluster-robust SEs; df reported as number of participant clusters minus 1.
reasoning: In the treatment condition, mean sharing intention for true headlines (M ≈ 3.49 on 1-6 scale, 0.498 rescaled to 0-1) was not significantly higher than for false headlines (M ≈ 3.52, 0.504); in fact the point estimate was very slightly in the opposite direction (b = -0.006 on 0-1 scale, t ≈ -1.12, p = 0.27 using OLS with participant-cluster-robust SEs over 13,200 observations from 440 treatment-condition participants × 30 headlines). The data thus do not reproduce the paper's claim that sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines in the treatment condition.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth dummy = 1 if GDP per capita growth ≥ 2% in each of years t…t+4 (5 consecutive years), starting at the survey year

operationalization_notes: Operationalization mirrors Table 3 column (1) of the paper: pooled OLS with Polity2 as the only control. Impartiality values were taken from the paper's appendix table (since the original paper provides them as the coded indicator); sustained growth was constructed from the supplied World Bank GDP per capita growth series (gdp.dta) using the paper's 5-year/2% definition.
reasoning: In a pooled OLS linear-probability model regressing the sustained-growth dummy (≥2% GDP/capita growth for 5 consecutive years starting at the survey year) on log(Impartiality index) and Polity2 across the 64 country-survey observations from Afrobarometer waves 1-4 (20 SSA countries), the coefficient on log impartiality is small and negative (b=-0.025, SE=0.103, t=-0.245, df=61, p=0.81). This provides no statistical support for the paper's claim that more impartial governments are more likely to experience sustained growth; the effect is statistically indistinguishable from zero and the point estimate even has the opposite sign to the paper's Table 3, column 1.

dependent_variable: Mean evaluation score (average of 5 items) for the 4.5-star vs. 2.5-star toaster (within-subjects)

reasoning: In the abstract-sound condition (group 5: C→F# with reverberation, single-measure/low-segmentation), participants rated the 4.5-star (aggregated-positive) toaster (M=4.64, SD=1.47) significantly higher than the 2.5-star (individualized-positive) toaster (M=3.32, SD=1.18), paired t(19)=2.39, p=.027, supporting the claim that the abstract sound shifts weight toward aggregated information, though the effect in the data is smaller than reported in the paper.

dependent_variable: National affluence (GDP per capita, PPP, US$ 2000)
main_predictor: Imports from the South (totalimport, in $ billions)

operationalization_notes: Followed Model 4 in Table 2 (Y2 = national affluence). Used the replication file northsouth_NoNA.xlsx; only South-trade variables are available, so North-North trade controls from the published model are omitted.

This reproduces the paper's finding of a positive indirect effect of Southern imports on Northern affluence.

dependent_variable: Average difference score (Utilitarian - Symbolic rating) across the four symbolic products (college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards). Higher values = more utilitarian.

model_specification: Independent-samples t-test on the average symbolic-product difference score, comparing branded vs. unbranded.
operationalization_notes: The claim targets the symbolic-product half of the level x product-type interaction reported in Study 1B of the original paper (p. 351). The most direct test is a between-subjects comparison of the symbolic-product Util-Symbol difference score across branded vs. unbranded conditions, with branded conditions (Sets A and B) pooled as in the original paper.
reasoning: For the four symbolic product categories (T-shirts, flags, class rings, greeting cards), the average difference score (Util - Symbol) was significantly higher (less negative, i.e., less symbolic / more utilitarian) in the branded condition (M = -2.09) than in the unbranded category condition (M = -2.66), t(555) = -4.07, p < .001. This supports the original claim that branding shifts attitudes toward symbolic product categories to be less symbolic and more utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA

operationalization_notes: Only aggregated summary statistics are available; the SEM path from self-regulation to GPA with no other predictors reduces to the zero-order correlation (r=.30), tested via its t-statistic with df=N-2.
reasoning: Using the Jung et al. summary statistics (N=366), the correlation between academic self-regulation (academic self-discipline) and semester GPA is r=.30, yielding t(364)=6.00, p<.001. This positive, significant association supports the SEM claim that self-regulation predicts higher GPA.

dependent_variable: Intentions to share/disseminate COVID-19 conspiracy theories (NOT AVAILABLE in dataset)

dependent_variable: Proportion of 36 forced-choice trials in which the participant chose the high-fWHR (right-side) face as more aggressive

operationalization_notes: Codebook indicates each Q1–Q36 records left/right choice on the forced-choice aggression judgement; following the published paradigm (Figure 1, high-transform face on right), 'Right' responses are scored as choices of the high-fWHR face. This mirrors the headline test in the original Study 1 (proportion above chance via one-sample t).
reasoning: Across 288 quality-screened participants, the mean proportion of trials on which the higher fWHR (right-side high-transform) face was chosen as more aggressive was 0.534, significantly greater than the 0.5 chance level, t(287)=5.10, p<.001. This replicates the paper's finding that higher fWHR faces are perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: Predicted total number of cabs divided by the maximum observed serial number (analogue to prediction/t_past, which equates the across-subject differences in observed maxima)
main_predictor: Number of examples observed (values_seen: 1, 3, or 10) — within-subjects

model_specification: One-way repeated-measures ANOVA (AnovaRM) with values_seen as the within-subjects factor
controls: None beyond the within-subjects design; normalization by max_value accounts for between-subject differences in the sampled stimuli
operationalization_notes: The paper's original analysis used a one-way within-subjects ANOVA on the prediction with examples-seen as the factor; because in the replication dataset the observed maxima vary across subjects (random number generator), I normalized the prediction by the max observed serial number to mirror the paper's design in which max was fixed.
reasoning: A one-way within-subjects ANOVA on the prediction/maximum-observed ratio across the three observation-count levels (1, 3, 10) for the taxicab condition yielded F(2,1340)=39.19, p<.001. Mean ratios decreased monotonically from 2.19 (1 obs) to 1.36 (3 obs) to 1.16 (10 obs), consistent with the claim that smaller predictions (relative to what has been observed) are made as more observations are provided.

dependent_variable: Social undermining (willingness to be matched; lower = more undermining), 1–7
main_predictor: TSC × ConditionCompetition interaction (TSC: 0=favorable/stable, 1=unfavorable/upward; Competition: 0=low, 1=high)
sample_definition: All retained participants from the experimental study, both within-subject TSC observations per participant (N=574 participants, 1148 observations)
model_specification: Linear mixed-effects model with random intercept by participant: Undermin ~ TSC*ConditionCompetition + (1|id)
operationalization_notes: TSC was manipulated within-subjects and Competition between-subjects; the directly relevant test of the moderation claim is the TSC × Competition interaction in a mixed model accounting for repeated measures within participant.
reasoning: Mixed-effects model on the experimental data (574 participants × 2 within-subject TSC conditions = 1148 obs) yielded a significant TSC × Competition interaction on the willingness-to-be-matched outcome (b = -0.578, z = -3.38, p < .001). Because lower scores indicate higher undermining, the negative interaction means the upward (unfavorable) TSC manipulation produced more undermining under high than low competition, supporting the moderation claim.

dependent_variable: Mean COVID-19-specific conspiracy belief endorsement (6 SpecCTs items, with reverse-coded items)

controls: None — the dataset does not include age, gender, education, lack of control, or trust variables
operationalization_notes: The provided dataset contains only 6 conspiracy items plus 2 COVID worry/threat items; it lacks the anxiety, lack-of-control, trust, and demographic variables used in the paper's path model. The most directly related testable piece of the claim is whether worry/threat (closest proxies for anxiety and risk perception) predict COVID conspiracy belief endorsement.
reasoning: Regressing COVID-19 conspiracy belief endorsement on the only available emotional-response proxies in the dataset (COVID1 = worry about spread, COVID3 = felt threat) yielded F(2,803)=32.83, p<.001, but the simple correlations were NEGATIVE (r=-.24 for worry, r=-.09 for threat). Thus, contrary to the claim that anxiety/risk perception predicts higher conspiracy belief, in this dataset higher COVID worry/threat is associated with LOWER endorsement of COVID conspiracy beliefs.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) on central-face trials

The direction is actually slightly opposite (angry marginally slower) and far from significance, so the claim that GAD participants were faster on angry than neutral trials does not reproduce in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Brand personality (sophistication) difference score: mean of post-scenario items (Q5_1–Q5_4) minus mean of pre-scenario items (Q2_1–Q2_4)

The pattern predicted by H2a/H2b — that the moderating effect of pseudorelevant information would emerge under high but not low outcome dependency — does not replicate in this Stage-2 dataset.

dependent_variable: Adoption of >=1 avoidance behavior (avoiding social events, public transport, eating out, grocery shopping, or staying home from work; from 'prep')

dependent_variable: Situational attributions scale (bidirectional version, Sit_AttB)

dependent_variable: Mean of four greedy behavioral inclination items (behav_incl_1-4)
main_predictor: Dispositional Greed Scale (DGS)

dependent_variable: Indicator = 1 if respondent chose the ambiguous candidate (derived from Q3 and the RND_01 presentation order)
main_predictor: Risk aversion (Q4 = 'prefer avoiding risks' = 1, else 0)
sample_definition: All respondents with valid (non-DK/refused) responses on Q1, Q2, Q3, Q4, RND_01, DOV_PRECISE, DOV_AMBIGUOUS (N = 2684)
model_specification: Probit: chose_ambiguous ~ risk_aversion + voter_certainty + distance_differential
controls: Voter certainty about own position and distance differential between voter and precise vs. ambiguous-midpoint position
operationalization_notes: Replicates the Table 3a unbranded-condition probit. Distance differential computed using DOV_PRECISE as precise candidate position and DOV_AMBIGUOUS code (2..6) as the midpoint of the ambiguous interval, matching the experimental design described in the codebook.
reasoning: In a probit regression mirroring the paper's Table 3a (unbranded condition) — DV = chose ambiguous candidate; predictors = risk aversion (Q4 = avoid risks), voter certainty (Q2 ≤ 2), and distance differential (|v−p| − |v−μ|) — the coefficient on risk aversion was −0.020 (SE 0.053, z = −0.38, p = .70). dependent_variable: ICE BofA US High-Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread (end-of-quarter, %), as a proxy for losses suffered by leveraged credit investors
main_predictor: Net percent of domestic banks tightening C&I lending standards to Large and Medium firms (SLOOS), as a proxy for negative fundamental / funding shocks

model_specification: OLS univariate time-series regression in levels: HYSpread_t = a + b*CreditStandards_t + e_t
operationalization_notes: The replication folder only contained the HY OAS and SLOOS series (the CDX HY spread file referenced in the data dictionary was not provided), so I could not compute the CDS-bond basis used in the paper's Table 2. reasoning: Regressing the quarterly end-of-period ICE BofA US High-Yield OAS (a proxy for losses borne by leveraged credit investors) on the SLOOS net-percent tightening of C&I credit standards (a proxy for negative fundamental/funding shocks) over 2010Q1-2020Q3 yields a positive but statistically insignificant slope (b=0.021, t=1.06, n=42, p=0.29). The directional sign is consistent with the claim (tighter standards -> wider HY spreads / losses for leveraged agents) but the relationship is not statistically detectable in the post-crisis sample provided.

dependent_variable: Intergroup Contact Scale with older workers (ICS_olderworkers)
main_predictor: WICS total score (mean of the five subscale means)

reasoning: Pooled OLS regression of standardized log search volume for panic buying (mean of 'panicbuying' and 'stockpile' Google Trends scores) on standardized log COVID-19 prevalence, with country fixed effects across the four claim-relevant countries (US, UK, Canada, Australia) from first confirmed case to 24 March 2020, yields b = 0.683, t(230) = 14.17, p < .001. This strong positive association supports the original claim that COVID-19 prevalence predicts panic-buying-related searches.

dependent_variable: Procedural justice (mean of pj1-pj7)

dependent_variable: PSS-10 mean perceived stress score (pss10_avg)

dependent_variable: Trust choice in the trust game (1 = Option L/trust, 0 = Option R/distrust)

dependent_variable: Desirability index = mean of S1_likely, S1_quality, S1_purchase (7-pt)

reasoning: Regressing the 3-item desirability index on contrast-coded clarity condition (1=clear, -1=conflicted), distribution (1=bimodal, -1=unimodal), and their interaction yielded a significant clarity x distribution interaction, b=-0.146, t(372)=-2.30, p=.022. In the conflicted/low-SCC condition the bimodal movie was rated more desirable than the unimodal one (M=4.98 vs 4.33), while in the clear condition the two were similar (4.60 vs 4.53), replicating the directional claim.

dependent_variable: Set of three behavioral reactions: Revenge, Avoidance, Reconciliation (3-item composites each)

A multivariate regression of the three outcomes on the two emotions provides a single omnibus test of this independence claim; Wilks' lambda for Anger (controlling for Sympathy) is reported as the focal statistic.
reasoning: A multivariate multiple regression of the three behavioral outcomes (Revenge, Avoidance, Reconciliation) on the two emotions (Anger, Sympathy) showed that Anger had a highly significant independent multivariate relation to the behavioral reactions (Wilks' Λ = 0.817, F(3,1113) = 83.29, p < .001); Sympathy was also independently significant (F(3,1113) = 42.01). This supports the claim that emotional reactions have independent relations with revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation.

dependent_variable: Mean recognition index (proportion of hits minus false alarms, averaged across joy and anger words per subject)

Because joy and anger are the only within-subject levels, the main effect of TASGRP is identical to the between-subjects effect on the per-subject mean of joy and anger recognition, which I computed directly.
reasoning: In a between-subjects ANOVA on the mean recognition rate across Joy and Anger words with Depth, Music, and Alexithymia group as factors, the main effect of Alexithymia group was highly significant, F(1,1088)=126.62, p<.001. High alexithymia scorers recognized far fewer joy/anger words (M=18.9%) than low scorers (M=46.3%), reproducing the original directional claim.

dependent_variable: EVOLVED: human beings developed from earlier species of animals (1=true/correct, 0=false)

operationalization_notes: Latent classes were estimated with stepmix (n_components=3, mixed binary_nan + categorical_nan emissions, 10 random inits). Classes were named by their patterns on Bible literalism, religious strength and science knowledge. The test directly mirrors the paper's between-class mean comparison on EVOLVED.

Among these two classes, 22.4% of Post-Seculars (273/1217) vs 56.3% of Traditionals (933/1656) endorsed that humans developed from earlier animals; chi-square(1)=329.75, p<<.001, matching the paper's direction (post-secular < traditional).

dependent_variable: Trendiness composite (mean of V18 trendy, V19 modern, V20 urban; 7-point scales)

dependent_variable: Interpersonal obstacle-behavior association (mean RT across 4 LDT trials, IntAsscM)

The claim specifically targets the within-MC relationship between expectations and obstacle-behavior associations, so the most direct test is the simple slope of IntExp_c in the full interaction model.

The direction is consistent with the original claim (higher expectations -> faster RT -> stronger associations; lower expectations -> weaker associations), but the effect is far from significant; the overall interaction (F change) is also nonsignificant, F(2,300) = 1.17, p = .31.

reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of H0: s = x_l (libertarian principle) among DW-treatment dictators yields W+=8, z=-3.38, p<0.001 (n=27, 18 non-zero differences), strongly rejecting that dictators' shares equal recipients' monetary contribution share. Consistent with the paper's conclusion that the libertarian principle fails to account for DW behavior.

dependent_variable: Under-diagnosed (=1 if hypertensive but not previously diagnosed)

reasoning: In the poor-health subsample, a probit of being under-diagnosed on education and controls yields a negative, statistically significant coefficient on years of education (b=-0.0322, z=-2.51, p=0.012, N=756; marginal effect ≈ -0.0125). More educated respondents in poor health are less likely to be under-diagnosed, i.e., more likely to be diagnosed, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological (harm-rejecting) responses in personal moral dilemmas (RH_PMD)

dependent_variable: Mean perceived societal good across the four organizational scenarios (SocGood_Artis, SocGood_Green, SocGood_Food, SocGood_Medtech; 1=great harm to 5=great good)

Numerical responses were extracted from the labeled categorical values (e.g., 'great good 5' → 5).

The For-Profit condition (M≈3.75) had the lowest perceived societal good, lower than the Non-Profit (M≈4.09) and Unspecified (M≈4.31) conditions, matching the direction reported in the paper.

operationalization_notes: The provided 'test data' study 2 file contains uniform-random simulated responses (means ~3.5 across all items, statuses 'Survey Test'), so the only usable participant data is the Roozenbeek et al. direct replication of Pennycook et al. GDP series is the provided gdp.dta (WB downloaded 2020), which may differ from vintage used in original paper.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's baseline pooled-OLS specification (Table 3, col. 1) — regressing a binary indicator of sustained growth (GDP per-capita growth ≥2% in each of the survey year and the next four years, from World Bank data) on log(Impartiality index) and Polity2 with country-clustered SEs — yields a coefficient on log(Impartiality) of -0.026 with t = -0.26 (p = 0.80, N = 63). dependent_variable: Within-subject difference in mean evaluation: 4.5-star toaster eval minus 2.5-star toaster eval (each averaged over 5 items)
main_predictor: Toaster type (aggregated-positive vs individualized-positive), within subjects, in the abstract-sound condition

model_specification: OLS with country fixed effects, five-year period dummies (1970-74 baseline), unemployment control, and country-clustered robust standard errors (FE-GLS in original)
controls: Country fixed effects, 5-year period dummies, unemployment rate; exports to the South included as second trade flow
operationalization_notes: Replication of paper's Model 4 (indirect effect: DV = national affluence) using the provided North-South trade panel (northsouth_NoNA.xlsx). Trade was expressed in billions of USD (raw available; population not provided so %GDP normalization could not be applied), but country FE absorb scale differences across countries. The sign and significance of imports from the South is the quantity of interest.
reasoning: In a two-way fixed-effects regression of national affluence (GDP per capita, $1000s, PPP) on imports from the South (in $billions), exports to the South, and unemployment for the 18 OECD countries 1970-2003, the coefficient on imports from the South is positive and highly significant (b=0.027, cluster-robust t=4.53, p<.001), consistent with the paper's claim that North-South imports raise Northern affluence (Model 4 in Table 2).

dependent_variable: Mean within-subject difference score (Util rating minus Symbol rating) across the four symbolic products
main_predictor: Branding condition (branded [Cond 3 or 4] vs. unbranded/category [Cond 1 or 2])
sample_definition: All participants across the 10 replication datasets who passed both attention checks (Attention1=7, Attention2=1) and the prior-participation screen (screenQ=2); N=557
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test comparing branded vs. unbranded mean symbolic-product difference scores
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the simple effect of branding on symbolic-category products (p. 351, Study 1b). The most direct test is a between-subjects comparison of the symbolic-product Util-Symbol difference score (higher = more utilitarian) between branded and unbranded conditions. Brand Set A and Brand Set B were pooled, mirroring the paper's collapsing across brand sets.
reasoning: For symbolic product categories (T-shirts, Flags, Class Rings, Greeting Cards), the mean Util-minus-Symbol difference score was significantly higher (less negative; more utilitarian, less symbolic) in the branded conditions (M = -2.09) than in the unbranded/category condition (M = -2.66), t(555) = 4.07, p < .001. This replicates the directional effect reported in the paper.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic self-regulation (academic self-discipline scale serving as SR indicator per Jung et al.)
sample_definition: Aggregate correlation/SD/mean data from Jung et al. (2017), N=366 college students
model_specification: OLS regression on standardized variables derived from the published correlation matrix (equivalent to a just-identified SEM path model) with GPA regressed on SR and SD simultaneously
operationalization_notes: The dataset is a summary correlation matrix used for replicating Zimmerman & Kitsantas (2014) via Jung et al. (2017); per the README, SR corresponds to 'academic self-discipline' and SD to the 'self-discipline facet'. The SEM path of interest reduces to a multiple regression of GPA on SR with SD as covariate.
