dependent_variable: Trust (binary: 1 = chose trust option in trust game, 0 = chose distrust option)
main_predictor: Interaction of Honesty-Humility (mean-centered) × Condition (0 = certainty, 1 = uncertainty)
sample_definition: All participants with valid responses on the DV, Condition, and all 10 HEXACO Honesty-Humility items (N = 844; 1 case excluded due to missing DV)
model_specification: Logistic regression: Trust ~ mean-centered Honesty-Humility + Condition + HH × Condition interaction
controls: Honesty-Humility main effect and Condition main effect included in the model; no additional covariates
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's Study 2 analytic approach, which used logistic regression with the binary trust decision as DV, mean-centered HH, experimental condition, and their interaction. HH was computed from 10 HEXACO-60 items (6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60) with reverse scoring for negatively-keyed items (12, 24, 30, 42, 48, 60; scored as 7 minus raw response). The trust game structure matches Study 2 (binary choice between Option L/trust and Option R/distrust).
reasoning: A logistic regression predicting trust (binary: Option L = trust vs Option R = distrust) from mean-centered Honesty-Humility, Condition (0 = certainty/control, 1 = uncertainty), and their interaction yielded a non-significant HH × Condition interaction (B = -0.088, SE = 0.150, z = -0.587, p = 0.557). While the interaction coefficient is in the predicted negative direction (self-uncertainty reducing trust more for high-HH individuals), the effect is small and far from statistically significant, failing to replicate the original Study 2 finding (B = -0.82, p < .01).

dependent_variable: Desirability index (average of likelihood to see, quality rating, and purchase likelihood; 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Interaction of self-concept clarity condition (clear vs. conflicted) × distribution type (bimodal vs. unimodal), contrast-coded
sample_definition: All usable participants from the SCORE 2.0 dataset (Exclusion = 0), which applied preregistered exclusion criteria including non-compliance with the manipulation by both independent raters, inability to see rating distributions, missing data, and test units
model_specification: OLS regression with contrast-coded predictors: clarity (1=clear, -1=conflicted), experimental (1=bimodal, -1=unimodal), and their interaction term
controls: Main effects of clarity and experimental condition (no additional covariates)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's analysis for Study 2B, I used the desirability index (average of three 7-point items) as the outcome and tested the clarity × distribution interaction as the key test of the claim. The contrast coding matches the paper's specification. The usable data sheet applies preregistered exclusion criteria.
reasoning: The interaction between self-concept clarity condition and distribution type was significant (t(372) = -2.30, p = .022), indicating that the effect of bimodal (vs. unimodal) rating distributions on product desirability is stronger when self-concept clarity is low. In the conflicted condition, bimodal products were rated more desirable (M = 4.98) than unimodal products (M = 4.33), whereas in the clear condition, there was little difference (M = 4.60 vs. M = 4.53). This supports the claim that people find products with bimodal rating distributions more desirable when they experience temporary low self-concept clarity.

dependent_variable: Anger and Sympathy (multivariate composite)
main_predictor: Experimental condition (malice vs. greed vs. control)
sample_definition: All participants who passed the comprehension check (passcomprehension=1), yielding n=1071 across three experimental conditions
model_specification: One-way MANOVA (Wilks' lambda) testing the multivariate effect of motive condition on anger and sympathy simultaneously
operationalization_notes: The claim asserts a mediation chain (motives → emotions → behaviors). The MANOVA tests the most critical first link: whether motive attributions shape emotional reactions. Composite scores for anger (mean of an1-an3) and sympathy (mean of sy1-sy3) were used as DVs, following the paper's measurement model. The malice/greed dummy codes served as the experimental manipulation following the paper's lab study design.
reasoning: A one-way MANOVA tested whether experimental conditions (malice, greed, control) shaped emotional reactions (anger, sympathy), which is the critical first link in the claimed mediation chain (motives → emotions → behaviors). The effect was non-significant, F(4, 2134) = 0.88, p = .475. While anger and sympathy significantly predicted revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation (supporting the emotion→behavior link), the motive→emotion link was not supported, and bootstrap mediation analyses confirmed non-significant indirect effects of motives on behaviors through emotions. The manipulation also failed: the greed condition was perceived as more malicious (M=4.33) than the malice condition (M=4.16) on the cruelty manipulation check.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 misperceptions (MisperpSc: mean of 21 misperception items)
main_predictor: Cognitive sophistication composite (CogSophSc: mean of z-scored CRT, science knowledge, numeracy, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity)
sample_definition: Participants with complete data on cognitive sophistication measures (filter_$ = 1), who passed at least 2 of 3 attention checks (N=87, U.S. sample)
model_specification: Pearson correlation / simple linear regression of MisperpSc on CogSophSc
controls: None (zero-order correlation, following the paper's Table 1 approach)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, cognitive sophistication was computed as the mean of 4 z-scored component measures (analytic thinking via CRT, numeracy, science knowledge, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity). The zero-order correlation was used as the primary test of the directional claim, consistent with how the paper presents this result in Table 1.
reasoning: Cognitive sophistication was a significant negative predictor of COVID-19 misperceptions (r = -0.40, t(85) = -4.05, p < .001), consistent with the paper's claim that higher cognitive sophistication predicts fewer COVID-19 misperceptions.

dependent_variable: Average recognition rate for joy and anger words (JOY% + ANG%)/2, where recognition rate = (hits - false alarms)/8 truncated at 0
main_predictor: Alexithymia group (Low vs High based on median split of TAS-20; ≤64 = Low, >64 = High)
sample_definition: All 1096 participants in the dataset with complete data on TAS-20, recognition measures, and condition assignments
model_specification: Between-subjects ANOVA: Avg_recognition ~ Depth × Music × Alexithymia (equivalent to the between-subjects main effect of alexithymia in the paper's 2×2×2×2 mixed ANOVA)
controls: Depth of processing (Deep vs Shallow) and Music condition (Happy vs Angry) included as between-subjects factors in the ANOVA model
operationalization_notes: The paper reported the main effect of alexithymia from a 2(LoP)×2(Music)×2(Alex)×2(WordType) mixed ANOVA on recognition rates. For a between-subjects effect (alexithymia), averaging across the within-subjects factor (WordType) and running a between-subjects ANOVA yields the same F-statistic. The recognition index is (hits-false alarms)/8, truncated at 0 as provided in the dataset (JOY% and ANG% columns).
reasoning: The main effect of alexithymia was highly significant, F(1, 1088) = 305.83, p < 0.001, with high alexithymia scorers recognizing fewer joy and anger words (M = 0.189) compared to low alexithymia scorers (M = 0.463). This replicates the original study's finding of F(1, 99) = 3.98, p < .05, confirming the claim that high alexithymia scorers recognize fewer anger words and joy words.

dependent_variable: Trendiness index (average of trendy, modern, and urban ratings, each 1-7)
main_predictor: Table surface condition (glass vs. wood)
sample_definition: All 69 participants in the replication dataset, all of whom received the interdependent self-view prime (based on V11 prompt content asking about events with family/friends); 34 in the glass table condition and 35 in the wood table condition
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing trendiness index between glass and wood table conditions
operationalization_notes: The dataset lacks an explicit self-view condition variable. The V11 writing prompt response text and codebook description indicate all participants received the interdependent self-view prime (writing about events with family/friends). The trendiness index was constructed following the paper's approach (averaging trendy, modern, and urban items). Since all participants appear to be interdependents, the simple effect of table type on trendiness directly tests the claim.
reasoning: The claim predicts interdependents will evaluate a neutral product as more trendy on a glass table (M=5.10) than a wood table (M=5.47), but the data shows the opposite pattern. An independent samples t-test on the trendiness index (average of trendy, modern, urban items) found no significant difference, t(67) = -1.31, p = .19, with the mean difference in the direction opposite to the predicted assimilation effect (Cohen's d = -0.32).

dependent_variable: moral_accept (binary: 1 = not morally acceptable, 2 = morally acceptable/utilitarian response to conflict dilemma)
main_predictor: salience condition (death vs. pain)
sample_definition: All 131 participants who completed the survey, with no exclusions based on attention or manipulation checks
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2×2 contingency table
operationalization_notes: The paper's key claim is that mortality salience reduces utilitarian responses on conflict moral dilemmas. moral_accept was identified as the conflict scenario based on its moderate utilitarian rate (~78%) compared to moral_accept1 (~95%), which aligns with the paper's pattern of conflict vs. no-conflict dilemmas. A utilitarian response was coded as moral_accept=2 (morally acceptable). The chi-square test directly tests whether the distribution of utilitarian vs. non-utilitarian responses differs by salience condition.
reasoning: The chi-square test of independence on the conflict moral dilemma (moral_accept) by salience condition (death vs. pain) yielded χ²(1) = 1.32, p = .25. Contrary to the paper's prediction that thinking about death makes people less utilitarian, the death condition actually had a higher utilitarian response rate (82.3%, 51/62) than the pain condition (73.9%, 51/69), though this difference was not statistically significant.

dependent_variable: Interpersonal obstacle-behavior association strength (mean RT on sequential priming trials where interpersonal obstacle word primes interpersonal behavior word; higher RT = weaker association)
main_predictor: Interaction between mental contrasting condition (dummy: MC vs. reverse contrasting reference) and centered interpersonal expectations of success
sample_definition: All participants from the direct replication dataset with valid interpersonal association RTs (IntAssocObs=0), valid accessibility RTs (IntAccessObs=0), and no missing data on IntAssocM, IntAccessM, or IntExp. N=313 across 3 conditions: mental contrasting (n=118), reverse contrasting (n=86), irrelevant content control (n=109).
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression: Step 1 entered centered interpersonal expectations, interpersonal accessibility mean RT, and two condition dummies (MC vs RC reference, ICC vs RC reference); Step 2 added two interaction terms (MC × centered expectations, ICC × centered expectations). F-change test assessed whether adding interactions improved the model.
controls: Accessibility of the interpersonal behavior (mean RT on trials with neutral prime and interpersonal behavior target), centered interpersonal expectations of success, condition dummy variables
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 analysis for the elaborated (interpersonal) concern, which was where the original effect was found. The paper's primary test was the F-change for the interaction terms in hierarchical regression, which directly tests whether mental contrasting produces expectancy-dependent obstacle-behavior associations. The claim about low expectations leading to weak associations requires a significant interaction as a prerequisite.
reasoning: The hierarchical regression F-change test for the Condition × Expectations interaction on interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations was non-significant, F(2, 306) = 0.81, p = .45, with a trivial R² change of 0.2% (vs. 9% in the original study). The specific MC × Expectations interaction was also non-significant, t(306) = -0.42, p = .68 (original: t(90) = 2.45, p = .02). While the direction was consistent with the prediction (negative coefficient, indicating higher expectations → stronger associations in MC), the effect was negligible (f² = 0.005). The replication data does not support the claim that mental contrasting paired with low expectations leads to weak obstacle-behavior associations.

dependent_variable: Dictator's kept share of the surplus (1 - s, where s is the proportion given away)
main_predictor: Libertarian share (xl = dictator's monetary contribution / total surplus)
sample_definition: All 27 dictators in the DW treatment (piece_rate=150, partner_piece_rate=200) with non-missing s and x values
model_specification: One-sample t-test on (s_kept - xl), testing H0: mean difference = 0 vs H1: mean difference ≠ 0
operationalization_notes: The libertarian principle predicts that the dictator keeps a share proportional to their monetary contribution (xl). Under H0, the mean of (s_kept - xl) equals zero. The one-sample t-test directly assesses whether observed behavior accords with the libertarian prediction. All dictators in the data are in the DW treatment, so no further subsetting was needed.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test on the difference between the dictator's kept share and the libertarian share (s_kept - xl) yields t(26) = 3.526, p = 0.0016. The mean difference is 0.121 (dictators keep 12.1 percentage points more than the libertarian share), which is significantly different from zero. This rejects the null that the libertarian principle accounts for observed behavior, supporting the paper's claim that in the DW treatment, the libertarian principle does not explain dictators' choices.

dependent_variable: underdiagnosed (1 = hypertensive but not diagnosed, 0 = diagnosed)
main_predictor: years of education
sample_definition: Hypertensive adults in poor general health from the IFLS 2007 survey
model_specification: Probit regression of underdiagnosis on education and controls
controls: log per capita expenditure, time preference, risk preference, distance to health center, sex (female indicator)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's split-sample approach from Table 0, I estimated separate probit models for respondents in poor vs. good general health. The claim is tested via the education coefficient in the poor health subsample, which should be negative (more education → less underdiagnosis → higher diagnosis probability). The same specification as the paper was used: education, log PCE, time preference, risk preference, distance to health center, and female indicator.
reasoning: In a probit model of underdiagnosis on the poor health subsample (n=756), the education coefficient is negative and significant (z = -2.485, p = 0.013), indicating that more educated respondents have a higher probability of being diagnosed with hypertension. In contrast, the same model on the good health subsample (n=2375) yields a non-significant education effect (z = -1.534, p = 0.125). This supports the claim that education increases disease detection only conditional on being in poor health.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological judgments (proportion of 'Inappropriate' responses)
main_predictor: Group × Dilemma Type interaction (OBS vs CON × Personal vs Impersonal vs Non-moral)
sample_definition: All participants with complete data (filter_$=1 and non-missing RH_PMD, RH_NMD, RH_CMD), N=152 (OBS=75, CON=77)
model_specification: 2 (Group: between-subjects) × 3 (Dilemma Type: within-subjects) mixed ANOVA on proportion of deontological responses
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's analytic approach, the key test for the claim that social observation promotes deontological judgments 'especially for personal moral dilemmas' is the Group × Dilemma Type interaction in a mixed ANOVA. The interaction directly tests whether the effect of social observation differs across dilemma types. The paper reported a significant interaction (F = 4.779, p = .014) with a selective increase for personal dilemmas, but this was not replicated in the present dataset.
reasoning: The 2 (Group: OBS vs CON) × 3 (Dilemma Type: Personal, Impersonal, Non-moral) mixed ANOVA yielded a non-significant Group × Dilemma Type interaction, F(2, 300) = 0.122, p = 0.885, η²p = 0.0008. The simple effect of group on personal moral dilemmas was also non-significant, t(150) = 0.600, p = 0.549, Cohen's d = 0.097, with OBS (M = 0.642) only marginally higher than CON (M = 0.627). The data provides no evidence that social observation promoted deontological judgments, let alone especially for personal moral dilemmas.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (COVID-19 worry/concern, 1-5 Likert scale)
main_predictor: female (gender: 0=male, 1=female)
sample_definition: All respondents from Germany with binary gender identification (male/female), excluding 121 respondents with gender=3 (other).
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed)
operationalization_notes: Used mh_anxiety_1 as the measure of COVID-19 concern/worry, as it most directly captures the 'concern about COVID-19' construct in the available data. The paper discusses fear and worry about COVID-19 as the primary concern measure, and this variable maps onto that construct. Gender was coded as a binary variable (male/female) consistent with the claim's framing.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing COVID-19 concern (mh_anxiety_1) between women (M=3.0748, SD=1.1091) and men (M=2.8896, SD=1.1411) yielded t(10069)=8.25, p<.001, with a small effect size (Cohen's d=0.16). Women reported significantly higher concern about COVID-19 than men, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Percentage-point change in proportion of population not staying at home, averaged over March 19–28, 2020 minus the reference week of March 1–7, 2020 (negative values indicate more social distancing)
main_predictor: County-level share of votes for Trump in the 2016 election (trump_share)
sample_definition: All U.S. counties with complete data on mobility measures from BTS transportation data, voting data, ACS socioeconomic/demographic variables, and rurality (N = 3,114 counties)
model_specification: Cross-sectional OLS regression with state fixed effects (50 state dummy variables, dropping one reference state), controlling for county-level sociodemographic characteristics, industry employment, rurality, and age distribution
controls: Income per capita, percent male, percent Black, percent Hispanic, percent with college degree, percent employed in retail, percent employed in transportation, percent employed in health/education/social services, percent rural, age distribution (13 decade-of-life variables), state fixed effects
operationalization_notes: The original paper used proprietary Unacast cell-phone data measuring average distance traveled; this replication uses publicly available BTS data (Trips by Distance) with the proportion of population not staying at home as the mobility proxy. The social distancing measure is the percentage-point change in this proportion from a pre-COVID reference week (March 1–7, 2020) to the COVID period (March 19–28, 2020). The model specification follows the paper's methods: OLS with state fixed effects and the same set of covariates including age distribution, rurality, and industry employment shares.
reasoning: The OLS regression coefficient for Trump vote share on the percentage-point change in mobility (proportion not staying at home) was positive and statistically significant (b = 1.32, t = 3.50, p < 0.001, 95% CI: 0.58–2.06). Since the dependent variable is the change in mobility (COVID period minus reference period, where negative values indicate more social distancing), a positive coefficient means higher Trump vote share is associated with less reduction in mobility, i.e., reduced social distancing. This supports the paper's claim that greater Republican political orientation was associated with reduced social distancing among U.S. counties.

dependent_variable: Social distancing (composite mean of 4 items: avoiding social gatherings, avoiding groups of 10+, maintaining >6ft distance, following government guidelines)
main_predictor: Political conservatism (composite mean of 3 items: conservative views, Republican preference, reverse-scored liberal identification)
sample_definition: All 322 observations in the final dataset (filtered for attention check and other exclusions applied by original authors)
model_specification: Simple ordinary least squares regression of social distancing on conservatism (testing total effect)
controls: None (bivariate model testing total effect, consistent with the paper's first step in mediation analysis)
operationalization_notes: The paper first establishes the total effect of conservatism on social distancing before testing mediation. Following this approach, the simple regression/correlation directly tests the claim. The mediators (perceived health risk, media accuracy, well-informed) were not available in the dataset, so the full mediation model could not be replicated. The bivariate relationship is the most direct test of whether conservatism inversely predicts social distancing.
reasoning: A simple linear regression of social distancing on political conservatism yielded a significant negative coefficient (B = -0.135, t(320) = -3.26, p = .001), indicating that greater conservatism was associated with lower compliance with social distancing. The Pearson correlation was r = -.179. This supports the paper's claim that political conservatism inversely predicted compliance with social distancing behaviors aimed at preventing the spread of COVID-19.

dependent_variable: Academic achievement composite (standardized average of 8th-grade reading and math IRT scale scores: X7RSCALK5, X7MSCALK5)
main_predictor: Social-emotional problems composite (standardized average of teacher-reported externalizing X7TCHEXT, teacher-reported internalizing X7TCHINT, child-reported peer victimization PEERVIC, and child-reported social anxiety SOCIALANX)
sample_definition: ELL children identified by X12LANGST == 1 (language status = ELL) in the ECLS-K dataset, with valid data on the social-emotional problems composite and achievement composite (n = 2,339 of 2,941 ELL children)
model_specification: OLS multiple regression of achievement composite on social-emotional problems composite with race and gender controls
controls: Race (Asian/Pacific Islander dummy, Other race dummy; Hispanic as reference), Gender (female dummy)
operationalization_notes: Used ECLS-K round 7 (8th grade) variables as specified in the data dictionary, since the paper's round 5 (3rd grade) SDQ-I self-report variables were not available in the public-use dataset. Social-emotional problems composite combines both teacher-reported (externalizing, internalizing) and child-reported (peer victimization, social anxiety) measures, each standardized and averaged with at least 2 of 4 measures required. Achievement composite averages standardized reading and math IRT scores. This operationalization directly tests the claim that fewer social-emotional problems are linked to higher achievement among ELL children.
reasoning: Among ELL children, social-emotional problems were significantly negatively associated with academic achievement (b = -0.304, t(2334) = -11.86, p < .001), confirming the paper's claim that fewer social-emotional problems are linked to higher achievement scores. The partial correlation was r = -0.238. Although the data uses different measures (8th-grade teacher-reported and child-reported measures vs. the paper's 3rd-grade self-reported SDQ-I), the directional finding is consistent with the original study's SEM result (r = -.388, p < .001).

dependent_variable: Average perceived societal good across 4 scenarios (1 = great harm to 5 = great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition (For-Profit vs. Non-Profit vs. Unspecified)
sample_definition: All participants who completed the study (Finished = 1), had non-missing condition assignment, and provided ratings on all four societal good items (N = 364)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA with firm motive condition as the between-subjects factor and average societal good as the dependent variable
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 3 design, I averaged the societal good ratings across the four organizational scenarios (artisanal crafts, green tech, healthy food, medical tech) for each participant. The condition variable maps: 1 = Non-Profit, 2 = Unspecified, 3 = For-Profit, as confirmed by the data dictionary. The one-way ANOVA directly tests the main effect of firm motive on perceived societal good, which is the core of the claim on p. 680.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA found a significant main effect of firm motive on perceived societal good, F(2, 361) = 36.91, p < .001. The For-Profit condition (M = 3.75, SD = 0.58) showed substantially lower perceived societal good than both the Non-Profit (M = 4.31, SD = 0.43) and Unspecified (M = 4.09, SD = 0.53) conditions, confirming that labeling an organization as for-profit reduced perceptions of the societal good it accomplishes.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth (binary: GDP per capita growth >= 2% for >= 5 consecutive years starting from survey year)
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index (log of weighted share of respondents perceiving their ethnic group is never treated unfairly by government)
sample_definition: All country-year observations from Afrobarometer Rounds 1-4 (1999-2009) with valid impartiality and Polity2 data, excluding countries with only one observation (Burkina Faso, Liberia) for the fixed effects model. 20 countries, 62 observations.
model_specification: Linear probability model (OLS) with country fixed effects and year fixed effects (LSDV approach), standard errors clustered by country
controls: Polity2 (democracy index), country fixed effects, year fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's preferred specification (Table 3, column 7), I used a fixed effects linear probability model. The Impartiality index was computed from Afrobarometer survey responses (share reporting their group is 'never' treated unfairly, using sample weights). Sustained growth was coded as 1 if GDP per capita growth >= 2% for 5 consecutive years starting from the survey year, using World Bank GDP data (2020 vintage). Differences from the original study may arise from GDP data revisions between the 2015 and 2020 World Bank vintages, which affect which observations are coded as sustained growth.
reasoning: In a linear probability model with country and year fixed effects (N=62, 18 countries), the coefficient on Log Impartiality index is positive (0.20) but not statistically significant (t=0.84, p=0.40, clustered SE=0.24). The 95% CI [-0.26, 0.66] includes zero. The bivariate correlation between impartiality and sustained growth is actually negative (r=-0.10). These results do not provide significant evidence that government impartiality increases the likelihood of sustained growth, contrary to the original study's finding, likely due to GDP data revisions affecting the sustained growth coding.

dependent_variable: Toaster evaluation (mean of 5 rating items on 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Information type (4.5-star aggregated vs. 2.5-star individualized), within-subjects
sample_definition: Participants in the abstract sound condition (group 5) with filter = 1 (excluding 4 participants with technical/hearing problems from this group, leaving N = 16)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing toaster45_mean vs toaster25_mean within the abstract sound group
operationalization_notes: The claim specifically concerns the within-group comparison for the abstract sound condition, so the analysis is restricted to that group. The paper reports this as a paired comparison of evaluation means for the two toasters, tested within the abstract sound group. The filter variable was used to exclude participants with technical or hearing problems, consistent with the paper's exclusion criteria.
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing evaluations of the 4.5-star toaster (M = 5.14, SD = 0.72) vs. the 2.5-star toaster (M = 2.97, SD = 0.79) within the abstract sound group yielded t(15) = 7.86, p < .001, confirming that participants who listened to the abstract sound strongly favored the toaster with the positive aggregated information over the toaster with the positive individualized information.

dependent_variable: ln(GDP per capita)
main_predictor: ln(imports from the South)
sample_definition: 18 OECD countries, years 1970-2003, observations with non-missing values for GDP per capita, imports from the South, exports to the South, and unemployment
model_specification: Two-way fixed effects OLS regression with country dummy variables and 5-year period indicators, clustered standard errors by country
controls: ln(exports to the South), unemployment rate, country fixed effects (17 dummies), period indicators (6 dummies: 1975-79, 1980-84, 1985-89, 1990-94, 1995-99, 2000-03)
operationalization_notes: Log-transformed variables were used because total GDP (needed to express trade as percentage of GDP, as in the original paper) was not available in the dataset. The log-log specification captures the same directional relationship (elasticity of affluence with respect to imports). Period indicators follow the paper's 5-year grouping. The specification matches Model 4 of Table 2 in the original paper, which tests the effect of North-South trade on national affluence.
reasoning: A two-way fixed effects regression of ln(GDP per capita) on ln(imports from the South), controlling for ln(exports to the South), unemployment, country fixed effects, and period indicators (5-year groups), yields a positive and statistically significant coefficient on ln(imports from the South) of 0.153 (t = 2.96, p = 0.003 two-sided). This supports the paper's claim that imports from the South have a positive effect on national affluence in economically advanced countries.

dependent_variable: Average benefit-symbolism difference score across 4 symbolic products (college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards); difference score = Utilitarian rating - Symbolism rating per product
main_predictor: Level (category vs. brand); category = Cond 1 & 2 (unbranded products), brand = Cond 3 & 4 (branded products)
sample_definition: Participants who completed the survey (Finished=1, Progress=100), passed both attention checks (Attention1=7, Attention2=1), and had complete data for all 4 symbolic product ratings
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing average difference score for symbolic products between category-level and brand-level conditions
operationalization_notes: The claim specifically concerns symbolic product categories. Following the paper's Study 1b methodology, I computed a difference score (benefit rating minus symbolism rating) for each of the 4 symbolic products and averaged them per participant. Category-level participants (Cond 1 & 2) rated unbranded products; brand-level participants (Cond 3 & 4) rated branded products. The prediction is that branding increases the difference score (makes it less negative), indicating less symbolic and more utilitarian attitudes.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing the average benefit-symbolism difference score (Util - Symbol) for symbolic products between category-level (M = -2.63, SD = 1.62, n = 298) and brand-level (M = -2.12, SD = 1.68, n = 283) conditions showed that branding significantly increased the difference score, t(579) = 3.73, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.31. This indicates that branding makes attitudes toward symbolic product categories less negative on the difference score (i.e., less symbolic and more utilitarian), consistent with the original claim.

dependent_variable: GPA (Semester GPA)
main_predictor: AcadSR (Academic self-discipline, corresponding to self-regulation)
sample_definition: All 366 participants from Jung et al. (2017) replication dataset
model_specification: Path analysis (SEM with observed variables): GPA regressed on AcadSR and SDfacet, using the correlation matrix with n=366
operationalization_notes: The original paper used SEM with latent factors (SR and SD) each measured by multiple indicators. The Jung et al. replication data provides only single observed variables per construct, so a path analysis (SEM with observed variables) was conducted where GPA is regressed on both AcadSR (self-regulation) and SDfacet (self-discipline). This mirrors the paper's key SEM test of whether SR predicts GPA while controlling for SD. Standardized regression coefficients and t-tests were computed from the published correlation matrix.
reasoning: The path from self-regulation (AcadSR) to GPA was positive and statistically significant (standardized β = 0.336, t(363) = 4.855, p < .001), while the self-discipline facet did not significantly predict GPA (β = -0.052, p = .456). This replicates the original paper's SEM finding that SR predicts GPA but SD does not.

dependent_variable: Belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories (mean of 4 items, 0-10 scale)
main_predictor: National narcissism (mean of 3 items: Germany deserves special treatment; Not many people seem to fully understand the importance of Germany; I will never be satisfied until Germany gets the recognition it deserves; 0-10 scale)
sample_definition: German participants from Study 3 with complete data on national narcissism, national identification, and conspiracy theory belief items (N=1551 after excluding 24 participants with missing values on any key variable)
model_specification: OLS linear regression predicting conspiracy theory belief from national narcissism, controlling for national identification
controls: National identification (mean of 2 items: I identify as German; Being German is an important reflection of who I am; 0-10 scale)
operationalization_notes: The claim refers to sharing/disseminating conspiracy theories (H2), but the available data (Study 3) did not measure dissemination intentions. Conspiracy theory belief (H1) was used as the DV instead, as it is the closest available operationalization and mediates the sharing relationship in the paper's framework. Following the paper's method, national identification was included as a covariate to isolate the unique effect of national narcissism from general ingroup positivity.
reasoning: National narcissism was positively associated with belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories (B = 0.59, SE = 0.024, t(1548) = 24.44, p < .001), controlling for national identification. Although the original claim specifically addresses sharing (dissemination intentions), the available data (German sample from Study 3) only measures conspiracy theory belief, not sharing intentions. Belief is the mediator of the sharing relationship per the paper, and the strong positive association supports the same directional conclusion as the original study.

dependent_variable: Proportion of trials on which the face with higher fWHR/masculinity was chosen as more aggressive
main_predictor: Facial width-to-height ratio / masculinity transform (higher vs. lower cue value)
sample_definition: Study 1 participants who indicated their data should be used (Quality = 'Yes'), N = 139 out of 150 total
model_specification: One-sample t-test against chance level (0.50), following the paper's analytical approach
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's approach of a one-sample t-test against chance. Because fWHR and masculinity trials could not be separated in the available data (no trial-type mapping was provided), the proportion was computed across all 36 trials combining both fWHR and masculinity transforms. The side on which the higher-cue face appeared was inferred from the majority response per trial and responses were recoded so that 1 = chose the face with the higher cue value. Study 1 (male faces only) was used as the primary dataset.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test against chance (0.50) showed that participants chose the face with higher fWHR/masculinity as more aggressive significantly above chance levels (M = 0.571, SD = 0.095, t(138) = 8.79, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.75), supporting the claim that faces with increased fWHR are perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: money (bribe/transfer amount demanded by Public Official in BG or proposed by Participant B in UG)
main_predictor: briberygame (BG vs UG treatment frame)
sample_definition: BG Public Officials and UG Participant Bs with non-missing money values (full sample including zero demands), all waves
model_specification: Welch's independent samples t-test comparing mean bribe/transfer amounts between BG and UG treatments
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the average bribe amount being lower in BG than UG. I used the 'money' variable which captures the bribe demanded by public officials (BG) or amount proposed for self by participant B (UG), using the full sample including zeros. This aligns with the paper's Table 1 'Bribe/transfer amount (full sample)' row. Welch's t-test was chosen to account for the substantially unequal variances between groups (BG has much larger variance due to many zero demands).
reasoning: The average bribe/transfer amount in the Bribery Game (M = 0.578, SD = 0.725, n = 199) was significantly lower than in the Ultimatum Game (M = 0.910, SD = 0.481, n = 195), Welch's t(344.68) = -5.37, p < .001. This confirms the paper's claim that corruption is less extensive in the bribery frame, as the average bribe amount demanded by Public Officials in BG is substantially and significantly lower than the amount proposed by Participant Bs in the strategically identical UG.

dependent_variable: t/t_past ratio (estimated total number of cabs divided by the largest observed cab number)
main_predictor: Number of observations (1, 3, or 10 examples of cab serial numbers)
sample_definition: Taxicab condition participants with all 3 estimates, excluding those whose estimates were less than t_past (largest observed value) and outliers beyond 3 SD from the mean within each observation condition
model_specification: One-way within-subjects ANOVA with number of observations (1, 3, 10) as the repeated factor
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, responses were screened to exclude participants who gave estimates below t_past (not understanding the task) and outliers >3 SD from the mean. The dependent variable was the t/t_past ratio as described in the paper. The within-subjects ANOVA matches the original analysis approach reported for the taxicab scenario.
reasoning: A one-way within-subjects ANOVA on the taxicab condition (dependent variable: t/t_past ratio) revealed a highly significant effect of the number of observations, F(2, 1148) = 127.92, p < .001. The mean t/t_past ratios decreased monotonically from 1.85 (1 observation) to 1.33 (3 observations) to 1.15 (10 observations), confirming that smaller predictions were made as more observations were provided.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total (binary indicator of election fraud from last-digit test)
main_predictor: v.elday.pc.2 (squared election-day violence per capita)
sample_definition: Districts with complete data on all variables (375 out of 389 districts, excluding 14 with missing electrification or per-capita expenditure data)
model_specification: Logistic regression with quadratic violence term (election-day violence and its square), standard errors clustered at the regional command level (4 clusters)
controls: Number of closed polling stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure (1,000 AFN), distance from Kabul (km), elevation (m)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 1 Model 1 specification exactly. The inverted U-shape claim is tested via the significance and sign of the quadratic violence coefficient—the most direct test of whether the violence-fraud relationship is curvilinear with an inverted U shape.
reasoning: Replicating Model 1 (logit regression of last-digit fraud indicator on election-day violence and its square, with controls and standard errors clustered at the regional command level), the coefficient on the quadratic violence term is -13.748 (SE = 4.720, z = -2.91, p = 0.0036). The significantly negative quadratic term confirms the inverted U-shape: fraud increases with violence at low levels but decreases at high levels, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Social undermining (unwillingness to be matched with coworker, 1-7 scale, reverse-coded so lower = more undermining)
main_predictor: TSC × Competition interaction (temporal social comparison × organizational competition)
sample_definition: All 574 participants in the analytical dataset who passed exclusion criteria (doubt checks and previous participation check), with 2 observations each (one favorable TSC, one unfavorable TSC), totaling 1148 observations
model_specification: Linear mixed model with random intercept for participant: Undermin ~ TSC + Competition + TSC×Competition + (1|id), where TSC is within-subjects and Competition is between-subjects
controls: None (analytical dataset contains only id, ConditionCompetition, TSC, and Undermin; no additional covariates available)
operationalization_notes: The paper used multilevel ordered logistic regression (MEOLOGIT in Stata) for this within-between mixed design. I used a linear mixed model as the closest available alternative in Python, which properly accounts for the within-subject nesting via random intercepts. The 7-point undermining scale has sufficient granularity to be treated as approximately continuous. The key test is the TSC × Competition interaction coefficient, which directly tests whether the TSC-undermining relationship differs by competition level.
reasoning: The TSC × Competition interaction in the linear mixed model was significant (z = 3.38, p = .0007), indicating that the relationship between unfavorable temporal social comparison and social undermining (measured as unwillingness to be matched) was stronger under high competition (mean TSC effect = -0.70) than under low competition (mean TSC effect = -0.13). This supports the claim that competition moderates the TSC–undermining relationship, with a stronger positive relationship under high competition.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs (mean of 6 SpecCTs items)
main_predictor: COVID1 (worry about COVID spread, anxiety proxy) and COVID3 (sense of threat, risk perception proxy)
sample_definition: All 806 participants across three samples (Survey 1 USA, Survey 2a USA, Survey 2b UK); no exclusions
model_specification: OLS multiple regression with COVID1 and COVID3 as predictors of COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs
controls: none (no demographic or other control variables available in the dataset)
operationalization_notes: The original paper tested a full mediation model (risk perception/trust → anxiety/lack of control → conspiracy beliefs) using SEM with 12-item anxiety and lack of control scales, risk perception, trust in institutions, and demographics. The available replication dataset only contains 6 conspiracy belief items, 2 COVID perception items (COVID1: worry about spread; COVID3: sense of threat), and a sample identifier. COVID1 serves as the closest available proxy for anxiety, and COVID3 for risk perception/threat. The full mediation model cannot be tested due to missing variables (no trust measure, no separate anxiety/lack of control scales, no demographics).
reasoning: The claim predicts that anxiety and lack of control positively predict conspiracy beliefs. Using COVID1 (worry about COVID spread) as an anxiety proxy and COVID3 (sense of threat) as a risk/lack of control proxy, the overall model is significant (F(2,803)=32.83, p<.001), but the key anxiety proxy (COVID1) shows a strong negative association with conspiracy beliefs (b=-0.34, t(803)=-7.69, p<.001) — the opposite direction from the claim. People more worried about COVID spread actually endorse fewer conspiracy beliefs. While COVID3 becomes positively associated in the multiple regression (b=0.16), its zero-order correlation is negative (r=-.086), and this reversal is driven by a suppression effect from the highly correlated COVID1 (r=.75).

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) to peripheral target letters when the central face displayed an angry vs. neutral expression
main_predictor: Valence of central face (angry vs. neutral) within the GAD group
sample_definition: All participants classified as Group 1 (likely GAD) in the dataset (n = 63)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing mean RT for angry-face trials vs. neutral-face trials within the GAD group
operationalization_notes: The paper's reported analysis was a paired contrast of angry vs. neutral RTs within the GAD group using F(1,13)=9.35. The equivalent paired t-test was applied here to the full GAD group in the provided dataset. The dataset contains 63 GAD participants (vs. 14 in the original Experiment 1), with RTs in a different range (~486 ms vs. ~650-700 ms), but the task structure (central face with angry/happy/neutral expressions) matches the original design.
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing angry vs neutral face RTs within the GAD group yielded t(62) = 0.47, p = .64. The mean difference was 1.45 ms in the opposite direction (angry RTs were slightly slower, not faster, than neutral). The claim that GAD group RTs were faster for angry compared with neutral faces is not supported by this dataset.

dependent_variable: Brand personality impression difference scores (post-exposure sophistication minus pre-exposure sophistication, averaged across 4 items: upper class, good looking, charming, glamorous)
main_predictor: Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction (under high outcome dependency)

controls: None (ANOVA with two manipulated factors and their interaction)
operationalization_notes: The claim (H2a) specifically predicts that under high outcome dependency, consistent behavior has a more positive impact and inconsistent behavior has a more negative impact when pseudorelevant information is not disclosed vs. disclosed. The most direct test is the Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction within the high outcome dependency subsample. The DV was computed as the mean of Q5_1-Q5_4 (post) minus the mean of Q2_1-Q2_4 (pre), following the paper's reported method of using difference scores. Both Stage1 and Stage2 datasets were combined as they share the same experimental design and measures.
reasoning: The Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction on brand personality impression difference scores was not significant under high outcome dependency (F(1, 611) = 0.773, p = 0.380, partial η² = 0.001). While the cell means were directionally consistent with the hypothesis (consistent behavior without disclosure: M = 0.113 vs. with disclosure: M = -0.015; inconsistent behavior without disclosure: M = -0.700 vs. with disclosure: M = -0.660), the effects were negligible and the interaction failed to reach statistical significance.

dependent_variable: Adoption of ≥1 avoidance behavior (binary), coded from prep items: avoiding social events, avoiding public transport, eating out less, shopping for groceries less, staying home from work
main_predictor: Trust in government/authorities (dichotomized: high [5–7] vs low [1–4]) based on Govresponse_2: 'How much do you trust the country's politicians to deal effectively with the pandemic?' (1–7 scale)
sample_definition: Australian respondents from the Winton Centre COVID-19 Risk Perception study with non-missing data on all analysis variables (outcome, predictor, and all covariates)
model_specification: Multivariate logistic regression with avoidance behavior adoption as the binary outcome and trust in government/authorities as the main predictor, adjusted for demographics and worry
controls: Age (quota_age categories), gender (DemGen), minority/ethnicity status (ethnic_min), education (DemEdu), and worry about coronavirus (FinitePool_2, 1–7 scale)
operationalization_notes: The paper's trust measure (2 items on 5-point Likert about government decisions and authorities' handling) was operationalized using Govresponse_2 (trust in politicians on 1–7 scale), the closest available analog, dichotomized at the midpoint. Avoidance behaviors were identified from prep variable items that involve avoiding social contact or public spaces (items 4,5,6,8,10). The model specification mirrors the paper's Model 2, which adjusted for demographics and worry with P<0.25 in univariate analyses.
reasoning: In an adjusted logistic regression (n=660), high trust in government/authorities was not significantly associated with adoption of ≥1 avoidance behavior (aOR = 1.076, 95% CI: 0.673–1.719, z = 0.31, p = 0.76). While the direction is positive, consistent with the paper's claim, the effect is negligible and far from statistically significant, providing no evidence that greater trust in government predicts more avoidance behaviors in this dataset.

dependent_variable: CMMSRC (reverse-coded current money management stress; higher = more positive/less stress)
main_predictor: Group (1=Failure frame, 2=Success frame)
sample_definition: Participants with Include=1 (met exclusion criteria; excluded those who filled in same item for every response, left writing prompt blank, or used nonsense words)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed) comparing CMMSRC between success and failure frame groups
operationalization_notes: Used the pre-computed CMMSRC variable (reverse-coded CMMS scale average) as the DV, consistent with the paper's reporting of the reverse-scored scale. Filtered to included participants only based on the Include variable. The paper's original analysis used an ANOVA framework (F-test); the t-test is equivalent and more directly tied to the directional claim.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test on reverse-coded current money management stress (CMMSRC) showed that success frame participants (M=3.003, SD=1.096) reported significantly more positive (i.e., lower) current money management stress than failure frame participants (M=2.559, SD=0.858), t(260)=3.65, p=.0003. This supports the original study's claim that success framing reduces perceived money management stress relative to failure framing.

dependent_variable: Situational Attribution Style (Sit_AttB)
main_predictor: Dispositional Attributions (Disp_AttB)
sample_definition: Respondents in the bidirectional experimental condition (BiDummy == 1) with complete data on all analysis variables
model_specification: OLS linear regression with HC1 robust standard errors
controls: Perceived risk of victimization, perceived crime trend, news consumption, conservatism, religiosity, family victimization, education, female, white, age
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 3, I regressed situational attribution style on dispositional attributions and the same set of control variables, using only the bidirectional group. The paper argues that acquiescence bias in unidirectional batteries masks the true negative relationship between attribution styles; the bidirectional condition minimizes this bias, revealing the significant hydraulic relation.
reasoning: In the bidirectional group, OLS regression with robust standard errors shows that dispositional attributions significantly predict situational attributions (b = -0.223, robust SE = 0.045, t = -4.94, p < .001, N = 642). The negative coefficient indicates a hydraulic relation: higher dispositional attributions are associated with lower situational attributions, consistent with the paper's claim that this relationship is highly significant when items are formulated bidirectionally.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE (Perceived Stress Scale-10 total score)
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME (ordinal 1-6, higher = higher income)
sample_definition: N=2035 Italian adults (18 excluded due to missing gender/other gender), all with complete data on the regression variables
model_specification: OLS multiple linear regression with PSS-10 score as outcome and sociodemographic predictors (age, gender/male, education, household members, monthly income)
controls: Age, gender (male), education (years), number of family/household members
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, I used the first hierarchical regression step (sociodemographic model, Table 1 in the paper) as the most direct test of the income-stress association. The 18 participants with 'other' gender were excluded due to missing coding on the BE MALE variable, consistent with the paper's approach. Monthly income is coded as an ordinal variable (1-6) and treated as continuous in the regression, as in the original analysis.
reasoning: In a multiple linear regression predicting PSS-10 perceived stress scores from sociodemographic variables (age, gender, education, household members, monthly income), the coefficient for monthly income was negative and statistically significant (B = -0.463, t(2029) = -3.465, p = .00054), confirming that higher income is associated with lower levels of perceived stress. This replicates the paper's finding from their first hierarchical regression step.

dependent_variable: Behavioral inclination composite (mean of 4 items: food inclination, sex inclination, friend inclination, phone inclination)
main_predictor: DGS (Dispositional Greed Scale score)
sample_definition: Participants who completed the survey (Finished = 1), N = 492
model_specification: OLS regression: behavioral inclination composite = intercept + DGS + MVS
operationalization_notes: The paper tested the claim using partial correlations between DGS/MVS and each behavioral inclination separately. I operationalized 'greedy behavioral tendencies' as a composite (mean) of all four behavioral inclination items, and tested whether DGS predicts this composite after controlling for materialism (MVS). The t-test for the DGS coefficient in this regression directly tests whether DGS predicts behavioral tendencies over and above materialism.
reasoning: An OLS regression predicting the mean of four behavioral inclination items from DGS (controlling for MVS) showed that DGS was a significant predictor (b = 0.716, t(489) = 17.31, p < .001), indicating that the Dispositional Greed Scale predicts greedy behavioral tendencies over and above materialism. MVS was also significant but with a much smaller coefficient (b = 0.114, t = 2.17, p = .031). This strongly supports the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: chose ambiguous candidate (1=yes, 0=no)
main_predictor: risk aversion (1=prefer avoiding risks, 0=otherwise)
sample_definition: all respondents with valid responses to Q2 (certainty), Q3 (candidate choice), and Q4 (risk preference), excluding those who skipped or refused
model_specification: probit regression with robust standard errors
controls: voter certainty (1=extremely or very sure, 0=otherwise), distance differential (|v-p| - |v-μ|)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 3 (unbranded model specification), the probit model predicts choosing the ambiguous candidate from risk aversion, voter certainty, and distance differential. The dataset lacks an explicit branding condition variable, so all valid observations were analyzed together. Risk aversion was coded as 1 if Q4=2 (prefer avoiding risks), 0 otherwise, matching the paper's operationalization. Voter certainty = 1 if Q2∈{1,2}, 0 otherwise. Distance differential = |respondent position - precise candidate position| - |respondent position - midpoint of ambiguous candidate interval|.
reasoning: The probit model coefficient for risk aversion is -0.020 (z = -0.38, p = 0.70), indicating a trivially small and statistically insignificant effect. While the direction is consistent with the claim (negative), the effect size is negligible and far from conventional significance levels. Risk-averse respondents chose the ambiguous candidate 47.1% of the time vs. 49.7% for others—a difference of only 2.6 percentage points that does not approach statistical significance.

dependent_variable: ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread (quarterly average, in percentage points)
main_predictor: Net percentage of domestic respondents tightening standards for C&I loans for large and medium firms (CreditStandards)
sample_definition: All quarterly observations from 2010Q1 to 2020Q2 where both HY bond spread data and credit standards survey data are available (n=42)
model_specification: OLS linear regression of HY spread levels on credit standards levels: HY_Spread = α + β × CreditStandards + ε
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 2 approach of univariate regressions on credit standards, the claim 'negative fundamental shock leads to losses for leveraged agents' is tested by examining whether credit standards tightening (a proxy for negative fundamental shocks per the paper's Figure 5 and Table 2) predicts wider HY bond spreads (which reflect declining bond prices and thus losses for leveraged agents who hold these risky securities). The HY spread is used as the dependent variable because it directly reflects the pricing environment for risky assets held by leveraged agents, and wider spreads indicate mark-to-market losses.
reasoning: The OLS regression of the quarterly high-yield bond spread on credit standards yields a positive coefficient of 0.040 (t = 2.412, p = 0.021, R² = 0.127), indicating that when banks tighten credit standards (a negative fundamental shock), HY spreads widen (reflecting losses for leveraged agents holding these bonds). This supports the paper's claim that negative fundamental shocks lead to losses for leveraged agents. The result is robust to Newey-West HAC correction (z = 2.60, p = 0.009).

dependent_variable: Model fit of WICS factor structure (20 items)
main_predictor: Factor structure (five correlated factors vs. one general factor)
sample_definition: All participants in the dataset with complete data on all 20 WICS items (N=581 out of 597 total)
model_specification: Confirmatory factor analysis with maximum likelihood estimation comparing a five correlated-factor model (LGS, PIA, WIR, WGI, IC) to a single-factor model, using chi-square difference test
controls: None (model comparison test of factor structure)
operationalization_notes: The claim that WICS is a 'valid and reliable multidimensional measure' was operationalized as testing whether the five-factor structure fits significantly better than a unidimensional structure. The chi-square difference test between nested CFA models directly tests the multidimensionality claim—the most distinctive component of the overall validity assertion. The five-factor model uses the paper's proposed structure of five correlated factors, each measured by 4 items (reverse-scored where applicable).
reasoning: A confirmatory factor analysis chi-square difference test comparing the five-factor WICS model to a one-factor model yielded Δχ²(10) = 1637.30, p < .001, strongly supporting the multidimensional factor structure. The five-factor model (CFI = 0.891, RMSEA = 0.071) fit substantially better than the one-factor model (CFI = 0.510, RMSEA = 0.146), confirming that WICS captures distinct subscales (Lack of Generational Stereotypes, Positive Intergenerational Affect, Workplace Intergenerational Retention, Workplace Generational Inclusiveness, Intergenerational Contact) rather than a single construct.

dependent_variable: Q9_1: Stockpiling intentions ('I am planning to buy more food or supplies than usually'; 1–5 Likert scale)
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility (mean of 16 HEXACO-100 items, reverse-scored where appropriate)
sample_definition: All 314 participants in the dataset with non-missing HEXACO and stockpiling intention data (Study 2 participants)
model_specification: Simple OLS linear regression of stockpiling intentions on Honesty-Humility
operationalization_notes: Honesty-Humility was computed as the mean of 16 HEXACO-100 items (HE_1–HE_16), with 10 items reverse-scored (HE_1, HE_2, HE_6, HE_7, HE_9, HE_11, HE_12, HE_14, HE_15, HE_16) based on standard HEXACO scoring conventions (items describing low-HH behavior are reverse-coded on the 1–7 scale as 8 minus the raw value). The dependent variable was the single stockpiling intentions item. The regression was run without covariates, consistent with the paper's initial reporting of the HH–intention association before mediation analysis.
reasoning: A simple OLS regression of stockpiling intentions (Q9_1) on Honesty-Humility yielded a significant negative association (t(312) = -9.51, p < 0.001, r = -0.47), indicating that higher Honesty-Humility predicts lower stockpiling intentions—or equivalently, higher intentions to refrain from stockpiling. This supports the paper's claim that Honesty-Humility is positively associated with intentions to refrain from stockpiling, though the effect size in this dataset (r = -0.47) is larger than what the paper reported (r = -0.24), possibly due to differences in sample composition (N = 314 vs. 401) or reverse-scoring of HEXACO items.

dependent_variable: Cumulative COVID-19 deaths per county as of June 11, 2020
main_predictor: Percentage of uninsured individuals (ages 19-64) at the county level
sample_definition: Non-urban counties (density < 1000 residents per square mile) with complete data on all variables and no spatial islands, as of June 11, 2020
model_specification: Spatial lag model (GM_Lag / spatial 2SLS) with queen contiguity weights matrix (row-standardized), estimating direct and indirect effects of predictors on COVID-19 deaths
controls: Percentage of farm workers, percentage of non-English speaking households, percentage of individuals in poverty, population density (residents per square mile), percentage of residents aged 65+, and number of high-risk days (days since first case minus days under shelter-in-place orders)
operationalization_notes: The paper's significant finding for the uninsured-mortality association was in non-urban counties. I used the ACS S2701_C05_012E variable (% uninsured ages 19-64) as the proxy for 'percentage of uninsured individuals under the age of 65' (the SAHIE data used by the paper was not directly available in the dataset). The spatial lag model specification follows the paper's methodology of using a spatial contiguity matrix with a lag of the dependent variable. Islands (counties with no neighbors in the queen contiguity matrix) were removed to ensure model convergence.
reasoning: In the spatial lag model for non-urban counties, the percentage of uninsured individuals (ages 19-64) was significantly associated with lower COVID-19 mortality (z = -3.03, p = 0.002, coefficient = -0.37). This confirms the paper's finding that higher uninsured rates are associated with lower reported COVID-19 mortality, which the authors interpreted as potential undercounting of deaths among the uninsured.

dependent_variable: Dessert choice (chocolate cake vs. fruit salad)
main_predictor: Decision condition (delegated vs. independent decision recall)
sample_definition: All participants from both rounds of data collection who completed the study and chose a dessert (N=399)
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on a 2×2 contingency table (condition × dessert choice), without Yates correction
operationalization_notes: Following the original study's analytic approach for Study 3, which used a chi-square test on the 2×2 contingency table of decision condition by dessert choice. The original paper reported χ²(1, 36) = 5.46, p < .03 with 70.6% vs 31.6% chocolate cake shares. The provided dataset combines both rounds of data collection (first and second), as no exclusion criteria were documented beyond study completion.
reasoning: The chi-square test on the contingency table of condition (delegated vs. independent) × dessert choice (chocolate cake vs. fruit salad) was not significant (χ²(1, N=399) = 1.28, p = .257). Contrary to the claim, the chocolate cake choice share was lower in the delegated condition (60.7%, 122/201) than in the independent condition (66.2%, 131/198), a direction opposite to the original study's finding.

dependent_variable: VIX intraday log range (log(VIX High) - log(VIX Low)), proxy for market-wide illiquidity
main_predictor: log(VIX Close) with one lead and one lag
sample_definition: Daily VIX observations from January 3, 2007 through December 31, 2009 (matching the paper's study period), after dropping rows with missing lagged/lead values
model_specification: OLS log-log regression with Newey-West (HAC, maxlags=5) standard errors: log(range_t) = α + β1·log(VIX_t) + β2·log(VIX_{t-1}) + β3·log(VIX_{t+1}) + day-of-week dummies + ε
controls: Day of week dummies (Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday)
operationalization_notes: The stock-level CRSP data (NASDAQ_2010_19.csv/sas7bdat) referenced in the ReadMe was not present in the data directory, so individual stock liquidity measures (quoted spread, effective spread, depth, etc.) could not be computed. As the best alternative, the VIX intraday range (High-Low) was used as a proxy for market-wide illiquidity/stress, following the logic that wider intraday variation in implied volatility reflects less stable and less liquid market conditions. The model structure follows the paper's regression model (6) with VIX leads/lags and day-of-week controls, testing the sum of VIX coefficients (Σβ) as the key measure of VIX's total effect.
reasoning: The sum of VIX coefficients (β1+β2+β3 = 0.026) from a log-log regression of the VIX intraday range (log(High)-log(Low), used as a proxy for market-wide illiquidity) on contemporaneous, lagged, and lead values of log(VIX Close) is positive and highly significant (t = 3.32, p = 0.0009). This indicates that higher market uncertainty is associated with wider intraday VIX variation, consistent with the claim that VIX exerts a market-wide impact on liquidity. The contemporaneous VIX coefficient alone is 0.17 (t = 3.40, p < 0.001). Stock-level CRSP data was not available in the dataset, so the VIX intraday range serves as the best available proxy for market stress/illiquidity.

dependent_variable: Perceived sandwich size (1='much smaller than average' to 7='much larger than average')
main_predictor: Pitch condition (high-pitch voice [Condition A] vs. low-pitch voice [Condition B])
sample_definition: All included participants from the cleaned dataset (615 participants who passed attention checks and had no exclusion criteria), with Condition A coded as high pitch and Condition B coded as low pitch based on the direction of the size mean difference being consistent with the hypothesis.
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed), equivalent to one-way ANOVA F-test with 1 degree of freedom
controls: None, consistent with the original study's between-subjects design
operationalization_notes: The original Study 1 used a simple between-subjects ANOVA comparing size perceptions across two pitch conditions. I followed the same approach using the replication data. Condition B was identified as the low-pitch condition based on its higher mean size rating being consistent with the predicted direction of the hypothesis. The analysis uses the cleaned/included participants dataset as provided.

reasoning: The F-test comparing the full mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + Controls) against the partial mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + CR + CP + NCR + NCP + Controls) yielded F(4, 159) = 19.31, p < 0.001, strongly rejecting the null hypothesis that the four direct paths from operant leadership to OCB are jointly zero. dependent_variable: Contribution amount (0–125 points contributed to the shared account)

operationalization_notes: Used the three outcome variance conditions matching the original paper's design: no variance (bonus = 600), gains-only (bonus = (400, 800)), and losses-and-gains (bonus = (0, 1200)). This confirms the paper's claim that dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to migration. The coefficient is -0.0006 (SE = 0.0005) in the regression of HP-detrended migration rate on the standardized national employment gap and the standardized SD of state employment gaps.

dependent_variable: response latency (in ms) for angry-to-neutral transition, averaged across exemplars per participant

I operationalized the 'anger lasting longer' component using the angry-to-neutral transition (where higher latency = anger perceived to persist longer), as this is the most direct measure of perceived anger duration. Men have approximately 2.4 times higher odds of being in the low compliance group compared to women, after controlling for age, marital status, children, education, employment, household income, smoking, and Big 5 personality traits.

dependent_variable: Death (binary: 1=died, 0=survived, constructed from fecha_def)

dependent_variable: Perceived stress (PSQ score at follow-up)
main_predictor: Own optimism (LOT-R score at baseline; actor effect)

model_specification: APIM regression: own stress predicted by own optimism (actor effect) and partner's optimism (partner effect), with cluster-robust standard errors to account for dyadic non-independence
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's APIM framework, the actor effect of optimism on stress was tested by regressing each individual's perceived stress on their own optimism and their partner's optimism. Cluster-robust SEs were used to handle the non-independence of dyad members. The paper treated dyads as interchangeable (non-distinguishable), which the pooled regression approach accommodates.
reasoning: The APIM actor effect of own optimism on own perceived stress (controlling for partner's optimism) was significant and negative (t = -8.76, df = 199, p < 0.001, β = -0.558), confirming that more optimistic individuals reported lower levels of stress. This supports the paper's claim, though the effect size is larger than the paper's reported β = -0.25, likely due to the scored dataset containing 101 couples versus the paper's 85.

dependent_variable: Negative affect (T2), computed as the sum of 10 PANAS negative affect items rated 1-5
main_predictor: Realistic threat (T1), computed as the mean of 5 COVID-19 realistic threat items rated 1-4
sample_definition: Participants with both T1 (earlier survey) and T2 (later survey, approximately one week later) data, excluding one test/participant with 28 duplicate rows. Participants with missing data on key variables were also excluded. N = 255.
model_specification: Simple linear regression (OLS) of T2 negative affect on T1 realistic threat, with no covariates
operationalization_notes: The paper used SEM with both realistic and symbolic threat as simultaneous predictors, finding a significant unique effect of realistic threat (b = 4.02, p < .001). I tested the most direct version of the claim—'positively associated'—using a simple regression of T2 negative affect on T1 realistic threat. This approach directly tests whether a positive association exists without requiring the stronger test of a unique effect controlling for symbolic threat. The composite scores for realistic threat (mean of 5 items) and negative affect (sum of 10 PANAS items) follow standard scoring conventions described in the paper.
reasoning: A simple linear regression of T2 negative affect on T1 realistic threat yielded a significant positive association (b = 2.041, t(253) = 2.113, p = .036, r = .132). Higher realistic threat at T1 predicted higher negative affect one week later at T2, consistent with the paper's claim. Note that in a simultaneous regression controlling for symbolic threat, the unique effect of realistic threat was not significant (p = .129), suggesting the bivariate association may partly reflect shared variance with symbolic threat, but the direct positive association claimed by the paper is supported.

dependent_variable: Cooperate (binary: 0=work alone, 1=work together/attempt risky coordination)
main_predictor: Knowledge level (1=Private, 2=Secondary shared, 3=Tertiary shared, 4=Common knowledge)

model_specification: Chi-square test of independence on a 4×2 contingency table (knowledge level × cooperate decision)
operationalization_notes: Exclusion criteria followed the paper's method of removing participants who failed comprehension questions about the payoff structure. The four knowledge conditions map onto the claim's categories: private (level 1), shared (levels 2-3, i.e., secondary and tertiary knowledge), and common knowledge (level 4, broadcast/loudspeaker). The omnibus chi-square test across all four conditions directly tests whether knowledge level affects coordination decisions, with the pattern of means confirming the directional claim.

Cooperation rates increased across knowledge levels: private (38.6%), secondary (43.3%), tertiary (54.7%), and common knowledge (70.1%), consistent with the claim that common knowledge facilitates more coordination attempts than shared or private knowledge.

dependent_variable: Intention to Support the nonprofit (ITS: composite of ITS1_1, ITS2_1, ITS3_1)

The a-path (FIT×SIM → COP) and b-path (COP → ITS) were estimated via OLS regression, and the indirect effect (a×b = 0.0126) was tested using the Sobel z-test.

This was tested as the product-of-coefficients indirect effect (a×b) with a Sobel z-test, following the paper's approach. The paper used SEM with latent variables (Mplus MLR estimator); this reanalysis uses OLS with composite scores as a tractable approximation. The direct interaction on ITS was not significant (p = .908), consistent with the paper's framework where the joint effect operates indirectly through mediators.

The interaction significantly predicts COP (b = .056, p = .010), and COP significantly predicts ITS (b = .227, p < .001), supporting the moderated mediation model where fit and similarity jointly affect intention to support the nonprofit indirectly through clarity of positioning.

dependent_variable: Physical distancing (self-reported curtailing of social contact, single item b7)

dependent_variable: SNARC slope (regression weight of magnitude predicting dRT, where dRT = median RT right - median RT left per digit)
main_predictor: Digit magnitude (in a within-subject regression), with the group-level test being whether the mean slope under verbal load differs from zero
sample_definition: Subjects in the verbal working memory condition who passed inclusion criteria: ≥25% correct WM recall in dual-task and overall parity RT within 4 SD of group median. 94 subjects had valid SNARC slopes.
model_specification: Per subject, dRT values (right RT - left RT) for each digit were regressed on digit magnitude to obtain a SNARC slope. A one-sample t-test was then conducted on these slopes against zero to test whether the SNARC effect exists under verbal load.

operationalization_notes: The paper's primary test of the claim was whether the SNARC slope (magnitude regression weight) differs from zero in the verbal load condition. Following their regression approach (Fias et al., 1996), dRTs were computed per digit per subject, regressed on magnitude, and the resulting slopes were tested against zero via one-sample t-test. This is the most direct test of whether verbal load abolished the SNARC effect.

Using the same regression approach described in the paper (dRT = median RT right - median RT left per digit, regressed on magnitude), the one-sample t-test on SNARC slopes in the verbal load condition shows a highly significant negative slope (mean = -7.94, t(93) = -6.68, p < 0.001), indicating a robust SNARC effect is still present under verbal load. This directly contradicts the paper's finding that the slope did not differ from zero under verbal load (t(19) = 0.18, p = .86).

dependent_variable: T3_panas_joviality (joviality at end of following workweek)

The paper controlled for demographics in Step 1, prior affect in Step 2, and entered all five weekend experience predictors simultaneously in Step 3. The direction is consistent with the original claim (β = 0.15, p < .01), but the effect does not reach conventional significance levels, suggesting the evidence is inconclusive.

dependent_variable: Autism identification (proportion of students identified with autism out of total enrollment, ages 6-21)

controls: Race (6 dummy variables: Black, Hispanic, Asian, PI, AI, Two or More; White as reference category)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methodology of using logistic regression on autism count data, I constructed a binomial GLM testing whether Ohio had lower autism identification rates than California after controlling for racial composition. Autism counts came from IDEA child count data; enrollment by race was computed by multiplying total enrollment (NCES table 203.20) by racial percentage distribution (NCES table 203.70). This operationalization directly tests the state-level claim while accounting for the paper's documented racial disparities.
