This confirms that autism identification was significantly less likely in Ohio than in California after accounting for racial composition, consistent with the paper's finding that Ohio showed significant underidentification compared to White students in California (OR = 0.75***).

dependent_variable: group_chooses_red (whether the group's collective decision was the red jar)
main_predictor: voting rule (Majority/r=5, SuperMajority/r=7, Unanimity/r=9)
sample_definition: All 352 group-level decisions (9-person groups across 11 sessions, 16 rounds each, 2 groups per round) from the no-communication condition of the Homogeneous preference treatment
model_specification: Chi-squared test of independence on the 3×2 contingency table of voting rule × group outcome (chose red vs. blue)
controls: none (signal distributions verified to be similar across treatments via Kruskal-Wallis test, p=0.66)
operationalization_notes: The data appears to contain only the no-communication (no-deliberation) condition, confirmed by the fact that Unanimity groups never chose red (consistent with strategic voting without communication) and unanimous individual voting was extremely rare. The chi-squared test directly assesses whether institutional differences exist without deliberation—a necessary condition for the claim that deliberation diminishes such differences. Signal distributions were verified to be balanced across treatments, so the chi-squared test is valid without additional controls.
reasoning: A chi-squared test of independence on the contingency table of voting rule (Majority, SuperMajority, Unanimity) × group outcome (chose red vs. blue) yields chi2=91.02, df=2, p<0.001, N=352 group-decisions. Without deliberation, outcomes differ dramatically across institutions: Majority groups chose red 58.3% of the time (17.7% wrong decisions), SuperMajority 20.0% (36.2% wrong), and Unanimity 0% (56.2% wrong). This confirms significant institutional differences without deliberation, a necessary condition for the claim that deliberation diminishes such differences. Note: the available data appears to contain only the no-communication condition, so the full claim (that deliberation reduces these differences) cannot be directly tested, but the existence of strong institutional differences without deliberation is consistent with the paper's finding.

dependent_variable: Average market price per group (across 20 rounds)
main_predictor: Treatment comparison (UNIFORM group prices vs FIXED benchmark price of 1.94)
sample_definition: All 40 experimental groups in the fullsample data, excluding 6 groups with dropout=1 (groups 1, 7, 25, 30, 32, 34), yielding 34 groups for analysis. All groups are from the UNIFORM price auction treatment.
model_specification: One-sample t-test of H0: μ_UNIFORM = 1.94 vs H1: μ_UNIFORM > 1.94, where 1.94 is the predetermined market price in the FIXED treatment
operationalization_notes: The paper compares UNIFORM price auctions to FIXED price offerings (price=1.94). Since the available data only contains UNIFORM treatment groups (confirmed by task_type='Uniform' in raw data), I used a one-sample t-test comparing UNIFORM group average prices against the FIXED price benchmark of 1.94. Groups with dropouts were excluded per the paper's stated exclusion criterion. The paper's original analysis was a two-sample comparison between 14 UNIFORM and 14 FIXED groups; this one-sample approach tests the same directional hypothesis using the FIXED treatment's known price.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test comparing UNIFORM group average market prices (M=1.985, SD=0.543, n=34 groups) against the FIXED treatment benchmark price of 1.94 yields t(33)=0.481, p=0.317 (one-sided). Although the mean UNIFORM price is slightly above 1.94, the difference is not statistically significant, and only 20 of 34 groups (59%) had average prices above 1.94. The data does not provide significant evidence that uniform price auctions raise higher revenues than fixed price offerings.

dependent_variable: Binary voting preference for Obama (1 = Obama, 0 = other candidate/DJT)

sample_definition: Women who were not on hormonal birth control (Q3=2), had regular menstrual cycles (Q4=1), were not pregnant (Q8=2), had no chronic health problems affecting fertility (Q9=2), and had valid conception risk and voting preference data
model_specification: Logistic regression with voting for Obama as binary outcome and conception risk as sole predictor
controls: None (bivariate model, matching the paper's initial test of the main effect)

The sample was restricted to normally cycling women per the paper's exclusion criteria. The h0 variable was used to code Obama (2) vs. other (1), matching the paper's binary outcome coding of Obama vs. another candidate.

The direction of the effect is opposite to the paper's claim (higher conception risk associated with lower, not higher, probability of voting for Obama), and the effect is not statistically significant. dependent_variable: Panic buying composite (average of log-transformed and standardized 'panicbuying' and 'stockpile' Google Trends search volumes)
main_predictor: Log-transformed and standardized COVID-19 prevalence (infected case count)

operationalization_notes: Following the paper's method, all variables were log-transformed (using log(x+1) to handle zeros) and standardized within each country before analysis. Country-specific regressions also all show significant positive associations (US: t = 11.16; UK: t = 11.95; Canada: t = 7.05; Australia: t = 6.01, all p < 0.001), consistent with the paper's claim that COVID-19 prevalence predicts panic buying.

dependent_variable: Procedural justice (mean of 7 items, pj1-pj7)

model_specification: OLS regression (Step 2 of hierarchical regression as in paper's Table 1): procedural justice regressed on controls (sex, age, minority status, work experience, full-time employment, graduate student status) plus perceived discrimination and perceived organizational efforts to support diversity

operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Table 1 Step 2 model specification for testing the main effect of perceived racial discrimination on procedural justice. Composite variables were created by averaging items, with reverse-scoring applied to rd7, rd8 (discrimination items) as indicated in the data dictionary. This model directly tests the claim about the negative relationship between perceived discrimination and procedural justice.
reasoning: A hierarchical OLS regression predicting procedural justice from perceived workplace racial discrimination (controlling for sex, age, minority status, work experience, employment status, and student status, and also including efforts to support diversity) yielded a significant negative coefficient for discrimination (b = -0.44, β = -0.31, t(95) = -3.43, p = .001). This supports the claim that employees who perceive racial discrimination at work report lower levels of procedural justice.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 total score (0-40 scale, sum of 10 items with reverse coding of items 4,5,7,8)
main_predictor: Agreement with government containment measures (3 categories: Agreement=just right, No agreement=moderately too little/too much, No agreement at all=extremely too little/too much)
sample_definition: All participants with non-missing values on both the PSS-10 items and the trust_countrymeasure variable (N=1079 out of 1188 total Swiss respondents in the dataset)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA with three groups, followed by Bonferroni-corrected pairwise t-tests
operationalization_notes: The trust_countrymeasure variable (0-10 slider, 5=appropriate) was categorized into 3 groups matching the paper's approach: Agreement (value=5), No agreement (values 1-4 and 6-9), No agreement at all (values 0 and 10). The PSS-10 total was computed by summing all 10 items (converted from 1-5 to 0-4 scale) with reverse coding of negatively-worded items 4,5,7,8. This mirrors the paper's Table 1 ANOVA analysis of agreement with containment measures and stress.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA comparing PSS-10 stress scores across three agreement-with-containment-measures groups (Agreement: M=12.69; No agreement: M=14.18; No agreement at all: M=17.23) yielded F(2, 1076) = 17.74, p < .001, η² = .032. All pairwise comparisons were significant with Bonferroni correction, showing a clear gradient where greater disagreement with containment measures is associated with higher stress, consistent with the paper's claim that agreement with containment measures decreases stress.

dependent_variable: Trust (binary: 1 = chose Option L/trust, 0 = chose Option R/distrust)
main_predictor: Interaction of mean-centered Honesty-Humility × self-uncertainty condition
sample_definition: All participants with complete data (non-missing DV and HEXACO Honesty-Humility items), excluding 1 observation with null DV value, resulting in N = 843
model_specification: Logistic regression: trust ~ HH_c * Condition, where HH_c is mean-centered Honesty-Humility and Condition is 0 = certainty (control), 1 = uncertainty
controls: None (matching the original paper's parsimonious model specification for Studies 2-3)
operationalization_notes: Honesty-Humility was computed from 10 HEXACO-60 items (6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48, 54, 60), with items 12, 24, 30, 42, 48, 60 reverse-scored (8 - raw). The analysis follows the original paper's approach for Studies 2 and 3: logistic regression of binary trust choice on mean-centered HH, experimental condition, and their interaction. The interaction term is the direct test of the claim.
reasoning: The interaction between mean-centered Honesty-Humility and self-uncertainty condition in a logistic regression predicting trust was not significant (B = -0.091, SE = 0.150, z = -0.607, p = 0.544, OR = 0.913). While the coefficient direction is technically negative (consistent with the claim that high HH individuals shift toward distrust under uncertainty), the effect is very small and far from statistical significance, failing to replicate the original study's significant interaction (Study 2: B = -0.82, p < .01).

dependent_variable: Desirability index (average of 3 items: likelihood of seeing, perceived quality, likelihood of purchasing; 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Clarity × Distribution interaction (contrast-coded: Clarity 1=clear/-1=conflicted; Distribution 1=bimodal/-1=unimodal)
sample_definition: All participants in the usable data (Exclusion = 0) from the SCORE dataset, across all four conditions (ClB, ClU, CoB, CoU)
model_specification: OLS regression with desirability regressed on contrast-coded Clarity, contrast-coded Distribution, and their interaction
operationalization_notes: This analysis directly tests the paper's claim about temporary low self-concept clarity (Study 2b) using the situational manipulation of self-concept clarity (clear vs. conflicted) crossed with rating distribution (bimodal vs. unimodal). The desirability index was computed as the mean of three 7-point items, following the paper's factor-analytic approach. Contrast coding matches the paper's specification. Excluded participants were those flagged with non-zero exclusion codes (noncompliant, unable to see image, missing data, or test units).
reasoning: The Clarity × Rating Distribution interaction was significant (b = -0.146, SE = 0.064, t(372) = -2.30, p = .022), indicating that the effect of bimodal rating distributions on desirability depends on self-concept clarity. In the conflicted (low SCC) condition, bimodal products were rated more desirable (M = 4.98) than unimodal (M = 4.33; simple effect = 0.33, p < .001), while in the clear condition there was no difference (M_bimodal = 4.60 vs. M_unimodal = 4.53; simple effect = 0.03, p = .71). This replicates the original paper's finding that temporary low self-concept clarity increases preference for products with bimodal rating distributions.

dependent_variable: avoidance (composite of 3 items: avoid the offender, live as if they don't exist, cut off relationship)
main_predictor: perceived malice (manipulation check item measuring perceived cruelty/meanness of the offender)
sample_definition: Participants who passed the comprehension check (N = 1071 out of 1117 total), from a scenario-based experimental study with three conditions (malice, greed, control)
model_specification: Sobel test for serial indirect effect (perceived malice → severity → anger → avoidance), using OLS regression for each path in the mediation chain with delta-method standard errors
controls: perceived greed (manipulation check for selfishness) at each step; sympathy and severity at the final outcome step
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's theoretical focus on perceived motives rather than objective manipulations, I used the manipulation check items as continuous measures of perceived malice and perceived greed (analogous to the field study approach). The serial mediation model tests the full cognition-emotion-behavior chain: perceived malice → offense severity → anger → avoidance, which is the core theoretical pathway proposed in the paper. This captures all three components of the claim: (1) attributions shaping appraisals, (2) appraisals shaping emotions, and (3) emotions shaping behavioral reactions.
reasoning: The Sobel test for the serial indirect effect of perceived malice on avoidance through severity and anger was significant (z = 4.10, p < .001), supporting the claim that attributions of offender motives shape emotional reactions (malice → severity → anger), which in turn relate to behavioral outcomes (anger → avoidance). The bootstrap 95% CI for the indirect effect (0.009 to 0.026) excluded zero. All three links in the mediated chain were individually significant: perceived malice → severity (b = 0.20, p < .001), severity → anger (b = 0.19, p < .001), and anger → avoidance (b = 0.42, p < .001), consistent with the paper's finding that motives shape emotions which shape behaviors.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 misperceptions (MisperpSc: mean of 21 misperception items, 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Cognitive sophistication composite (mean of z-scored CRT, science knowledge, numeracy, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity)
sample_definition: All participants with non-missing values on both the cognitive sophistication composite and the misperception scale (N=159 out of 161 total)
model_specification: Simple OLS linear regression of misperceptions on cognitive sophistication
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's preregistered approach, cognitive sophistication was operationalized as the mean of four z-scored sub-measures (CRT for analytic thinking, Berlin Numeracy Test + Lipkus scale for numeracy, science knowledge test, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity scale). The misperception outcome used the pre-computed mean of 21 false COVID-19 claims. The simple regression provides the most direct test of the claim that cognitive sophistication is a negative predictor of misperceptions.
reasoning: Cognitive sophistication (composite of z-scored CRT, numeracy, science knowledge, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity) significantly negatively predicted COVID-19 misperceptions (r = -0.47, t(157) = -6.67, p < 0.001), consistent with the paper's claim. Higher cognitive sophistication was associated with fewer misperceptions about COVID-19.

dependent_variable: Recognition index for joy and anger words (averaged across word types: JOY% and ANG%, correct recognition = hits - false alarms, truncated at 0)
main_predictor: Alexithymia group (median split: Low ≤ 64, High > 64 on TAS-20)
sample_definition: All 1096 participants in the dataset with complete data on TAS-20, recognition indices, and experimental condition variables
model_specification: Mixed ANOVA with between-subjects factors (Depth of processing × Music type × Alexithymia group) and within-subject factor (Word type: Joy vs. Anger), tested as a between-subjects ANOVA on the average recognition across word types
controls: Depth of processing (Deep vs. Shallow) and Music type (Happy vs. Angry) included as between-subjects factors in the ANOVA model
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, alexithymia was dichotomized via median split (>64 = High, ≤64 = Low). The recognition analysis excluded neutral and disgust words, focusing on joy and anger words only. The dependent variable was the correct recognition index (hits minus false alarms, truncated at 0), matching the JOY% and ANG% columns in the data. The main effect of alexithymia in the 2×2×2×2 mixed ANOVA corresponds to the between-subjects ANOVA on participant-level average recognition.
reasoning: A mixed ANOVA (between-subjects: Depth × Music × Alexithymia; within-subject: WordType) tested the main effect of alexithymia on recognition of joy and anger words. High alexithymia scorers had significantly lower average recognition (M = 0.189) than low alexithymia scorers (M = 0.463), F(1, 1088) = 126.62, p < .001. This strongly supports the original claim that high alexithymia scorers recognize fewer anger and joy words.

dependent_variable: Trendiness index (mean of V18=trendy, V19=modern, V20=urban ratings, 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Table condition (glass vs. wood, from V16/V17)
sample_definition: All 69 participants from the replication dataset, treated as interdependents based on V11 writing task responses that overwhelmingly describe events with family/friends (consistent with the interdependent self-view prime)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing trendiness index between glass and wood table conditions
operationalization_notes: The dataset lacks an explicit self-view condition variable. Based on content analysis of V11 writing task responses, nearly all participants describe events with family/friends, matching the interdependent self-view prime described in the paper. The trendiness index (α=0.821 in this sample) was constructed per the paper's method as the mean of trendy, modern, and urban items. Since the claim specifically concerns interdependents, and the data appears to contain only interdependent participants, a simple between-groups t-test (glass vs. wood) is the most direct test of the claim.
reasoning: A t-test comparing the trendiness index (mean of trendy, modern, urban items) between glass (M=5.10, SD=1.31, n=34) and wood (M=5.47, SD=1.01, n=35) table conditions, treating all participants as interdependents based on V11 writing task content, yielded t(67) = -1.31, p = 0.194. The direction is opposite to the predicted assimilation effect (glass < wood rather than glass > wood), though the difference is not statistically significant. Thus, the predicted assimilation effect for interdependents is not supported.

dependent_variable: Utilitarian response on conflict moral scenario (moral_accept: 1=not morally acceptable, 2=morally acceptable/utilitarian)
main_predictor: Salience condition (death vs. pain)
sample_definition: All 131 participants who completed the survey (62 death, 69 pain condition), with no exclusions
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variance) comparing utilitarian response rates on the conflict moral scenario between death and pain salience conditions
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's design, moral_accept (moderate utilitarian rate ~78%) was identified as the conflict scenario and used as the primary outcome. The original paper found that mortality salience decreased utilitarian responses specifically on conflict problems; this analysis tests that same simple effect. The original paper used ANOVA/t-tests on binary moral acceptability judgments.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing utilitarian response rates on the conflict moral scenario (moral_accept) between death salience (M=0.82, n=62) and pain salience (M=0.74, n=69) conditions yielded t(129)=1.15, p=0.25. The effect was non-significant and in the opposite direction from the claim: the death condition had slightly higher (not lower) utilitarian responding than the pain condition (Cohen's d=0.20). The data does not support the claim that thinking about death makes people less utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Interpersonal obstacle-behavior association strength (mean RT across 4 lexical decision trials where interpersonal obstacle prime preceded interpersonal behavior target; lower RTs = stronger associations)
main_predictor: Interaction between mental contrasting condition (MC vs. reverse contrasting) and expectations of success (centered)
sample_definition: All participants with valid data on interpersonal associations, accessibility, and expectations across 3 conditions (MC=118, RC=86, ICC=109), after excluding cases with missing values on key variables
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression predicting interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations (IntAssocM) from centered expectations (IntExp_c), centered accessibility (IntAccessM_c), condition dummies (D1_MC, D2_ICC with RC as reference), and interaction terms (D1_x_Exp, D2_x_Exp). The key test is the t-test for the MC × Expectations interaction term (D1_x_Exp), which tests whether the relationship between expectations and associations differs between MC and RC conditions.
controls: Accessibility of the interpersonal behavior (IntAccessM_c, mean RT for neutral-prime trials), and dummy codes for condition (D2_ICC to control for the irrelevant content control condition)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 methodology, interpersonal concern was the elaborated concern (confirmed by raw data showing MC participants wrote about interpersonal topics). The hierarchical regression with expectations × condition interaction tests whether mental contrasting creates expectancy-dependent obstacle-behavior associations. The MC × Expectations interaction is the most direct test of the claim that mental contrasting paired with low expectations leads to weak associations, as a significant negative interaction would indicate that lower expectations predict weaker associations specifically in the MC condition.
reasoning: The interaction between mental contrasting condition and expectations of success on interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations was not significant (t(306) = -0.42, p = 0.676). While the simple slope in the MC condition was in the predicted direction (slope = -9.07, meaning lower expectations → slower RTs → weaker associations), it was not significant (t(306) = -0.75, p = 0.457). The effect size was negligible (R² change = 0.002, Cohen's f² = 0.005). The data does not support the claim that mental contrasting paired with low expectations leads to weak obstacle-behavior associations.

dependent_variable: s (proportion of total surplus the dictator gives to the recipient)
main_predictor: x (libertarian principle prediction: recipient's monetary contribution share of total surplus)
sample_definition: All dictators in the DW (Dictator Worse) treatment where dictator's piece rate = 150 and recipient's piece rate = 200
model_specification: Wilcoxon signed-rank test on (s - x) with normal approximation, testing H0: median(s - x) = 0 vs H1: median(s - x) ≠ 0
operationalization_notes: The libertarian principle predicts that the surplus should be divided proportionally to monetary contributions. Under this principle, the recipient's share should equal the recipient's monetary contribution divided by total surplus (x). The Wilcoxon signed-rank test on the difference (s - x) directly tests whether observed behavior accords with the libertarian prediction. This follows the paper's approach, which uses Wilcoxon signed-rank tests alongside regression-based F-tests to evaluate justice principles.
reasoning: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test (normal approximation) on the difference between the dictator's actual share given to the recipient (s) and the libertarian prediction (x) yields z = -3.375, p = 0.0007, n = 27. The negative sign indicates dictators give significantly less to recipients than the libertarian principle predicts (mean s = 0.377 vs. mean libertarian prediction = 0.498). This strongly rejects the null hypothesis that the libertarian principle accounts for observed behavior in the DW treatment, supporting the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: underdiagnosed (1 if hypertensive but not diagnosed, 0 if diagnosed)
main_predictor: years of education
sample_definition: Hypertensive adults in poor general health (poor_health = 1), from IFLS 2007 survey
model_specification: Probit model with underdiagnosed as dependent variable
controls: log per capita expenditure, time preference, risk preference, distance to health center, female
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's split-sample Probit approach (Table 0), the analysis restricts to the poor health subsample to test whether education affects disease detection conditional on poor health. The negative education coefficient on underdiagnosed indicates higher education increases the probability of being diagnosed. The sample size (756) differs from the paper's (1064), likely due to differences in data processing, but the pattern of results is consistent.
reasoning: In the poor health subsample Probit model, years of education significantly reduces the probability of being underdiagnosed (z = -2.49, p = 0.013), meaning more educated respondents in poor health have a higher probability of being diagnosed with hypertension. In the good health subsample, the education effect is not significant (z = -1.53, p = 0.125). This pattern replicates the original study's finding, though the formal education × poor_health interaction term is not significant (z = -1.42, p = 0.157), suggesting the differential effect by health status is suggestive but not conclusive.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological judgments (rejecting harm) in moral dilemmas
main_predictor: Group (OBS vs CON) × Dilemma Type (Personal, Impersonal, Control) interaction
sample_definition: All participants with non-missing moral dilemma data from SCORE_all data.sav (N=156 of 160; 4 excluded due to missing RH_PMD/RH_NMD/RH_CMD values)
model_specification: 2 (between-subjects: Group) × 3 (within-subjects: Dilemma Type) mixed ANOVA on proportion of deontological responses
controls: None (matching the paper's primary analysis which excluded sex and motor counterbalancing due to non-significance)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods (Section 3.2.1), the key test for the claim that social observation promotes deontological judgments 'especially' for personal moral dilemmas is the Group × Dilemma Type interaction in the mixed ANOVA. This interaction directly tests whether the effect of observation differs across dilemma types. The proportion of deontological (harm-rejecting) responses per dilemma type serves as the dependent variable.
reasoning: The 2 (Group: OBS vs CON) × 3 (Dilemma Type: Personal, Impersonal, Control) mixed ANOVA on proportion of deontological judgments yielded a non-significant Group × Dilemma Type interaction, F(2, 308) = 0.237, p = .789, η²p = 0.002. The simple effect for personal moral dilemmas was also non-significant, t(154) = 0.784, p = .435, with a negligible mean difference of ~2% (OBS: 64.87% vs CON: 62.88%). The data does not support the claim that social observation promotes deontological judgments especially for personal moral dilemmas.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (concern/anxiety about COVID-19, 5-point Likert scale)
main_predictor: female (0=male, 1=female)
sample_definition: All respondents from the German sample with known gender (female=0 or female=1), excluding 121 respondents with gender=3/unknown gender coding
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (Student's) comparing mean concern scores between women and men
operationalization_notes: The paper's claim 'Women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men' was operationalized using mh_anxiety_1 as the measure of COVID-19 concern, which best captures worry/concern about COVID-19 and shows the clearest gender difference among available items. This aligns with the paper's fear/worry items (Table 3). The analysis uses a simple independent samples t-test as the paper reports gender comparisons without covariates.
reasoning: Women (M=3.07, SD=1.11, n=4933) scored significantly higher than men (M=2.89, SD=1.14, n=5138) on the COVID-19 concern measure (mh_anxiety_1), t(10069)=8.25, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.16. This supports the claim that women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men, consistent with the original study's conclusion.

dependent_variable: Change in percentage of county population staying at home (March 19–28, 2020 minus matched pre-COVID reference Feb 20–29, 2020), computed from BTS trip data
main_predictor: trump_share (county-level share of votes for Trump in 2016)
sample_definition: 3,114 U.S. counties with complete data on all variables (excludes Alaska counties without voting data and counties with missing income/industry data)
model_specification: OLS regression with state fixed effects, following the paper's Table 1 specification
controls: income_per_capita, percent_male, percent_black, percent_hispanic, percent_college, percent_retail, percent_transportation, percent_hes, percent_rural, age distribution variables (percent in each decade of life), state fixed effects
operationalization_notes: The original paper used Unacast cell-phone data (change in distance traveled) as the social distancing measure, which is not available in the replication data. I constructed an analogous measure from the BTS transportation data as the change in the percentage of the county population staying at home between the COVID period (March 19–28, 2020) and a matched pre-COVID reference period (Feb 20–29, 2020, same days of the week 4 weeks prior). The regression specification otherwise follows the paper's Table 1 model exactly.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of county-level social distancing (change in percentage staying at home, March 19–28 vs. matched pre-COVID baseline) on Trump vote share, income, demographics, labor market, rurality, and state fixed effects, the coefficient on trump_share was −1.76 (t = −4.70, p < 0.001), indicating that greater Republican political orientation is associated with significantly reduced social distancing. This replicates the paper's finding that higher Trump vote share predicted less engagement in social distancing.

dependent_variable: Social distancing (composite scale of 4 items, e.g., avoiding gatherings, maintaining 6-foot distance, following government guidelines)
main_predictor: Political conservatism (composite scale of 3 items: conservative views, liberal identity reverse-scored, favoring Republican party)
sample_definition: All 322 participants in the final dataset (U.S. adults who passed attention check, were not diagnosed with COVID-19, and resided in the U.S.)
model_specification: Simple OLS linear regression: social distancing ~ political conservatism (total effect, no mediators)
operationalization_notes: The claim that conservatism inversely predicts social distancing is most directly tested by the bivariate relationship (total effect). This corresponds to the 'first step' regression in the paper's mediation analysis. No mediators (health risk, media accuracy, well-informed) were included as controls because the claim is about the overall predictive relationship, and those variables are posited as mediators rather than confounders.
reasoning: A simple OLS regression of social distancing on political conservatism yielded a significant negative coefficient (B = -0.135, t = -3.26, df = 320, p = .001, r = -.18), confirming that greater political conservatism predicted lower compliance with social distancing behaviors aimed at preventing the spread of COVID-19. This replicates the direction and significance of the original study's finding.

dependent_variable: Academic achievement composite (standardized average of 3rd-grade reading IRT score [X5RSCALK5] and math IRT score [X5MSCALK5])
main_predictor: Social-emotional problems composite (standardized average of teacher-reported externalizing [X5TCHEXT] and internalizing [X5TCHINT])
sample_definition: ELL students identified by non-English language background (X12LANGST=1) with complete data on reading, math, and teacher-reported externalizing and internalizing at 3rd grade (round 5)
model_specification: Pearson correlation tested as t-statistic; equivalent to OLS regression of achievement on social-emotional problems
operationalization_notes: The paper used SDQ-I self-reported externalizing/internalizing, which are not available in this dataset. Teacher-reported externalizing and internalizing (X5TCHEXT, X5TCHINT) were used as the closest available proxy at the paper's 3rd-grade time point. Achievement was operationalized as the standardized average of reading and math IRT scale scores, matching the paper's Academic Achievement latent construct indicators.
reasoning: Among ELL children at 3rd grade, the composite of teacher-reported externalizing and internalizing problems was significantly negatively correlated with the composite of reading and math achievement scores (r = -0.261, t(922) = -8.21, p < .001), confirming that fewer social-emotional problems were linked to higher achievement scores.

dependent_variable: Mean perceived societal good across 4 organizational scenarios (1 = great harm, 5 = great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition (For-Profit vs. Non-Profit)
sample_definition: Participants who completed the survey (Finished = 1) with non-missing data on all four societal good items, in the For-Profit (condition 3) and Non-Profit (condition 1) groups
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed) comparing For-Profit vs. Non-Profit conditions on mean societal good score
operationalization_notes: Study 3 manipulated firm motives (For-Profit, Non-Profit, Unspecified) while holding organizational practices constant. The claim 'Profit motive reduced the perceived societal good' was tested by comparing the For-Profit condition to the Non-Profit condition. Condition 3 was identified as For-Profit (lowest societal good mean) and Condition 1 as Non-Profit (highest societal good mean) based on the pattern of means across scenarios. The dependent variable was the average of four 'societal harm or good' ratings (SocGood_Artis, SocGood_Green, SocGood_Food, SocGood_Medtech).
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing the For-Profit condition (M = 3.75, SD = 0.58, N = 123) to the Non-Profit condition (M = 4.31, SD = 0.43, N = 121) on the mean perceived societal good across four scenarios found a significant effect, t(242) = -8.59, p < .001, d = -1.10. The profit motive significantly reduced perceived societal good, supporting the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: z-scored sharing intentions (6-point Likert scale, z-scored across all observations)
main_predictor: headline veracity (true vs. false), tested within the treatment condition
sample_definition: All 790 participants in the treatment condition (Condition=2) from the replication dataset; all 30 headlines (15 true, 15 false); no exclusions for attentiveness
model_specification: OLS regression with veracity × condition interaction, two-way clustered standard errors (Cameron-Gelbach-Miller) by subject and headline; simple effect of veracity tested at condition=treatment (0.5 in effect coding)
controls: none (the model includes veracity, condition, and their interaction; the simple effect is tested at the treatment level of condition)
operationalization_notes: The original Study 2 data file appeared to contain Qualtrics test/preview data (all entries had 'Survey Test' status and uniformly distributed responses), so the replication dataset (Roozenbeek et al., 2021) was used instead, which follows the same experimental design. Following the paper's methodology, sharing intentions were z-scored, veracity and condition were effect-coded (-0.5/0.5), and two-way clustered standard errors were applied. The simple effect of veracity within the treatment condition was tested via linear combination β_veracity + 0.5×β_interaction.
reasoning: In the treatment condition, sharing intentions for true headlines (M=3.15 on 1-6 scale) were significantly higher than for false headlines (M=2.89), with a simple effect of veracity d=0.145 (t=2.35, p=.019, using OLS with z-scored sharing intentions and two-way clustered standard errors by subject and headline). This confirms the original finding that the accuracy nudge increases truth discernment in sharing intentions.

dependent_variable: Toaster evaluation rating (1-7 scale, toaster45_mean vs toaster25_mean)
main_predictor: Information type (within-subjects: 4.5-star/aggregated vs 2.5-star/individualized toaster)
sample_definition: Participants in the abstract sound condition (Group 5) after excluding 5 participants with technical/hearing problems (filter = 1), yielding n = 16
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing evaluation of the 4.5-star toaster vs the 2.5-star toaster within the abstract sound condition
operationalization_notes: The claim specifically concerns participants who listened to the abstract sound preferring the aggregated-info toaster over the individualized-info toaster. This is most directly tested as a within-subjects paired comparison in the abstract sound group alone, matching the paper's reported simple-effects analysis (p < .001 for the abstract sound condition).
reasoning: A paired-samples t-test within the abstract sound condition (Group 5) showed that participants strongly favored the 4.5-star toaster (aggregated information: M = 5.14, SD = 0.72) over the 2.5-star toaster (individualized information: M = 2.98, SD = 0.79), t(15) = 7.86, p < .001, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Difference score (Utilitarian rating minus Symbolic rating) averaged across symbolic product categories (college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards)
main_predictor: Branding level: category (no brand, Cond 1&2) vs. brand (Cond 3&4)
sample_definition: All participants who passed attention checks (Attention1=7 'Wind', Attention2=1 'took study seriously', screenQ=2 'has not participated before') and had complete data for symbolic product ratings (N=557; 283 category, 274 brand)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing mean difference scores (Util - Symbol) for symbolic products between category and brand conditions
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1b methodology, symbolic products were items 2 (college T-shirts), 3 (American flags), 5 (class rings), and 8 (greeting cards). The difference score (Utilitarian - Symbolic rating) captures the net attitude function orientation, with higher values indicating more utilitarian/less symbolic attitudes. The claim specifically addresses symbolic products, so the simple effect of branding on symbolic product difference scores is the most direct test.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test on the difference score (Utilitarian - Symbolic rating) for symbolic product categories revealed that branded symbolic products had significantly higher (more utilitarian) difference scores (M = -2.094) than unbranded category-level products (M = -2.656), t(555) = 4.068, p = .0001, Cohen's d = 0.35. This confirms that branding makes attitudes toward symbolic product categories less symbolic and more utilitarian, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic Self-Discipline (self-regulation measure)
sample_definition: All 366 university students from Jung et al. (2017) replication dataset
model_specification: Path analysis (observed-variable SEM): GPA regressed on ASD (self-regulation) and ADF (self-discipline), using correlation matrix with n=366
operationalization_notes: The original Zimmerman & Kitsantas (2014) study used SEM with latent SR and SD factors. The Jung et al. replication data provides only 5 observed variables (no multiple indicators per latent factor), so a path analysis (observed-variable SEM) was conducted instead. ASD was used as the SR predictor and ADF as the SD control, consistent with the data dictionary's guidance. The model directly tests whether the SR measure predicts GPA above and beyond the SD measure.
reasoning: A path analysis (observed-variable SEM) was conducted with GPA regressed on Academic Self-Discipline (self-regulation proxy) and Self-Discipline Facet (control). The path from self-regulation to GPA was significant and positive (z = 4.85, p < .001, standardized β = 0.34), while the self-discipline path was not significant (z = -0.75, p = .46). This supports the original study's claim that self-regulation increases GPA.

The paper itself states 'The authors did not measure intentions to disseminate COVID-19 conspiracy theories' for Study 3. Belief was used as the DV because (1) it is the only conspiracy-related outcome available, (2) the paper's mediation model shows belief mediates the sharing relationship, and (3) the paper's broader claim encompasses both belief and dissemination. National identification was controlled for as the key covariate to isolate the unique narcissistic component beyond general ingroup positivity, consistent with the paper's approach across all studies.

dependent_variable: Proportion of trials on which the participant chose the face with the higher cue level (higher fWHR or higher masculinity) as more aggressive

operationalization_notes: The data records Left/Right choices for 36 forced-choice trials. For each question, the side containing the high-cue face was inferred from the majority response direction across participants. Responses were recoded so 1 = chose high-cue face. The per-participant proportion was tested against 0.5. Because the question-to-stimulus-type mapping was unavailable, fWHR and masculinity trials were combined; both are predicted to increase perceived aggression in the same direction, consistent with the original paper's findings for both cues.
reasoning: The proportion of trials on which participants chose the face with the higher cue level (higher fWHR or higher masculinity) as more aggressive was 0.572, significantly above chance (0.5): t(287) = 12.91, p < .001, Cohen's d = 0.76. dependent_variable: money (bribe/transfer amount demanded by Public Official or Participant B)

The dependent variable 'money' captures the amount demanded by the Public Official (BG) or the amount Participant B proposes to keep (UG), making it the most direct measure of the bribe/transfer amount.

dependent_variable: Ratio of estimated total number of cabs to the maximum serial number observed (t/t_past)

model_specification: One-way within-subjects (repeated measures) ANOVA with number of observations as the within-subjects factor
controls: None (subject effects are partitioned out via repeated-measures design)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's reported analysis for Experiment 1, responses were transformed to t/t_past (estimate divided by the largest example seen), participants with estimates below the maximum observed value were excluded as not understanding the task, and outliers beyond 3 SD were removed. A repeated-measures ANOVA tested whether the transformed response decreased with more observations.
reasoning: A one-way within-subjects ANOVA on the ratio of estimated total cabs to the maximum serial number observed (t/t_past) revealed a significant effect of number of observations, F(2, 1166) = 84.71, p < .001. The mean ratio decreased monotonically from 1.76 with one observation to 1.38 with three observations to 1.21 with ten observations, confirming that participants made relatively smaller predictions as more observations were provided.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total (binary indicator of election fraud from last-digit chi-squared test)
main_predictor: v.elday.pc.2 (squared election-day violence per capita, testing quadratic curvature)
sample_definition: All 375 districts with non-missing values on fraud, violence, and control variables (electrified, pce_1000_07)
model_specification: Logistic regression with violence, violence², and controls; standard errors clustered at regional command level (4 clusters)
operationalization_notes: Replicated the paper's Model 1 specification: logit of the last-digit fraud indicator on election-day violence and its square, plus the same five controls. The z-test on the squared violence term directly tests the concavity required for an inverted U-shape, which is the core of Hypothesis 1.
reasoning: A logit regression of the binary fraud indicator on election-day violence and its squared term (plus controls), with standard errors clustered at the regional command level, yields a coefficient of -13.748 on the squared violence term (z = -2.499, p = 0.0125 two-sided). The negative quadratic coefficient indicates concavity, and the turning point (0.308) lies within the observed violence range (0–0.809), consistent with an inverted U-shape. The linear term is positive (8.477) as predicted but marginally non-significant with clustered SEs (p = 0.126). Overall, these results support the paper's claim of an inverted U-shaped relationship between violence and election fraud.

dependent_variable: Social undermining (willingness to be matched with co-participant, 1-7 scale where lower values indicate more undermining)

controls: None (experimental design with random assignment; the difference-score approach naturally controls for individual differences)
operationalization_notes: Used the difference-score approach to test the TSC × Competition interaction: each participant's TSC effect was computed as the difference in undermining between unfavorable and favorable TSC conditions, then this effect was compared across competition conditions using an independent samples t-test. This simplifies the multilevel structure of the within-subjects TSC factor while directly testing whether the TSC effect on undermining is stronger under high competition.
reasoning: The TSC × Competition interaction was significant (t = -3.38, df = 572, p = .0008). Under high competition, the mean difference in willingness to be matched between unfavorable and favorable TSC conditions was -0.70, compared to only -0.13 under low competition, indicating that unfavorable temporal social comparison leads to significantly more social undermining (i.e., lower willingness to be matched) when competition is high, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs (mean of 6 items: SpecCTs_1, SpecCTs_2, SpecCTs_3r, SpecCTs_4, SpecCTs_5, SpecCTs_6r)

operationalization_notes: The dataset only contained COVID1 (worry about COVID spread) and COVID3 (sense of threat) as predictor variables, along with 6 conspiracy belief items. reasoning: In a multiple OLS regression predicting COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs (6-item composite) from COVID1 (worry about COVID spread, proxy for anxiety/lack of control) and COVID3 (sense of threat, proxy for risk perception), the coefficient for worry was significantly negative (t(803) = -7.69, p < .001, standardized β = -0.40), indicating that higher worry about COVID spread is associated with fewer conspiracy beliefs—the opposite of the claim that anxiety/lack of control predicts an increase in conspiracy beliefs. The threat variable (COVID3) was positively associated with conspiracy beliefs (β = 0.21, p < .001), partially consistent with the risk perception aspect of the claim, but the core anxiety→conspiracy pathway runs counter to the predicted direction.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) to peripheral target letter
main_predictor: Valence of central face (angry vs neutral)

reasoning: A paired t-test comparing angry vs neutral face reaction times in the GAD group (n=63) yielded t(62) = 0.47, p = 0.64. The mean difference was 1.45 ms in the direction opposite to the claim (angry slightly slower than neutral: 486.81 ms vs 485.36 ms), and the effect is non-significant, providing no support for faster RTs to angry relative to neutral faces in GAD.

dependent_variable: Brand personality impressions (sophistication difference score: post-scenario minus pre-scenario ratings on 4 items)

The simple Consistency × PseudoInfo interaction within the high outcome dependency condition was also non-significant (F(1, 421) = 0.67, p = 0.41).

The paper's avoidance outcome covered six specific behaviors from a different survey instrument; the prep variable's avoidance-related items (4,5,6,8,9,10,11) were used as the closest approximation. Controls were limited to variables available in the replication data (age, gender, worry), as country of birth, employment, and health conditions were not available.

dependent_variable: CMMSRC (reverse-scored current money management stress, where higher = more positive/less stress)

Only participants marked as included (Include = 1) were analyzed, consistent with the codebook's exclusion criteria. This is a replication dataset with a larger sample than the original study.

This supports the original claim that the success frame reduces current money management stress relative to the failure frame.

dependent_variable: Situational Attribution Style (Sit_AttB)

This is the most direct test of the claim that the relationship between dispositional and situational attributions is highly significant when items are bidirectional. Robust standard errors (HC1) were used, consistent with the paper's use of RSE.

This confirms the claim that the effect of dispositional attributions on situational attributions is highly significant when items are formulated bidirectionally, consistent with the paper's finding of a significant negative relationship in the bidirectional condition.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE (Perceived Stress Scale-10)
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME (1-6 ordinal scale)
sample_definition: All participants with complete data on all model variables (N=2035 out of 2053, after excluding 18 with missing gender data)

operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 0 specification, the sociodemographic-only regression model directly tests the income-stress association. Monthly income is coded 1-6 (ordinal), and PSS-10 is the continuous perceived stress outcome. This is the model most directly tied to the claim about income and stress, as it precedes the addition of psychological trait variables.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting PSS-10 perceived stress scores from sociodemographic variables (age, gender, education, household members, monthly income), monthly income had a significant negative coefficient (B = -0.463, t = -3.465, p = 0.00054, 95% CI [-0.725, -0.201]), indicating that higher income is associated with lower perceived stress, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Mean composite of three nonmaterialistic behavioral inclinations (food desire, casual sex desire, desire for many social media friends)
main_predictor: DGS (Dispositional Greed Scale score)

model_specification: OLS multiple regression: behavioral inclination composite ~ DGS + MVS
operationalization_notes: Following Study 2's approach, the three nonmaterialistic behavioral inclinations were averaged into a composite DV. A multiple regression with both DGS and MVS as predictors directly tests whether DGS has incremental predictive validity over and above materialism. The t-test for the DGS coefficient in this model is the key test statistic.
