A simplified analysis using VIX intraday range as a crude proxy for market stress is possible but would not constitute a valid test of the liquidity claim, as VIX intraday range measures intraday VIX volatility rather than stock market liquidity.

dependent_variable: Size perception of the advertised sandwich on a 7-point scale (1 = 'much smaller than average' to 7 = 'much larger than average')
main_predictor: Pitch condition (Condition A vs. Condition B, corresponding to high-pitched vs. low-pitched voice in the radio advertisement)
sample_definition: All included participants from the cleaned dataset (615 of 985 total, after excluding those who failed attention checks, had incomplete responses, were duplicates, or had hearing impairments)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA with pitch condition as the independent factor and size perception as the dependent variable, consistent with the original Study 1 analysis
controls: None, matching the original Study 1 analysis which used a simple one-way ANOVA with no covariates
operationalization_notes: The analysis follows the paper's Study 1 methodology: a one-way ANOVA comparing size perceptions between two pitch conditions of a radio ad for a Cosmo's sandwich. The dataset appears to be a replication conducted at UNLV (not the original Study 1 data which had N=94). Condition B showed higher size ratings than Condition A, consistent with B being the low-pitch condition per the paper's prediction, but the effect was not statistically significant.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA comparing sandwich size perceptions between the two pitch conditions yielded F(1, 613) = 2.53, p = 0.112, which is not statistically significant at α = .05. The mean difference was in the direction predicted by the claim (Condition B: M = 5.21 vs. Condition A: M = 5.09, Cohen's d = 0.13), but the effect was small and non-significant, failing to replicate the original study's significant finding of F(1, 93) = 6.38, p < .05.

dependent_variable: Composite of four COVID-19 danger attitude measures: finitepool_2 (worry about coronavirus, 1-7), canadaq_1 (getting sick can be serious, 1-5), canadaq_2 (I will probably get sick, 1-5), canadaq_3 (COVID-19 will NOT affect many people, reverse-coded, 1-5)
main_predictor: Sex (1=female, 2=male)
sample_definition: Respondents aged 18+ residing in Spain with complete data on all four dependent variables (n=681; 346 female, 335 male)
model_specification: One-way MANOVA (Pillai's trace) with sex as the independent variable and four COVID-19 danger attitude measures as dependent variables, following the paper's analytic approach of using MANOVA with Pillai's trace
operationalization_notes: The original paper's nine specific 0-10 rating scale items (personal concern, social alarm, knowledge, control, compliance, stay home, hand washing, 1.5m distance, mask use) are not present in the replication dataset. I used the four available variables that best capture attitudes toward the dangers of the COVID-19 pandemic: worry about coronavirus, perceived seriousness of illness, perceived personal risk, and perceived scope of the pandemic (reverse-coded). This operationalization preserves the core construct of 'responsible attitudes toward dangers' while working with the available data.
reasoning: A MANOVA (Pillai's trace) testing the multivariate effect of sex on four COVID-19 danger attitude measures (worry about coronavirus, perceived seriousness of getting sick, perceived personal risk, and perceived scope of the pandemic) yielded a significant effect: Pillai's trace = 0.0425, F(4, 676) = 7.50, p < .001. Women scored higher than men on all four measures, consistent with the claim that women have more responsible attitudes toward the dangers of the COVID-19 pandemic.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 attack rate (cumulative confirmed cases per 100,000 population as of April 14, 2020)
main_predictor: Age-standardized prevalence of tobacco smoking among persons 15+ (2016 WHO data)
sample_definition: All 27 EU member states with available data on COVID-19 cases, deaths, population, and smoking prevalence
model_specification: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (non-parametric test for monotonic association), tested via t-approximation
controls: none (bivariate ecological correlation as in the original study)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods exactly: Spearman's rank correlation was used due to non-normality of data. COVID-19 data were aggregated by country from the replication dataset (summing cases across provinces/territories for France, Netherlands, and Denmark), then attack rate was computed as total confirmed cases / population × 100,000. The t-statistic was derived from the Spearman's rho using the formula t = rho × sqrt((n-2)/(1-rho²)).
reasoning: Spearman's rank correlation between age-standardized prevalence of tobacco smoking and COVID-19 attack rate across 27 EU member states was rho = -0.476 (t = -2.70, df = 25, p = 0.012), indicating a statistically significant negative correlation. This supports the claim that countries with higher smoking prevalence tend to have lower COVID-19 attack rates, consistent with the original study's finding.

dependent_variable: Computer and Information Literacy (CIL) score (mean of 5 plausible values PV1CIL–PV5CIL)
main_predictor: Student sex (S_SEX: 0=Boy, 1=Girl)
sample_definition: All Korean students in the ICILS 2018 dataset with valid sex and CIL plausible values (N=2,875; 1,497 boys and 1,378 girls)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (two-sided), comparing mean CIL score between female and male students
operationalization_notes: The CIL score was computed as the average of the 5 plausible values provided in ICILS 2018. A simple independent samples t-test was chosen as the most direct test of the directional claim about gender differences in ICT literacy scores. This parallels the paper's Model 2 HLM (which added gender as the first individual-level predictor), though without the multilevel structure or additional covariates.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing CIL scores between female (mean=559.19) and male (mean=520.10) students shows that female students score significantly higher than male students by 39.09 points (t(2873)=11.65, p<0.001), consistent with the paper's claim that female students' ICT literacy scores are higher than male students'.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 responsible behavior (mean of 5 behavioral items: avoiding physical contact, washing hands, avoiding going out, coughing/sneezing in elbow, wearing mask)
main_predictor: COVID-19 worry (single item on 1-7 scale asking how worried participants are for themselves and their family)
sample_definition: Participants with complete data on all key variables (behavior, worry, unfounded beliefs, knowledge, anxiety, CRT, AOT, faith in intuition, science curiosity); n = 550
model_specification: OLS multiple regression predicting behavior from worry, unfounded beliefs, knowledge, anxiety, cognitive reflection, AOT, faith in intuition, and science curiosity, approximating the structural portion of the paper's SEM
controls: Unfounded beliefs (mean of conspiracy + treatment beliefs), COVID-19 knowledge (mean of 6 items), trait anxiety (mean of 4 items), cognitive reflection (mean of 3 CRT items), actively open-minded thinking (mean of 9 AOT items with reverse coding), faith in intuition (mean of 5 items), science curiosity (standardized mean of 5 science-related items)
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary analysis is an SEM where worry predicts behavior while controlling for unfounded beliefs, knowledge, and individual differences. I approximated this with an OLS regression using composite scores instead of latent variables, since the dataset is a replication sample (~550 participants) rather than the original Croatian sample (~962 in SEM). The worry variable is a single observed item as in the paper. The worry→behavior path is the direct test of the claim.
reasoning: A multiple regression predicting COVID-19 responsible behavior from worry, controlling for unfounded beliefs, knowledge, anxiety, cognitive reflection, actively open-minded thinking, faith in intuition, and science curiosity (approximating the paper's SEM structural model), yielded a positive and highly significant worry coefficient (b = 0.221, standardized β = 0.418, t(541) = 9.91, p < 0.001). This confirms the paper's claim that greater worry about COVID-19 leads to more responsible COVID-19 behavior.

dependent_variable: Leadership experiences (Leader_Exp_Total)
main_predictor: Openness to experiences (Oppenness_Total)
sample_definition: All participants in the Popper Data for Correlations dataset with non-missing values on both openness to experiences and leadership experiences (N=215)
model_specification: Pearson bivariate correlation with t-test for significance
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns a positive relation between openness to experiences and leadership experiences. The most direct test is the bivariate Pearson correlation, matching the zero-order correlation reported in Table 1 of the paper. The analysis uses the pre-computed total scores from the 'Popper Data for Correlations.csv' file.
reasoning: A Pearson correlation between openness to experiences and leadership experiences yielded r = 0.2198, which is positive and statistically significant (t(213) = 3.29, p = .001). This confirms the paper's claim of a positive relation between openness to experiences and leadership experiences, consistent with the paper's reported correlation of .26**.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 confirmed cases per million people (as of April 3, 2020)
main_predictor: Democracy Index (EIU, 0-100 scale)
sample_definition: All 150 countries in the replication dataset with complete data on all variables
model_specification: OLS linear regression with constant (replicating the paper's Model 1, no lag)
controls: Annual average temperature, international trade openness (% of GDP)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 1 specification, the dependent variable is computed as COVID cases divided by population times one million. The three predictors (temperature, openness, democracy) match the paper's final model after they excluded insignificant variables (precipitation, population density). The t-statistic for the democracy coefficient directly tests the directional claim.
reasoning: The OLS regression of COVID-19 cases per million (as of April 3, 2020) on democracy index, controlling for annual temperature and trade openness, yields a positive and highly significant coefficient for democracy (t = 4.41, p < 0.001). This confirms the claim that the number of confirmed COVID-19 cases is higher in countries with stronger political democracy.

dependent_variable: Hoax beliefs (1 = definitely not a hoax to 6 = definitely a hoax)
main_predictor: CRT proportion correct (proportion of 7 Cognitive Reflection Test items answered correctly)
sample_definition: All participants who passed the attention check (end = 'complete'), excluding those who failed the attention check (end = 'att_fail' or 'non-binary')
model_specification: Bivariate Pearson correlation between CRT proportion correct and hoax belief rating, with associated t-test
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's primary analysis method: CRT was scored as proportion correct across 7 items (3 original Frederick items + 4 Thomson & Oppenheimer non-numeric items), and hoax beliefs were measured on a 1-6 scale. The bivariate correlation is the most direct test of the claim that lower analytic thinking predicts higher hoax beliefs. All complete cases from both waves were included to maximize power and generalizability.
reasoning: The bivariate Pearson correlation between CRT proportion correct and hoax beliefs was r = -0.119, t(2138) = -5.55, p < 0.001, indicating that individuals with lower analytic-thinking scores were significantly more likely to believe the COVID-19 pandemic was a hoax. This supports the same directional conclusion as the original study, though the effect size is considerably weaker (r = -0.12 vs. the paper's reported r = -0.46).

dependent_variable: Containment-related behavior (mean of Q2_1-Q2_6: disinfecting hands, avoiding social contacts, washing hands, avoiding crowds, not touching face, staying home)
main_predictor: COVID-19 hoax belief (mean of Q2_18, Q2_19, reverse-coded Q2_20)
sample_definition: All 104 observations with complete data on the key variables (no exclusion criteria beyond missing data)
model_specification: OLS linear regression with containment-related behavior regressed on hoax belief, human-made belief, and political orientation
controls: Human-made conspiracy belief (mean of Q2_21, Q2_22, reverse-coded Q2_23) and political orientation (Q21, 1=extremely liberal to 7=extremely conservative)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 analysis, the dependent variable is containment-related behavior (items identified from the factor analysis in Table 1), the main predictor is the hoax belief scale, and the model simultaneously includes human-made belief and political orientation as covariates. Items Q2_7 and Q2_8 were excluded from the containment scale per the paper's note about cross-loading items.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting containment-related behavior (mean of 6 items: hand disinfecting, avoiding social contacts, hand washing, avoiding crowds, not touching face, staying home) from hoax belief (mean of 3 items), human-made belief, and political orientation, hoax belief was a significant negative predictor: B = -0.278, t(100) = -3.41, p = .001. This supports the claim that believing COVID-19 is a hoax is inversely related to containment-related behaviors.

dependent_variable: Rehearsal strategies (mean of REH_1–REH_4 from MSLQ)
main_predictor: Mastery-approach orientation (mean of MAp_1–MAp_3 from AGQ)
sample_definition: Participants who passed both attention checks (ATTN_1=1, ATTN_2=7) and had complete data on all goal orientation and rehearsal items (N=978)
model_specification: OLS multiple regression with all four achievement goal orientations (mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) as simultaneous predictors of rehearsal strategy use
controls: Mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goal orientations
operationalization_notes: The original paper used SEM with latent variables where achievement goals simultaneously predicted learning strategies. The multiple regression with observed composite scores is the closest OLS equivalent, testing whether MAp predicts rehearsal while controlling for other goal orientations, consistent with the SEM framework. Composite scores were computed as item means.
reasoning: A multiple regression with all four achievement goal orientations predicting rehearsal strategies revealed that mastery-approach orientation was a significant positive predictor (b = 0.327, t(973) = 9.368, p < .001), supporting the original study's claim that mastery-approach orientation positively predicts the use of rehearsal strategies. The bivariate correlation was also positive and significant (r = .324, p < .001).

dependent_variable: PANAS affect scores (positive and negative subscale means, per item on 1-5 scale)
main_predictor: Block type (progressive vs. stagnant)
sample_definition: All 346 participants in Stage 1 with complete data across both blocks and both PANAS subscales; one participant with duplicate rows was deduplicated by keeping first occurrence
model_specification: 2 (Block: progressive vs. stagnant) × 2 (Scale Valence: positive vs. negative) repeated-measures ANOVA, testing the Block × Valence interaction
controls: None (within-subjects design where participants serve as their own controls)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's reported analysis method, I tested the Block × Scale Valence interaction using a repeated-measures ANOVA. The interaction tests whether the effect of block type differs for positive vs. negative affect, which is the direct statistical test of whether progressive processing yields 'relatively better moods.' I used mean PANAS item responses per subscale as the paper describes analyzing 'participants' mean responses to the positive and negative affect scales.'
reasoning: A 2×2 repeated-measures ANOVA (Block × Scale Valence) on Stage 1 data yielded a non-significant Block × Valence interaction, F(1, 345) = 0.004, p = .948. The mean difference in mood (positive minus negative affect) between progressive and stagnant blocks was negligible (0.003 on a per-item scale, Cohen's d = 0.004). There is no evidence that progressive processing results in better moods than stagnant processing.

dependent_variable: Canadachoice (binary: 1 = chose Canadian/system-supporting brand, 0 = chose international brand)
main_predictor: Interaction of HighLowThreat × mean-centered SystemJustification
sample_definition: Participants in the indirect system support condition (DirectIndirectsystemsupport = 0), all observations with complete data
model_specification: Logistic regression: Canadachoice ~ HighLowThreat + MeansCentered + HighLowThreat × MeansCentered
controls: None (consistent with the paper's Study 1 analysis)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 approach, I tested the interaction between threat condition (high vs. low threat) and system confidence (continuous, mean-centered) on choosing an indirect system-supporting product. The indirect condition was selected because the claim specifically focuses on individuals seeking consumption choices that allow them to 'indirectly' defend the system. System justification was computed from 8 items (Q3_1-Q3_8, with pro-system items reverse-coded) so higher scores indicate greater confidence in the system.
reasoning: The logistic regression interaction between threat condition and mean-centered system justification on choosing an indirect system-supporting product was not statistically significant (Z = -0.945, p = 0.345, N = 245). While the direction of the interaction was consistent with the claim (negative, meaning threat increases system-supporting choices more for low-confidence individuals), the effect was not significant. The simple effect of threat at -1 SD of system confidence was also non-significant (Z = 1.503, p = 0.133). The data do not provide statistically significant support for the claim that low system-confidence individuals seek indirect consumption choices to defend the system when it is threatened.

dependent_variable: Proportion of correctly identified competition winners (out of 8 trials)
main_predictor: Visual-only condition (tested against chance level of 1/3 for 3-alternative forced choice)
sample_definition: All participants in the Visual-only condition (N=96) from the between-subjects replication data across both phases
model_specification: One-sample t-test against chance level (1/3)
operationalization_notes: The core of the claim that novices can select winners through visual cues alone was tested by comparing Visual condition accuracy against chance (33.3%), matching the paper's primary analytical approach of one-sample t-tests against chance for each condition. The Visual condition data combines both phases of data collection.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test comparing Visual condition accuracy (M=0.350, SD=0.147) against chance level (1/3=0.333) was not significant, t(95)=1.13, p=0.26, Cohen's d=0.12. Visual performance was not significantly above chance, nor significantly different from Audio (M=0.309, p=0.17) or Audiovisual (M=0.340, p=0.75) conditions. The data does not support the claim that novices can identify competition winners through visual cues alone.

dependent_variable: toned (desire for toned and defined muscles, 0-4 scale)
main_predictor: age (continuous, 18-25 years)
sample_definition: Males aged 18-25 who completed the survey, consented, and passed the attention check (N=2438 from phase 2 data, which includes all phase 1 participants plus additional recruits)
model_specification: OLS regression with heteroscedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors, modeling toned as a function of age, sexuality_cat (3 levels: heterosexual [reference], mostly_heterosexual, gay_bisexual), geographic region, and weight status
controls: sexual orientation (3 categories), geographic region (13 categories), weight status (3 categories)
operationalization_notes: The original paper measured 'desire for bigger muscles' (ages 9-19), which is not available in this dataset. The closest available variable is 'desire for toned/defined muscles' (ages 18-25). In the original study, these were distinct constructs with different developmental trajectories (bigger muscles increased with age; toned muscles did not). The analysis follows the paper's modeling approach (GEE adapted to cross-sectional OLS with robust SEs, controlling for geographic region and weight status, testing and dropping non-significant age × sexual orientation interactions). The non-significant negative age effect contradicts the claim of increasing muscularity desires with age, though this may partly reflect the construct and age-range mismatch.
reasoning: Testing whether muscularity desires increase with age using the available 'desire for toned/defined muscles' variable (closest proxy for 'desire for bigger muscles'), OLS regression with robust SEs yielded a non-significant negative age coefficient (β = -0.013, t(2420) = -1.51, p = 0.13), which does not support the claim of an increase. The age × sexual orientation interaction was non-significant (F(2, 2418) = 0.17, p = 0.85), consistent with the 'regardless of sexual orientation' part of the claim. However, the available outcome variable (toned/defined muscles) differs from the original construct (bigger muscles), which showed distinct developmental trajectories in the original study.

dependent_variable: Relationship satisfaction (PRQC mean score across 18 items)
main_predictor: Partner's ideal discrepancies on warmth/trustworthiness (partner's rating of how well the actor matches the partner's ideals, 6-item mean)
sample_definition: 233 heterosexual couples (466 individuals), excluding 26 same-sex couples from the 259 total couples in the dataset
model_specification: APIM multilevel model (MixedLM with REML) predicting actor satisfaction from actor ideal discrepancies, partner ideal discrepancies, and sex (effect coded: men=1, women=-1), with dyad as the grouping variable
controls: Actor's ideal discrepancies on warmth/trustworthiness, participant sex (effect coded)
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's APIM approach, I computed scale scores from raw items matching the Partner Ideal Scales and PRQC, restricted to heterosexual couples, grand-mean centered predictors, and tested the partner effect on the warmth/trustworthiness dimension—the most theoretically central dimension in the ideal standards model and the dimension showing the strongest effects in the original study.
reasoning: Using APIM with multilevel modeling on the warmth/trustworthiness dimension, the partner effect of ideal discrepancies on relationship satisfaction was significant and positive (z = 6.677, p < 0.001, standardized β = 0.208). This confirms that individuals whose partners rate them as less closely matching their ideals report lower relationship satisfaction, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Creativity
main_predictor: Intrinsic motivation
sample_definition: All 67 independent samples from the meta-analysis dataset that reported a correlation between intrinsic motivation and creativity
model_specification: Random-effects meta-analysis using Fisher's z transformation with DerSimonian-Laird estimator for tau-squared, testing whether the meta-analytic mean correlation differs from zero
operationalization_notes: The paper's core claim about intrinsic motivation being positively related to creativity is a bivariate relationship, so the most direct test is a meta-analytic test of the mean correlation across all available studies. I used the liu.csv data file which contains 67 studies with IM-creativity correlations and sample sizes. A random-effects model was chosen due to substantial heterogeneity (I²=93.2%), and Fisher's z transformation was used to properly handle the sampling distribution of correlations.
reasoning: A random-effects meta-analysis of 67 independent samples (N=19,290) using Fisher's z transformation yielded a weighted mean correlation of r=0.285 between intrinsic motivation and creativity (z=10.38, p<0.001, 95% CI [0.23, 0.34]), strongly supporting the claim that intrinsic motivation is positively related to creativity.

dependent_variable: Organizational citizenship behavior (OCB), composite of 4 supervisor-rated subscales (Sportsmanship, Civic Virtue, Courtesy, Altruism)
main_predictor: Operant leadership (4 dimensions: Contingent Reward, Contingent Punishment, Non-contingent Reward, Non-contingent Punishment)
sample_definition: 167 employee-supervisor dyads with complete data on all study variables, after removing one outlier for tenure (>50 years) and excluding 3 cases with missing tenure data
model_specification: OLS regression F-test comparing full mediation model (OCB regressed on Trust + controls only) vs partial mediation model (OCB regressed on Trust + all 4 operant leadership dimensions + controls), following Baron & Kenny mediation framework
controls: Tenure with leader (years), Organizational level (1-3 scale)
operationalization_notes: The F-test directly evaluates whether the 4 direct paths from operant leadership to OCB are jointly zero (full mediation) vs non-zero (partial mediation). Composites were created per the paper's measurement model: CR from 10 items (2 reverse-coded), CP from 5 items, NCP from 4 items, NCR from 4 items, Trust from 6 items (1 reverse-coded), OCB as average of 4 subscale means. The paper's original test used SEM chi-square difference (Δχ²=7.76[4], ns), but our F-test on the observed composites rejects full mediation (F=14.85, p<.001), primarily due to NCP's persistent direct effect on OCB.
reasoning: The F-test comparing the full mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + controls, with direct effects of operant leadership constrained to zero) versus the partial mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + CR + CP + NCR + NCP + controls) yields F(4,159) = 14.85, p < .001, strongly rejecting full mediation. Non-contingent punishment retains a significant direct effect on OCB (β = -0.218, t = -4.44, p < .001) even after controlling for Trust, contradicting the claim that trust fully mediates the relationship.

dependent_variable: PASAverage (Prostitution Attitudes Scale score; higher = more favorable attitudes toward prostitution)
main_predictor: WritingCondition (0 = dental pain control, 1 = mortality salience/death)
sample_definition: European American participants (EuropeanAmerican=1) with non-missing PASAverage values
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variance) comparing PASAverage between mortality-salience and control conditions
operationalization_notes: The claim specifically concerns the simple effect of mortality salience on prostitution attitudes among European Americans. The PAS score is the primary DV from Study 1, with higher scores reflecting more favorable attitudes. The claim predicts lower PAS in the MS condition, but the data show a non-significant trend in the opposite direction.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing PAS scores (higher = more favorable attitudes toward prostitution) between mortality-salience (M=1.37, SD=1.41, n=92) and control (M=1.27, SD=1.29, n=101) conditions among European Americans yielded t(191)=0.56, p=.58. The non-significant difference was in the opposite direction from the claim: the mortality-salience condition showed slightly more favorable (not more negative) attitudes toward prostitution.

dependent_variable: log mean mortality rate (log of country-level mean daily increase in COVID-19 deaths during the ascending phase)
main_predictor: International Arrivals (millions, 2018)
sample_definition: 37 countries reporting at least 25 COVID-related deaths with available data for all chosen determinants, as specified in the original study
model_specification: OLS multivariable linear regression with 11 predictors plus intercept
controls: log population, air pollution, mean temperature, population density, prevalent neoplasms, prevalent hypertension, WHO health index, urban population %, GDP per capita, mean stringency index
operationalization_notes: Used Data_for_Replication.csv filtered to the 37 study countries. The original paper's model included 14 predictors; 3 (BCG vaccination coverage, UV radiation, % population aged 65+) were not available in the provided data files and were omitted. The mean stringency index was computed from the daily stringency index data (covid.stringency.index.final.csv) averaged over the period through 08/06/2020.
reasoning: In a multivariable OLS regression predicting log mean mortality rate from international arrivals and 10 control variables across 37 countries, the coefficient for international arrivals was 0.030 (SE=0.012), yielding t(25)=2.571, p=0.016. This positive, statistically significant effect supports the claim that greater international arrivals predicts greater COVID-19 severity, consistent with the paper's reported multivariable coefficient of 0.033 (p=0.003).

dependent_variable: Contribution to the shared account (points, 0-125 endowment)
main_predictor: Outcome prospect condition (losses-and-gains vs. no-variance + gains-only, within-subjects)
sample_definition: All 320 participants who completed all 4 rounds of the threshold public goods game (endowment=125, threshold=300), from sessions mccarta_feele, mccarta_qualtrics, and mccarta_prolific
model_specification: Paired t-test (within-subjects) comparing each participant's mean contribution across losses-and-gains rounds [(0,1200) and (200,1000) bonuses] vs. non-losses rounds [600 and (400,800) bonuses]
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Hypothesis 2 test, contributions in losses-and-gains conditions (where the minimum possible per-person return from the public good falls below the average required individual contribution of 75) were compared against contributions in the combined no-variance and gains-only conditions. The losses column in the data already encodes this classification. The paired t-test is equivalent to the repeated-measures ANOVA contrast (F with 1 numerator df) reported in the original paper.
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing each participant's mean contribution in losses-and-gains rounds (M=73.20) vs. non-losses rounds (M=73.75) yielded t(319) = -0.578, p = 0.564. While the direction favors the hypothesis (slightly lower contributions in loss-prospect conditions), the difference is trivially small and far from statistical significance, failing to reproduce the original study's finding of F(1,61) = 4.73, p < .05.

dependent_variable: HP-detrended intercounty migration rate (HPmigration)
main_predictor: Standardized standard deviation of state employment gaps (StateEmploymentGapz)
sample_definition: Annual US data from 1948-2009, excluding years with missing CPS migration data (1972-75, 1977-80, 1995)
model_specification: OLS regression of HP-detrended migration rate on standardized national employment gap and standardized SD of state employment gaps
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 1 column 2 specification, which tests whether dispersion in local economic conditions (measured as the cross-state SD of employment gaps) is related to migration after controlling for the national business cycle. The employment gap is the only business cycle measure available in the provided data. The dependent variable is the cyclical component from an HP filter applied to the intercounty migration rate.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of the HP-detrended intercounty migration rate on the standardized national employment gap and the standardized SD of state employment gaps (1948-2009, excluding 1995), the coefficient on the dispersion measure (StateEmploymentGapz) is 0.144 with SE 0.092, yielding t(50) = 1.56, p = 0.125. This is not significant at conventional levels, confirming the paper's claim that dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to migration.

dependent_variable: Mean response latency (seconds) for detecting when anger disappeared from the face in the angry-to-neutral transition
main_predictor: Target age (old vs young) for White faces
sample_definition: All participants who had valid data for both old White and young White angry-to-neutral conditions. Trials were excluded if: response was a quit command (Ctrl+Q), latency was ≤0, <0.5s (anticipatory), or >17s (beyond movie duration). Latencies were averaged across the two exemplar faces per condition per participant.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing mean response latency for old White vs young White faces in the angry-to-neutral (transition type 3) condition
operationalization_notes: The claim mentions both 'anger lasting longer' and 'appearing sooner' on old vs young White faces. I focused on the 'anger lasting longer' component, operationalized as the angry-to-neutral transition where a longer latency indicates the participant perceived anger as persisting longer. A paired t-test directly comparing old vs young White faces was chosen as the most direct test of the claim, consistent with the paper's simple effects analysis approach.
reasoning: A paired-samples t-test on the angry-to-neutral transition showed that participants perceived anger as lasting significantly longer on old White faces (M = 11.75s, SD = 1.93s) compared to young White faces (M = 10.48s, SD = 2.17s), t(54) = 4.87, p < .001, d = 0.66. This replicates the original study's finding that anger is perceived as lasting longer on old compared to young White faces.

dependent_variable: Not following social distancing (binary: keep_distance ≤ 4, where keep_distance is 'I keep my distance from other people as much as possible' on a 1-7 scale)
main_predictor: Male (1 = male, 0 = female)
sample_definition: All respondents in the replication dataset with complete data on all analysis variables (N = 3,892), including both survey rounds
model_specification: Logistic regression (logit model) with Wald z-test for the male coefficient
controls: Age categories (20-29, 30-39, 50-59, 60+, ref: 40-49), marital status (not married), children under 18 (none), education (junior high/high school), employment (non-regular, self-employed, not working; ref: regular employee), household income categories (ref: 4,000-5,999K JPY), smoking habit, Big 5 personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness)
operationalization_notes: The paper's original DV was a binary indicator of not avoiding the 'three overlapping Ms' (closed spaces, crowded places, close-contact settings), which was not available as a single variable in the dataset. I used keep_distance ('I keep my distance from other people as much as possible') as the most direct measure of social distancing behavior, dichotomized at ≤4 (midpoint or below = not following). The model specification follows the paper's logit approach with similar controls, though the drinking habit variable was not available in the replication data.
reasoning: A logistic regression predicting not following social distancing (keep_distance ≤ 4 on a 1–7 scale) found that being male significantly increases the odds of not following social distancing (z = 6.80, p < 0.001, OR = 2.31, 95% CI: 1.82–2.95), controlling for age, marital status, children, education, employment, household income, smoking, and Big 5 personality traits. This strongly supports the claim that men have a lower likelihood of following social distancing, consistent with the original study's finding (OR = 1.635 for male).

dependent_variable: Preference for part-time work (Prefs_1, 1-5 scale)
main_predictor: Cluster membership (satisficer, free agent, maximizer) derived from Ward's hierarchical clustering on 24 desire items
sample_definition: Participants who were age 40+, currently seeking employment, completed the survey, passed both attention checks (Know_8=5, Social_12=1), and had ≤20 identical consecutive responses (SameResponse ≤ 20), yielding N=730
model_specification: One-way ANOVA with cluster membership as the grouping variable and part-time preference as the dependent variable
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's two-stage clustering approach, Ward's hierarchical method was used on standardized desire items to identify 3 clusters matching the paper's profiles. The hierarchical solution (rather than K-means) was retained as it produced cluster proportions closely matching the original (24.8%, 19.3%, 55.9% vs. 26.6%, 16.8%, 56.6%) and cluster patterns consistent with satisficers, free agents, and maximizers. Standard data quality filters were applied (attention checks, extreme same-response exclusion).
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA testing whether three clusters (satisficers, free agents, maximizers) differed in their preference for part-time work yielded F(2, 727) = 0.92, p = .398, with negligible effect size (η² = .0025). Group means were very similar: satisficers M = 2.86, free agents M = 2.65, maximizers M = 2.74. dependent_variable: Utilitarian score (0–2, sum of two binary moral acceptability items: moral_accept and moral_accept1, each coded as 1 for morally acceptable/utilitarian and 0 for not)
main_predictor: Salience condition (death vs. pain)
sample_definition: Participants who consented (Q1=2), passed the attention check (attn='c' or 'C'), and had satisfactory manipulation responses (satisfactory_manipulation_response1=1), yielding N=129 (62 death, 67 pain)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variance) comparing mean utilitarian score between death and pain salience conditions
operationalization_notes: The composite utilitarian score sums utilitarian responses across both moral scenarios. The paper's original experiments used t-tests comparing utilitarian response rates between mortality salience and control conditions, so an independent samples t-test on the composite score is the most direct analog. Exclusions followed the codebook criteria for attention and manipulation quality checks.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing composite utilitarian scores (sum of two binary moral acceptability items) between mortality salience (death) and control (pain) conditions found no significant effect, t(127) = 0.43, p = 0.67. The death condition (M = 1.76) was slightly but non-significantly MORE utilitarian than the pain condition (M = 1.72), opposite to the predicted direction. The claim that thinking about death makes people less utilitarian is not supported by this dataset.

dependent_variable: IntAssocM (mean reaction time for interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations, where faster RTs indicate stronger associations)
main_predictor: Interaction of mental contrasting condition dummy × expectations of success
sample_definition: Participants with no outliers on IntAssoc and IntAccess (IntAssocObs=0, IntAccessObs=0) and complete data on all analysis variables (n=313)
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression with F-change test: Step 1 entered expectations of success, accessibility of the behavior, and two dummy codes for condition (MC vs RC reference, ICC vs RC reference); Step 2 added two interaction terms (expectations × MC dummy, expectations × ICC dummy)
controls: IntAccessM (accessibility of the interpersonal instrumental behavior), expectations of success (IntExp), condition dummies (Dummy_MC, Dummy_ICC)
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's analytic approach for Study 1, focusing on the interpersonal domain (the elaborated concern) where the original study found significant expectancy-dependent obstacle-behavior associations. The F-change test for adding the condition × expectations interaction terms is the primary test reported in the original paper for this claim.
reasoning: The hierarchical regression F-change test for the interaction between condition and expectations on interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations was not significant (F(2,306) = 0.81, p = .45). The simple slope of expectations in the mental contrasting condition was also non-significant (β = -10.65, t(115) = -0.83, p = .41), indicating no evidence that mental contrasting paired with low expectations leads to weak obstacle-behavior associations in the replication data.

dependent_variable: s (proportion of the surplus the dictator gives away)
main_predictor: xl (libertarian share: proportion of the surplus the dictator should give away under the libertarian principle)
sample_definition: All dictators in the DW treatment (piece_rate=150, partner_piece_rate=200) from the cleaned dataset with valid s and x values
model_specification: Wilcoxon signed-rank test on deviations (s - xl) from the libertarian principle, testing H0: median(s - xl) = 0
operationalization_notes: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test directly tests whether dictators' actual giving systematically differs from the libertarian prediction. Under the DW treatment, the libertarian principle dictates that the dictator should give away the recipient's monetary contribution proportion (xl). Rejecting H0 that median(s-xl)=0 means the libertarian principle fails to account for observed behavior. This non-parametric test is appropriate given the non-normal distribution of deviations and is consistent with the paper's analytic approach.
reasoning: The Wilcoxon signed-rank test on deviations (s - xl) from the libertarian principle yields z = -3.38, p = 0.0007, strongly rejecting H0 that the libertarian principle accounts for observed behavior under the DW treatment. Of 27 dictators, 16 gave less than the libertarian share (s < xl), only 2 gave more, and 9 matched exactly. The negative z indicates dictators systematically give away less than the libertarian principle predicts, confirming the claim.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological (rejecting harm) judgments
main_predictor: Condition (OBS vs CON) × DilemmaType interaction
sample_definition: All participants with complete data on RH_PMD, RH_NMD, and RH_CMD (N=156; 78 per condition), excluding 4 participants with missing values
model_specification: 2 (Condition: observed vs control) × 3 (DilemmaType: personal, impersonal, non-moral) mixed ANOVA with Condition as between-subjects factor and DilemmaType as within-subjects factor
operationalization_notes: The claim that observation promotes deontological judgments 'especially for' personal moral dilemmas implies a Condition × DilemmaType interaction, making the mixed ANOVA interaction the most direct test. RH_PMD, RH_NMD, and RH_CMD represent the proportion of deontological responses for personal moral, non-personal (impersonal) moral, and control (non-moral) dilemmas respectively, following the study's design and codebook definitions.
reasoning: The Condition × DilemmaType interaction in the mixed ANOVA was non-significant (F(2, 308) = 0.237, p = 0.789, η²p = 0.0015), indicating no evidence that social observation differentially promotes deontological judgments for personal moral dilemmas. The simple effect of observation on personal moral dilemmas was also non-significant (t(154) = 0.784, p = 0.435, d = 0.13).

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (COVID-19 worry/concern, 5-point Likert scale)
main_predictor: gender (female vs. male)
sample_definition: All respondents with valid binary gender (female=0 or 1), excluding 121 respondents with gender=3 (non-binary/other)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variance assumed)
operationalization_notes: The mh_anxiety_1 variable was used as the primary concern/worry measure about COVID-19, consistent with the reproduction benchmark (matching t=8.2527). The paper claims women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men; this variable directly captures COVID-19 worry/concern on a 5-point Likert scale. Non-binary respondents (gender=3, n=121) were excluded as the claim specifically compares women and men.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing women (M=3.0748, SD=1.1091, n=4933) and men (M=2.8896, SD=1.1411, n=5138) on the COVID-19 concern measure (mh_anxiety_1) yielded t(10069)=8.2527, p<.001, with Cohen's d=0.1645. Women scored significantly higher on COVID-19 concern than men, supporting the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Percentage-point change in county mobility (% not staying at home, March 19–28 minus Feb 20–29, 2020)
main_predictor: County-level Trump vote share in 2016
sample_definition: U.S. counties with non-missing data on mobility change, Trump vote share, income per capita, demographic, education, industry, and rurality variables (N = 3,114 of 3,142 counties)
model_specification: OLS regression with state fixed effects, controlling for county-level sociodemographic characteristics
controls: Income per capita, percent male, percent Black, percent Hispanic, percent with college degree, percent employed in retail, percent employed in transportation, percent employed in health/education/social services, percent rural, age distribution (13 decade-of-life percentages), and state fixed effects (50 dummies)
operationalization_notes: The original paper used Unacast cell-phone data measuring distance traveled per person; the replication dataset provides BTS trips-by-distance data instead. I constructed a comparable mobility measure as the percentage-point change in the share of population not staying at home (pop_not_home / (pop_home + pop_not_home)) averaged over March 19–28, 2020 minus the same metric averaged over matched pre-COVID days (Feb 20–29, 2020). The regression specification follows the paper's Table 1 model with state fixed effects and IQR-scaled predictors (scaling does not affect t-statistics).
reasoning: In an OLS regression with state fixed effects and sociodemographic controls, the coefficient on Trump vote share was positive and highly significant (t = 4.70, p < 0.001), indicating that counties with greater Republican orientation showed less reduction in mobility (i.e., less social distancing) during March 19–28, 2020, relative to a pre-COVID reference period. This replicates the original study's finding that greater Republican political orientation was associated with reduced social distancing.

dependent_variable: Social distancing (composite of 4 items: avoided social gatherings, avoided groups of 10+, maintained 6ft distance, followed government guidelines; 1-6 scale)
main_predictor: Political conservatism (composite of 3 items: conservative views, liberal [reverse-scored], favor Republican party; 1-6 scale)
sample_definition: All 322 observations in the final dataset (US residents who passed attention check and were not diagnosed with COVID-19)
model_specification: Simple OLS regression (total effect / bivariate relationship), matching the paper's first step of mediation analysis testing Hypothesis 1
controls: None (testing total/bivariate effect as the most direct test of the claim)
operationalization_notes: The paper explicitly tests the claim 'political conservatism inversely predicted compliance with social distancing' as the total effect from a simple regression (first step of mediation), reporting B = -.20, p < .001 (Study 1) and B = -.11, p = .012 (Study 2). The available dataset lacks the mediator variables (perceived health risk, media accuracy, well-informed), so the simple regression of social distancing on conservatism is the most direct and appropriate test of the claim.
reasoning: A simple OLS regression of social distancing on conservatism yielded a significant inverse relationship (B = -0.135, t(320) = -3.26, p = .001, r = -.18), consistent with the paper's claim that political conservatism inversely predicted social distancing compliance. The effect is small in magnitude (R² = .03) but statistically reliable, replicating the paper's reported total effects in both Studies 1 and 2.

dependent_variable: Average perceived societal good across four organizational scenarios (1=great harm to 5=great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition (For-Profit vs. Non-Profit vs. Unspecified)
sample_definition: Participants who completed the survey (Finished=1), gave consent (Consent=1), and had no missing data on the four societal good ratings and condition variable (N=364)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA with three between-subjects groups, testing the main effect of firm motive condition on the average societal good rating across four scenarios
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 3 approach, the analysis tests the main effect of firm motive condition (For-Profit, Non-Profit, Unspecified) on perceived societal good, averaged across the four within-subject scenarios. The one-way ANOVA on subject means is equivalent to the between-subjects main effect in the mixed repeated-measures ANOVA reported in the original paper. Condition 1=Non-Profit, 2=Unspecified, 3=For-Profit per the data dictionary.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA on average perceived societal good across four scenarios found a significant main effect of condition (firm motive), F(2, 361) = 36.91, p < .001, ηp² = .170. The For-Profit condition had the lowest perceived societal good (M = 3.75, SD = 0.58), compared to Non-Profit (M = 4.31, SD = 0.43) and Unspecified (M = 4.09, SD = 0.53), confirming that the profit motive reduced the perceived societal good accomplished by the firm.

dependent_variable: Sharing intentions (1-6 Likert scale, averaged across headlines per participant separately for true and false headlines)
main_predictor: Headline veracity (true vs false)
sample_definition: Participants in the treatment condition (Condition=2) from the replication dataset, including all participants regardless of attentiveness following the paper's main analysis approach
model_specification: Paired t-test comparing participant-level average sharing intentions for true vs false headlines within the treatment condition
operationalization_notes: The original study 2 data file appeared to contain Qualtrics test/pilot data (uniform response distributions, no discernment), so the replication dataset was used instead. The paired t-test is the most direct test of the claim that true headlines receive higher sharing intentions than false headlines within the treatment condition, and is equivalent to the OLS regression approach with clustered SEs used in the paper.
reasoning: A paired t-test within the treatment condition (N=790) comparing average sharing intentions for true headlines (M=3.15) versus false headlines (M=2.89) yielded t(789)=9.33, p<.001, Cohen's d=0.33. This confirms the original study's claim that sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines in the treatment condition.

dependent_variable: Evaluation of toaster (mean of 5 items: interested, likely, confident, happy, general feeling; scale 1-7)
main_predictor: Information type (within-subjects: 4.5-star toaster favored by aggregated info vs. 2.5-star toaster favored by individualized info)
sample_definition: Participants in the abstract sound condition (group 5: C-F# harmonies, reverberation, nonsegmented/measure-1) who passed the filter (no technical/hearing problems), yielding n=16
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing evaluation of 4.5-star toaster vs. 2.5-star toaster within the abstract sound condition
operationalization_notes: The claim specifically refers to the abstract sound condition favoring the aggregated-info toaster, so the most direct test is a within-group paired comparison. The filter variable was used to exclude 4 participants with technical/hearing problems, consistent with the paper's reported exclusion of 5 total participants. The resulting means match the paper's reported values (M=5.14 and M=2.98).
reasoning: A paired t-test within the abstract sound condition (n=16, after excluding 4 participants for technical/hearing problems) showed that participants strongly favored the 4.5-star toaster (favored by aggregated information; M=5.14, SD=0.72) over the 2.5-star toaster (favored by individualized information; M=2.98, SD=0.79), t(15)=7.86, p<.001. This directly supports the original claim that abstract sound listeners strongly favored the toaster with positive aggregated information.

dependent_variable: GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted, national affluence)
main_predictor: Imports from the South as a share of GDP (lagged 1 year)
sample_definition: 18 OECD countries, 1971-2003 (after lagging explanatory variables), with complete data on GDP per capita, trade/GDP ratios, and unemployment
model_specification: Two-way fixed-effects GLS (Prais-Winsten FGLS with panel-specific AR(1) serial correlation correction, country and 5-year period fixed effects)
controls: Exports to the South as share of GDP (lagged 1 year), Unemployment rate (lagged 1 year), 5-year period indicators, country fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methodology (FE-GLS with country/period FE, lagged explanatory variables), I computed trade/GDP ratios using total GDP derived from OECD GDP per capita (PPP) multiplied by World Bank population data. The Prais-Winsten FGLS approach accounts for panel-specific AR(1) serial correlation, approximating the paper's Stata xtgls estimator. The coefficient is positive and significant (p < 0.01), consistent with the paper's finding, though the t-statistic (2.69) is smaller than the paper's (≈8.75), likely due to differences in GDP data sources, outlier removal, and exact GLS implementation.
reasoning: The FE-GLS regression (Prais-Winsten FGLS with panel-specific AR(1) correction) yields a significant positive coefficient for imports from the South as a share of GDP on national affluence (GDP per capita, PPP-adjusted): t(440) = 2.694, p = 0.007. A 1-percentage-point increase in the import/GDP ratio is associated with approximately a $362 increase in GDP per capita. This supports the paper's claim that North-South trade increases national affluence in economically advanced Northern countries.

dependent_variable: Average benefit-symbolism difference score (utilitarian rating minus symbolism rating, 1-7 scales) across four symbolic products (College T-shirts, American Flags, Class Rings, Greeting Cards)
main_predictor: Level: category (unbranded) vs. brand (branded), between-subjects
sample_definition: All participants from 10 replication datasets who passed all attention checks (Attention1=7 selecting Wind, Attention2=1 confirming serious participation, screenQ=2 confirming no prior participation), with non-missing utilitarian and symbolism ratings for the symbolic products
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test (equal variances) comparing brand vs. category conditions on the average benefit-symbolism difference score for symbolic products
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1b methods, the benefit-symbolism difference score was computed as Utilitarian rating minus Symbolism rating for each product, then averaged across the four symbolic product categories. Cond 1 and 2 were classified as category (unbranded) level; Cond 3 and 4 were classified as brand level. Participants failing attention checks were excluded. This simple-effects test is the most direct test of the specific claim about symbolic products becoming less symbolic and more utilitarian when branded.
reasoning: An independent-samples t-test comparing brand vs. category benefit-symbolism difference scores (utilitarian rating minus symbolism rating, averaged across symbolic products: College T-shirts, American Flags, Class Rings, Greeting Cards) revealed that branding significantly increased the difference score for symbolic products (Category mean = -2.66, Brand mean = -2.06), t(497) = 4.037, p < .001, indicating that branding makes attitudes toward symbolic product categories less symbolic and more utilitarian, consistent with the original paper's finding of t(204) = 3.54, p = .0005.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic Self-Discipline (corresponding to Self-Regulation)
sample_definition: All 366 undergraduate students from Jung et al. (2017) with complete data
model_specification: Path analysis (SEM with observed variables): GPA regressed on SR and SD simultaneously
operationalization_notes: The original study used SEM with latent factors (SR with 4 indicators, SD with 3 indicators). The replication data only has single observed proxies for SR (Academic Self-Discipline scale) and SD (Self-Discipline Facet from conscientiousness), so a path analysis with observed variables was used as the closest feasible SEM approach. The data dictionary explicitly maps Academic Self-Discipline to self-regulation and Self-Discipline Facet to self-discipline.
reasoning: A path analysis (SEM with observed variables) regressing GPA on Academic Self-Discipline (SR) and Self-Discipline Facet (SD) using the Jung et al. (2017) summary statistics (N=366) showed that SR significantly predicts GPA (z = 4.85, p < .001, standardized β = 0.34), while SD does not (z = -0.75, p = .46, β = -0.05). This replicates the original study's finding that self-regulation increases GPA.

dependent_variable: Belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories (mean of 4 items: bioweapon, conspiracy to take rights, hoax for financial gain, cover-up for economic crash)
main_predictor: National narcissism (mean of 3 items from Collective Narcissism Scale)
sample_definition: All 1575 participants from the German subset of Study 3 with complete data on all variables
model_specification: OLS linear regression: conspiracy belief regressed on national narcissism
controls: None (simple regression, following paper's Main Model specification for Study 3)
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns 'sharing' (dissemination) of conspiracy theories, but the available dataset (Study 3) only measures belief in conspiracy theories, not dissemination intentions—the paper itself notes Study 3 did not measure dissemination. Since the paper's mediation analysis (Studies 1-2) shows belief is the mechanism through which national narcissism leads to dissemination, testing the national narcissism → belief relationship is the most defensible test of the claim with the available data. The simple regression follows the paper's Main Model approach for Study 3; a model controlling for national identification also yields a significant positive effect (t = 24.68, p < .001).
reasoning: National narcissism significantly predicted belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories (B = 0.54, SE = 0.02, t(1573) = 24.01, p < .001, R² = .27). The positive relationship is highly significant, supporting the claim that higher national narcissism is associated with greater endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories—the key mediating pathway through which dissemination occurs per the paper's mediation model.

dependent_variable: Proportion of trials on which participant chose the face with higher fWHR/masculinity as more aggressive (across 36 forced-choice trials)
main_predictor: Facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR) and facial masculinity transform level (combined across trial types, as fWHR and masculinity trials could not be separated in the available data)
sample_definition: Participants from Processed_Data.csv (Study 1, male face stimuli) who self-reported their data quality as 'Yes' (n=139 out of 150 total)
model_specification: One-sample t-test against chance level (0.50), following the original paper's primary analytic approach
operationalization_notes: The original paper separately analyzed fWHR (24 trials) and masculinity (12 trials) using one-sample t-tests against chance. Because the trial-to-stimulus-type mapping was not available in the data, all 36 trials were combined. Responses were recoded per trial so that the majority direction reflected choosing the higher-trait (more aggressive) face, accounting for the randomized side-of-screen assignment described in the paper. The combined measure tests the claim that facial structure cues (fWHR and masculinity) are associated with perceived aggression; both were expected to show positive effects per the original findings. Only male face stimuli appear to be present in this dataset, so the female-face component of the claim could not be independently tested.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test against chance (0.5) on the proportion of trials where participants chose the face with higher fWHR/masculinity as more aggressive yielded t(138) = 8.79, p < .001, with a mean proportion of 0.571 (95% CI [0.555, 0.587]). This significantly-above-chance rate of selecting the high fWHR/masculinity face as more aggressive supports the original study's claim that faces with increased fWHR are perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: money (amount demanded by public official in BG / amount proposed by Participant B in UG, including zeros)
main_predictor: briberygame (Bribery Game vs Ultimatum Game treatment)
sample_definition: B-side participants (Public Officials in BG, Participant B in UG) with non-missing money values; 10 participants with missing money excluded
model_specification: Welch's t-test (unequal variances) comparing mean money amounts between BG and UG treatments
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns average bribe amounts across the two treatments. The 'money' variable captures the amount demanded/proposed in both frames. Using the full sample (including zeros for those who did not demand a bribe) is the most natural interpretation of 'average bribe amount' and aligns with the paper's OLS specification (1) in Table 2. A Welch t-test is appropriate given unequal variances across groups.
reasoning: The average bribe amount in the Bribery Game (M=0.578, n=199) was significantly lower than the average ultimatum amount in the Ultimatum Game (M=0.910, n=195), Welch's t(344.68)=-5.37, p<0.001. This supports the original study's claim that the average bribe amount is lesser in the harassment bribery game than in the strategically identical but neutrally framed ultimatum game.

dependent_variable: ratio of estimated total to maximum observed value (t_total/t_past)
main_predictor: number of observations seen (1, 3, or 10)
sample_definition: Participants in the taxicab condition who provided estimates for all three observation levels, excluding those who gave any estimate below the maximum observed value (misunderstood task) and outliers beyond 3 SD from the mean on the ratio measure
model_specification: One-way within-subjects (repeated measures) ANOVA with values_seen (1, 3, 10) as the within-subjects factor
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, the dependent variable was the ratio of the participant's estimate to the largest observed value (t_past), participants who estimated below t_past were excluded, and responses >3 SD from the mean were treated as outliers. The ANOVA model matches the paper's reported analysis for the taxicab scenario.
reasoning: A one-way within-subjects ANOVA on the ratio estimate/max_value (t_total/t_past) in the taxicab condition yielded F(2, 1166) = 84.71, p < .001, confirming that participants made significantly smaller predictions as more observations were provided. Mean ratios decreased monotonically from 1.76 (1 observation) to 1.38 (3 observations) to 1.21 (10 observations), consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Fraud by last-digit test (binary: 1 if chi-square test significant at 5% level for district)
main_predictor: Violence per 1,000 population (election day) and its squared term
sample_definition: All districts with complete data on all variables (N=375, dropping 14 observations with missing values on electrified/pce_1000_07)
model_specification: Logistic regression with violence, violence squared, and controls; standard errors clustered at the ISAF regional command level (4 clusters)
controls: Number of closed polling stations, electrification rate, per-capita expenditure (1,000 AFs), distance from Kabul (km), elevation (m)
operationalization_notes: I replicated Model 1 from Table 2 of the paper, which directly tests the inverted U-shape claim using the primary fraud measure (last-digit test) and election-day violence. The z-test on the squared violence coefficient is the most direct test of the concavity implied by the inverted U-shape. Clustered SEs at the regional command level were used as specified in the paper.
reasoning: In a logit regression of fraud (last-digit test, binary) on election-day violence (per capita), its square, and controls, the squared violence coefficient is -13.748 (z = -2.499, p = 0.0125), indicating a significant concave relationship consistent with an inverted U-shape. The linear violence term is positive (8.477) though not significant with clustered SEs (z = 1.530, p = 0.126), and the turning point (0.308) falls within the observed violence range (0–0.809).

dependent_variable: Social undermining (measured as willingness to be matched with the comparison person, reverse-coded: higher values = less undermining)
main_predictor: TSC × Competition interaction (TSC: 0=favorable, 1=unfavorable; Competition: 0=low, 1=high)
sample_definition: All 574 participants in the analytical data file who passed exclusion criteria (doubt checks and previous participation check), from the experimental study with within-subjects TSC manipulation and between-subjects competition manipulation
model_specification: Mixed-effects linear model (random intercept per participant) with fixed effects for TSC, Competition, and their interaction on the Undermin outcome
controls: None (the experimental design controls for confounds through randomization; the model includes only the main effects and their interaction)
operationalization_notes: The analytical dataset contains experimental data from Study 1a (within-subjects TSC, between-subjects Competition). The mixed-effects model accounts for the nested data structure (2 observations per participant). The Undermin variable is coded so that higher values indicate less undermining (more willingness to be matched); thus a negative interaction coefficient means the effect of unfavorable TSC on increasing undermining is stronger under high competition, consistent with the claim.
reasoning: The TSC × Competition interaction significantly predicted social undermining (z = -3.38, p = .0007) in a mixed-effects linear model. Under high competition, the mean difference in undermining between unfavorable and favorable TSC conditions was -0.70 on the willingness-to-be-matched scale, compared to only -0.13 under low competition. This confirms the claim that the positive relationship between temporal social comparison and social undermining is stronger when competition is high.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs (mean of 6 SpecCTs items)
main_predictor: COVID1 (worry about COVID spread, proxy for anxiety)
sample_definition: All 806 observations across 3 samples (Survey 1 USA, Survey 2a USA, Survey 2b UK) with complete data on all variables
model_specification: Simple OLS linear regression of conspiracy beliefs on COVID1
controls: None in the simple regression; a supplementary multiple regression with COVID3 as additional predictor showed COVID1 remained negative and COVID3 had a positive partial effect
operationalization_notes: The original paper measured anxiety and lack of control with dedicated multi-item scales not available in the dataset. COVID1 (worry about COVID spread) was used as the closest available proxy for anxiety, the central construct in the claim. COVID-19 conspiracy beliefs were computed as the mean of 6 SpecCTs items (including reverse-scored items already coded in the correct direction). The simple regression provides the most direct test of the claim's core directional prediction about anxiety predicting increased conspiracy beliefs.
reasoning: The claim predicts that anxiety and lack of control predict increased conspiracy beliefs, but the analysis shows that COVID1 (worry about COVID spread, the best available proxy for anxiety) significantly predicts FEWER conspiracy beliefs (r = -.237, t(804) = -6.92, p < .001). The negative relationship is opposite to the claim's predicted direction. In a multiple regression with both COVID1 and COVID3, COVID1 remains strongly negative (b = -0.343) while COVID3 (threat) shows a positive partial effect (b = 0.162), but the simple bivariate correlations for both proxies are negative (COVID1: r = -.237; COVID3: r = -.087), failing to support the claim that anxiety and lack of control predict increased conspiracy beliefs.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) to peripheral target letter
main_predictor: Face valence (angry vs. neutral), within-subjects
sample_definition: All participants classified as GAD (Group=1) in the dataset (n=63), corresponding to 'likely GAD' per the data dictionary
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test (angry vs. neutral mean RT), equivalent to the planned contrast F-test reported in the original paper
operationalization_notes: The paper reported a planned contrast (angry vs. neutral) within the GAD group following a Group×Valence ANOVA. The most direct test of the directional claim is a paired comparison of angry and neutral mean RTs within the GAD group, which I implement as a paired t-test. The dataset contains 63 GAD participants (vs. 14 in the paper's Experiment 1), but no variable distinguishes the original subsample, so the full GAD group was analyzed.
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing mean reaction times for angry (M=486.81 ms) vs. neutral (M=485.36 ms) faces within the GAD group (n=63) yielded t(62)=0.47, p=.64. The direction was opposite to the claim—angry-face RTs were slightly slower, not faster, than neutral-face RTs—by a negligible 1.45 ms (paired Cohen's d=0.06). The claim of faster RTs for angry compared with neutral faces in the GAD group is not supported by the data.

dependent_variable: Brand personality impression difference score (post-interaction sophistication minus pre-interaction sophistication, each averaged across 4 nine-point items)
main_predictor: Three-way interaction of Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information × Outcome Dependency
sample_definition: All 858 respondents from the Stage2 data file with non-missing brand personality impression scores
model_specification: 2 (Consistency: consistent vs inconsistent) × 2 (Pseudorelevant Information: disclosed vs not disclosed) × 2 (Outcome Dependency: high vs low) between-subjects ANOVA on difference scores
controls: None (following the paper's original analytical approach)
operationalization_notes: The claim involves both brand personality impressions and brand attitudes, but brand attitude items (bad/good, unfavorable/favorable, dislike/like) were not available in the dataset. The analysis focused on brand personality impressions using the sophistication difference score approach described in the paper. The three-way interaction is the most direct statistical test of the claim, as it tests whether the Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction differs across levels of Outcome Dependency. Pseudorelevant Information coding: 0 = info disclosed, 1 = info not disclosed.
reasoning: The three-way interaction (Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information × Outcome Dependency) on brand personality impression difference scores was not significant (F(1, 850) = 0.484, p = .487, partial η² = .0006). The claim predicts that under high outcome dependency, consistent (inconsistent) behavior would affect brand personality impressions more positively (negatively) when pseudorelevant information is not disclosed versus disclosed. While the cell means under high outcome dependency show a pattern in the predicted direction (consistent+no_info: 0.13 vs consistent+info: -0.02; inconsistent+no_info: -0.72 vs inconsistent+info: -0.68), the interaction effect is negligible and far from statistical significance.

dependent_variable: Binary avoidance behavior (performed ≥1 of 7 avoidance-related prep items: avoiding social events, avoiding public transport, eating out less, shopping for groceries less, cooking at home more, staying home from work, purchasing extra supplies)
main_predictor: Trust in government/authorities (dichotomized high vs low, based on mean of Govresponse_2 [trust in politicians to deal with pandemic] and Govresponse_6 [effectiveness of official response], threshold ≥4 on 1-7 scale)

operationalization_notes: The paper's original trust measure (two 5-point Likert items about government decisions and authorities' performance) was proxied using Govresponse_2 and Govresponse_6 (7-point scales) averaged and dichotomized at the midpoint. Avoidance behaviors were constructed from the prep variable's avoidance-related items (4,5,6,8,9,10,11). This supports the original study's claim that trust in government predicts avoidance behavior adoption, with the effect in the same positive direction, though the effect size is smaller than the paper's reported aOR of 5.5, likely due to different survey instruments and variable operationalizations.

dependent_variable: CMMSRC (reverse-scored Current Money Management Stress scale, where higher = more positive/lower stress)

model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equal variances assumed), equivalent to one-way ANOVA F-test
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 3a approach, the dependent variable is the reverse-scored CMMS scale (CMMSRC) where higher values indicate more positive/less stressed perceptions. The paper reported F(1,104)=7.66 for this effect; the t-test is the most direct test for a two-group comparison. Only included participants (Include=1) were analyzed, consistent with the codebook's exclusion criteria.

This replicates the original study's finding that framing success vs. failure affects perceived current money management stress in the predicted direction.

Robust standard errors were used as specified in the paper's analytic strategy section. The pre-computed scale variables (Disp_AttB, Sit_AttB) from the processed dataset were used.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE (perceived stress scale-10 total score)
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME

This is the model most directly testing the claim about income and perceived stress while controlling for basic demographics.
reasoning: In a multiple linear regression predicting PSS-10 SCORE from sociodemographic variables (age, gender, education, household members, monthly income), the coefficient for Monthly Income was B = -0.463 (SE = 0.134, t = -3.465, p = 0.00054), confirming that higher income is significantly associated with lower perceived stress, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Composite of 3 non-materialistic behavioral inclinations (eating chips, casual sex, social media friends)
main_predictor: DGS (Dispositional Greed Scale score)
