model_specification: OLS multiple regression with DGS and MVS as simultaneous predictors of the non-materialistic behavioral inclination composite
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 2 approach, the key test is whether DGS predicts behavioral inclinations after controlling for materialism. The paper's Table 5 shows partial correlations for each item; I created a composite of the 3 non-materialistic inclinations (chips, sex, friends) as the most direct test of the claim, since the paper argues greed uniquely predicts non-materialistic desires. The t-test for the DGS coefficient in a regression controlling for MVS directly tests 'over and above materialism.'
reasoning: In a multiple regression predicting a composite of non-materialistic behavioral inclinations (chips, sex, friends) from both DGS and MVS, the DGS coefficient was highly significant (t(489) = 15.65, p < .001, partial r = .58), while MVS was not (t(489) = 1.54, p = .12, partial r = .07). This confirms that the Dispositional Greed Scale predicts greedy behavioral tendencies over and above materialism.

dependent_variable: HY bond yield spread (ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread, quarterly end-of-period)
main_predictor: Credit standards (LargeandMedium: net percentage of banks tightening C&I loan standards for large/medium firms)
sample_definition: All quarterly observations with overlapping data for both HY spread and credit standards, spanning 2010:Q1 through 2020:Q2 (42 quarters)
model_specification: OLS linear regression of HY bond yield spread on credit standards (univariate), analogous to the paper's Table 2 specification but using bond spread instead of CDS-bond basis
operationalization_notes: The paper's Table 2 regresses the CDS-bond basis on credit standards to test the model's prediction that margin constraints drive deviations from the Law of One Price. Since CDX (CDS spread) data was unavailable, I used the HY bond yield spread alone as a proxy for losses to leveraged agents (wider spreads = lower bond prices = losses). Credit standards tightening (LargeandMedium) serves as the proxy for negative fundamental shocks / binding margin constraints. This is a weaker test than the paper's because the bond spread includes both fundamental risk and margin premium components, whereas the basis isolates the margin premium.
reasoning: The OLS regression of the HY bond yield spread on credit standards (LargeandMedium) yields a positive coefficient (0.021, t = 1.06, p = 0.29, n = 42), directionally consistent with the claim that negative fundamental shocks (credit tightening) lead to losses for leveraged agents (wider bond spreads). However, the effect is not statistically significant, and the R² is only 0.028. The weak result likely reflects the absence of CDX data needed to compute the CDS-bond basis (the paper's preferred dependent variable that isolates the margin premium), forcing use of the raw bond spread which conflates fundamental risk and margin effects.

dependent_variable: Positive contact with older workers (ICS-OW, Intergroup Contact Scale for older workers)
main_predictor: WICS total score (WIAStotal)
sample_definition: Workers aged 40 or younger (age40 = 1) with complete data on all regression variables (N = 446 after listwise deletion of missing values on age, work hours, years with employer, JSS, AOWS-adjusted-log, SIC, WICS total, and ICS-olderworkers)
model_specification: Hierarchical multiple regression with 3 steps: Step 1 = demographics (age, weekly work hours, years with employer); Step 2 = added JSS, AOWS-adjusted-log, SIC; Step 3 = added WICS total. F-change test for Step 3 evaluates incremental validity of WICS.
controls: Age, weekly work hours, years with employer, job satisfaction (JSS), attitudes toward older workers (AOWS log-adjusted), and intergenerational tension (SIC)
operationalization_notes: The claim that WICS is a 'valid and reliable multidimensional measure' encompasses multiple psychometric properties. The most directly testable directional hypothesis from the available Study 3 data is incremental validity—the prediction that WICS scores significantly predict criterion variables (positive intergroup contact) above and beyond other established measures. I used the younger group (age ≤ 40) with ICS-olderworkers as the criterion, following the paper's Study 3 methodology exactly. The F-change test for adding WICS to the model is the key statistical test of this incremental validity claim.
reasoning: A hierarchical multiple regression tested whether WICS adds incremental predictive power for positive intergroup contact above and beyond demographics, job satisfaction, attitudes toward older workers, and intergenerational tension. The F-change for adding WICS was F(1, 438) = 37.95, p < .001, with ΔR² = .071 and standardized β = .32 for WICS in the final model. This strongly supports the validity of WICS as a measure of intergenerational climate, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Q9_1 (stockpiling intention: 'I am planning to buy more food or supplies than usually', 1-5 Likert scale)
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility (reverse-coded mean of 16 HEXACO-100 items, HE_1 through HE_16)
sample_definition: All participants in the dataset with valid data on both HH and Intention (N = 314); one header row excluded
model_specification: OLS linear regression (bivariate)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's bivariate analysis approach for the HH-Intention relationship. HH was scored by reverse-coding 10 negatively-keyed items (HE_1, HE_2, HE_6, HE_7, HE_9, HE_11, HE_12, HE_14, HE_15, HE_16) using 8 - original before computing the mean of all 16 items. The paper's standardized beta of -0.24 equals the zero-order correlation, indicating no covariates were used in this specific test.
reasoning: An OLS regression of stockpiling intention (Q9_1) on reverse-coded Honesty-Humility yielded t(312) = -9.51, p < 0.001, r = -.47. The negative coefficient indicates that higher Honesty-Humility predicts lower stockpiling intention, which is equivalent to a positive association with refraining from stockpiling — consistent with the paper's claim. The effect size (r = -.47) is larger than the paper's reported r = -.24, likely due to differences in the available dataset (N = 314 vs. the paper's N = 401).

dependent_variable: deaths (cumulative COVID-19 deaths per county as of June 11, 2020)
main_predictor: pct_uninsured_u65 (percentage of uninsured individuals under age 65, computed as weighted average of under-19 and 19-64 uninsured rates from ACS S2701)
sample_definition: Non-urban US counties (density < 1000 residents per square mile), excluding territories (PR, GU, AS, MP, VI), counties with missing data, and spatial islands (counties with no queen contiguity neighbors)
model_specification: Spatial lag model (spatial two-stage least squares / GM_Lag) with queen contiguity spatial weights matrix, row-standardized
controls: pct_non_english (households), pct_farmworkers, pct_poverty, density (residents per sq mile), pct_over_65, high_risk_days (days since first case minus SIP days)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods, I used a spatial autoregressive (lag) model for non-urban counties where the paper found the uninsured effect significant. The uninsured variable was derived from ACS S2701 as a population-weighted average of uninsured rates for under-19 and 19-64 age groups. Farmworker data was from NASS/Bureau of Economic Analysis, with missing values imputed as 0. The claim is specifically tested in the non-urban subsample as stated in the paper's results section.
reasoning: In a spatial lag (GM_Lag) model for non-urban counties (n=2842), the coefficient for percentage uninsured under 65 was -0.361 (z = -2.654, p = 0.008), indicating that higher uninsured rates are associated with significantly lower reported COVID-19 mortality. This replicates the paper's finding that percentage of uninsured individuals was associated with lower reported COVID-19 mortality in non-urban/rural counties.

dependent_variable: Dessert choice (chocolate cake vs. fruit salad)
main_predictor: Decision recall condition (delegated vs. independent)
sample_definition: All 125 participants in the first-round analytic dataset who completed both the decision recall manipulation and the dessert choice measure
model_specification: Chi-square test of independence (2×2 contingency table), consistent with the paper's reported analysis
operationalization_notes: Used the analytic dataset_firstround.sav which corresponds to Study 3's two-condition (delegated vs. independent) design with dessert choice as the self-regulatory depletion measure. The paper reported using a chi-square test (and logistic regression) for this comparison, so a chi-square test of independence was used.
reasoning: The chi-square test on the analytic dataset (N=125) showed no significant association between decision recall condition and chocolate cake choice, χ²(1) = 0.085, p = .770. The delegated condition had 58.7% choosing chocolate cake vs. 61.3% in the independent condition — a non-significant difference in the opposite direction from the original claim (which predicted greater chocolate cake choice in the delegated condition).

dependent_variable: log(VIX intraday quoted spread) = log((High - Low) / ((High + Low)/2))
main_predictor: log(VIX Close) — sum of contemporaneous, lagged, and lead coefficients (ΣVIX)
sample_definition: Daily VIX observations from January 3, 2007 through December 31, 2009 (the paper's stated sample period), excluding observations with missing lag/lead values
model_specification: OLS levels regression following paper's model (a): log(LM_t) = α + β₁·log(VIX_t) + β₂·log(VIX_{t-1}) + β₃·log(VIX_{t+1}) + ε, with Newey-West (HAC, 10 lags) standard errors
controls: Lagged and lead values of log(VIX) per paper's specification; no additional controls available without stock-level data
operationalization_notes: The stock-level data file (NASDAQ_2010_19.csv) was not present in the data directory, precluding replication of the paper's individual stock liquidity regressions. As an alternative, the VIX intraday quoted spread—computed from VIX High and Low as (High-Low)/((High+Low)/2), mirroring the paper's quoted spread formula—was used as a proxy for market-wide liquidity conditions. The regression follows the paper's model (a) specification with log-log elasticity form and HAC standard errors.
reasoning: The sum of VIX coefficients (UEL = 0.289) in the log-log regression of VIX intraday spread on contemporaneous, lagged, and lead values of log(VIX) is positive and highly significant (t = 3.41, p = 0.0007), indicating that higher market uncertainty is associated with wider VIX intraday spreads—a proxy for lower market liquidity. This is consistent with the paper's claim that VIX exerts a market-wide impact on liquidity. Note: the stock-level NASDAQ data file (NASDAQ_2010_19.csv) referenced in the ReadMe was not available, so the VIX intraday quoted spread (High-Low)/midpoint—analogous to the paper's quoted spread formula—was used as a proxy for market liquidity conditions.

dependent_variable: Size (7-point scale: 'much smaller than average' to 'much larger than average')
main_predictor: Pitch condition (Condition A = high pitch, Condition B = low pitch)
sample_definition: All included participants from the cleaned dataset (n=615), with 301 in Condition A and 314 in Condition B
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing Size between the two pitch conditions
operationalization_notes: Condition assignment (A=high pitch, B=low pitch) was inferred from the direction of the mean difference, consistent with the paper's prediction that low pitch should yield higher size ratings. The paper reports F-tests from one-way ANOVA for this comparison; the t-test is equivalent (t²=F for 1 df between groups). The cleaned included participants dataset was used as provided.
reasoning: The difference in size ratings between the low-pitch condition (M=5.21) and high-pitch condition (M=5.09) was in the predicted direction but not statistically significant (t(613)=1.59, p=.112, Cohen's d=0.13). The small effect size and non-significant p-value do not support the claim that lower voice pitch leads to significantly larger product size perceptions in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Five attitude/behavior measures: worry about coronavirus (finitepool_2), perceived seriousness of coronavirus (canadaq_1), perceived likelihood of catching coronavirus (personal_8), prosociality (prosocial), and count of precautionary behaviors taken (prep_count)
main_predictor: Sex/gender (1=female, 2=male)
sample_definition: Adults aged 18 and older residing in Spain with complete data on all dependent variables (n=682; 347 female, 335 male)
model_specification: One-way MANOVA with Pillai's trace, following the paper's approach of testing multivariate gender differences across multiple attitude measures
operationalization_notes: The original paper used a Google Forms survey with 9 measures on 0-10 scales; the replication dataset uses the Winton Centre survey with different scales (1-7, 1-5, 0-11 count). The 5 selected variables capture the two key dimensions of 'responsible attitudes toward the dangers': (1) taking the threat seriously (worry, perceived seriousness, risk perception) and (2) acting responsibly (prosociality, precautionary behaviors). The MANOVA approach mirrors the paper's multivariate analysis strategy. The prep_count variable was computed from the multi-select prep question by counting the number of precautionary behaviors endorsed.
reasoning: A one-way MANOVA (Pillai's trace) testing gender differences across five measures of responsible attitudes toward COVID-19 dangers yielded a significant multivariate effect (Pillai's trace = 0.038, F(5, 676) = 5.29, p = .0001). Women scored higher than men on all five measures: worry about coronavirus (M=6.46 vs 6.04, p<.001), perceived seriousness of coronavirus (M=4.47 vs 4.29, p=.006), perceived likelihood of catching coronavirus (M=4.68 vs 4.42, p=.021), prosociality (M=5.86 vs 5.61, p=.009), and precautionary behaviors (M=7.39 vs 7.06, p=.089). These results support the claim that women have more responsible attitudes toward the dangers of the COVID-19 pandemic than men.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 attack rate (cumulative confirmed cases per 100,000 population as of April 14, 2020)
main_predictor: Age-standardized prevalence of tobacco smoking among persons 15+ years (2016 WHO data)
sample_definition: All 27 EU member states with country-level data (excluding sub-national/province rows for France, Denmark, and UK territories)
model_specification: Spearman's rank correlation with t-test approximation (t = rho * sqrt((n-2)/(1-rho^2)), df = n-2)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methods: used Spearman's rank correlation due to non-normality of data, computed attack rate as cumulative confirmed cases divided by population times 100,000. Only country-level rows retained from the replication dataset (province-level rows for France and Denmark were excluded). The t-statistic is the standard test for significance of Spearman's rho.
reasoning: Spearman's rank correlation between age-standardized prevalence of tobacco smoking and COVID-19 attack rate across 27 EU member states was -0.4757 (t = -2.70, df = 25, p = 0.012), confirming a statistically significant negative correlation consistent with the original study's finding that countries with higher smoking prevalence had lower COVID-19 attack rates.

dependent_variable: CIL (Computer and Information Literacy) score, using 5 plausible values (PV1CIL-PV5CIL)
main_predictor: Gender (male = 1 if boy, 0 if girl; S_SEX variable)
sample_definition: Korean students from ICILS 2018 with valid gender responses (S_SEX = 0 or 1), yielding 2,875 students (1,497 boys, 1,378 girls) in 150 schools
model_specification: Two-level hierarchical linear model with random intercept for schools, analyzed separately for each of 5 plausible values and combined using Rubin's rules; REML estimation
controls: None (baseline model testing only the gender effect, analogous to the paper's Model 2)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's HLM approach, I used a two-level model (students within schools) with the male indicator as the sole fixed effect and a random school intercept. The ICILS 2018 Korean data was used as the available dataset. Each of the 5 CIL plausible values was analyzed separately, and results were combined using Rubin's rules for multiple imputation to properly account for measurement uncertainty in the CIL scores.
reasoning: The two-level HLM (students nested in schools) with 5 CIL plausible values combined via Rubin's rules yields a male coefficient of -34.83 (SE = 4.06), t(1229) = -8.59, p < 0.001, indicating that female students score approximately 35 points higher than male students on the ICILS CIL scale. This strongly supports the paper's claim that female students' ICT literacy scores are higher than male students' scores.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 Responsible Behavior (mean of 4 items: RespBeh1-4)
main_predictor: COVID-19 Worry (CWorry, single item, 1-7 scale)

model_specification: OLS linear regression of behavior on worry
operationalization_notes: The dependent variable was computed as the mean of the 4 responsible behavior items (avoiding physical contact, washing hands, avoiding going out, coughing/sneezing in elbow), matching the original paper's measure. The predictor was the single-item COVID-19 worry measure (CWorry). A simple bivariate regression provides the most direct test of the claim that greater worry leads to more responsible behavior. The positive and significant coefficient supports the original study's conclusion.
reasoning: An OLS regression of COVID-19 responsible behavior (mean of 4 items: avoiding physical contact, washing hands, avoiding going out, coughing/sneezing in elbow) on COVID-19 worry (single item, 1-7 scale) yielded a significant positive coefficient (b = 0.232, t(549) = 11.12, p < .001), indicating that greater worry about COVID-19 predicts more responsible COVID-19 behavior. This replicates the original study's claim that greater worry leads to more responsible COVID-19 behavior.

dependent_variable: Leadership experiences (Leader_Exp_Total)
main_predictor: Openness to experiences (Oppenness_Total)
sample_definition: All observations with non-missing values on both openness to experiences and leadership experiences (N=215 from the Popper Data for Correlations dataset)
model_specification: Pearson correlation with t-test for significance of r (H0: ρ = 0)
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns a bivariate positive relation between openness to experiences and leadership experiences. The most direct test is the Pearson correlation and its associated t-test, matching the correlation matrix reported in the paper's Table 1. No controls were included because the claim is about the zero-order relation.
reasoning: A Pearson correlation between openness to experiences (Oppenness_Total) and leadership experiences (Leader_Exp_Total) yielded r = 0.22, t(213) = 3.29, p = .001, confirming a statistically significant positive relation consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 confirmed cases per million people (cumulative as of April 3, 2020)
main_predictor: EIU Democracy Index (0-100 scale)
sample_definition: All 150 countries in the replication dataset with available data on COVID cases, population, temperature, trade openness, and democracy index
model_specification: OLS linear regression with HC1 heteroscedasticity-robust standard errors
controls: Annual average temperature (°C, averaged 1961-1999), trade openness (exports of goods and services as % of GDP, 2016)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Model 1 specification (no lag), the dependent variable is COVID cases per million computed by dividing cumulative cases through April 3, 2020 by population in millions. The paper's three retained predictors (temperature, openness, democracy) are used, with HC1 robust standard errors to address the heteroscedasticity the paper itself acknowledges.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of COVID-19 cases per million people (as of April 3, 2020) on annual temperature, trade openness, and the EIU Democracy Index, the democracy coefficient is positive and statistically significant (b = 7.896, t(146) = 4.065, p < 0.001 with HC1 robust SEs), confirming the claim that countries with stronger political democracy had higher numbers of confirmed COVID-19 cases.

dependent_variable: Containment-related behavior (mean of 6 items: disinfecting hands, avoiding social contacts, washing hands, avoiding crowds, not touching face, staying home in quarantine)
main_predictor: COVID-19 hoax belief (mean of 3 items including 1 reverse-coded item)
sample_definition: All participants who passed the attention check (Q21 = 7) from the Study 1 US MTurk sample; 2 participants excluded for failing the attention check, yielding N = 102
model_specification: OLS linear regression with both conspiracy beliefs (hoax and human-made) entered simultaneously as predictors of containment-related behavior
controls: SARS-Cov-2 human-made belief (entered simultaneously as the other CT predictor)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's primary analytic approach (Step 1 regression), both conspiracy belief types are entered simultaneously to predict containment-related behavior, allowing the unique effect of hoax belief to be isolated from the overlapping human-made belief. The containment composite uses the 6 items identified by the paper's EFA as loading on the containment factor (items 1-6 in Table 1). Participants failing the attention check were excluded.
reasoning: An OLS regression predicting containment-related behavior from both conspiracy belief types found that COVID-19 hoax belief was significantly and negatively associated with containment behavior (B = -0.274, SE = 0.082, t(99) = -3.34, p = .001, β = -0.49), while human-made belief was not a significant predictor (B = 0.176, p = .066). This confirms the claim that believing COVID-19 is a hoax is inversely related to containment-related behaviors.

dependent_variable: Rehearsal strategies (mean of REH_1, REH_2, REH_3, REH_4)
main_predictor: Mastery-approach orientation (mean of MAp_1, MAp_2, MAp_3)
sample_definition: Participants who passed both attention checks, did not revoke consent, and had non-missing values on key variables (N = 977)
model_specification: OLS multiple regression with rehearsal as outcome and all four achievement goal orientations (mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, performance-avoidance) as predictors
controls: Mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goal orientations
operationalization_notes: The paper used SEM with latent variables; I used OLS regression with observed composite scores, which is the most direct way to test the directional claim. Including all four achievement goals as predictors mirrors the SEM approach where paths from all goal orientations to learning strategies were estimated simultaneously. Participants who failed attention checks or revoked consent were excluded.
reasoning: A multiple regression predicting rehearsal strategies from all four achievement goal orientations found that mastery-approach orientation was a significant positive predictor (unstandardized b = 0.33, standardized β = 0.30, t(972) = 9.36, p < .001), controlling for mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance orientations. This supports the original study's claim that a mastery-approach orientation positively predicts the use of rehearsal strategies.

dependent_variable: PANAS subscale mean scores (positive affect and negative affect)
main_predictor: Block type (progressive vs stagnant) × Scale Valence (positive vs negative) interaction
sample_definition: All participants in the Stage 1 dataset with complete data for both block types (N = 346, within-subjects design)
model_specification: 2 (Block: progressive vs stagnant) × 2 (Scale Valence: positive vs negative) repeated-measures ANOVA on mean PANAS subscale scores
controls: None — both factors are within-subjects manipulations
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's primary analysis for Experiment 1, I computed mean PANAS positive and negative affect scores per participant per block, then tested the Block × Valence interaction. This interaction captures whether the pattern of positive versus negative affect differs between progressive and stagnant processing conditions, which is the most direct statistical test of the claim that progressive processing yields 'relatively better moods.' Used Stage 1 data as it contains the stagnant vs progressive block comparison corresponding to the claim.
reasoning: The Block × Valence interaction in a 2 (Block: progressive vs stagnant) × 2 (Valence: positive vs negative) repeated-measures ANOVA was completely non-significant, F(1, 345) = 0.004, p = .95. Positive affect was negligibly higher after progressive blocks (M = 2.703) versus stagnant (M = 2.675), and negative affect was also slightly higher (not lower) after progressive (M = 1.587) versus stagnant (M = 1.561), yielding an interaction contrast of only 0.003 with ηp² ≈ 0.00001. The data provides no evidence that processing progressive word lists leads to better moods than processing stagnant word lists.

dependent_variable: Canadachoice (binary: 1 = chose Canadian/system-supporting brand, 0 = chose international brand)
main_predictor: Interaction of HighLowThreat (1 = system threat, 0 = no threat) × MeansCentered (mean-centered system justification score)
sample_definition: Participants in the indirect product condition (DirectIndirectsystemsupport = 0), where products provide indirect system support; n = 245 of 497 total
model_specification: Logistic regression: Canadachoice ~ HighLowThreat * MeansCentered
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 and Study 5 approach, the most direct test of the claim that low system-confidence individuals seek indirect consumption choices to defend the system under threat is the interaction between threat condition and system confidence predicting product choice in the indirect condition. System justification was computed by reverse-coding pro-system items (Q3_1, Q3_2, Q3_4, Q3_5, Q3_6, Q3_8) and averaging all 8 items, then mean-centered. The indirect condition was selected because the claim specifically concerns indirect system defense through consumption.
reasoning: A logistic regression in the indirect product condition testing the interaction between system threat (HighLowThreat) and mean-centered system confidence (MeansCentered) on choosing a Canadian brand (Canadachoice) yielded a non-significant interaction (z = -0.945, p = .345). While the negative direction of the coefficient (B = -0.207) is consistent with the claim that low-confidence individuals seek indirect system defense under threat, the effect is far from statistical significance and thus provides no reliable evidence supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Postshift negative affect
main_predictor: Difference between direct care TAS and indirect care TAS coefficients (Wald test of equality)
sample_definition: 208 matched daily observations from 52 nurses who completed pre-shift surveys, post-shift surveys, and person-level measures, with valid affect scores and task accomplishment data
model_specification: Two-level hierarchical linear model (HLM) with random intercepts for participants, Level 1 predictors group-mean centered (preshift negative affect, direct care TAS, indirect care TAS), Level 2 predictors grand-mean centered (nurse-physician relations, psychological resilience), and cross-level interactions (NP relations × direct/indirect TAS, resilience × direct/indirect TAS)
controls: Preshift negative affect, nurse-physician relations, psychological resilience, NP relations × direct TAS, NP relations × indirect TAS, resilience × direct TAS, resilience × indirect TAS
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 3 specification, postshift negative affect was modeled with preshift negative affect as a covariate to capture change. Direct care TAS was computed as the average satisfaction across 6 direct patient care tasks (oral hygiene, skin care, teaching patients/family, comforting/talking to patients, developing/updating care plans, preparing patients for discharge), excluding administering medication and completing treatments per the paper's footnote 2. Indirect care TAS was the average across 3 indirect tasks (charting, reviewing diagnostic test results, patient history reviews). The claim was tested via a Wald test of the difference between the two TAS coefficients.
reasoning: A Wald test comparing the direct care TAS coefficient (-2.253) to the indirect care TAS coefficient (-0.697) in a multilevel model predicting postshift negative affect (controlling for preshift affect, nurse-physician relations, resilience, and their cross-level interactions) yielded z = -2.852, p = .002 (one-tailed). This indicates that the effect of direct care task accomplishment satisfaction on negative affect is significantly larger (more negative) than the effect of indirect care task accomplishment satisfaction, supporting the claim that the impact is larger for direct care nursing tasks.

dependent_variable: Proportion of correct winner identifications across 8 ensemble competition triads
main_predictor: Condition (Visual-only modality, tested against chance level of 1/3)
sample_definition: All 96 participants in the Visual-only condition from the analytic data file, across both phases of data collection
model_specification: One-sample t-test comparing Visual accuracy against chance (1/3), matching the paper's primary analysis approach
operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 used one-sample t-tests against chance (1/3) as the primary test of whether novices could identify winners through each modality. I followed this approach, using the Visual analytic data which has per-participant accuracy scores. The claim requires Visual accuracy to be significantly above chance; since it is not (t(95)=1.13, p=0.26), the claim is unsupported by this data.
reasoning: A one-sample t-test against chance (1/3) showed that Visual-only accuracy (M=0.350, SD=0.147) was not significantly above chance, t(95)=1.13, p=0.26. The original study found Visual accuracy at 46.4% (significantly above chance), but this replication data shows Visual accuracy at only 35.0%, a negligible effect (Cohen's d=0.12). The data does not support the claim that novices could identify competition winners through visual cues alone.

dependent_variable: toned (desire for toned and defined muscles, 0-4 scale)
main_predictor: age (continuous, 18-25 years)
sample_definition: All male participants aged 18-25 who completed the Qualtrics survey and provided consent, with non-missing values on toned, age, sexuality_cat, geo, and weight_status (n = 2,438)
model_specification: OLS linear regression predicting desire for toned/defined muscles from age, sexual orientation category, geographic region, and weight status, following the paper's GEE model specification adapted for cross-sectional data
controls: sexual orientation category (heterosexual referent, mostly heterosexual, gay/bisexual), geographic region of residence, weight status (underweight, normal, overweight)
operationalization_notes: The claim references 'desire for bigger muscles' but the dataset only contains 'desire for toned and defined muscles' (toned). The paper itself found these constructs differ: bigger muscles desire increased with age (β = .10) while toned muscles desire did not (β = -.01). The analysis uses the toned variable as the closest available muscularity concern measure. The paper's GEE approach was adapted to OLS regression since the data is cross-sectional rather than longitudinal.
reasoning: The age effect on desire for toned/defined muscles is non-significant (t(2420) = -1.52, p = .129) and in the opposite direction (β = -0.013) from the claim that muscularity desire increases with age. The age × sexual orientation interaction was also non-significant (F = 0.17, p = .846), supporting the 'regardless of sexual orientation' portion but with no meaningful age effect to moderate. Critically, the available outcome (desire for toned/defined muscles) differs from the claim's construct (desire for bigger muscles), and the paper itself found these behave differently.

dependent_variable: Actor's relationship satisfaction (PRQC composite of 18 items)
main_predictor: Partner's warmth/trustworthiness ideal discrepancies (partner's rating of how well the actor matches partner's ideals on 6 warmth/trustworthiness items)
sample_definition: All 259 heterosexual romantic couples (518 individuals) in the dataset who provided consent and were in current, exclusive, heterosexual relationships
model_specification: Multilevel Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) with dyad as grouping variable, actor's ideal discrepancies and partner's ideal discrepancies as predictors, sex (effect coded: women=-1, men=1) as covariate, and actor's PRQC relationship satisfaction as outcome
controls: Actor's own ideal discrepancies, participant sex (effect coded)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's APIM approach (Campbell & Kashy, 2002; Kenny et al., 2006), data from both partners were nested within dyads. The warmth/trustworthiness dimension was chosen as the primary test because it is the most theoretically central dimension in the ISM and showed the most consistent partner effects across both studies in the original paper. All continuous predictors were grand-mean centered. Partner effect tests whether the partner's rating of how well the actor matches their ideals predicts the actor's own relationship satisfaction.
reasoning: Using an Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) with multilevel modeling, the partner effect of warmth/trustworthiness ideal discrepancies on actor's relationship satisfaction was highly significant (z = 7.891, p < .001, unstandardized b = 0.223, standardized β = 0.230). This confirms that individuals are less satisfied when they fail to match their partner's ideal standards, consistent with the original study's claim.

dependent_variable: Stroop interference score (log-transformed mean RT on incongruent trials minus log-transformed mean RT on congruent trials)
main_predictor: Stereotype threat condition (condit 'd' = threat vs 'j' = control, validated by post-task manipulation check showing higher threat concern in 'd' group)
sample_definition: All 304 participants with valid Stroop task data (correct and non-anticipatory responses ≥300ms) from the replication dataset
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (equivalent to one-way ANOVA with 2 levels) on log-transformed Stroop interference scores, following the original paper's analysis approach
controls: Error-based interference was examined as a check for speed-accuracy trade-off (not significant), but not included as a covariate in the primary model following the original paper's primary analysis
operationalization_notes: The condit variable (d/j) was interpreted as the stereotype threat manipulation based on the post-task manipulation check: participants in condit='d' reported significantly higher threat concern (M=3.63 on 4-point scale) than condit='j' participants (M=2.90), t=7.10, p<.0001. Stroop interference was computed per the original paper's method: erroneous responses and RTs <300ms were excluded, RTs were log-transformed, and interference was calculated as mean log(RT) on incongruent trials minus mean log(RT) on congruent trials.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing Stroop interference scores (log-transformed RT difference between incongruent and congruent trials) between the stereotype threat condition (condit='d', N=160, M=0.1283) and control condition (condit='j', N=144, M=0.1343) yielded t(302) = -0.42, p = .68. While the direction is consistent with the claim (threat has lower interference, suggesting better cognitive control), the effect is negligible (Cohen's d = -0.05) and far from statistically significant, even with a sample nearly 5 times larger than the original Study 1 (63 participants). The data does not replicate the original finding of F(1,61) = 8.69, p = .004.

dependent_variable: creativity
main_predictor: intrinsic motivation
sample_definition: All 68 independent samples from the meta-analysis dataset that reported a correlation between intrinsic motivation and creativity
model_specification: Random-effects meta-analysis of correlation coefficients using the Fisher z transformation with DerSimonian-Laird estimator for between-study variance (τ²)
operationalization_notes: The paper's Table 1 reports the bivariate meta-analytic correlation between intrinsic motivation and creativity as the primary evidence for Hypothesis 1. I used the Meta-analysis_liu_SCORE.csv dataset which contains k=68 effect sizes matching the paper's reported k, applied a random-effects meta-analysis via Fisher z transformation (the standard method for synthesizing correlations), and tested whether the mean correlation is significantly greater than zero using a one-tailed z-test.
reasoning: A random-effects meta-analysis of 68 independent samples (N=19,695) using the Fisher z method yielded a significantly positive mean correlation between intrinsic motivation and creativity (r̄ = .28, z = 10.31, p < .001). After correcting for measurement error (creativity reliability = .88, intrinsic motivation reliability = .80), the corrected correlation was ρ̄ = .33, consistent with the paper's reported ρ = .34. The relationship is unambiguously positive and statistically significant.

dependent_variable: Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB) — supervisor-rated composite of Sportsmanship, Civic Virtue, Courtesy, and Altruism subscales
main_predictor: Four operant leadership dimensions (Contingent Reward, Contingent Punishment, Non-contingent Reward, Non-contingent Punishment) testing direct effects on OCB after controlling for Trust
sample_definition: 168 employee-supervisor dyads with complete data on all variables (from 170 matched dyads, 2 excluded due to missing tenure data)
model_specification: Nested F-test comparing OLS regression models: Full mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + Tenure with Leader + Organizational Level) vs. Partial mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + CR + CP + NCR + NCP + Tenure with Leader + Organizational Level). H0: all 4 direct effects of operant leadership on OCB = 0 (full mediation).
controls: Tenure with leader (years), Organizational level (3-point scale)
operationalization_notes: Scales computed per item content: CR (Q3_1-Q3_10, items 9-10 reverse coded), CP (Q3_11-Q3_15), NCR (Q3_20-Q3_23; praise regardless of performance), NCP (Q3_16-Q3_19; punishment without cause). Data dictionary labels for NCR/NCP were swapped relative to item content and corrected. Trust = mean of Q4_1-Q4_5 (5-item Podsakoff measure). OCB = mean of 4 supervisor-rated subscales. Tenure capped at 40 years to address data entry errors. The F-test directly evaluates the full mediation claim by testing whether the 4 direct paths from operant leadership to OCB are jointly zero when Trust is included.
reasoning: The F-test comparing the full mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + Controls) to the partial mediation model (OCB ~ Trust + 4 Operant Leadership dimensions + Controls) yielded F(4, 160) = 18.47, p < .001, strongly rejecting the null hypothesis of full mediation. Specifically, non-contingent punishment (NCP) retains a significant direct effect on OCB (β = -0.22, t = -4.58, p < .001) even after controlling for Trust, indicating the mediation is partial rather than full. While indirect effects through Trust are significant for CR, CP, and NCR, the NCP→OCB path is direct-only (indirect effect through Trust not significant), contradicting the claim of full mediation.

dependent_variable: PASAverage (Prostitution Attitudes Scale average; higher scores = more favorable attitudes toward prostitution)
main_predictor: WritingCondition (mortality salience vs. dental pain control)
sample_definition: European American participants (EuropeanAmerican=1) who passed the pre-filter criteria (filter_$=1), with non-missing PASAverage scores
model_specification: Independent samples t-test (two-tailed) comparing PASAverage between mortality-salience and control conditions for European Americans
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's design, the claim concerns the simple effect of condition on prostitution attitudes among European Americans only. The PAS measure was reverse-coded such that higher scores reflect more favorable attitudes. The original paper found more negative attitudes (lower PAS) in the MS condition; in this dataset the direction reverses but the effect is non-significant.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test on European Americans' PAS scores (higher = more favorable toward prostitution) comparing mortality-salience (M=1.88, SD=1.02, n=39) vs. control (M=1.67, SD=1.03, n=43) yielded t(80)=0.92, p=.36. The direction is opposite to the original claim: European Americans in the MS condition had slightly more positive (not more negative) attitudes toward prostitution, but this difference was not significant.

dependent_variable: log(mean mortality rate) — the natural logarithm of the country-level mean daily increase in COVID-19 deaths during the ascending phase of the epidemic curve
main_predictor: International Arrivals (millions) in 2018
sample_definition: 37 countries reporting >25 COVID-related deaths by 08/06/2020 with complete data, excluding China, matching the paper's inclusion criteria
model_specification: Multivariable OLS linear regression with log(mean mortality rate) as the outcome
controls: Log population, median age, air pollution, mean temperature, population density, prevalent neoplasms, prevalent hypertension, WHO health index, urban population %, GDP per capita, hospital beds per 10,000
operationalization_notes: Used the Data_for_Replication.csv dataset filtered to the 37 countries specified in the paper. The outcome and main predictor match the paper's specification. I could not include UV radiation, BCG vaccination coverage, or stringency index as these variables were not available in the dataset; median age was used instead of % population aged 65+ for the same reason. Despite these minor differences, the results closely replicate the paper's reported coefficient and p-value for international arrivals.
reasoning: Multivariable OLS regression with log(mean mortality rate) as outcome and international arrivals as the main predictor, controlling for 11 other country-level determinants, yields a positive and statistically significant coefficient for international arrivals (β = 0.030, t = 3.34, p = 0.003, 95% CI: 0.011–0.049). This confirms the paper's finding that greater international arrivals predict greater COVID-19 first-wave severity.

dependent_variable: contribution amount (points allocated to shared account, 0-125)
main_predictor: outcome prospect condition (losses-and-gains vs. no variance + gains-only, coded by the 'losses' variable)
sample_definition: All 320 participants who completed the study across 4 rounds, each playing in both losses-and-gains and gains-only/no-variance conditions
model_specification: Paired t-test comparing within-participant mean contributions across the two prospect conditions
operationalization_notes: The 'losses' variable in the dataset classifies each round as gains-only (0) or losses-and-gains (1) based on whether the minimum possible per-person return from the public good exceeds the average required per-person contribution (75 points). With threshold=300 and 4-person groups: BONUS=600 and (400,800) are gains-only; BONUS=(200,1000) and (0,1200) are losses-and-gains. Each participant's mean contribution was computed separately for each condition type, then compared via paired t-test, matching the within-subjects design of the original study.
reasoning: A paired t-test comparing each participant's mean contribution in losses-and-gains prospect conditions (M = 73.20) versus no variance and gains-only conditions (M = 73.75) yielded t(319) = -0.58, p = 0.56. While the direction of the tiny mean difference (-0.55 points on a 125-point scale) is consistent with the original claim, the effect is negligible and far from statistically significant. The original study's finding of lower contributions under loss prospects does not replicate in this dataset.

dependent_variable: HP-detrended inter-county migration rate (percentage points)
main_predictor: Standardized cross-state standard deviation of state employment gaps (dispersion measure)
sample_definition: Annual US data from 1948 to 2009, excluding years without CPS migration data (1972-1975, 1977-1980); 54 observations
model_specification: OLS regression of HP-detrended migration rate on standardized national employment gap and standardized dispersion of state employment conditions
controls: Standardized national employment gap (HP cyclical component of log national employment, computed from continuous monthly employment series with April-March annual averaging)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 1 column 2 specification, the national employment gap was computed by applying an HP filter (λ=100) to the log of national nonfarm employment using a continuous monthly series (PAYNSA) averaged to April-March annual frequency. The dispersion measure is the cross-state SD of state employment gaps as provided in the replication data (StateEmploymentGapSD), standardized within the 1948-2009 sample. The DV is the HP-detrended migration rate (HPmigration) from the replication data.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of the HP-detrended inter-county migration rate on the standardized national employment gap and the standardized cross-state dispersion of employment conditions (SD of state employment gaps), the coefficient on the dispersion measure is 0.0137 (SE = 0.0466), yielding t(51) = 0.29, p = 0.77. This is far from statistical significance, confirming the paper's claim that dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to migration. The national employment gap itself is significant (t = 2.86, p = 0.006), consistent with procyclical migration.

dependent_variable: Mean response latency (seconds) for perceiving anger has disappeared from the face in the angry-to-happy transition
main_predictor: Target age (old vs. young) within White targets
sample_definition: 51 participants who completed all 4 conditions of the angry-to-happy transition (after excluding latencies <0.5s or >17s and subjects with fewer than 40 valid trials out of 48)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing old White vs. young White faces, following up on the significant age × race interaction from a 2×2 within-subjects ANOVA
operationalization_notes: The angry-to-happy transition was selected as the most canonical test of 'anger lasting longer' from the Hugenberg & Bodenhausen (2003) paradigm adapted by this study. In this transition, a face morphs from angry to happy, and participants press a key when anger is no longer visible; higher latency means anger is perceived to persist longer. Data cleaning excluded implausibly fast (<0.5s, suggesting inattention) and impossibly slow (>17s, beyond movie duration) responses.
reasoning: For the angry-to-happy transition, participants showed significantly longer latencies for old White faces (M = 12.09s) compared to young White faces (M = 10.70s), t(50) = 5.278, p < .001, indicating anger was perceived as lasting longer on old White faces. This strongly supports the original study's claim about anger lasting longer on old compared to young White faces.

dependent_variable: Not following social distancing (binary: composite score ≤ 5 on 1-7 scale from three items: avoiding crowded places, avoiding poorly ventilated spaces, keeping distance)
main_predictor: Male (1 = male, 0 = female)
sample_definition: All 3,892 survey respondents with complete data on the model variables
model_specification: Logistic regression (logit model)
controls: Age groups (20-29, 30-39, 50-59, 60+; ref: 40-49), not married, no children under 18, low education, work status (nonregular employee, self-employed, not working; ref: regular employee), household income categories, smoking habit, drinking habit, Big 5 personality traits (extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, openness)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's approach of a logit model with male as the key predictor and controls for demographics and personality, I constructed a composite social distancing score from three items corresponding to the '3Ms' (avoiding poorly ventilated closed spaces, avoiding large gatherings, keeping distance). Since the exact 'avoid the three overlapping Ms' question from the original paper was not available in this dataset, I used a threshold of ≤ 5 on the 1-7 composite scale to define non-compliance, yielding approximately 24% non-compliance (similar to the paper's ~20%).
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting not following social distancing (composite ≤ 5 on a 1-7 scale from three social distancing items: avoiding crowds, avoiding poorly ventilated spaces, keeping distance), the male coefficient was 0.768 (z = 8.123, p < 0.0001), corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.155 (95% CI: 1.790–2.593). This means men have significantly higher odds of not following social distancing compared to women, which is equivalent to a lower likelihood of following social distancing. This strongly supports the original paper's finding (OR = 1.635, p < 0.001).

dependent_variable: Preference for part-time work (Prefs_1, 1=doesn't matter to 5=must have)
main_predictor: Cluster membership (3 clusters: free agents, satisficers, maximizers derived from 24 desire items)
sample_definition: Participants who consented, were age 40+, were currently seeking employment, completed the survey, and had non-missing desire items (N=771 from the replication dataset)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA comparing part-time preference means across three clusters
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's two-stage cluster analysis (Ward's hierarchical method to identify 3 clusters, then K-means for final assignments) on the 24 Desire items, followed by a one-way ANOVA on the Part-time preference item. The hierarchical analysis confirmed the 3-cluster solution (largest fusion coefficient jump from 3→2 clusters). Cluster labels were assigned based on pattern matching with original study: Cluster 0 (low family/generative)=free agents, Cluster 1 (moderate all)=satisficers, Cluster 2 (high all)=maximizers.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA on part-time work preference (Prefs_1) across three clusters of mature job seekers (free agents, satisficers, maximizers) identified via two-stage cluster analysis (Ward's method + K-means) yielded F(2,768) = 0.046, p = .955, with eta-squared ≈ 0.0001. The three clusters showed nearly identical part-time preference means (2.74–2.77 on a 1–5 scale), providing no evidence that cluster membership is associated with preference for part-time work, contrary to the original finding of F = 5.46, p < .01.

dependent_variable: Death (binary: 1 = died from COVID-19, 0 = survived)
main_predictor: Sex (male = 1, female = 0)
sample_definition: COVID-19 positive patients aged 25 and older with admission date on or before April 23, 2020, identified via the origsamp variable in the replication dataset
model_specification: Multiple logistic regression predicting mortality from sex, age groups, comorbidity combinations, pregnancy, immunosuppression, pneumonia, hospitalization, intubation, ICU, and health service sector
controls: Age groups (50-74, ≥75; reference 25-49), CKD, COPD, combined chronic disease categories (7 categories; reference = none), pregnancy, immunosuppression, pneumonia, hospitalization, intubation, ICU, health service sector (IMSS, ISSSTE, SSA, other; reference = private)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Table 4 specification, I fitted a logistic regression for death with sex as the key predictor and the same covariates. The sample (n=17,465) is larger than the paper's original n=10,544 likely because the July 2020 data release includes additional retrospectively-reported cases; the origsamp variable was used as the best available approximation of the original April 23 data cutoff, restricted to ages 25+ as in the paper's regression model.
reasoning: A logistic regression for mortality with sex (male) as the main predictor, controlling for age groups, CKD, COPD, combined chronic disease categories, pregnancy, immunosuppression, pneumonia, hospitalization, intubation, ICU admission, and health service type, yielded a z-statistic of 9.37 for the male coefficient (OR = 1.64, p < 0.001). This confirms the paper's claim that men had significantly higher risk of death compared to women.

dependent_variable: Perceived stress (Perceived Stress Questionnaire score at follow-up)
main_predictor: Dispositional optimism (Life Orientation Test-Revised score at baseline)
sample_definition: All individuals from 101 couples with complete optimism and stress data in the scored dataset
model_specification: Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) estimated via OLS regression with cluster-robust standard errors (clustered by couple), with own optimism and partner's optimism as predictors of own perceived stress
controls: Partner's optimism (as required by APIM specification to separate actor and partner effects)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methodology, I used the APIM framework to test the actor effect of optimism on stress. The APIM was specified for interchangeable dyads (actor and partner effects constrained equal across gender, as the paper found the omnibus test of distinguishability was non-significant). The actor effect directly tests the claim that more optimistic individuals report lower stress. The scored dataset provided composite optimism (LOT-R) and stress (PSQ) scores for both partners.
reasoning: The Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM) actor effect of optimism on perceived stress was significant and negative: b = -0.305, t(199) = -8.76, p < .001, indicating that more optimistic individuals reported lower levels of stress. This replicates the original study's finding of a significant negative actor effect (β = -0.25, p < .001) linking optimism to lower perceived stress.

dependent_variable: Cooperate (binary: 1 = attempted risky coordination/work together, 0 = work alone)
main_predictor: Knowledge level (1 = Private, 2 = Secondary, 3 = Tertiary, 4 = Common Knowledge)
sample_definition: Participants who consented, completed the survey, and passed all three payoff comprehension checks (CC1=4, CC2=1, CC3=3 for their assigned role). Participants missing Knowledge or Cooperate values were excluded.
model_specification: Chi-square test of independence on the 4×2 contingency table of knowledge level × coordination choice
operationalization_notes: The analysis follows the paper's approach of using chi-square tests to compare coordination rates across knowledge conditions. The data appears to be from a single payoff condition ($1.60 alone/$1.80 together based on comprehension check answer options). Exclusion was based on comprehension checks matching the paper's ex post exclusion procedure. The omnibus 4-level chi-square test is the primary test reported in the paper's Table 1 for each payoff condition.
reasoning: A chi-square test of independence across the four knowledge conditions was significant, χ²(3, N=249) = 15.49, p = .001. The proportion attempting risky coordination was highest with common knowledge (0.706), compared to tertiary/shared knowledge (0.547), secondary/shared knowledge (0.433), and private knowledge (0.386). This supports the claim that common knowledge leads to more coordination attempts than shared or private knowledge.

dependent_variable: ITS (intention to support the nonprofit, mean of 3 items)
main_predictor: FIT × SIMILAR interaction (mean-centered product of measured fit and similarity)
sample_definition: All participants with complete data on FIT, SIMILAR, COP, ITS, and TRUST composite scores (N=907 out of 911 total)
model_specification: Moderated mediation tested via Sobel z-test: Step 1 (mediator model) COP ~ FIT_c + SIM_c + FIT×SIM_c + TRUST; Step 2 (DV model) ITS ~ FIT_c + SIM_c + FIT×SIM_c + COP + TRUST. Indirect effect = a×b tested with Sobel's method.
operationalization_notes: The paper's claim on p.449 refers to H2b (moderated mediation), where the FIT × SIMILAR interaction indirectly affects intention to support through clarity of positioning. I used OLS regression with composite scores (instead of SEM with latent variables) to test this. FIT and SIMILAR were mean-centered before creating the interaction term, consistent with standard practice for moderated mediation analysis. The Sobel z-test provides the inferential test of the indirect effect.
reasoning: The Sobel test of the indirect effect of the FIT × SIMILAR interaction on intention to support the nonprofit (ITS) through clarity of positioning (COP) yielded z = 2.48, p = .013. The interaction significantly predicted COP (b = 0.056, t = 2.60, p = .010), and COP significantly predicted ITS (b = 0.332, t = 8.28, p < .001). The bootstrap 95% CI for the indirect effect [0.003, 0.036] excluded zero. This supports the claim that relational fit and similarity jointly affect intention to support the nonprofit via clarity of positioning.

dependent_variable: Physical distancing (self-report: 'I am massively curtailing social contact'), 1-5 Likert scale
main_predictor: Empathy for those most vulnerable (mean of 3 items: concern, compassion, being moved), 1-5 Likert scale
sample_definition: US participants from Study 1 (N=63 available in dataset; original study reported N=322); all observations with complete data on empathy and distancing items included
model_specification: Pearson correlation with t-test for significance of the correlation coefficient
controls: none (consistent with the paper's primary reported analysis in Study 1)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Study 1 method, I used the self-related physical distancing item (not the other-related item) and the 3-item affective empathy composite. The Likert items were recoded from their 8-12 coding to a standard 1-5 scale. Only the US subsample was available in the provided dataset (63 of the original 322 participants); the UK and German samples were not included in the data file.
reasoning: The Pearson correlation between empathy (mean of 3 affective empathy items for those most vulnerable) and self-reported physical distancing is r = 0.51, t(61) = 4.63, p < .001, confirming a significant positive association. This replicates the direction and significance of the original study's reported r = .54 for the US sample, supporting the claim that empathy motivates physical distancing.

dependent_variable: SNARC regression slope (slope of dRT = RT_right - RT_left regressed on digit magnitude, computed per subject)
main_predictor: Deviation of SNARC slope from zero under verbal load condition (one-sample test)
sample_definition: Subjects in the verbal working memory condition who: (1) self-reported paying attention, (2) achieved ≥75% parity accuracy in both baseline and load phases. RT trimmed to 200–2000ms; only correct trials used.
model_specification: One-sample t-test testing whether the mean SNARC regression slope under verbal load differs from zero. SNARC slopes computed per subject by regressing dRT (mean RT for right-hand responses minus mean RT for left-hand responses) on digit magnitude (1-4, 6-9).
operationalization_notes: Following the standard SNARC analysis (Dehaene et al., 1993), dRT was computed as the difference between right-hand and left-hand mean RTs for each digit, then regressed on digit magnitude. A negative slope indicates a SNARC effect. The one-sample t-test directly tests whether the SNARC effect is present (slope ≠ 0) under verbal load, which is the most direct test of the claim that verbal load 'abolished' the SNARC effect. Exclusion criteria ensured data quality while maintaining a reasonable sample size.
reasoning: The claim states that verbal memory load abolished the SNARC effect in parity judgment. However, a one-sample t-test on SNARC regression slopes (dRT regressed on digit magnitude) in the verbal load condition shows a mean slope of -8.04, which is significantly different from zero (t(96) = -6.07, p < .001). A negative slope indicates the SNARC effect is present (small numbers → faster left responses, large numbers → faster right responses). The verbal load did NOT abolish the SNARC effect; it remained robust.

dependent_variable: d' (signal detection sensitivity index, computed from hit rate and false alarm rate across all test trials)
main_predictor: Version (starting small vs. random condition)
sample_definition: All participants who passed the attention check (attnPrompts = 'ok'), yielding 38 in the SS group and 32 in the random group (70 total)
model_specification: Independent samples t-test comparing mean d' between SS and random groups
operationalization_notes: Following the original paper's primary analysis (a t-test on mean d'-values comparing SS vs. random groups in Experiment 1), d' was computed for each participant using the log-linear correction for extreme hit/false-alarm rates. Participants flagged as 'notTrying' on the attention check were excluded. The original paper reported t(26) = 3.94, p = .001 with SS d' = 1.51 vs. random d' = 0.08; the replication data show no such effect.
reasoning: An independent samples t-test comparing mean d' values between the SS group (M = 0.096, SD = 0.627) and the random group (M = 0.000, SD = 0.212) yielded t(68) = 0.83, p = 0.41. The SS group did not significantly outperform the random group, and neither group performed significantly above chance. The original claim that SS outperforms random learning is not supported by the replication data.

dependent_variable: T3_panas_joviality (joviality at end of following workweek)

The test statistic comes from the relaxation coefficient in Step 3.
controls: Demographics (age, gender, having children, contract work hours/week, days worked/week), T1 joviality (autoregressive control), and other weekend experiences (psychological detachment, mastery, control, non-work hassles) entered simultaneously with relaxation in Step 3
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's methodology, I used hierarchical regression with T3 joviality as the outcome and relaxation as the key predictor, controlling for demographics and the autoregressive effect of T1 joviality. All five weekend experience variables were entered simultaneously in Step 3 as in the original study. The k17 dataset was used as the primary analysis dataset because it has the larger sample size and complete data across all three measurement occasions.
reasoning: A hierarchical regression predicting joviality at the end of the following workweek (T3) from weekend relaxation, controlling for demographics (age, gender, children, work hours, work days), T1 joviality, and other weekend experiences (detachment, mastery, control, hassles), yielded a positive but non-significant coefficient for relaxation: t(325) = 1.727, p = 0.085 (two-tailed), standardized β = 0.098, partial r = 0.095. The direction is consistent with the original claim, but the effect does not reach conventional significance levels.

dependent_variable: Autism identification (binary: 0 = no autism, 1 = autism)
main_predictor: State (Ohio vs California, California as reference)

controls: Race (7 categories: White [reference], Black, Hispanic, Asian, Pacific Islander, American Indian/Alaska Native, Two or More Races)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's Part 3 methodology, I used logistic regression with state and race as categorical predictors, with California and White as reference categories. The Ohio state coefficient directly tests whether autism identification differs between Ohio and California after accounting for racial composition. Autism counts came from IDEA data (Age 6-21), and enrollment counts were computed from NCES total enrollment and racial percentage distributions.

This confirms that, after controlling for racial composition, autism identification was significantly less likely in Ohio than in California.

dependent_variable: group_chooses_red (indicator that the group decision was the red jar)
main_predictor: voting rule / treatment (Majority r=5, SuperMajority r=7, Unanimity r=9)

model_specification: OLS linear probability model at the group level: group_chooses_red ~ C(treatment) + red_signal_grp; reported statistic is the joint cluster-robust F test that the two voting-rule coefficients are zero.
controls: Number of red private signals in the group (red_signal_grp); standard errors clustered by session.
operationalization_notes: The paper evaluates institutional differences in collective outcomes by comparing group decisions across threshold rules while conditioning on the group signal profile. The supplied data contain group decisions, voting rules, and red-signal counts but no separate communication/no-communication indicator, so I tested whether institutional differences remained in the available group-decision data using the signal-count control.

The raw red-choice rates also differed sharply by institution (58.3% majority, 20.0% supermajority, 0.0% unanimity), so this analysis does not show diminished institutional differences.

dependent_variable: Group mean market price in the uniform price auction, averaged over rounds
main_predictor: Offering mechanism, operationalized as uniform-auction price compared against the fixed-offering price benchmark of 1.94

operationalization_notes: The paper's revenue claim is tied directly to market price because the supply is fixed and subscription is generally near complete; the paper also analyzes group-level results due to within-group dependence. The fixed-price treatment price is exogenously set at 1.94, so I tested whether uniform-auction group mean prices exceed that benchmark.
reasoning: Using group-level average uniform-auction prices and excluding groups flagged for dropout or bankruptcy, the mean price was 1.9567 versus the fixed-price benchmark of 1.94. A one-sided one-sample t-test gave t(31)=0.174, p=0.432, so the data do not provide evidence that uniform price auctions raise higher revenues than fixed price offerings in this sample.

dependent_variable: Binary intention to vote for Barack Obama from Q20, coded 1 = Barack Obama and 0 = Donald Trump/a different candidate/no support or unsure
main_predictor: Conception risk (oddconcept)

model_specification: Point-biserial Pearson correlation between conception risk and binary Obama vote intention, tested with the equivalent t test for zero correlation
operationalization_notes: The paper tested the simple claim with a point-biserial correlation using a dichotomous Obama-vs-other vote preference outcome among normally cycling women; I used the corresponding Obama preference item and conception-risk variable in the provided dataset with eligibility exclusions matching the methods.
reasoning: Using a point-biserial correlation test, conception risk was not positively related to intending to vote for Barack Obama in the eligible analytic sample, t(302) = -0.758, p = 0.449 (equivalent r = -0.044). The observed association was slightly negative and statistically inconclusive, so it does not support the claimed positive relationship.

dependent_variable: Panic-buying search composite: average of within-country standardized log1p Google Trends scores for 'panic buying' and 'stockpile'

operationalization_notes: The paper used cross-temporal analyses within the four countries, log transformation and standardization, and a panic-buying composite from 'panic buying' and 'stockpile'. I used a single pooled fixed-effects version of that analysis to produce one main test of the claim's panic-buying outcome.
reasoning: In a pooled within-country fixed-effects regression for the four focal countries, standardized log COVID-19 infections positively predicted the panic-buying search composite, B = 0.683, t(230) = 16.46, p = 9.44e-41. This supports the claimed positive relationship for the panic-buying component of the broader claim.

dependent_variable: Mean procedural justice score across pj1-pj7
main_predictor: Mean perceived workplace racial discrimination score across rd1-rd8

operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim using composite scale means and a controlled regression; I therefore used the same scale construction and Step 2 regression specification, using the largest available participant dataset rather than copying any statistic from the article.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting mean procedural justice, perceived workplace racial discrimination had a negative coefficient (b = -0.311) after adjustment for the paper's demographic controls and perceived organizational efforts to support diversity. The coefficient was statistically different from zero, t(96) = -3.49, p = 0.00073, supporting the claim that higher perceived racial discrimination is associated with lower procedural justice.

dependent_variable: PSS10_avg perceived stress composite score
main_predictor: agreement with containment measures, operationalized as 5 - abs(Trust_countrymeasure - 5), where higher values indicate judging the measures closer to appropriate
sample_definition: Swiss respondents in the provided dataset with non-missing PSS10_avg and Trust_countrymeasure values
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of PSS10_avg on the continuous agreement score
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods identify perceived stress as the PSS-10 score and agreement with containment measures as whether government measures were judged appropriate versus too little/too much. In the provided replication data, Trust_countrymeasure is an 0-10 item centered at 5 = appropriate, so I used closeness to 5 as a continuous agreement score and tested its unadjusted association with stress.
reasoning: In the Swiss complete-case sample, higher agreement with the country's preventive measures predicted lower perceived stress, b = -0.0647 PSS10-average units per agreement-score point, t(1077) = -5.09, p = 4.25e-7. This supports the claim that agreement with containment measures is associated with decreased stress.

dependent_variable: Binary trust-game choice, recoded 1 = trust/Option L and 0 = distrust/Option R
main_predictor: Interaction of mean-centered Honesty-Humility score with self-uncertainty condition (0 = certainty control, 1 = self-uncertainty)

operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Studies 2 and 3 main analysis: a binary trust-game outcome was regressed on Honesty-Humility, experimental self-uncertainty condition, and their interaction. Honesty-Humility was computed as the mean of the 10 HEXACO-60 Honesty-Humility items, reverse-scoring negatively keyed items.
reasoning: I fit the Study 2/3-style logistic regression predicting trust from mean-centered Honesty-Humility, self-uncertainty condition, and their interaction. The Honesty-Humility × self-uncertainty interaction was in the predicted negative direction but was not statistically significant, z = -0.623, p = 0.534, so these data do not provide clear evidence that high-Honesty-Humility participants shifted toward distrust under self-uncertainty.

dependent_variable: Desirability index: mean of likelihood of seeing the movie, perceived movie quality, and likelihood of buying the movie
main_predictor: Interaction between temporary self-concept clarity condition (clear vs conflicted/low clarity) and rating distribution (bimodal vs unimodal)

operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Study 2b operationalization of temporary self-concept clarity threat and product desirability, using contrast coding clear = 1, conflicted = -1, bimodal = 1, unimodal = -1.

With coding clear = 1, conflicted/low clarity = -1, bimodal = 1, and unimodal = -1, the negative interaction indicates a larger bimodal-over-unimodal preference in the conflicted/low-clarity condition, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: composite revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation scores
main_predictor: composite anger and sympathy scores

dependent_variable: COVID-19 misperceptions composite score (MisperpSc)

dependent_variable: Participant-level average of corrected recognition indices for joy and anger words, computed as (hits - false alarms)/8 for each emotion category and then averaged
main_predictor: Alexithymia group from the TAS-20 median split (TASGRP: low vs high)

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that EVOLVED was answered True/scientifically correct (humans developed from earlier species of animals); false, don't know, and no answer were coded 0 among respondents to whom the item was administered.
main_predictor: Assigned latent class membership: post-secular versus traditional from a three-class latent class analysis of science knowledge, science attitudes, Bible views, and religious affiliation strength.

dependent_variable: Mug trendiness index: mean of ratings for trendy, modern, and urban (V18-V20)

dependent_variable: Participant-level proportion of utilitarian responses across moral_accept and moral_accept1, coded 1 when the action was judged morally acceptable (response = 2) and 0 otherwise.

The available dataset contains two moral acceptability outcomes, so I averaged these binary utilitarian-response indicators per participant and compared conditions.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) on interpersonal obstacle-prime / instrumental-behavior-target lexical decision trials; lower values indicate stronger obstacle-behavior association

controls: Interpersonal behavior accessibility reaction time, centered expectation, condition main effects, and expectation-by-condition interaction terms
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim in Study 1 using interpersonal obstacle-behavior association RTs adjusted for mere accessibility of the behavior. I followed that specification and used the observed low expectation value in this dataset to test whether mental contrasting yielded weaker associations than the control conditions.
reasoning: At the observed low end of expectations (IntExp = 2), the adjusted contrast comparing mental contrasting to the average of the reverse-contrasting and irrelevant-control conditions was not significant, t(306) = -0.314, p = .754. The estimated difference was -19.9 ms, where lower reaction time indicates stronger rather than weaker obstacle-behavior associations, so the data do not support the claimed weak associations under low expectations.

dependent_variable: s, the proportion of the surplus that the dictator gave to the recipient
main_predictor: libertarian-principle predicted recipient share x_l, computed as the recipient's monetary contribution divided by total surplus
sample_definition: Dictator-worse treatment observations in cleaned_data.dta with playerdictator = 1, dictator piece rate = 150, partner piece rate = 200, and nonmissing s and x_l; 27 paired observations were available, with 18 nonzero differences used by the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test on nonzero paired differences s - x_l gave z = -3.376, p = 0.00037, rejecting the hypothesis that behavior follows the libertarian principle in the direction of lower-than-libertarian giving.

dependent_variable: diagnosed with hypertension before the IFLS survey (1 = diagnosed, computed as 1 - underdiagnosed)

operationalization_notes: The paper tests disease detection with probit models split by general health status; I followed that approach for the poor-health subgroup and reversed the underdiagnosis outcome so the coefficient directly represents probability of diagnosis.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological judgments/rejecting harm responses (RH_PMD, RH_NMD, RH_CMD)

reasoning: A 2 (social observation condition) × 3 (dilemma type) mixed ANOVA on participants' proportions of deontological/rejecting-harm responses showed no condition × dilemma-type interaction, F(2, 308) = 0.237, p = 0.789. The observed group was only slightly higher than control for personal dilemmas (0.649 vs. 0.629), and the pattern was not selectively stronger for personal dilemmas.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1, treated as a 5-point COVID-19 anxiety/worry/concern score with higher values indicating greater concern
main_predictor: gender, operationalized as female versus male using the binary female indicator
sample_definition: Respondents in data_0948.csv from Germany with non-missing mh_anxiety_1 and binary gender/female coding; excluded 121 respondents with non-binary/uncoded gender, yielding N = 10071.
model_specification: Unweighted independent-samples equal-variance t-test comparing mean mh_anxiety_1 scores for women versus men, with the reported contrast defined as women minus men.
operationalization_notes: The paper frames the claim in terms of gender differences in COVID-19 worry/concern measured on Likert-type items, so I tested the mean gender difference on the available COVID-19 anxiety/worry item in the German respondent data.
reasoning: Women had higher scores on the COVID-19 anxiety/worry item than men (M_women = 3.075, M_men = 2.890). An independent-samples t-test for the women-minus-men contrast was significant, t(10069) = 8.253, p = 1.74e-16, supporting the claim that women are more concerned.

dependent_variable: Average percentage change in estimated per-resident miles traveled during March 19-28, 2020 relative to day-of-week-matched baseline days in Feb 24-Mar 1, 2020
main_predictor: 2016 county-level Trump vote share
sample_definition: U.S. counties with complete BTS trip-distance mobility data for the baseline and March 19-28 windows and nonmissing voting and county covariate data (N=3113)
