operationalization_notes: Following the paper's cross-sectional OLS approach, I used the available trip-distance data to approximate average distance traveled per resident from distance-bin midpoints, then compared March 19-28 mobility to a pre-COVID weekday-matched reference week. The Trump-share coefficient directly tests whether Republican political orientation predicts less social distancing.
reasoning: In an OLS model with state fixed effects and county covariates, the coefficient for Trump's 2016 county vote share was positive for percentage change in mobility (t(3045) = 4.98, p = 6.83e-7). Because more negative mobility change indicates more distancing, this positive association means more Republican-oriented counties had less reduction in mobility, consistent with reduced social distancing.

dependent_variable: Base-10 log of reflected social distancing composite (soc_dist_log_reflected; higher values indicate lower social distancing compliance)
main_predictor: Political conservatism composite (mean of conservative ideology, reverse-coded liberal identification, and Republican preference items)
sample_definition: Complete cases in the final dataset: U.S. respondents with no COVID-19 diagnosis who passed the attention check and were retained in the provided final data file (N = 322).
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression with the transformed/reflected social distancing composite as the outcome and conservatism as the sole predictor; the reported t test is for the conservatism slope.
operationalization_notes: The paper computed arithmetic-average composites for social distancing and conservatism and noted strong negative skew in social distancing, addressed by a base-10 logarithmic transformation of reflected scores. I used that provided transformed/reflected social-distancing variable to test the total ideology-compliance relationship corresponding to Hypothesis 1.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of log-reflected social-distancing compliance on political conservatism, conservatism significantly predicted higher reflected scores, b = 0.0286, t(320) = 3.82, p = 0.00016. Because the dependent variable is reflected, higher scores indicate less social-distancing compliance, so this supports the claim that conservatism was inversely associated with compliance.

dependent_variable: Composite academic achievement: mean of within-sample z-scored X7RSCALK5 reading IRT and X7MSCALK5 mathematics IRT scores
main_predictor: Composite social-emotional problems: mean of within-sample z-scored X7TCHEXT teacher-reported externalising and X7TCHINT teacher-reported internalising scores
sample_definition: Records with X12LANGST == 1 (used as the available ELL/language-status indicator) and complete nonnegative data on X7RSCALK5, X7MSCALK5, X7TCHEXT, and X7TCHINT; special negative missing codes and blanks excluded
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of the achievement composite on the social-emotional problems composite; the reported t test is for the slope, equivalent to a Pearson correlation test
operationalization_notes: The paper modeled academic achievement as reading and mathematics scores and social-emotional problems as internalizing/externalizing problems. The provided data dictionary identified corresponding achievement and teacher-reported internalizing/externalizing variables, so I combined these into composites and tested their association within the ELL/language-status subsample.
reasoning: Among children coded as ELL/language-minority in the available language-status variable, the social-emotional problems composite was negatively related to the reading/mathematics achievement composite, t(2045) = -12.43, p = 2.93e-34 (equivalent r = -0.265). Thus, children with fewer teacher-reported social-emotional problems tended to have higher achievement scores.

dependent_variable: Mean perceived societal good rating across the four organization scenarios (SocGood_Artis, SocGood_Green, SocGood_Food, SocGood_Medtech; 1 = great harm, 5 = great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition, coded as for-profit (condition = 3) versus unspecified motive baseline (condition = 2)
sample_definition: All participants in the SAV dataset assigned to the for-profit or unspecified condition with complete societal-good ratings for all four scenarios; no exclusions were applied.
model_specification: Independent-samples t test comparing participant-level mean societal-good ratings between for-profit and unspecified-motive conditions, using equal variances.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 directly tested this claim by manipulating firm motives between subjects and averaging societal-good judgments across four within-subject organization scenarios. I used the for-profit versus unspecified-motive contrast as the clearest test of whether adding a profit motive reduces perceived societal good relative to a baseline without stated motives.
reasoning: Participants in the for-profit condition rated the organizations as accomplishing less societal good on average (M = 3.746) than participants in the unspecified-motive condition (M = 4.087). This difference was statistically significant, t(242) = -4.795, p = 2.84e-6, supporting the claim that a profit motive reduced perceived societal good.

dependent_variable: Sharing intention for each headline, rescaled from the 6-point Likert response so 1=0 and 6=1
main_predictor: Headline veracity within the treatment condition (true vs false), tested as the veracity + veracity-by-treatment linear contrast
sample_definition: Study 2 rows in the provided data with valid headline-sharing ratings; all treatment and control ratings were used in the model (877 participants, 26,310 headline ratings), with the reported contrast evaluating the treatment condition (440 treatment participants)
model_specification: Linear regression at the headline-rating level: scaled sharing intention ~ veracity * treatment; two-way cluster-robust standard errors clustered by participant and headline; reported t test is the treatment-condition simple slope for veracity
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's stated rating-level linear-regression approach with sharing intentions rescaled to [0,1] and tests the claim directly as the true-versus-false difference among treated participants.
reasoning: In a rating-level OLS model with two-way cluster-robust standard errors, the simple effect of veracity within the treatment condition was negative rather than positive (true minus false = -0.0062 on the 0-1 sharing scale), t(26306) = -1.45, p = .147. Thus, in this analysis the treatment-condition sharing intentions for true headlines were not significantly higher than for false headlines.

dependent_variable: Indicator for sustained growth: GDP per capita growth at least 2% in each of the five years following the Afrobarometer fieldwork year
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index, the log of the within-country weighted share of respondents saying their group is never treated unfairly by the government
sample_definition: Country-survey observations from Afrobarometer rounds 1-4 with valid impartiality data, matched Polity2 data, and five future GDP per capita growth observations through 2013; Zambia 2009 and Zimbabwe 2009 were excluded for lacking five future years, leaving 62 observations from 20 countries.
model_specification: Pooled OLS linear probability model with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; test is the t-test for the Log Impartiality index coefficient.
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's baseline approach: construct the survey-based impartiality index using respondent weights, define sustained growth as five consecutive future years of at least 2% GDP per capita growth, and estimate a pooled linear probability model controlling for Polity2.
reasoning: In a baseline linear probability model, the coefficient for log perceived impartiality was negative and not statistically distinguishable from zero (t(59) = -0.49, p = 0.628). This does not support the claim that more impartial governments were more likely to enter sustained growth spells in this reanalysis.

dependent_variable: Evaluation rating of the toaster favored by aggregated information versus evaluation rating of the toaster favored by individualized information; analyzed as the within-participant difference (4.5-star toaster mean minus 2.5-star toaster mean).
main_predictor: Information type within the abstract sound condition (aggregated-information toaster vs individualized-information toaster).
sample_definition: Participants assigned to the abstract sound condition (group = 5) who were retained in the study's analysis filter (filter = 1), excluding participants marked for technical or hearing problems; N = 16.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing toaster45_mean and toaster25_mean within the abstract sound group.
operationalization_notes: The cited claim refers specifically to participants in the abstract sound condition favoring the toaster with positive aggregated information over the toaster with positive individualized information, so I tested the within-subject difference in the two toaster evaluation means in that condition, using the same exclusion filter described in the paper.
reasoning: Among the 16 included participants in the abstract-sound condition, the mean evaluation was higher for the toaster favored by aggregated information (M = 5.1375) than for the toaster favored by individualized information (M = 2.9750). A paired-samples t-test on these two evaluations gave t(15) = 7.858, p = 1.07e-6, supporting the claim that abstract-sound participants favored the aggregated-information toaster.

dependent_variable: National affluence, measured as GDP per capita in thousands of USD (PPP series in the supplied GDPcapita variable)
main_predictor: One-year-lagged imports from the South, measured as totalimport in billions of USD
sample_definition: Country-years for the 18 OECD countries from 1970-2003 with complete lagged imports from the South, lagged exports to the South, lagged unemployment, and GDP per capita; excluded the paper-identified outlier country-years Norway 1999-2003 and Belgium 1998-1999 where present.
model_specification: OLS linear regression with country fixed effects and five-year period fixed effects; test statistic is the t test for the lagged imports-from-South coefficient.
controls: One-year-lagged exports to the South, one-year-lagged unemployment rate, country fixed effects, and five-year period indicators (1970-74 reference).
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's indirect-effects equation in which national affluence is regressed on imports from the South, exports to the South, controls, country fixed effects, and period effects, with predictors lagged one year. The supplied replication file contains South trade totals rather than GDP-normalized trade shares, so imports were scaled to billions of USD for estimation.
reasoning: In a two-way fixed-effects regression predicting GDP per capita, the coefficient on lagged imports from the South was positive (0.0267 thousand USD per additional billion USD of imports) and statistically significant, t(419)=4.25, p=2.65e-5. This supports the claimed positive relationship between a Northern country's imports from the South and national affluence.

dependent_variable: Participant-level average benefit-minus-symbolism difference score across the four symbolic products: college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, and greeting cards
main_predictor: Branding condition: branded product/brand set versus unbranded category-level product
sample_definition: All observations in the combined data with Cond equal to 1, 2, 3, or 4 and complete utilitarian and symbolic ratings for all four symbolic products; Cond 1/2 were treated as unbranded category conditions and Cond 3/4 as branded conditions
model_specification: Independent-samples pooled-variance t-test comparing the mean symbolic-product difference score in branded versus unbranded category conditions
operationalization_notes: The paper tested attitude function shifts using benefit-minus-symbolism difference scores, with higher values indicating more utilitarian and less symbolic attitudes. Because the target claim is specifically about symbolic product categories, I averaged the difference scores over the symbolic products and tested the simple brand-versus-category effect.
reasoning: Branded versions of the symbolic products had a higher mean benefit-minus-symbolism score (M = -2.066) than unbranded category versions (M = -2.614). This positive brand-category difference was statistically significant, t(607) = 4.09, p = 0.000049, indicating that branding made attitudes toward symbolic categories less symbolic/more utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic self-discipline (ASD), treated as the self-regulation measure
sample_definition: All observations represented in the aggregate correlation matrix; N = 366 with variables ASD, self-discipline facet, and semester GPA.
model_specification: OLS multiple regression reconstructed from the reported correlation/covariance matrix: semester GPA regressed on ASD and self-discipline facet; main test is the t-test for the ASD coefficient.
operationalization_notes: The available data are aggregate means, SDs, and correlations rather than individual records. The readme identifies ASD as corresponding to self-regulation and GPA as the focal dependent variable; including the self-discipline facet mirrors the paper's SEM comparison of self-regulation with self-discipline as simultaneous predictors of academic achievement.
reasoning: Using the provided correlation matrix for N = 366, academic self-discipline/self-regulation positively predicted semester GPA after controlling for the self-discipline facet, t(363) = 4.85, p = 1.79e-6. This supports the claim that self-regulation is positively related to GPA in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Mean endorsement of four COVID-19 conspiracy theory belief items (conspiracy_theories__1 to conspiracy_theories__4)
main_predictor: Mean national/collective narcissism score from three items (collective_narcis__1 to collective_narcis__3)
sample_definition: Complete cases in ReplicationData_Sternisko_covid_GG7d.csv with non-missing values on all three national narcissism items and all four COVID-19 conspiracy belief items; N = 1552.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of the averaged COVID-19 conspiracy belief scale on the averaged national narcissism scale.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3/data dictionary for the supplied dataset includes national narcissism and COVID-19 conspiracy belief items but explicitly does not include dissemination intentions. I therefore tested the closest available component of the claim: whether higher national narcissism is associated with stronger endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories.
reasoning: In the supplied cleaned dataset, national narcissism positively predicted endorsement of COVID-19 conspiracy theories, b = 0.539, t(1550) = 23.91, p = 8.46e-108, N = 1552. This is a strong positive association in the same direction as the original study's claim, although the supplied data did not include a direct dissemination-intention outcome.

dependent_variable: Participant-level proportion of fWHR forced-choice trials in which the high-fWHR face was selected as more aggressive
main_predictor: High versus low facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR) face within each pair
sample_definition: Processed_Data.csv participants with Quality == 'Yes' (N=139); included the 24 fWHR trials corresponding to Q1-Q24, following the Study 1 design described in the paper
model_specification: One-sample t-test of each participant's mean high-fWHR choice proportion against chance level 0.5
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 used 24 fWHR pairs and 12 masculinity pairs; I treated Q1-Q24 as the fWHR trials in the processed dataset and used the right-side response as selecting the higher-fWHR version, consistent with the provided stimulus examples/processed coding.
reasoning: Among participants who indicated their data should be used, the mean proportion of fWHR trials on which the higher-fWHR/right-side face was chosen as more aggressive was 0.533, significantly above chance, t(138)=3.14, p=0.0021. This supports the directional claim that increased fWHR is associated with greater perceived aggressiveness in the available forced-choice data.

dependent_variable: money: amount of bribe demanded by the public official or amount proposed/kept by Participant B
main_predictor: game frame / treatment (briberygame: harassment bribery game vs ultimatum game)
sample_definition: Decision-maker observations only: survey 2 public officials in the bribery game and survey 4 Participant Bs in the ultimatum game, excluding observations with missing money values; zero amounts were retained as part of the full sample average.
model_specification: Welch independent-samples t-test comparing mean money between bribery game and ultimatum game groups.
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the average bribe/transfer amount across the bribery and strategically identical ultimatum frames, so I compared the full-sample amount variable for the roles that set this amount, matching the paper's descriptive mean-comparison approach.
reasoning: Among decision-makers with observed amount data, the mean amount demanded/proposed was lower in the bribery game (M = 0.578, n = 199) than in the ultimatum game (M = 0.910, n = 195). A Welch two-sample t-test gave t(344.68) = -5.37, p = 1.42e-7, supporting the claim that the average amount is lower in the bribery frame.

dependent_variable: Participant's estimate of the total number of taxi cabs divided by the maximum cab serial number observed so far
main_predictor: Number of observed taxi-cab serial-number examples (1, 3, or 10)
sample_definition: Taxicab-condition observations from the JSON data files; included participants with complete responses at 1, 3, and 10 examples, excluding participants with any estimate below the current maximum observed serial number and excluding participants with any normalized response more than 3 SD from its condition mean.
model_specification: One-way within-subjects repeated-measures ANOVA on normalized estimates across the three levels of examples seen.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Experiment 1 analysis strategy for the taxicab scenario: screen implausible responses, normalize each prediction by the largest example provided, and test the within-subject effect of number of examples.
reasoning: In the taxicab condition, normalized estimates of total fleet size decreased as more cab serial-number observations were shown: M=1.85 with 1 observation, M=1.33 with 3 observations, and M=1.15 with 10 observations. A one-way repeated-measures ANOVA found a strong effect of number of observations, F(2,1148)=127.92, p=6.99e-51, supporting the claim that predictions became smaller relative to the largest observed serial number as more examples were provided.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total, a binary indicator for district-level fraud from the Beber-Scacco last-digit chi-square test on total vote counts
main_predictor: election-day violence per capita (v.elday.pc) and its squared term (v.elday.pc.2)
sample_definition: Afghan districts in the replication data with non-missing dependent variable, election-day violence variables, and all controls; N=375 after dropping missing electrification/per-capita expenditure controls
model_specification: Logistic regression with an intercept; Wald chi-square test that the linear and squared election-day violence coefficients are jointly zero; covariance matrix clustered by regional command without small-sample correction
controls: number of closed stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure in 1000 AFs, distance from Kabul, elevation
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's main Table 2 Model 1 specification for the inverted-U claim, using the last-digit fraud indicator and election-day violence; the joint Wald test provides one main statistic for the curvilinear violence-fraud relationship, with coefficient signs used to assess the claimed direction.
reasoning: I fit a district-level logit model for last-digit fraud including election-day violence and its square, with the paper's controls and regional-command clustered standard errors. The two violence terms were jointly significant, χ²(2, N=375)=35.225, p=2.24e-8; the fitted coefficients were positive for violence (8.477) and negative for violence squared (-13.748), matching an inverted-U pattern.

dependent_variable: Social undermining, operationalized as reverse-coded willingness to be matched with the potential partner (8 - original Undermin rating)
main_predictor: Temporal social comparison condition (unfavorable vs favorable) moderated by competition condition (high vs low)
sample_definition: All 574 participant IDs in the analytical CSV; each participant contributed two observations, one favorable and one unfavorable temporal social comparison rating, with competition as a between-participant condition.
model_specification: Computed each participant's within-person difference in reversed social undermining for unfavorable minus favorable TSC, then regressed this difference score on competition condition; the reported t test is the competition coefficient.
controls: None; static social comparison was held constant by design in this Study 1a-style dataset.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1a method used a mixed design with TSC manipulated within participants and competition between participants, and measured undermining by reluctance to be matched with a coworker. I therefore tested the TSC × competition interaction via the equivalent difference-score regression, reverse-coding the original matching-preference item because the data dictionary states lower original values indicate higher undermining.
reasoning: Using reversed matching preference so that higher scores indicate greater social undermining, the unfavorable-minus-favorable TSC effect was larger under high competition (M_diff = 0.705) than low competition (M_diff = 0.127). The between-condition test of this within-person difference was significant, t(572) = 3.384, p = 0.000764, supporting the claim that the TSC-undermining relationship is stronger under high competition.

dependent_variable: Mean endorsement of the six coronavirus-specific conspiracy theory items (SpecCTs_1, SpecCTs_2, SpecCTs_3r, SpecCTs_4, SpecCTs_5, SpecCTs_6r)
main_predictor: Mean of COVID1 and COVID3, representing current worry about and perceived threat from the coronavirus spread
sample_definition: All 806 observations in the provided cleaned dataset with complete data on the six conspiracy items, COVID1, COVID3, and sample identifier; no cases were excluded.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression: COVID conspiracy belief composite regressed on COVID worry/threat composite and categorical sample indicators.
controls: Survey sample fixed effects using the sample variable (1 = Survey 1 USA, 2 = Survey 2a USA, 3 = Survey 2b UK). No age, gender, education, trust, risk-perception, or lack-of-control controls were available in the provided dataset.
operationalization_notes: The paper's focal mediation model included risk perception, trust in institutions, anxiety, lack of control, and demographic covariates, but the provided dataset contained only COVID-specific conspiracy items, two COVID worry/threat items, and sample identifiers. I therefore tested the core available component of the claim: whether COVID-related worry/threat predicts higher COVID-specific conspiracy belief endorsement.
reasoning: In an OLS regression, the composite of current COVID worry/threat negatively predicted the mean COVID-specific conspiracy-belief scale after adjusting for survey sample, b = -0.140, t(802) = -4.69, p = 3.18e-6. Thus, in the provided data, stronger COVID-related worry/threat was associated with lower, not higher, endorsement of COVID conspiracy beliefs.

dependent_variable: Participant-level mean reaction time in milliseconds, contrasted as NeutralM minus AngryM
main_predictor: Central face valence: angry versus neutral, within the GAD/likely-GAD group
sample_definition: Rows with Group = 1 (coded in the data dictionary as likely GAD) and nonmissing AngryM and NeutralM; n = 63
model_specification: One-sample paired-samples t test of the within-participant neutral-minus-angry mean RT contrast against zero
operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 tests this claim using mean reaction times to peripheral target letters after centrally presented angry versus neutral faces in the GAD group. The available dataset contains participant-level condition means, so I directly tested the same within-group valence contrast using the Group = 1 coding.
reasoning: Among participants coded as the GAD/likely-GAD group, mean RT was 486.81 ms for angry faces and 485.36 ms for neutral faces. A paired t test on the contrast neutral minus angry RT gave t(62) = -0.471, p = 0.639, so the data do not support faster responses for angry than neutral faces.

dependent_variable: Change in brand personality impressions: mean post-scenario Hansen Design sophistication rating (Q5_1-Q5_4) minus mean pre-scenario rating (Q2_1-Q2_4)
main_predictor: Employee behavior consistency (consistent vs inconsistent) × pseudorelevant information disclosure (no pseudorelevant information vs disclosed pseudorelevant information)
sample_definition: Participants in the final Stage 2 data file with high outcome dependency (Outcome Dependency = 1) and complete pre- and post-sophistication scale items; first Qualtrics header row excluded.
model_specification: Two-way between-subjects ANOVA/OLS with sum-coded factors, testing the Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction within the high outcome-dependency subsample.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this hypothesis using brand-personality difference scores after first exposing participants to a sophisticated brand ad; because the target claim is specifically under high outcome dependency, I restricted to that subsample and tested whether pseudorelevant information moderated the effect of behavior consistency on the change score.
reasoning: Among high outcome-dependency participants, the Behavior Consistency × Pseudorelevant Information interaction on change in brand sophistication was not significant, F(1, 420) = 0.836, p = 0.361. The cell means were only weakly in the predicted direction: no-information vs information was 0.154 vs -0.021 for consistent behavior and -0.723 vs -0.683 for inconsistent behavior, so this analysis does not provide clear support for the claim.

dependent_variable: Aversiveness/disturbing rating, rescaled from 1-7 in the raw files to 0-6, averaged within participant for each item type
main_predictor: Humor topic/type: Covid Verbal versus Non-Covid Verbal
sample_definition: Participants with non-missing completion timestamps in both deidentified survey parts and at least one valid aversiveness rating in both compared item blocks (N = 916)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test on within-participant mean aversiveness for Covid Verbal items versus Non-Covid Verbal items
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary contrast for this claim compares Covid Verbal with structurally similar Non-Covid Verbal humor. I followed the stimulus-type order and counts described in the Methods, treating the six 36-item survey blocks as Covid Verbal items pic1-pic72 and Non-Covid Verbal items pic145-pic216, and used participant-level means to test the directional aversiveness difference.
reasoning: Among participants who completed both survey parts, mean aversiveness was higher for the Covid verbal item block (M = 0.766 on the 0-6 rescaled scale) than for the non-Covid verbal item block (M = 0.723). The paired-samples test of participant-level mean differences was significant, t(915) = 5.96, p = 3.52e-9, supporting greater aversiveness for Covid humor.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for adopting at least one avoidance-related preparation behavior in the last month: avoiding social events, avoiding public transport, eating out less, shopping for groceries less, cooking at home more, or staying home from work.
main_predictor: Mean of Govresponse_2 and Govresponse_3: trust in the country's politicians and national scientific/medical advisors to deal effectively with the pandemic.
sample_definition: Australian respondents in replication_data.csv with usable preparation-response data and complete data on trust, age group, gender, and coronavirus worry; missing prep responses were treated as no selected behavior only when the respondent's overall missingness proportion was <= 0.20, otherwise excluded.
model_specification: Logistic regression with a Wald z test for the government/authority trust coefficient.
controls: Categorical age group, categorical gender, and continuous personal worry about coronavirus/COVID-19 (FinitePool_2).
operationalization_notes: The paper tested avoidance behavior using logistic regression adjusted for demographics and worry; the provided dataset did not contain the exact Seale behavior/trust items, so I used the closest available government/authority trust items and coded avoidance from the multi-select preparation question.
reasoning: In an adjusted logistic regression predicting whether respondents had adopted any avoidance-related preparation behavior, the government/authority trust composite had a positive but non-significant coefficient (Wald z = 1.38, p = 0.166; OR = 1.13 per 1-point increase). Thus, this operationalization does not provide clear evidence that greater trust is associated with adopting avoidance behaviors after adjustment.

dependent_variable: Current money management stress composite (CMMS; higher scores indicate greater stress)
main_predictor: Writing prompt frame/group: success frame versus failure frame
sample_definition: Participants in the analysis dataset with Include = 1 and non-missing CMMS values; n = 262 (131 failure, 131 success)
model_specification: Independent-samples equal-variance t-test comparing mean CMMS in the success-frame group to the failure-frame group
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3a tests whether the current-finance success versus failure writing prompt affects current money management stress; therefore I used the included Study 3a observations and compared the CMMS composite directly between the two randomized groups.
reasoning: Among included participants, the success-frame group had lower current money management stress (M = 2.997) than the failure-frame group (M = 3.441). An independent-samples t-test on CMMS gave t(260) = -3.65, p = .00032, supporting the claimed directional effect.

dependent_variable: Situational attribution style scale (Sit_AttB)
main_predictor: Dispositional attribution style scale (Disp_AttB)
sample_definition: Respondents in the cleaned Qualtrics adult dataset assigned to the bidirectional questionnaire condition (BiDummy = 1 / Bal_Group = 1), with complete data on the model variables.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of situational attributions on dispositional attributions and the paper's control variables, using HC1 robust standard errors.
controls: Perceived victimization risk, perceived crime trend, news consumption, conservatism, religiosity, family victimization, education, female, White, and age.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's multivariate test of the relationship between attribution styles in the bidirectional group, using the cleaned reverse-coded attribution scales and the same set of controls described in the methods section.
reasoning: In the bidirectional questionnaire group, an OLS model with robust standard errors showed that dispositional attributions significantly negatively predicted situational attributions, b = -0.223, robust t(630) = -4.94, p = 9.96e-7. This supports the claimed significant hydraulic relationship when items are formulated bidirectionally.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME
sample_definition: Participants from the overall dataset with complete data on PSS-10 score, monthly income, gender, age, education, and family members; 18 participants missing gender were excluded, yielding N = 2035.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of PSS-10 SCORE on MONTHLY INCOME and sociodemographic covariates; the main result is the t test for the monthly income coefficient.
controls: BE MALE, AGE, EDUCATION, FAMILY MEMBERS
operationalization_notes: The paper tested the income claim in its sociodemographic regression predicting PSS-10 stress. I followed that model's final sociodemographic specification, treating monthly income as an ordinal numeric predictor and perceived stress as a continuous outcome.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting PSS-10 perceived stress scores, monthly income had a negative coefficient (B = -0.463) and was statistically significant, t(2029) = -3.465, p = 0.00054. Thus, higher income was associated with lower perceived stress in this sample.

dependent_variable: Mean of nonmaterial behavioral inclination items: chips, casual sex, and social-network friends
main_predictor: Dispositional Greed Scale score (DGS)
sample_definition: Participants in the analytic dataset with Finished = 1 and complete DGS, MVS, and behavioral inclination data
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of the nonmaterial behavioral inclination mean on DGS and MVS with an intercept
operationalization_notes: Study 2 tested whether greed predicts desires for nonmaterial goods beyond materialism; therefore I aggregated the three nonmaterial inclination items and tested the unique DGS coefficient while controlling for materialism.
reasoning: In a linear regression predicting the average of the three nonmaterial greedy behavioral inclinations, DGS had a positive unique association controlling for MVS, b = 0.708, t(489) = 15.65, p = 4.85e-45. This supports the claim that dispositional greed predicts greedy behavioral tendencies over and above materialism.

dependent_variable: Indicator equal to 1 if the respondent chose the ambiguous candidate in Q3, using RND_01 to identify whether the ambiguous candidate was Candidate A or Candidate B
main_predictor: Risk aversion, coded 1 for respondents who said they prefer avoiding risks (Q4 = 2), 0 for preferring taking risks or having no preference
sample_definition: All respondents with valid self-placement (Q1), certainty (Q2), candidate choice (Q3), risk preference (Q4), candidate position, and presentation-order data; skipped/refused/nonresponse codes were excluded
model_specification: Survey-weighted probit regression with HC1 robust standard errors
controls: Voter certainty, coded 1 for extremely sure about own position (Q2 = 1), and distance differential |v - p| - |v - mu| computed from Q1, DOV_PRECISE, and DOV_AMBIGUOUS
operationalization_notes: This mirrors the paper's unbranded-candidate probit analysis for causal mechanisms: ambiguous-candidate choice is regressed on risk aversion while adjusting for certainty about own position and spatial proximity. I used the provided post-stratification weight to estimate the population relationship in the supplied survey data.
reasoning: Using a weighted probit model following the paper's causal-mechanism specification, risk aversion had a negative coefficient for choosing the ambiguous candidate (b = -0.150, robust SE = 0.0529), z = -2.84, p = 0.0045. Thus, in this operationalization, respondents who preferred avoiding risks were significantly less likely to choose the ambiguous candidate.

dependent_variable: Quarter-end ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread (BAMLH0A0HYM2)
main_predictor: Net percent of domestic respondents tightening C&I loan standards for large and medium firms (LargeandMedium)
sample_definition: All quarterly observations with overlapping CI_Data survey values and BAMLH0A0HYM2 quarter-end observations, 2010:Q1 through 2020:Q2 (n=42). Daily BAML observations were collapsed to the last available trading day in each survey quarter-end month.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression: HYSpread_t = alpha + beta * LargeandMedium_t + error_t; the reported test is the two-sided t test of beta = 0.
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's empirical use of Federal Reserve credit-standards data as a proxy for bad funding/credit states, I treated tighter credit standards as the negative-shock/bad-state measure. I used high-yield credit spreads as the available proxy for losses in leveraged risky-credit positions, since wider spreads imply lower risky bond values.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of quarter-end high-yield option-adjusted spread on the Fed senior-loan-officer tightening measure, the estimated slope was positive (0.0213 percentage points of HY spread per 1 percentage-point increase in tightening), but the t statistic was only 1.06 with 40 df (p = 0.294). Thus this operationalization does not provide statistically reliable evidence that worse/tighter credit conditions are associated with losses in leveraged/risky-credit positions.

dependent_variable: ICS_olderworkers: positive contact with older workers index
main_predictor: WIAStotal: WICS total score
sample_definition: Participants coded as age40 == 1 (40 years old or younger) with complete data on the outcome, WICS, age, weekly work hours, years with employer, JSS, AOWS adjusted log score, and SIC; n = 446.
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression; compared a model with demographics, JSS, AOWSadjustedlog, and SICmean to the same model plus WIAStotal, reporting the partial F test for the added WICS term.
controls: Age, weekly work hours, years with current employer, JSSmean, AOWSadjustedlog, and SICmean.
operationalization_notes: Following Study 3, I tested incremental criterion validity by asking whether WICS explains additional variance in intergenerational contact beyond demographics, job satisfaction, and other age-attitude measures. I used the larger younger-worker subgroup and its designated criterion outcome, contact with older workers.
reasoning: In the younger-worker subgroup, adding the WICS total score to the regression significantly improved prediction of positive contact with older workers, F(1, 438) = 37.95, p = 1.64e-9. The WICS coefficient was positive (B = 1.04), supporting the study's claim that WICS has criterion/incremental validity as a measure of workplace intergenerational climate.

dependent_variable: Future intention to refrain from stockpiling, operationalized from Q9_1 (the item about planning to buy more food/supplies than usual, coded so higher values indicate refraining/not planning to buy more).
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility score, computed as the mean of HE_1 through HE_16 as coded in the dataset, with higher scores indicating greater Honesty-Humility.
sample_definition: Study 2 observations in ColumbusOSF.csv after removing the embedded label row and retaining complete cases on HE_1-HE_16 and Q9_1; N=314.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of future refrain intention on Honesty-Humility.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies Study 2's future stockpiling-intention item as the direct test of the claim, so I used that item and the 16-item Honesty-Humility scale described in the methods. I used a bivariate OLS model because the reported claim is the zero-order directional association between Honesty-Humility and future refraining intentions.
reasoning: In an OLS regression within the Study 2 data, higher Honesty-Humility significantly predicted greater future intention to refrain from stockpiling, t(312)=11.42, p=1.87e-25. This is a positive and statistically clear association, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Cumulative reported COVID-19 deaths in the county on 2020-06-11
main_predictor: Percent of civilian noninstitutionalized residents under age 65 who were uninsured, derived from ACS S2701 age-specific total and uninsured counts
sample_definition: U.S. county observations in the 50 states on 2020-06-11, excluding Puerto Rico, District of Columbia, counties with density >= 1000 residents per square mile, and observations with missing model variables; missing farm-labor counts were treated as zero before computing farm-worker percentage.

dependent_variable: binary dessert choice, coded as chocolate cake versus fruit salad

The supplied processed dataset contained Left/Right choices rather than trial-level covariates, so the analysis used the side coding of the high-fWHR face in the questionnaire as the response indicator.
reasoning: In the final processed dataset after excluding participants who said their data should not be used, participants chose the high-fWHR-coded face on average in 53.39% of the 36 forced-choice aggression trials. This was significantly above chance, t(287)=5.10, p=6.20e-7, supporting the claim that higher-fWHR faces were perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: money: amount of bribe demanded by the public official or amount Participant B proposed to keep
main_predictor: game frame/treatment (bribery game vs ultimatum game)

operationalization_notes: The abstract claim concerns the average bribe/ultim amount being lower in the harassment bribery frame; therefore I compared the observed demanded/retained amount across the two strategically identical frames, including zero demands to capture overall average corruption extent.
reasoning: In the decision-maker sample with valid amounts, the mean demanded/retained amount was lower in the bribery game (M = 0.578, n = 199) than in the ultimatum game (M = 0.910, n = 195). A one-sided Welch two-sample t-test for BG < UG gave t(344.68) = -5.37, p = 7.10e-08, supporting the claim that the average bribe/retained amount is lower in the bribery frame.

dependent_variable: Estimated total number of taxicabs divided by the maximum observed cab serial number
main_predictor: Number of observations/examples seen (1, 3, or 10)

model_specification: One-way repeated-measures ANOVA with values_seen as a within-subject categorical factor on the normalized estimates.
operationalization_notes: This follows the Experiment 1 analysis strategy in the paper: taxicab responses were scaled by the largest example observed, and the effect of the number of examples was tested within subjects.
reasoning: In the taxicab condition, normalized estimates of the fleet size decreased as the number of observed cab numbers increased: mean response/max observed number was 1.85 after 1 observation, 1.33 after 3 observations, and 1.15 after 10 observations. A repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong effect of number of observations, F(2, 1148) = 127.92, p = 6.99e-51, consistent with smaller relative predictions after more examples.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that the district-level last-digit chi-square fraud test for total vote counts was significant at the 5% level (fraudchi2_total)
main_predictor: Election-day insurgent attacks per 1,000 population (v.elday.pc) and its squared term (v.elday.pc.2); main test is the squared term

operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's primary test of the inverted-U claim: the forensic last-digit fraud measure is regressed on election-period violence and its square, adjusting for the development and geography controls described in the methods.
reasoning: In a district-level logit model, the election-day violence coefficient was positive (8.477) and the squared violence coefficient was negative (-13.748). The cluster-robust z test for the squared term was z = -2.913, p = 0.0036, supporting a concave/inverted-U relationship between violence and fraud.

dependent_variable: Social undermining, reverse-coded from willingness to be matched with the comparison participant (8 - Undermin; higher = more undermining)

model_specification: Cumulative ordered logistic regression predicting reverse-coded social undermining from TSC, competition, and their interaction; standard errors clustered by participant ID to account for the within-person TSC manipulation.
operationalization_notes: This follows the Study 1 behavioral operationalization most directly tied to the stated moderation claim: TSC was manipulated within participants, competition was manipulated between participants, and undermining was the ordinal matching-preference measure where lower willingness to match implies greater undermining.
reasoning: I reverse-coded the matching-preference item so that higher scores indicated greater social undermining. In a cumulative logit model, the unfavorable temporal social comparison × high-competition interaction was positive and statistically significant (b = 0.602, z = 3.163, p = .0016), indicating that unfavorable temporal comparison increased undermining more in the high-competition condition than in the low-competition condition.

dependent_variable: Mean endorsement of COVID-specific origin/conspiracy beliefs (SpecCTs_4, SpecCTs_5, SpecCTs_6r)
main_predictor: Mean COVID worry/threat composite (COVID1 and COVID3)

controls: Categorical survey sample fixed effects (sample identifiers 1, 2, and 3)
operationalization_notes: The provided dataset did not contain the paper's full measures of institutional trust or lack of control. I therefore used the available COVID worry/threat items as the closest operationalization of COVID-related anxiety/risk, and averaged the available origin/plot conspiracy items while excluding the hoax/minimization-like items, consistent with the paper's rationale for excluding a flu/hoax conspiracy item.
reasoning: In an OLS regression controlling for survey sample, the COVID worry/threat composite did not positively predict endorsement of COVID origin/conspiracy items, b = -0.021, t(802) = -0.599, p = .549. Thus, in the available data, I did not find evidence for the claimed positive relationship between COVID-related anxiety/threat and conspiracy beliefs.

dependent_variable: Participant-level mean reaction time in milliseconds
main_predictor: Central face valence: angry versus neutral
sample_definition: Participants with Group = 1 (likely GAD) and nonmissing AngryM and NeutralM values; n = 63. The provided mean RT variables were used, which reflect the task scoring with incorrect responses and time outliers summarized in the dataset.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing AngryM to NeutralM within the GAD group, with the t statistic computed for AngryM - NeutralM.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 claim is a within-GAD comparison of reaction times when the centrally presented face is angry versus neutral; the dataset provides subject-level mean RTs for these two valence conditions, making a paired t-test the most direct operationalization.
reasoning: Within participants coded as likely GAD, mean RT was not faster for angry faces (M = 486.81 ms) than for neutral faces (M = 485.36 ms). A paired-samples t-test on AngryM minus NeutralM gave t(62) = 0.47, p = 0.639, so the data do not support the claimed faster responding to angry than neutral central faces.

dependent_variable: Change in brand personality impression: post-interaction Hansen Design sophistication mean minus pre-interaction sophistication mean, using Q5_1-Q5_4 and Q2_1-Q2_4
main_predictor: Employee behavior consistency × pseudorelevant-information condition interaction; pseudorelevant-information code 0 = disclosure present, 1 = no disclosure

operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim with Study 2 using brand-personality change scores. Because the claim specifically concerns high outcome dependency and both consistent and inconsistent employee behavior, I tested whether pseudorelevant information moderated the effect of behavior consistency on sophistication change within the high-dependency participants.
reasoning: In the high outcome-dependency subsample, the employee behavior consistency × pseudorelevant-information interaction on change in brand sophistication was not significant, F(1, 420) = 0.836, p = 0.361. The cell means were directionally consistent but small: inconsistent behavior produced changes of -0.683 with disclosure versus -0.723 without disclosure, while consistent behavior produced changes of -0.021 with disclosure versus 0.154 without disclosure.

dependent_variable: Aversiveness/disturbing rating, rescaled from 1-7 to 0-6 and averaged within participant by humor category
main_predictor: Humor category: Covid-19 humor items versus non-pandemic humor items
sample_definition: Respondents in the deidentified survey data who completed both survey parts and had non-missing aversiveness means for both Covid-19 and non-pandemic item sets; N = 915 participants
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing participant-level mean aversiveness for pooled Covid-19 humor items against participant-level mean aversiveness for non-pandemic verbal humor items
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's focus on aversiveness and its item Type factor, I pooled Covid Verbal, Covid Meme, and Covid Strip items as Covid-19 humor and compared them to Non-Covid Verbal items; participant-level averaging provides a direct within-subject test of whether Covid-19 humor is more aversive.
reasoning: I compared each participant's mean aversiveness rating for Covid-19 humor items with their mean rating for non-pandemic verbal humor items on the 0-6 rescaled response scale. Covid-19 humor was rated more aversive (M = 0.909) than non-pandemic humor (M = 0.553), paired t(914) = 23.16, p = 9.45e-94, supporting the claimed aversiveness mark.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for having adopted at least one avoidance behavior in the last month
main_predictor: High trust in government/official COVID-19 information (govtrustQ1 >= 5 on a 1-7 scale vs. 1-4)
sample_definition: Australian respondents in replication_data.csv with non-missing preparation behavior, government trust, age category, gender, and COVID-19 worry variables; N = 580

controls: Age category (quota_age), gender (DemGen), and worry about coronavirus (FinitePool_2)
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's focus on adoption of avoidance-related behaviors and trust in government/authorities, I coded avoidance as selecting any of the available preparation options corresponding to avoiding social events, avoiding public transport, eating out less, shopping for groceries less, or staying home from work. I dichotomized government/official-source trust into high vs. low to mirror the paper's high/low trust comparison and adjusted for available demographic and worry variables.
reasoning: In a logistic regression, high trust in government/official COVID-19 information was positively associated with reporting at least one avoidance behavior (b = 0.766, OR = 2.15), z = 2.67, p = 0.0076. Thus, respondents with higher trust were significantly more likely to adopt avoidance behaviors, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Reverse-coded current money management stress scale average (CMMSRC; higher values indicate more positive/lower stress)
main_predictor: Valence frame / writing prompt group (success frame vs. failure frame)
sample_definition: Participants in the Study 3a dataset with Include = 1, nonmissing CMMSRC, and assigned to group 1 (failure) or group 2 (success); N = 262.
model_specification: Independent-samples t test comparing mean CMMSRC between success-frame and failure-frame groups, using the pooled-variance two-sample t test equivalent to a one-way ANOVA with two groups.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3a method directly tests this manipulation using the reverse-scored current money management stress scale so that higher scores are more positive; I therefore compared included success- and failure-frame participants on CMMSRC without covariates.
reasoning: Among included participants, the reverse-coded current money management stress score was higher (more positive/lower stress) in the success-frame group (M = 3.003, n = 131) than in the failure-frame group (M = 2.559, n = 131). An independent-samples t test gave t(260) = 3.65, p = 0.00032, supporting the claimed directional effect.

dependent_variable: Situational attributions scale (bidirectional items, reverse-coded as in the processed data)
main_predictor: Dispositional attributions scale (bidirectional items, reverse-coded as in the processed data)
sample_definition: Respondents in the Qualtrics dataset assigned to the bidirectional questionnaire condition with complete data on the outcome, predictor, and controls (BiDummy = 1; N = 642).

controls: Perceived victimization risk, perceived crime trend, news consumption, conservatism, religiosity, family victimization, education, female, White, and age.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies this claim with Table 4's multivariate test of the hydraulic relation for attribution styles; I therefore used the bidirectional condition and matched that model specification using the processed scale variables in the Qualtrics dataset.
reasoning: In the bidirectional-question group, dispositional attributions negatively predicted situational attributions after adjustment for the same control variables, b = -0.223 with robust SE = 0.045. The effect was highly statistically significant, t(630) = -4.94, p = 9.96e-7, supporting the claimed hydraulic relationship.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME
sample_definition: Participants in the overall dataset with complete data on PSS-10 score, gender coded as BE MALE, age, education, family members, and monthly income; this excludes the 18 participants with missing BE MALE/other gender, yielding N = 2035.

controls: AGE, BE MALE, EDUCATION, FAMILY MEMBERS
operationalization_notes: The paper tested the income claim as part of a sociodemographic multiple regression predicting continuous PSS-10 perceived stress; I used that direct model and report the t test for the monthly income coefficient.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting PSS-10 perceived stress, monthly income had a negative adjusted association with stress (B = -0.463, t(2029) = -3.465, p = 0.00054). Thus, higher income was associated with lower perceived stress in this sample.

dependent_variable: Mean of the three nonmaterial behavioral inclination items: not wanting to stop eating chips, liking casual sex with as many people as possible when single, and wanting as many social-network friends as possible
main_predictor: Dispositional Greed Scale (DGS), recomputed as the mean of the seven greed items
sample_definition: Consenting respondents in the analytic dataset who finished the survey with Progress = 100 and had nonmissing data on the three behavioral inclination items, DGS items, and MVS items (N = 492)
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of the nonmaterial greedy-tendency composite on DGS and MVS; the reported test is the t test for the DGS coefficient
controls: Material Values Scale (MVS), recomputed as the mean of the nine materialism items with the simple-life item reverse-coded
operationalization_notes: Study 2 was designed to test whether greed, beyond materialism, predicts desires for nonmaterial goods. I therefore combined the three nonmaterial inclination items into a single outcome and tested the unique DGS coefficient while controlling for materialism.
reasoning: Among completed respondents, the recomputed DGS positively predicted a composite of nonmaterial greedy behavioral inclinations after controlling for recomputed materialism scores, b = 0.708, t(489) = 15.65, p = 4.85e-45. This supports the claim that DGS predicts greedy tendencies over and above materialism.

dependent_variable: Indicator for choosing the ambiguous candidate in Q3, coded from candidate order randomization RND_01
main_predictor: Risk aversion indicator, coded 1 for respondents who preferred avoiding risks in Q4 and 0 for preferring taking risks or having no preference
sample_definition: All observations in the provided dataset with a valid candidate choice (Q3 = Candidate A or B), valid risk response (Q4 = 1, 2, or 3), valid certainty response (Q2 = 1 through 5), and observed candidate/voter positions; N = 2684
model_specification: Probit regression with HC1 robust standard errors; reported statistic is the z test for the risk-aversion coefficient
controls: Voter certainty indicator (extremely sure about own position) and distance differential |voter - precise candidate| minus |voter - midpoint of ambiguous candidate interval|
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Table 3 causal-mechanism specification as closely as possible using the available candidate-choice data: ambiguous-candidate choice is regressed on risk aversion while controlling for self-position certainty and proximity-based distance differential.
reasoning: In a probit model of choosing the ambiguous candidate, the coefficient for risk aversion was negative but extremely small and not statistically distinguishable from zero (b = -0.0155, robust SE = 0.0532, z = -0.291, p = 0.771). Thus, in these data the direction is consistent with risk-averse respondents being less likely to choose the ambiguous candidate, but the evidence is inconclusive.

dependent_variable: Quarterly average ICE BofA US High Yield Index Option-Adjusted Spread, in basis points
main_predictor: Net percentage of banks tightening C&I loan standards for large and medium firms
sample_definition: All overlapping quarterly observations from 2010:Q1 through 2020:Q2 with nonmissing high-yield spread and Senior Loan Officer Survey credit-standards data (n=42)
model_specification: OLS regression of quarterly average high-yield option-adjusted spread on credit-standards tightening with an intercept; t-test of the slope coefficient
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's use of credit standards as a measure of tight funding/bad times, I used higher credit-standard tightening as the negative funding/fundamental-shock proxy and high-yield spread widening as the observable implication of losses on risky credit positions held by leveraged agents.
reasoning: In a quarterly OLS regression, tighter C&I credit standards were associated with wider high-yield corporate bond spreads: slope = 4.014 basis points per percentage point tightening, t(40) = 2.41, p = 0.0205. Since wider credit spreads imply mark-to-market losses for levered holders of risky credit, the estimated positive relationship supports the claim.

dependent_variable: Intergroup Contact Scale index for contact with older workers (ICS_olderworkers)
main_predictor: WICS total score (WIAStotal), entered as the final block in a hierarchical regression
sample_definition: Participants coded as age40 == 1 (40 years old or younger), excluding cases with missing data on the outcome, WICS, or covariates; N = 446 complete cases
model_specification: Hierarchical ordinary least squares regression; main test is the nested-model F change comparing the model with demographics, JSS, AOWS, and SIC to the same model plus WICS total
controls: Age, weekly work hours, years with current employer, JSS mean score, log-transformed adjusted AOWS score, and SIC mean score
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 used hierarchical regression to test WICS incremental validity by predicting contact with differently aged coworkers. reasoning: In the age-40-and-younger complete-case sample, adding WICS total scores to the regression significantly improved prediction of positive contact with older workers, F(1, 438) = 37.95, p = 1.64e-09, increasing R² by about .071. This supports the study's conclusion that WICS has incremental/criterion validity as a measure of workplace intergenerational climate.

dependent_variable: Future intention to refrain from stockpiling, computed as 6 - Q9_1 ('I am planning to buy more food or supplies than usually') so higher values indicate greater intended refraining
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility composite from the 16 HEXACO Honesty-Humility items, reverse-scoring negatively keyed items and averaging

model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of recoded future refraining intention on Honesty-Humility
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns future intentions, which the paper measured in Study 2 with Q9_1. I followed the paper's direct personality-intention test but recoded the stockpiling-intention item so the outcome directly represents intention to refrain from stockpiling.
reasoning: In an OLS regression, Honesty-Humility positively predicted the recoded future intention-to-refrain score, b = 0.671, t(312) = 9.508, p = 5.45e-19, N = 314. Thus, higher Honesty-Humility was associated with stronger intentions to refrain from stockpiling in the future.

dependent_variable: Cumulative reported COVID-19 deaths in the county on 2020-06-11
main_predictor: Percentage of residents under age 65 who were uninsured, derived from ACS S2701 under-19 and age-19-to-64 uninsured counts and denominators
sample_definition: U.S. counties in the 50 states with FIPS codes, classified as non-urban by population density <1000 residents per square mile, observed on 2020-06-11, and with complete data on the outcome, predictor, and covariates; missing farm-labor counts were treated as zero.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; the main test is the robust t-test for the uninsured-percentage coefficient.
controls: Percent farm workers, percent limited-English-speaking households, percent below poverty line, percent age 65 or older, residents per square mile, and high-risk epidemic days up to 2020-06-11.
operationalization_notes: The paper's claim was reported for the non-urban fully adjusted county model, so I analyzed non-urban counties and adjusted for the same social-demographic covariates and epidemic-stage measure. I used a non-spatial adjusted linear model as the single reproducible test of the directional association from the provided county-level data.
reasoning: In a fully adjusted non-urban county model, the coefficient for percent uninsured under age 65 was negative (b = -0.489 deaths per percentage point) and statistically significant, t(2841) = -3.58, p = 0.00035. Thus, higher uninsured percentage was associated with lower reported COVID-19 deaths in this operationalization.

dependent_variable: Binary dessert choice, coded 1 for chocolate cake and 0 for fruit salad
main_predictor: Decision-recall condition: delegated/dependent decision recall versus independent decision recall
sample_definition: All observations in analytic dataset_secondround.sav with nonmissing decisiontype and dessert choice; no additional exclusions were applied (N=274).

operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 identifies dessert choice as the depletion measure and reports a logistic regression comparing delegated versus independent recall, so I used the same binary outcome and condition contrast on the provided clean analytic dataset.
reasoning: Using the clean analytic second-round dataset, the chocolate-cake choice share was 85/138 = 61.6% in the delegated/dependent recall condition versus 93/136 = 68.4% in the independent recall condition. A no-controls logistic regression likelihood-ratio test did not support the claimed greater cake choice after delegated recall, χ²(1, N=274) = 1.389, p = .239; the observed direction was actually lower in the delegated condition.

dependent_variable: CMD risk, coded 1 for at least 8 affirmative symptoms on the available SRQ symptom items and 0 otherwise

operationalization_notes: The paper modeled CMD risk using an SRQ cut-point and adjusted logistic regression among ever-in-union women. The available data file contained SRQ items p622a-p622q, so I mirrored the paper's threshold by coding CMD risk as 8 or more affirmative symptoms and tested the current emotional IPV coefficient in the fully adjusted IPV model.

dependent_variable: Perceived sandwich size rating (Size; 1 = much smaller than average, 7 = much larger than average)

model_specification: One-way between-subjects ANOVA / OLS regression of Size on pitch condition
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 tested this claim by comparing perceived size ratings between participants randomized to the low-voice versus high-voice radio advertisement; I used the analogous cleaned included participant data and the focal Size outcome without covariates.
reasoning: Using the cleaned included-participants dataset, the lower-pitched condition had a slightly higher mean perceived size than the higher-pitched condition (5.213 vs. 5.086), but the one-way ANOVA was not statistically significant, F(1, 613) = 2.53, p = .112. dependent_variable: Estimated point of subjective equality / apparent target duration, operationalized as mean comparison duration in milliseconds; duration compression is 307 ms minus this PSE
main_predictor: Prime-target vertical spatial distance: overlap (0°) versus +4° separation
sample_definition: Thirteen participants represented in the analysis-ready CSV files; included final-task-block observations with vdist equal to 0 or +4 and all prime-orientation conditions, excluding other spatial distances.
model_specification: Within-subject paired t test on subject-level means for +4° minus 0° PSE, after computing means within each subject, spatial distance, and orientation-difference condition and averaging the two orientation differences equally.
controls: Orientation difference was controlled by equal averaging across the 22.5° and 67.5° conditions within each spatial-distance condition; no additional covariates.
operationalization_notes: Experiment 2 tested spatial proximity using adaptive comparison durations/PSEs; the direct test of the quoted 0° versus 4° claim is a paired within-subject comparison of PSE-derived compression between those two spatial-distance levels.
reasoning: Using participant-level PSE proxies from the final adaptive block, the mean comparison duration was lower when prime and target overlapped (0°: 233.72 ms) than when separated by +4° (256.72 ms), implying greater duration compression at 0°. The paired comparison, averaged equally over the two orientation-difference conditions, was significant, t(12)=2.21, p=.0477.

dependent_variable: Personal worry about coronavirus/COVID-19 (finitepool_2; 1 = not at all worried, 7 = very worried)

A Welch two-sample t-test gave t(593.15) = 4.64, p = 4.29e-6, supporting the claim that women's attitudes toward the pandemic danger were more serious/responsible than men's.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 attack rate through April 14, 2020, computed as confirmed cases per 100,000 population
main_predictor: Age-standardized prevalence of tobacco smoking among persons aged 15+ in 2016

dependent_variable: ICT literacy test score
main_predictor: student gender
sample_definition: intended sample was all student records with nonmissing ICT literacy score and gender, excluding schools with 15 or fewer respondents as in the paper; unavailable in supplied data
model_specification: intended test was the t-statistic for the gender coefficient in a two-level linear model with students nested in schools
controls: individual and school-level controls described in the paper would be used if the original microdata were available
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods link this claim to the HLM analysis of ICT literacy score, but the supplied files contain no analyzable original microdata from which to recompute that model.
