The files named Helper student/princ/teacher are variable-name lists only, and Summary statistics.csv contains only marginal summaries/counts, not the joint data needed to estimate the gender effect on ICT literacy score.

dependent_variable: Mean responsible COVID-19 behavior score from RespBeh1-RespBeh4
main_predictor: COVID-19 related worry (CWorry single item)
sample_definition: Participants in the provided dataset with complete data on RespBeh1-RespBeh4, CWorry, unfounded belief items, knowledge items, trait anxiety items, CRTSc, AOT, FaithSc, and SciCurSc; mask behavior item was excluded to match the paper's four-item behavior measure
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of the four-item responsible behavior mean on CWorry and covariates; reported statistic is the t test for the CWorry coefficient
controls: Unfounded COVID-19 beliefs composite from ConspBelief1-ConspBelief8 and TreatBelief1-TreatBelief6, COVID-19 knowledge mean Know1-Know6, trait anxiety mean Anx1-Anx4, CRTSc, AOT, FaithSc, and SciCurSc
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods define COVID-19 responsible behavior as the mean of four recommended behaviors and COVID-19 worry as a single item. I used an observed-variable OLS analogue of the paper's SEM regression component so the main result is the adjusted test of worry predicting responsible behavior.
reasoning: In an OLS regression mirroring the paper's structural prediction of responsible behavior, COVID-19 worry positively predicted responsible behavior, b = 0.212, t(523) = 9.255, p = 5.49e-19. This supports the claim that greater worry is associated with more responsible COVID-19 behavior in the provided data.

dependent_variable: Leader_Exp_Total (mean leadership experiences score)
main_predictor: Oppenness_Total (mean openness to experiences score)
sample_definition: All observations in Popper Data for Correlations.csv with non-missing openness, leadership-experience, and trait-anxiety scale scores; N = 215.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of leadership experiences on openness to experiences and trait anxiety; the reported test is the t test for the openness coefficient.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested H4 in a structural model where leadership experiences were predicted by openness to experiences and trait anxiety; I approximated that structural path using the provided cleaned composite scale scores rather than copying the reported SEM coefficient.
reasoning: Using the cleaned scale-score dataset, openness to experience positively predicted leadership experiences after adjusting for trait anxiety, b = 0.225, t(212) = 3.34, p = 0.00098, N = 215. This supports a positive relation between openness and leadership experiences, consistent with the original claim.

dependent_variable: Confirmed COVID-19 cases per one million population on 03 April 2020, computed as COVID_12_31_04_03 / popData2019 * 1,000,000
main_predictor: Economist Intelligence Unit democracy index, 2019, as provided in the dataset on a 0-100 scale
sample_definition: All 150 countries in /workspace/data/COVID replication.dta with complete data on confirmed cases, population, democracy, annual temperature, and trade openness
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression with an intercept; the reported test is the conventional t-test for the democracy coefficient
controls: Annual average temperature and trade openness (trade_recent)
operationalization_notes: The paper's main modeling approach regressed cases per million on country-level characteristics and then focused on temperature, openness, and democracy after excluding precipitation and population density as insignificant; I used that no-lag OLS specification on the replication dataset.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of confirmed COVID-19 cases per million as of 03 April 2020 on democracy, annual temperature, and trade openness, the democracy coefficient was positive (8.81 additional cases per million per one-point increase on the 0-100 EIU democracy index). This effect was statistically significant, t(146)=4.41, p=2.01e-5, supporting the claim that confirmed cases were higher in countries with stronger political democracy.

dependent_variable: Hoax rating: extent to which the participant believed the COVID-19 pandemic was a hoax, coded 1 = definitely not a hoax to 6 = definitely a hoax
main_predictor: CRT proportion correct across the seven Cognitive Reflection Test items
sample_definition: All rows in Stanley_covid_b3G4_98g_FullDataSet_IncludingNonRelevant.csv with AttCheckSCORE = 5 and nonmissing CRT and Hoax data; both data-collection waves included
model_specification: Pearson bivariate correlation between CRT proportion correct and Hoax rating
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim with a bivariate correlation between average CRT performance and the hoax-belief item after excluding attention-check failures. I followed that specification, scoring the seven CRT items as correct/incorrect and averaging them; semantically correct variants were accepted for the bat-and-ball and Emily items.
reasoning: Using the attention-check-passing observations, CRT proportion-correct was negatively correlated with belief that COVID-19 was a hoax, r(2144) = -0.1204, p = 2.20e-08. Because higher hoax scores indicate greater endorsement of the hoax belief, this supports the claim that lower analytic-thinking is associated with greater hoax belief.

dependent_variable: Mean self-reported containment-related behavior across disinfecting hands, avoiding social contacts, washing hands, avoiding crowds, not touching face, and staying home/quarantine items
main_predictor: Mean COVID-19 hoax belief scale: virus presented as dangerous to mislead, experts mislead/virus no worse than flu, and reverse-coded belief experts say virus is dangerous
sample_definition: Participants in the provided dataset who passed the attention check by selecting strongly agree on Q21 and had complete data on the outcome, hoax belief, human-made belief, and political orientation
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of containment-related behavior on COVID-19 hoax belief, with the t test for the hoax-belief coefficient as the main test
controls: SARS-CoV-2 human-made conspiracy belief scale and political orientation
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 methods describe forming a containment-related behavior composite from hygiene and distancing/quarantine behaviors and testing the focal hypothesis by regressing that composite on the two specific conspiracy-belief scales plus political orientation; I applied that specification to the available original data.
reasoning: In an OLS regression, stronger COVID-19 hoax belief significantly predicted lower containment-related behavior, b = -0.265, t(96) = -3.275, p = 0.00147. This supports the claimed inverse relationship between hoax belief and behaviors such as handwashing and physical distancing.

dependent_variable: Mean rehearsal strategy score from REH_1-REH_4
main_predictor: Mean mastery-approach achievement goal score from MAp_1-MAp_3
sample_definition: Respondents with consent/progress complete, Student Status = Yes, passed both attention checks, Course_Type = Social Sciences, and complete achievement-goal and rehearsal items; N = 243.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression predicting the rehearsal subscale mean from mastery-approach plus the other three achievement-goal subscale means.
controls: Mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance achievement-goal subscale means
operationalization_notes: The paper tested paths from achievement goals to learning-strategy use in an educational psychology course; a social-sciences course subsample and AGQ/MSLQ subscale means provide a direct item-level analogue to the reported mastery-approach to rehearsal path.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of the rehearsal-strategy mean on achievement-goal subscale means among valid social-sciences-course respondents, mastery approach had a positive coefficient (b = 0.372) and was statistically detectable, t(238) = 5.28, p = 2.91e-7. This supports the claim that a mastery-approach orientation positively predicted rehearsal strategies.

dependent_variable: Mean positive affect score on the PANAS after each block
main_predictor: Association block type: progressive versus stagnant
sample_definition: Participants in mason_data_stage2.csv with positive PANAS responses for both progressive and stagnant blocks; observations were averaged within participant, block, and subscale, so the duplicated participant ID was treated as one participant.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test of within-participant mean positive PANAS after progressive blocks minus after stagnant blocks
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns Experiment 1's progressive versus narrowly constrained/stagnant word-list manipulation. Following the paper's focal simple-effects analysis, I operationalized better mood as higher positive PANAS affect after the block and tested the within-subject progressive-stagnant difference.
reasoning: Using the full cumulative dataset, mean positive PANAS ratings were only slightly higher after progressive blocks than after stagnant blocks (mean paired difference = 0.022). A paired-samples t-test did not support the claimed advantage, t(483) = 0.931, p = 0.353.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that the participant chose the Canadian/national product option
main_predictor: High system threat versus low/no threat, evaluated at low system confidence (one SD below the analytic-sample mean)
sample_definition: Final combined Stage 2 dataset; included participants who reported Canadian citizenship (Q16 = 1), were assigned to the indirect/plain national-product support condition (DirectIndirectsystemsupport = 0; Q10/controlchoice), and had nonmissing threat, system-confidence, and choice data.
model_specification: Logistic regression of Canadian product choice on threat condition, mean-centered continuous system confidence, and their interaction; the reported z test is the linear contrast for the effect of threat at one SD below mean system confidence.
operationalization_notes: The paper tests this claim by examining whether low-system-confidence participants under verbal system threat increase indirect national-brand choices. I therefore focused on the indirect choice condition and used the Aiken-and-West-style simple threat contrast at low system confidence.
reasoning: In the indirect/plain national-product choice condition among Canadian citizens, the estimated high-threat versus low-threat contrast at one SD below mean system confidence was positive (log-odds = 0.622), corresponding to z = 1.51, p = .131. Thus, the direction was consistent with the claim, but the evidence was not statistically conclusive in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Postshift negative affect
main_predictor: Contrast between within-person direct care task accomplishment satisfaction and indirect care task accomplishment satisfaction slopes
sample_definition: Finished, nonmissing paired preshift and postshift diary observations from PreShift_3.csv and PostShift_3.csv, matched by participant ID and date; 205 shift-level observations from 53 participants.
model_specification: Random-intercept linear mixed model with participant as the grouping variable; postshift negative affect was regressed on group-mean-centered preshift negative affect, group-mean-centered indirect care TAS, and group-mean-centered direct care TAS. The reported statistic is a Wald z test of beta_direct_TAS - beta_indirect_TAS = 0.
controls: Group-mean-centered preshift negative affect; participant random intercept.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested changes in affect by predicting postshift affect while controlling preshift affect and group-mean-centered Level 1 predictors; I used negative affect because both direct and indirect TAS are expected to reduce postshift negative affect and the coefficient contrast directly tests whether direct-care TAS has the larger effect.
reasoning: In a multilevel model predicting postshift negative affect, the within-person coefficient for direct-care task accomplishment satisfaction was more negative than the coefficient for indirect-care task accomplishment satisfaction (direct b = -2.377, indirect b = -0.780). The Wald contrast for direct minus indirect was significant, z = -2.99, p = .0028, indicating a larger impact for direct-care tasks.

dependent_variable: Participant accuracy: proportion of the 8 ensemble competition trials in which the actual winner was selected
main_predictor: Presentation modality contrast: visual-only condition versus pooled audio-only and audiovisual conditions
sample_definition: All participant-level observations in the processed analytic Audio, Visual, and Audiovisual CSV files; each participant contributed their mean Correct score across 8 sets. This yielded 96 visual-only, 32 audio-only, and 32 audiovisual novice participants across the two data-collection phases.
model_specification: Welch independent-samples t test comparing mean accuracy in the visual-only condition to mean accuracy in the pooled audio-only/audiovisual conditions
operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 tested novices' ability to select winners from 6-second clips across audio-only, video-only, and video-plus-sound conditions. I used the same participant-level accuracy outcome and chose a single planned contrast focused on the claim that visual cues alone outperform auditory or combined auditory-visual information.
reasoning: Using participant-level accuracy across the eight ensemble competitions, the visual-only condition averaged 0.350 correct (96 participants) versus 0.324 correct in the pooled audio-only and audiovisual conditions (64 participants). A Welch independent-samples t test gave t(124.33) = 1.02, p = 0.309, so this dataset does not provide clear evidence that novices identified winners better from visual cues alone than from auditory-containing presentations.

dependent_variable: Desire for toned/defined muscles, 0=Never to 4=Always
main_predictor: Age in years
sample_definition: All observations in phase2_final_data.csv with nonmissing toned/defined-muscles score, age, sexual orientation category, geographic region, and weight status; male participants aged 18-25 years (N=2438).
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression treating the 0-4 muscularity-concern item as continuous: toned ~ age + sexual orientation + geographic region + weight status.
controls: Sexual orientation category, geographic region, and weight status.
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed muscularity-concern items as continuous outcomes adjusted for sexual orientation, region, and weight status. The provided dataset did not contain the original desire-for-bigger-muscles item or adolescent ages 9-19, so I used the available analogous muscularity concern item, desire for toned/defined muscles, in the largest cleaned dataset.
reasoning: In the available data, age was not a significant positive predictor of muscularity concern: the adjusted slope for age predicting desire for toned/defined muscles was negative (b = -0.013 per year), t(2420) = -1.52, p = .129. Thus this analysis does not support an increase in the available muscularity-concern outcome with age.

dependent_variable: Mean Perceived Relationship Quality Components Inventory score across 18 items
main_predictor: Partner's overall rating of how well the actor matches the partner's ideal standards, averaged across the 17 Partner Ideal Scale items
sample_definition: Opposite-sex couples in SCOREdata06AUG20.dta with both partners consenting and committing to provide thoughtful answers; 232 dyads, represented as 464 actor-level observations
model_specification: Actor-partner interdependence mixed linear model with actor observations nested in dyads and a random intercept for dyad; continuous predictors grand-mean centered
controls: Actor's own overall partner-ideal match rating and actor sex effect-coded as male = 1, female = -1
operationalization_notes: The paper tested partner effects separately for ideal-standard dimensions; to conduct one analysis of the broad claim, I averaged all 17 ideal-match items into a single overall ideal-standards score and tested the partner effect on relationship quality while retaining the paper's APIM logic.
reasoning: In a dyadic mixed model, actors reported higher relationship quality when their partner rated the actor as more closely matching the partner's ideal standards, b = 0.214, z = 6.48, p = 9.18e-11. Because higher ideal-match scores indicate less failure to meet the partner's standards, this supports the claim that people are less satisfied when they fail to match their partner's ideals.

dependent_variable: Stroop interference score: mean response time on correct incongruent color-word trials minus mean response time on correct neutral XXXX trials, in seconds
main_predictor: Stereotype threat versus control condition, coded from the condition-response key in each Stroop file (d treated as stereotype threat, j as control)
sample_definition: All participants with usable test-trial Stroop data and non-missing interference scores; incorrect trials were excluded before computing condition-specific mean response times, leaving N = 304 participants.
model_specification: Independent-samples t test comparing participant-level Stroop interference scores between stereotype-threat and control groups; equal-variance t test.
operationalization_notes: Study 1 tested the claim with a simplified Stroop task; reduced Stroop interference is the most direct measure of greater cognitive control capacity, so I compared interference scores between the two randomized instruction conditions.
reasoning: Using participant-level Stroop interference scores, the putative stereotype-threat condition had slightly lower interference than control (M = 0.114 s vs. 0.134 s), but the independent-samples t test was not statistically significant, t(302) = -1.26, p = .210. Thus the data do not provide clear evidence that stereotype threat facilitated immediate cognitive control capacity.

dependent_variable: Current Health Behavior: Social Distancing composite (mean of Q26_1, Q26_2, Q26_3, Q26_4, Q26_5, and Q26_7)
main_predictor: SD3 Psychopathy composite
sample_definition: Rows in Blagov2020_ReplicationOSFclean.csv after removing the Qualtrics metadata row; observations with complete CHB social distancing, SD3 psychopathy, gender, corrected age, and physical health-risk controls were included (N = 449).
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of CHB Social Distancing on SD3 Psychopathy and covariates; the reported t-test is for the SD3 Psychopathy coefficient, equivalent to a partial correlation test.
controls: Gender, age, and physical health-risk status
operationalization_notes: The paper tested health-behavior endorsement using social-distancing/hygiene composites and planned partial correlations controlling for gender, age, and health condition. I selected the current social-distancing composite and SD3 psychopathy because the claim specifically highlights psychopathy predicting low health-behavior endorsement.
reasoning: In a regression/partial-correlation test controlling for gender, age, and physical health-risk status, SD3 psychopathy negatively predicted current social-distancing endorsement, t(444) = -3.67, p = 0.00027 (partial r = -0.172). Thus, higher psychopathy was associated with lower endorsement of this health behavior.

dependent_variable: creativity
main_predictor: intrinsic motivation
sample_definition: All independent study samples in Meta-analysis_liu_SCORE.csv with a non-missing intrinsic motivation-creativity correlation; k = 68, total participant N = 19,695.
model_specification: DerSimonian-Laird random-effects meta-analysis of Fisher-z transformed Pearson correlations, with inverse-variance weights and a z test of the pooled effect against zero.
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the bivariate positive relationship between intrinsic motivation and creativity, so I used the study-level intrinsic motivation-creativity correlations from the original meta-analytic dataset and summarized them meta-analytically.
reasoning: Using the 68 independent study samples with an intrinsic motivation-creativity correlation (total N = 19,695), a random-effects meta-analysis of Fisher-z transformed correlations gave a pooled correlation of r = 0.282. The test of the pooled Fisher-z effect against zero was z = 10.31, p = 6.20e-25, indicating a positive relationship.

dependent_variable: Post-test anti-Black attitudes, computed as the mean of post-test anti-Black items on the 0-5 scale with items 6 and 10 reverse-keyed
main_predictor: Communication positivity (PosImp), tested as its simple slope at low pre-test IMS (-1 SD)
sample_definition: All readable observations in the provided merged replication dataset with complete variables; all 30 observations were Black-target cases, with no White-target cases available
model_specification: OLS ANCOVA: post-test anti-Black attitudes regressed on pre-test anti-Black attitudes, centered EMS, centered IMS, centered communication positivity, and the centered communication positivity x IMS interaction; reported statistic is the simple slope of communication positivity at IMS = -1 SD
controls: Pre-test anti-Black attitudes and pre-test EMS
operationalization_notes: The paper tested whether communication positivity predicted post-test anti-Black attitudes as a function of target race and IMS while controlling for pre-test anti-Black attitudes. Because the provided dataset contained no target-race variation, I implemented the closest estimable Black-target-only version of that model using the available PosImp communication-positivity variable.
reasoning: Using the available data, all participants were in the Black-target condition, so the Black-versus-White target comparison in the original claim could not be estimated. In a Black-target-only ANCOVA, the simple slope of communication positivity on post-test anti-Black attitudes at low IMS (-1 SD), controlling for pre-test anti-Black attitudes and EMS, was positive but not statistically significant, t(24)=1.49, p=.150.

dependent_variable: Supervisor-rated organizational citizenship behavior composite (15 OCB items, with negatively worded sportsmanship items reverse-coded, averaged)
main_predictor: Four employee-rated operant leader behavior composites: contingent reward, contingent punishment, non-contingent reward, and non-contingent punishment
sample_definition: Matched employee-supervisor dyads in the provided Stage 1 files with complete data on OCB, trust, operant-leadership composites, tenure with supervisor, and organizational level; all included respondents passed the attention checks; N=168.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of OCB on trust, the four operant-leadership composites, tenure with supervisor, and organizational level; main statistic is an omnibus nested-model F-test of the four direct operant-leadership coefficients equal to zero after trust is included.
controls: Tenure with direct supervisor in years/months and organizational level
operationalization_notes: The paper tested full mediation by comparing a fully mediated model with a partial-mediation model including direct paths from the four operant-leadership dimensions to OCB. I used the same conceptual comparison with observed scale composites because the provided dataset contains item-level employee ratings of leadership/trust and supervisor ratings of OCB, but not the original LISREL setup.
reasoning: I tested the key full-mediation implication by asking whether the four operant-leadership dimensions still had direct associations with supervisor-rated OCB after adding employee trust and the paper's controls. The direct paths remained jointly significant, F(4,160)=24.00, p=1.45e-15, so this operationalization does not support full mediation by trust.

dependent_variable: Prostitution Attitudes Scale average score (PASAverage; higher values reflect more favorable attitudes toward prostitution)
main_predictor: WritingCondition (death/mortality-salience condition vs dental-pain control condition)
sample_definition: European American respondents only (EuropeanAmerican = 1), restricted to completed surveys (Finished = 1) with nonmissing PASAverage and WritingCondition.
model_specification: Independent-samples pooled-variance t-test comparing PASAverage between mortality-salience and control conditions within European Americans; t is oriented as mortality-salience minus control.
operationalization_notes: This directly follows Study 1's planned contrast for the claim: within European Americans, compare PAS attitudes after the mortality-salience prime versus the dental-pain control prime, using the PAS outcome described in the paper.
reasoning: Among completed European American respondents, mean PAS scores were very similar in the death/mortality-salience condition (M = 1.304, n = 83) and the dental-pain control condition (M = 1.257, n = 98). Because higher PAS scores indicate more favorable attitudes toward prostitution, the small difference was not in the claimed negative direction and was not statistically significant, t(179) = 0.230, p = 0.818.

dependent_variable: BMI
main_predictor: Neuroticism
sample_definition: Intended sample would be adult respondents with nonmissing BMI, neuroticism/personality items, and covariates; unavailable because individual-level data were not provided.

controls: Intended controls: gender, age, education, and chronic disease, following the paper's cross-sectional model.
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods indicate OLS regressions of body-weight measures on Big Five traits with demographic/health controls. I selected the cross-sectional BMI model as one direct test of the claim, but the necessary record-level data were absent.

The available TSV files are variable dictionaries/univariate summaries and the IFLS .txt files are documentation/codebooks rather than raw data, so the association between neuroticism and BMI/body-weight measures cannot be estimated from the supplied materials.

dependent_variable: Mean of the China travel-ban item and the all-of-Asia travel-ban item
main_predictor: Perceived Infectability subscale score
sample_definition: Study 1A American MTurk observations in Goh2020OSF.csv with nonmissing China and Asia travel-ban items and computable PVD subscale scores (complete-case analysis for variables in the model).
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of mean China/Asia travel-ban support on Perceived Infectability and Germ Aversion; the reported statistic is the t test for the Perceived Infectability coefficient.
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary Study 1A analyses used regression models with Perceived Infectability and Germ Aversion as simultaneous predictors of travel-ban support. I averaged the two target outcomes named in the claim (China and all of Asia) to produce one outcome and tested the unique association with Perceived Infectability.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting the average of support for travel bans from China and all of Asia, Perceived Infectability had a positive coefficient when controlling for Germ Aversion, b = 0.275, t(256) = 3.33, p = .001. Thus, higher Perceived Infectability was associated with greater endorsement of these travel bans in the American data.

dependent_variable: Natural log of the country-level mean mortality rate, computed as the mean slope of LOWESS-smoothed daily COVID-19 deaths from the first day with more than 2 deaths to the smoothed peak or 2020-06-08.
main_predictor: International arrivals in 2018, measured in millions.
sample_definition: The 37 countries listed in the paper as included in the primary analysis; all had complete data for the variables used in the fitted model.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of log mean mortality rate on international arrivals and covariates selected using a univariable p<0.30 screening rule, following the paper's approach.
controls: Natural log population, median age, air pollution, mean January-May temperature, prevalent neoplasms, prevalent hypertension, WHO health index, percent urban population, GDP per capita (PPP), and mean stringency index.
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's linear-regression framework and recomputed the mortality-slope outcome from the daily death data using LOWESS smoothing. Because some paper covariates such as BCG coverage and UV exposure were not available in the supplied data files, the multivariable model used the available covariates that passed the paper-style p<0.30 univariable screening; median age was used as the available age-structure measure.
reasoning: In a multivariable OLS model, international arrivals had a positive coefficient of 0.0360 on log mean mortality rate per additional million arrivals, with t(25)=3.106 and p=0.00468. Thus, higher international arrivals significantly predicted greater severity of the first COVID-19 wave in this operationalization.

dependent_variable: Points contributed to the shared account in each public-goods dilemma, averaged within participant over condition type
main_predictor: Outcome prospect type: losses-and-gains prospects versus no-variance/gains-only prospects
sample_definition: All 320 participants in the cleaned dataset with complete contribution data for all four medium-threshold bonus conditions; each participant contributed one losses-and-gains average and one no-variance/gains-only average.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test of each participant's mean contribution in losses-and-gains conditions [(0,1200) and (200,1000) bonuses] against their mean contribution in no-variance/gains-only conditions [600 and (400,800) bonuses].
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim in Study 1 with a within-subject planned contrast on contributions. The available cleaned data contain the same contribution task at threshold 300, for which (200,1000) and (0,1200) imply possible losses relative to the 75-point average required contribution, while 600 and (400,800) do not.
reasoning: Using the cleaned complete-participant data, mean contribution was 73.20 points in the losses-and-gains prospect trials versus 73.75 points in the no-variance/gains-only trials. The paired within-participant contrast was small and not significant, t(319) = -0.58, p = 0.564, so this dataset does not reproduce a significant reduction in contributions under loss prospects.

dependent_variable: HP-detrended intercounty migration rate, expressed as a proportion (HPmigration/100)
main_predictor: standardized standard deviation of state employment gaps (StateEmploymentGapz)
sample_definition: Annual CPS aggregate intercounty migration observations for MigYear 1948-2009 with nonmissing migration and employment-gap variables; years when the CPS migration question was not asked are absent, yielding 54 observations.
model_specification: OLS time-series regression testing the t statistic for the coefficient on StateEmploymentGapz.
controls: standardized national employment gap (NationalEmploymentGapz) and an intercept
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's aggregate analysis of whether dispersion in local conditions explains migration: regress detrended aggregate migration rates on a national business-cycle measure and the cross-state dispersion of the corresponding state employment gaps.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of HP-detrended intercounty migration on the standardized dispersion of state employment gaps, controlling for the standardized national employment gap, the dispersion coefficient was positive but not statistically significant, t(51)=1.60, p=0.115. Thus this analysis does not provide evidence that dispersion in local employment conditions is significantly related to migration.

dependent_variable: Participant-level composite response latency bias in seconds for anger-relevant White-face transitions; onset transitions were coded young latency minus old latency and offset transitions were coded old latency minus young latency, then averaged.
main_predictor: Target age for White faces (old vs young), within subjects.
sample_definition: Participants with complete 48-trial experiment data; trials were included only if the response latency was greater than 0 and no more than the 17-second movie duration; participants needed nonmissing means for all White anger-relevant age-by-transition cells.
model_specification: One-sample t-test of the within-participant old-versus-young White anger-bias composite against zero, after averaging across the two face exemplars per cell and across happy-to-angry, neutral-to-angry, angry-to-happy, and angry-to-neutral transitions with directionally consistent coding.
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed response latencies from the facial emotion change-detection task separately by transition; to test the single verbal claim about White faces perceiving anger as both appearing sooner and lasting longer, I combined the four anger-relevant White-face transitions into one directionally coded within-subject composite.
reasoning: I formed a participant-level White-face anger bias score where positive values mean anger was detected sooner on old than young White faces for anger-onset transitions and lasted longer on old than young White faces for anger-offset transitions. The mean bias was positive (M = 1.13 s) and significantly greater than zero, t(53) = 7.20, p = 2.17e-9, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for following social distancing: response of 5-7 vs 1-4 to 'I keep my distance from other people as much as possible' (keep_distance/i48).
main_predictor: Male gender (1 = male, 0 = female).
sample_definition: Respondents in the provided dataset aged 20-64 with nonmissing sex, household income, occupation grouping, and model covariates; N = 3,119.
model_specification: Logistic regression of binary social-distancing adherence on male gender and covariates; reported statistic is the Wald z test for the male coefficient.
controls: Age category, marital status, no child under 18 in household, high/junior-high education indicator, employment category, household income category, smoking status, TIPI Big Five personality scores, and survey round.
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods used a logit model for social-distancing-related behavior with demographic, health-habit, and personality covariates. Because the supplied dataset contains a direct 7-point current behavior item on keeping distance from others, I dichotomized it into high adherence (5-7) versus lower adherence (1-4) and tested the adjusted male effect.
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting high social-distancing adherence, the coefficient for male was negative and statistically significant (z = -6.46, p = 1.05e-10; OR = 0.40). Men therefore had a lower adjusted likelihood of reporting that they kept distance from other people as much as possible.

dependent_variable: Prefs_1: rated criticality/preference for part-time work in future employment (1 = doesn't matter to 5 = must have)
main_predictor: Three job-seeker profile clusters (satisficer, free agent, maximizer) derived from the 24 work-desire items
sample_definition: Completed, consenting respondents who indicated being age 40+ and current job seekers, had valid self-reported age 40-100, and had complete data on the 24 desire items and part-time preference; N = 767.
model_specification: Ward hierarchical clustering on the 24 raw desire items was used to obtain three initial clusters; their centroids initialized a deterministic Lloyd k-means refinement. A one-way ANOVA then tested Prefs_1 across the three resulting clusters.
operationalization_notes: The paper formed satisficer/free-agent/maximizer profiles from the 24 desire items and tested work-characteristic preferences with one-way ANOVAs, so I followed that approach for the part-time preference item. No imputation was used because the analytic sample had no missing values on the variables used.
reasoning: Using a three-cluster solution from the 24 work-desire items, part-time work preference did not differ across the groups, F(2, 764) = 0.028, p = 0.972. The group means were nearly identical (satisficers M = 2.74, free agents M = 2.75, maximizers M = 2.77), so this analysis does not support the claimed variation in preference for part-time work.

dependent_variable: Death, coded 1 when FECHA_DEF was not 9999-99-99 and 0 otherwise
main_predictor: Male sex (SEXO = 2) versus female sex (SEXO = 1)
sample_definition: Records with ORIGSAMP = 1: SARS-CoV-2 positive patients aged 25 years or older with registry/admission date on or before April 23, 2020; complete cases on model covariates were retained for the regression.
model_specification: Multivariable logistic regression with a Wald z test for the male-sex coefficient.
controls: Age group indicators (50-74, >=75, reference 25-49), chronic kidney disease, COPD, diabetes/hypertension/obesity combination category indicators, pregnancy, immunosuppression, pneumonia, hospitalization, intubation, ICU admission, and health service sector indicators (IMSS, ISSSTE, SSA, other; private as reference).
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's mortality-model approach: restrict to adult positive cases in the study cutoff window and model death as the endpoint while adjusting for the same major clinical and service covariates used in Table 4.
reasoning: In a complete-case multivariable logistic regression for death among adult COVID-positive cases in the original-sample window, the coefficient for male sex was positive and highly significant (z = 9.23, p = 2.81e-20). The fitted odds ratio for men versus women was exp(0.490) = 1.63, indicating higher mortality risk for men.

dependent_variable: Perceived stress score at follow-up
main_predictor: Individual's own dispositional optimism score at baseline
sample_definition: All complete heterosexual couples in SCORE_scored_data_wrangled.csv/SCORE_scored_data.csv with both partners' optimism and stress scores available: 101 couples, 202 individuals.
model_specification: Actor-partner interdependence model implemented as a pooled individual-level linear regression of stress on own optimism and partner optimism, with standard errors clustered by dyad.
controls: Partner's optimism; cluster-robust dyad-level standard errors to account for non-independence within couples.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested the claim with a basic APIM linking baseline optimism to follow-up perceived stress. I therefore used the scored optimism and stress variables supplied with the dataset, reshaped couples to person-level records, and tested the actor effect of own optimism while accounting for partner optimism and dyadic clustering.
reasoning: In a dyadic actor-partner regression, own optimism negatively predicted follow-up perceived stress, b = -0.3049, t(100) = -8.76, p = 5.10e-14. Thus, more optimistic individuals reported lower stress than less optimistic individuals in this dataset.

dependent_variable: T2 negative affect, computed as the sum of the 10 PANAS negative-affect items
main_predictor: T1 realistic COVID-19 threat, computed as the mean of the five realistic-threat items
sample_definition: Participants in Kachanoff_Survey_deidentify.csv with a non-empty participant_id hash, two survey observations 5-10 days apart; first observation treated as T1 and earliest complete follow-up as T2; cases with missing T1 threat composites or T2 negative-affect composite excluded.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of T2 negative affect on T1 realistic threat and T1 symbolic threat; reported t test for the realistic-threat coefficient.
operationalization_notes: Study 3 tested whether T1 realistic and symbolic threats predicted criterion outcomes one week later in a simultaneous SEM. I approximated the path for the target claim with a simultaneous longitudinal regression using observed scale composites, which leaves the target coefficient as the unique association of realistic threat with subsequent negative affect.
reasoning: In a longitudinal regression, T1 realistic threat positively predicted T2 negative affect, but the coefficient was not statistically significant at the conventional two-sided .05 level, t(236)=1.84, p=.068. Thus the estimate was in the same direction as the published claim but was inconclusive in this reanalysis.

dependent_variable: Binary decision to attempt risky coordination / work together (Cooperate = 1) versus work alone (Cooperate = 0)
main_predictor: Common knowledge condition (Knowledge = 4) versus non-common knowledge conditions (Knowledge = 1 private, 2 secondary, or 3 tertiary)
sample_definition: Non-pilot complete responses from the dataset (records corresponding to N = 22–613), with Finished = 1, Progress = 100, non-missing Knowledge and Cooperate, and correct payoff comprehension answers for the respondent's role (both cooperate = 1.80, unilateral cooperate = 0, work alone = 1.60).
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on a 2 × 2 contingency table crossing common-vs-noncommon knowledge with the binary cooperation decision; no continuity correction.
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary procedure excludes participants who failed payoff comprehension checks and tests whether knowledge level affects the decision to work together. I dichotomized the knowledge manipulation as common knowledge versus all lower levels because the target claim contrasts common knowledge with shared or private knowledge.
reasoning: Among included participants, 47/67 (70.1%) in the common-knowledge condition chose to work together, compared with 83/180 (46.1%) in the combined non-common conditions (private, secondary, and tertiary knowledge). A Pearson chi-square test showed this difference was significant, χ²(1, N = 247) = 11.32, p = 0.00077, supporting the claim that common knowledge increased risky coordination attempts.

dependent_variable: Composite intention to support the nonprofit (mean of ITS1_1, ITS2_1, ITS3_1)
main_predictor: Mean-centered relational fit × sponsor-sponsee similarity interaction, tested as an indirect effect through clarity of nonprofit positioning
sample_definition: Finished respondents with complete data on the fit, similarity, clarity of positioning, attitude toward sponsorship, intention to support, trustworthiness, and experimental condition variables (N = 907); four unfinished/incomplete responses were excluded.
model_specification: Observed-variable OLS path analysis: clarity of positioning was regressed on mean-centered fit, similarity, their interaction, trustworthiness, and nonprofit-brand dummy; attitude toward sponsorship was regressed on fit, similarity, their interaction, and trustworthiness; intention to support was regressed on clarity of positioning and attitude toward sponsorship. The main statistic is a Sobel z test for (Fit × Similarity → clarity of positioning) × (clarity of positioning → intention to support), using HC3 robust standard errors.
controls: Sponsor trustworthiness; nonprofit brand dummy (Red Cross vs. Leukaemia Foundation) in the clarity-of-positioning path, following the paper's reported covariate structure.
operationalization_notes: The claim in the paper refers to the H2b moderated-mediation result, so I used the same constructs and mediation route but represented latent variables with their item means because the provided analysis was recomputed directly from the dataset rather than copied from the SEM output.
reasoning: Using observed scale composites in a path model mirroring the paper's moderated-mediation specification, the Fit × Similarity effect on clarity of positioning was positive and, multiplied by the clarity-to-intention path, gave an indirect effect of 0.0184. A Sobel test with HC3 robust path standard errors gave z = 2.05, p = .040, supporting a joint indirect effect on intention to support the nonprofit.

dependent_variable: Self-reported physical distancing item b7: massively curtailing social contact because of COVID-19
main_predictor: Affective empathy composite: mean of b1, b2, and b3 concern/compassion/moved items for those most vulnerable to COVID-19
sample_definition: All complete observations in the provided survey dataset that passed the attention check Q21 = strongly agree (62 of 63 respondents); the available file contains this survey rather than separate US/UK/Germany files.
model_specification: Bivariate ordinary least squares regression of physical distancing on empathy; reported t-test for the empathy slope, equivalent to Pearson correlation test.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 operationalized the claim with the same three-item affective empathy measure and the self-related physical distancing item, reporting the main association without covariates, so I used the analogous bivariate analysis on the provided data.
reasoning: Among the 62 participants passing the attention check, higher affective empathy was positively associated with stronger self-reported physical distancing, t(60)=4.39, p=0.000046 (Pearson r=0.493). This supports the study's claim that empathy is a motivation for physical distancing.

operationalization_notes: The paper suggests using fixed-effects panel models of gender-role/mothering attitudes before versus after first birth, but the required panel microdata are not present in /workspace/data.
reasoning: I could not compute a test statistic because the data directory contains only user-guide PDFs and a data-dictionary spreadsheet, not an analyzable respondent-level dataset. Since no original data file with observations is available to load and analyze, the claim cannot be independently tested from the provided materials.

dependent_variable: Per-subject SNARC slope: regression coefficient of dRT (median RT for right responses minus median RT for left responses) on digit magnitude
main_predictor: Task phase/condition within the verbal working-memory group: verbal load versus no-load baseline
sample_definition: Participants assigned to verbal working-memory load who recalled at least 25% of dual-task memory blocks, were not overall parity-RT outliers (>4 SD above the group median), and had complete correct-trial medians for both left and right responses for all eight digits in both phases; n=94 paired participants.
model_specification: For each participant and phase, correct parity trials were summarized by median RT for each digit and response side; dRTs were regressed on digit magnitude to obtain a SNARC slope. The main test was a paired-samples t-test comparing verbal-load slopes with baseline slopes.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's SNARC regression approach and focuses on the within-participant change from baseline to verbal memory load, which directly operationalizes the claim that a verbal load abolished/reduced the SNARC effect in the parity task.
reasoning: Among included verbal-load participants, the mean SNARC regression slope was -8.76 ms/digit at baseline and -7.94 ms/digit under verbal load. The paired comparison of load versus baseline slopes was not significant, t(93)=0.53, p=0.595, so these data do not support the claim that verbal load abolished or reduced the SNARC effect.

dependent_variable: Participant mean d-prime sensitivity across the 12 grammaticality-judgment test blocks
main_predictor: Training-input condition / Version (starting small vs random)
sample_definition: Consenting participants in the combined dataset with attnPrompts == 'ok'; all grammaticality-judgment test trials across blocks 1-12 were included for those participants (N = 70).
model_specification: For each participant and block, d′ was computed as z(hit rate) - z(false alarm rate), with loglinear correction ((count + 0.5)/(n + 1)); the participant outcome was the mean of these 12 block d′ values. Groups were compared with an equal-variance independent-samples t-test.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper’s Experiment 1 primary analysis comparing overall mean d′ performance between the starting-small and random training groups; attention-flagged participants were excluded because the dataset explicitly identifies them as not trying.
reasoning: Using participants who passed the attention-screening flag, the starting-small group had only slightly higher mean block-level d′ (M = 0.073) than the random group (M = -0.006). This difference was not statistically significant, t(68) = 0.83, p = 0.409, so the data do not support the claimed SS advantage in this reanalysis.

dependent_variable: T3_panas_joviality
main_predictor: req_relax
sample_definition: Complete cases in /workspace/data/data_k17.csv with nonmissing T3 joviality, weekend relaxation, demographics, T1 joviality, and other weekend-experience variables; N = 337.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression predicting T3 PANAS joviality from demographics, T1 joviality, and all weekend experience variables; the reported test is the t test for the weekend relaxation coefficient in the full model.
controls: gender, age computed from birthyear, having children, work hours per week, work days per week, T1 PANAS joviality, psychological detachment, mastery, control, and non-work hassles
operationalization_notes: The model follows the paper's hierarchical-regression specification for joviality at Time 3, using baseline joviality and the demographic controls plus all weekend recovery/hassle predictors entered in the final step.
reasoning: In the complete-case OLS regression, weekend relaxation had a positive coefficient for end-of-following-week joviality, but the test was not conventionally significant, t(325) = 1.727, p = 0.085. Thus, this reanalysis does not provide clear two-sided evidence for the claimed positive association.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that the respondent was arrested in a given month (monthly arrest status 1-98 coded 1; 0 or 99 coded 0).
main_predictor: Within-person divorce status: monthly divorced indicator minus the respondent-specific mean divorced proportion.
sample_definition: Ever-married respondents with an arrest history and nonmissing key baseline controls; valid observed person-months from 1997-2009 excluding invalid relationship/arrest months and widowed months; 830 respondents contributed 124,904 person-months.
model_specification: Binomial logistic generalized estimating equation with exchangeable working correlation by respondent; relationship states decomposed into within-person centered indicators and between-person respondent means; robust sandwich standard errors.
controls: Within-person legal separation and single indicators, age and age-squared; between-person mean divorce, legal separation, and single proportions; male, Black race, household members under age 18, intact family, disadvantage, parental education, early-risk index, and incarceration history.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies the within-individual effect of divorce among ever-married respondents with an arrest history as the central test of whether divorce increases arrest likelihood; I therefore modeled monthly arrest as a function of within-person divorce relative to married months, while controlling for the same relationship-state decomposition and baseline covariates described in the methods.
reasoning: In a population-average logistic GEE for 830 ever-married respondents with an arrest history, the within-person divorce coefficient was positive (b = 0.464; OR = 1.59) and statistically significant, z = 2.18, p = 0.029. Thus, months in which a respondent was divorced had higher odds of arrest than that same respondent's married months, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Autism identification among enrolled public school students, represented as autism count versus non-autism count in each state-by-race stratum
main_predictor: State indicator for Ohio compared with California
sample_definition: Students represented in the 2014 IDEA autism counts and 2014 NCES public elementary/secondary enrollment denominators for California and Ohio, across the seven reported racial/ethnic categories; Wyoming and all other states were not included in this focused comparison.
model_specification: Grouped binomial logistic regression with state-by-race strata: logit(Pr(autism identified)) = intercept + Ohio indicator + race fixed effects; the reported statistic is the Wald z test for the Ohio coefficient.
controls: Race/ethnicity categorical fixed effects for American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, Black/African American, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Two or More Races, and White
operationalization_notes: The paper's between-state analysis used logistic regression on aggregated count data with autism as the outcome and state and race as predictors. I operationalized the claim as the direct California-vs-Ohio version of that model, using the same age 6-21 IDEA autism counts and NCES enrollment denominators by race.
reasoning: In a grouped binomial logistic regression of autism identification on an Ohio-vs-California indicator controlling for race, the Ohio coefficient was negative (log-odds = -0.309; OR = 0.734), z = -34.42, p = 1.40e-259. Thus, autism identification was significantly less likely in Ohio than in California after adjustment for racial composition.

dependent_variable: group_chooses_red (indicator that the group decision was the red jar)
main_predictor: voting rule / institution (Majority, SuperMajority, Unanimity)
sample_definition: All available observations in Goeree_Econometrica_2011_1574_data.csv collapsed to one observation per unique sessioncode × round × groupid_in_session group-round; no group-rounds with nonmissing outcome and covariates were excluded.
model_specification: Linear probability model at the group-round level: group_chooses_red ~ C(treatment) + C(red_signal_grp), with a joint F-test of the two voting-rule dummy coefficients; standard errors clustered by sessioncode.
controls: Categorical fixed effects for red_signal_grp, the number of red private signals in the group.
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzes institutional differences in group outcomes conditional on the group's information. The provided dataset has voting-rule treatments and group signal counts but no explicit chat/no-chat or preference-condition indicator, so I treated the provided deliberation-session data as the relevant condition and tested whether institutions differ in group outcomes after controlling flexibly for information.
reasoning: In the provided data, voting rule strongly predicts the group red outcome after adjusting for the group's number of red signals, F(2,10)=57.52, p=3.27e-6. The adjusted differences are large: relative to majority rule, supermajority and unanimity reduce the probability of a red group outcome by about 0.416 and 0.577 respectively, so institutional differences remain pronounced rather than diminished.

dependent_variable: Group mean seller revenue per share across 20 uniform-auction rounds (operationalized as average market price/revenue per 100,000 shares)
main_predictor: Auction mechanism comparison: uniform-price auction revenue tested against the fixed-price offering benchmark of 1.94
sample_definition: Groups in fullsample_analysis.csv with dropout=0 and bankrupt=0; 32 valid uniform-auction groups, each averaged over 20 rounds
model_specification: One-sided one-sample t-test of group mean uniform-auction revenue per share against 1.94, the fixed offering price specified in the experimental design
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzes group-level outcomes because decisions within groups are interdependent and notes that fixed offerings used a predetermined price of 1.94; since the provided data contain uniform-auction group prices and validity flags, I tested whether valid groups' average uniform-auction revenue per share exceeded this fixed-price benchmark.
reasoning: Using valid group-level observations, the mean uniform-auction revenue per share was 1.9567 versus the fixed-offering benchmark price of 1.94. A one-sided one-sample t-test did not show that uniform auctions raised higher revenue, t(31)=0.174, p=0.432.

dependent_variable: Binary intended vote preference in the Obama-versus-Trump item: 1 = Barack Obama, 0 = Trump, different candidate, or no support/not sure
main_predictor: Conception risk (oddconcept actuarial fertility risk value)
sample_definition: Female respondents who reported no hormonal birth control, regular menstrual cycles, not pregnant, no chronic fertility-relevant health problems, planned to vote, and had nonmissing Q20 vote preference and conception-risk data
model_specification: Point-biserial (Pearson) correlation between binary Obama preference and conception risk
operationalization_notes: The paper's main-effect test used a point-biserial correlation with Obama preference coded 1 versus all other options coded 0 among normally cycling non-hormonal-contraceptive women; I applied the analogous coding to the available Obama vote-preference item and used the paper's participant-exclusion criteria adapted to the variables in the dataset.
reasoning: In the eligible sample, the point-biserial correlation between conception risk and intending to vote for Barack Obama rather than another/no candidate was r = -0.042 with df = 304, N = 306, p = 0.462. The association was not statistically significant and was slightly negative, so this analysis does not support the claimed positive relationship.

dependent_variable: Panic-buying search composite: mean of within-country z-scored log1p Google Trends values for 'panic buying' and 'stockpile'.
main_predictor: Within-country z-scored log1p total confirmed COVID-19 infected cases.
sample_definition: Daily observations from the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, and Australia from each country's first nonzero confirmed case through March 24, 2020; observations with zero cases before first confirmed case and New Zealand were excluded.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of the panic-buying composite on standardized log COVID-19 cases with country fixed effects.
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed log-transformed standardized time-series within countries through March 24, 2020. The provided dataset contains the panic-buying and stockpile search terms, so I tested the panic-buying component of the broader claim and pooled the four target countries with fixed effects to obtain one main statistic.
reasoning: In a pooled country-fixed-effects regression for the four stated countries, within-country standardized log COVID-19 cases positively predicted the standardized log panic-buying search composite, b = 0.683, t(230) = 16.46, p = 9.42e-41. This supports the claim component that higher COVID-19 prevalence was associated with greater panic-buying-related searches.

dependent_variable: Procedural justice scale score, computed as the mean of pj1-pj7
main_predictor: Perceived workplace racial discrimination scale score, computed as the mean of rd1-rd8
sample_definition: All 105 observations in 347d_m89_105participant_data.csv with complete data on the procedural justice items, racial discrimination items, organizational diversity-effort items, and covariates; no observations were missing on these variables.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of procedural justice on perceived workplace racial discrimination, perceived organizational efforts to support diversity, and demographic/work covariates; the reported test is the t test for the racial discrimination coefficient.
controls: Perceived organizational efforts to support diversity (mean of oesd1-oesd5), sex/gender as a categorical control, age, minority status, work experience, full-time employment status, and graduate-student status
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim with hierarchical regression predicting procedural justice from workplace racial discrimination while adjusting for demographic/work controls and perceived organizational efforts to support diversity. I used the same scale composites and control structure on the largest provided participant dataset, treating sex/gender categorically because the data include one non-binary-coded category.
reasoning: In an OLS regression matching the paper's procedural-justice analysis, higher perceived workplace racial discrimination significantly predicted lower procedural justice, b = -0.312, t(95) = -3.50, p = 0.00072. The negative coefficient supports the claim that employees reporting more race-based discrimination report lower procedural justice from the organization.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 total stress score, computed from pss10_avg as (pss10_avg - 1) * 10
main_predictor: Three-level agreement with government's containment/preventive measures category derived from trust_countrymeasure
sample_definition: Swiss respondents in the replication dataset with nonmissing PSS-10 average and nonmissing trust_countrymeasure/agreement response (N = 1079)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA/OLS model: PSS-10 total stress score ~ categorical agreement group
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's group-comparison approach, I treated the response midpoint of trust_countrymeasure (5 = appropriate measures) as agreement and collapsed responses symmetrically around that midpoint: 4-6 = agreement, 2-3 and 7-8 = no agreement, and 0-1 and 9-10 = no agreement at all.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA showed that PSS stress differed by agreement with the government's containment measures, F(2, 1076) = 9.98, p = 5.09e-05. The observed means were ordered in the claimed direction: agreement/appropriate measures M = 13.26, no agreement M = 14.08, and no agreement at all M = 16.02, indicating lower stress among respondents who agreed with the measures.

dependent_variable: Binary trust-game choice, coded 1 = Option L/trust and 0 = Option R/distrust
main_predictor: Interaction between mean-centered Honesty-Humility and experimental condition (0 = control/certainty, 1 = self-uncertainty)
sample_definition: Completed responses with nonmissing trust choice and complete data on the 10 Honesty-Humility HEXACO items; N = 842.
model_specification: Logistic regression of binary trust on mean-centered Honesty-Humility, condition, and their product interaction.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's Studies 2/3 analysis: binary trust-game behavior was regressed on Honesty-Humility, the self-uncertainty manipulation, and their interaction. Honesty-Humility was scored as the mean of HEXACO-60 items 6, 12R, 18, 24R, 30R, 36, 42R, 48R, 54, and 60R.
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting trust, the Honesty-Humility by self-uncertainty interaction was negative but not statistically significant, z = -0.623, p = .534. Thus, these data do not provide clear evidence that people high in Honesty-Humility shifted toward distrust under self-uncertainty.

dependent_variable: Mean of S1_likely, S1_quality, and S1_purchase (movie desirability index)
main_predictor: Interaction between self-concept clarity manipulation (clear = 1, conflicted/low clarity = -1) and rating distribution (bimodal = 1, unimodal = -1)
sample_definition: All observations in the 'All Usable data' sheet, i.e., participants retained after the documented exclusion criteria; N = 376.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of desirability on contrast-coded clarity condition, contrast-coded rating distribution, and their interaction.
operationalization_notes: This follows Study 2B's primary desirability analysis for temporary self-concept clarity threat: the three desirability items were averaged and regressed on the two experimental factors and their interaction using the contrast coding described in the paper/data dictionary.
reasoning: Using the cleaned usable sample, the clarity condition × rating distribution interaction predicting the three-item desirability index was significant, t(372) = -2.30, p = .022. With the paper's contrast coding, this negative interaction indicates that the bimodal-vs-unimodal desirability difference was larger under conflicted/low self-concept clarity (means: 4.98 vs. 4.33) than under clear self-concept clarity (4.60 vs. 4.53), supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Antisocial behavioral reaction composite: average of standardized revenge, standardized avoidance, and reverse-coded standardized reconciliation scale means
main_predictor: Perceived offender motives: malice/cruelty and greed/selfishness manipulation-check ratings; joint indirect effect through anger
sample_definition: Participants in the lab-scenario dataset who passed the comprehension check and had complete data on the focal scales (N=1071)
model_specification: Observed-variable mediation/path analysis using OLS scale-score regressions: anger was regressed on perceived malice, perceived greed, and offense severity; the behavioral composite was regressed on anger, sympathy, perceived malice, perceived greed, and offense severity. The main statistic is a 2-df Sobel/delta-method Wald chi-square test of the two indirect effects via anger.
controls: Offense severity in the anger model; offense severity, sympathy, and direct perceived malice/greed terms in the behavioral-outcome model
operationalization_notes: The paper tested a structural model with perceived motive attributions, emotions, and behavioral reactions. To obtain one reproducible test statistic from the available item-level data, I used the paper's scale groupings, represented the three behavioral outcomes with one directional composite, and tested whether distinct malice and greed attributions had indirect relations with behavior through anger.
reasoning: Using scale means, the joint delta-method Wald test for the two indirect paths from perceived malice and perceived greed to an antisocial behavioral-reaction composite through anger was significant, χ²(2)=40.79, p=1.39e-9. Both estimated indirect effects were positive (malice: 0.0195; greed: 0.0421), consistent with motive attributions shaping anger, which in turn related to more revenge/avoidance and less reconciliation.

dependent_variable: MisperpSc (mean COVID-19 misperceptions scale)
main_predictor: CogSophSc (omnibus cognitive sophistication composite: mean of z-scored CRT/analytic thinking, science knowledge, numeracy, and reverse-scored bullshit receptivity scales)
sample_definition: Participants in the SAV file with valid MisperpSc and CogSophSc values; this matched the provided SPSS filter variable filter_$ = 1 (NumbCorrectScreen > 1), yielding N=87.
model_specification: Pearson zero-order correlation between CogSophSc and MisperpSc.
operationalization_notes: The paper describes the main cognitive-sophistication result for misperceptions using the preregistered omnibus cognitive sophistication score and the overall misperception scale; a zero-order correlation is the most direct test of the stated negative association.
reasoning: In the analytic sample (N=87), the omnibus cognitive sophistication composite was significantly negatively correlated with COVID-19 misperceptions, r(85) = -0.402, p = 0.000113. This indicates that higher analytic/numerate/science-knowledge/bullshit-skepticism scores were associated with lower endorsement of COVID-19 misperceptions.

dependent_variable: Mean correct recognition index across joy words and anger words (JOY% and ANG% averaged per participant)
main_predictor: Alexithymia group from the TAS-20 median split (TASGRP: high vs low)
sample_definition: All complete participant-level observations in Vermeulen Data Submission.csv with non-missing depth condition, music condition, alexithymia group, JOY%, and ANG% (N = 1096)
model_specification: Between-subjects factorial ANOVA on participant-level mean recognition for joy and anger words: emo_mean ~ depth * music * alexithymia_group; the reported result is the type-III main effect of alexithymia group.
controls: Depth of processing condition, music condition, and their interactions with alexithymia group were included as design factors; no additional covariates.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim as the alexithymia main effect in the recognition analysis restricted to joy and anger words. Averaging JOY% and ANG% gives the between-subject outcome corresponding to that main effect while retaining the paper's between-subject design factors.
reasoning: Using the mean correct recognition index across joy and anger words, high alexithymia participants recognized substantially fewer words (M = 0.189) than low alexithymia participants (M = 0.463). The alexithymia-group main effect in the factorial ANOVA was significant, F(1,1088) = 303.154, p = 4.40e-60, supporting the directional claim.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that EVOLVED was answered True (human beings developed from earlier species of animals); other substantive/DK/NA responses coded 0 among respondents asked the item.
main_predictor: Modal latent class membership, comparing post-secular versus traditional classes from a 3-class latent class analysis of science- and religion-perspective indicators.
sample_definition: General Social Survey respondents from 2006, 2008, and 2010 with non-IAP responses on the science/religion indicators used for the latent class model (N = 2844); the chi-square test includes only respondents assigned to the post-secular or traditional latent classes (N = 1755).
model_specification: Three-class latent class model estimated by maximum likelihood/EM on the paper's science knowledge, science attitude, Bible-view, and religious-affiliation-strength indicators; post-estimation 2 x 2 Pearson chi-square test of latent class group by evolution response.
operationalization_notes: The paper ties the claim to the conditional means by latent class, so I operationalized perspectives with the same style of three-class LCA and then directly tested the post-secular-versus-traditional difference in the EVOLVED item. Science quiz items were coded correct versus not correct, with DK/NA treated as not correct for the binary evolution outcome.
reasoning: Using modal assignments from a three-class latent class model, 51 of 720 post-secular respondents (7.1%) versus 308 of 1035 traditional respondents (29.8%) answered that humans evolved from earlier species of animals. The difference is large and statistically significant, chi-square(1, N = 1755) = 134.17, p = 5.0e-31, supporting the claim that post-secular respondents were less likely than traditional respondents to give the evolution response.

dependent_variable: Mug trendiness index computed as the mean of trendy, modern, and urban ratings (V18, V19, V20)
main_predictor: Display table surface condition: glass table versus wood table
sample_definition: All valid participant rows in Zhu_Replication.csv after excluding the Qualtrics header row; participants with either V17=1 for glass table or V16=1 for wood table were included (N=69).

operationalization_notes: The paper tests this claim in Experiment 1 using a neutral mug and a trendiness index formed from the trendy, modern, and urban items. The provided replication dataset contains the interdependent self-view writing prompt and table-surface manipulation, so I directly compared the table conditions on that same trendiness index.
reasoning: Using the three-item trendiness index, participants in the glass-table condition rated the mug numerically less trendy (M = 5.10) than those in the wood-table condition (M = 5.47). dependent_variable: Percentage of utilitarian responses across the two moral acceptability items, coded as morally acceptable = utilitarian and averaged per participant

operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 directly tested the claim by comparing utilitarian responses to conflict moral scenarios after a death versus pain salience manipulation. The available dataset contains two moral acceptability responses and a death/pain salience assignment, so I used the participant-level percentage of morally acceptable responses as the utilitarian-choice outcome and applied the same basic between-condition comparison.
reasoning: Using participants who passed the manipulation-response quality screen, the mean utilitarian response percentage across the two moral-conflict scenarios was 87.90% in the death-salience group and 85.82% in the pain-salience control group. dependent_variable: Mean interpersonal obstacle-behavior association reaction time across the four critical lexical decision trials; higher/slower RT indicates weaker association.

model_specification: OLS regression predicting mean interpersonal obstacle-behavior RT from centered expectation (centered at the lowest observed value, 2), condition dummies with mental contrasting as the reference group, their interactions, and accessibility RT; the reported t test is the planned linear contrast of mental contrasting versus the average of both controls at expectation = 2.
controls: Mean interpersonal behavior accessibility reaction time from neutral-prime trials.
operationalization_notes: The paper operationalized obstacle-behavior association strength with lexical-decision RTs and controlled for mere accessibility of the behavior. I focused on the elaborated interpersonal concern and tested the low-expectation simple contrast most directly tied to the claim that mental contrasting with low expectations yields weak associations.
reasoning: Using the Study 1-style regression, the estimated contrast at the lowest observed expectation score (2) showed mental contrasting participants had only 24.6 ms slower obstacle-behavior reaction times than the average of the two control conditions, t(300)=0.389, p=0.697. Because slower RTs indicate weaker associations, this was in the predicted direction but far from statistically reliable.

dependent_variable: s: proportion of the surplus allocated to the recipient
main_predictor: x_l: recipient's monetary contribution divided by total monetary contribution (libertarian predicted recipient share)

operationalization_notes: The paper operationalizes whether a justice principle accounts for behavior by regressing the actual recipient share on the share predicted by that principle and testing whether the intercept is zero and the slope is one. I applied that specification to the DW treatment and the libertarian predicted share.
reasoning: For DW dictators, I regressed the recipient share given (s) on the libertarian predicted recipient share (x_l) and tested the joint restriction alpha=0 and beta=1. The heteroskedasticity-robust Wald/F test rejected the libertarian principle, F(2,25)=8.94, p=0.00118, so the observed allocations are not well accounted for by the libertarian benchmark.

dependent_variable: Prior hypertension diagnosis, coded 1 if the hypertensive respondent was not underdiagnosed and 0 if underdiagnosed

controls: Log per-capita expenditures, time preference, risk preference, travel time to health center, sex, age, and age squared
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's disease-detection specification, I tested whether education predicts diagnosis conditional on being hypertensive and in poor general health, using a probit model with the same core covariates described in the methods. I coded the outcome as diagnosed rather than underdiagnosed so the coefficient direction directly corresponds to the claim.
reasoning: In a probit model among hypertensive respondents in poor general health, the coefficient for years of education predicting prior hypertension diagnosis was positive (coef = 0.0322) and statistically significant, z = 2.51, p = 0.012. Thus, within the poor-health subgroup, more educated respondents had a higher probability of having been diagnosed.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological judgments, coded as the proportion of raw main-task APP responses marked Inappropriate/rejecting harm within each dilemma type
main_predictor: Social observation condition (experimental/observed vs. control) and its interaction with dilemma type
sample_definition: All participants in the main moral-dilemmas dataset with nonmissing condition assignment and complete raw APP responses for the 50 main-task dilemmas; N = 156 (78 control, 78 experimental/observed).

operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed proportions of deontological responses in a 2 × 3 mixed ANOVA and interpreted the claim as a social-observation effect that was especially pronounced for personal moral dilemmas; therefore I tested the group-by-dilemma-type interaction using proportions computed from the raw item-level responses (items 1-20 personal, 21-35 impersonal, 36-50 control).
reasoning: A 2 (condition) × 3 (dilemma type) mixed ANOVA on deontological-response proportions gave no evidence that the observation effect differed by dilemma type, F(2, 308) = 0.237, p = 0.789. The observed/experimental group was only slightly higher than control for personal dilemmas (0.649 vs. 0.629), with similarly small differences for impersonal and control dilemmas, so the data do not support a selective promotion of deontological judgments for personal moral dilemmas.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (5-point COVID-19 concern/anxiety item)
