model_specification: Pearson correlation between the mean z-scored achievement composite and the mean z-scored social-emotional problems composite.
operationalization_notes: The paper modeled academic achievement as reading and mathematics indicators and social-emotional problems as externalizing and internalizing indicators; I mirrored this with observed standardized composites and tested their direct association in the ELL group.
reasoning: Among children coded as ELL/non-English language status (X12LANGST = 1) with complete third-grade achievement and social-emotional data, the standardized achievement composite was negatively correlated with the standardized social-emotional problems composite, r(2045) = -0.265, p = 2.93e-34. Because higher problem scores indicate more externalizing/internalizing problems, this supports the claim that fewer social-emotional problems are linked to higher achievement scores.

dependent_variable: Mean of SocGood_Artis, SocGood_Green, SocGood_Food, and SocGood_Medtech ratings (1 = great harm, 5 = great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition coded as for-profit versus non-profit
sample_definition: Completed respondents (Finished = 1) in the Study 3 for-profit and non-profit conditions with nonmissing societal-good ratings for all four organization scenarios; unspecified-motive condition excluded for this focused contrast.
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test equivalent to OLS regression of mean perceived societal good on a binary for-profit indicator; reported t tests the for-profit coefficient.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 claim concerns the manipulated firm motive effect on the general societal-good item across four hypothetical organizations, so I averaged each subject's four societal-good ratings and tested the focal for-profit versus non-profit motive contrast.
reasoning: In completed Study 3 responses, the for-profit condition had lower average perceived societal good across the four scenarios (M = 3.746, n = 123) than the non-profit condition (M = 4.310, n = 121). An independent-samples t-test/OLS coefficient for a for-profit indicator was significant, t(242) = -8.59, p = 1.08e-15, supporting the claim that profit motive reduced perceived societal good.

dependent_variable: Sharing intention for each COVID-19 headline, with the 1-6 Likert response rescaled to 0-1
main_predictor: Headline veracity within the treatment condition (true vs false headline)
sample_definition: Treatment-condition participants in the Study 2 data file with headline sharing ratings; 440 participants contributed 30 ratings each, for 13,200 rating-level observations.
model_specification: Rating-level ordinary least squares regression of rescaled sharing intention on headline veracity, restricted to the treatment condition, with two-way cluster-robust standard errors clustered by participant and headline.
operationalization_notes: This directly tests the claim's simple effect by comparing sharing intentions for true versus false headlines within the accuracy-nudge treatment condition, following the paper's rating-level linear model approach with participant and headline clustering and rescaled sharing-intention outcome.
reasoning: Among treatment-condition ratings, mean rescaled sharing intention was 0.4975 for true headlines and 0.5037 for false headlines, giving a true-minus-false coefficient of -0.00621. A rating-level OLS model with two-way cluster-robust standard errors by participant and headline gave z = -1.45, p = 0.147, so the data analyzed here do not support significantly higher sharing intentions for true than false headlines in the treatment condition.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth indicator: GDP per capita growth of at least 2% in each of the five years following the survey year
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index, the weighted country-survey share of valid Afrobarometer respondents saying their ethnic/identity group is never treated unfairly by the government
sample_definition: Country-survey observations from Afrobarometer rounds 1-4 with valid unfair-treatment question responses, mergeable Polity2, and five subsequent years of GDP per capita growth data; 64 observations from 20 sub-Saharan African countries
model_specification: OLS linear probability model with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard error; reported test is the t-test for the log impartiality coefficient
controls: Polity2 democracy score for the survey country-year
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's core specification closely: a country-survey impartiality index from the first four Afrobarometer rounds, a five-year sustained-growth outcome based on the 2% GDP-per-capita-growth threshold, and Polity2 as the baseline control. I used the five years after the survey to preserve the paper's lagged-explanatory-variable logic.
reasoning: In a linear probability model of sustained growth on log perceived government impartiality, controlling for Polity2, the coefficient test for log impartiality was t(61) = -0.615, p = 0.541. The estimated association was negative and statistically indistinguishable from zero, so this reanalysis does not support the claim that perceived impartiality predicts a higher likelihood of sustained growth.

dependent_variable: paired difference in toaster evaluation score: mean evaluation of 4.5-star/aggregated-information toaster minus mean evaluation of 2.5-star/individualized-information toaster
main_predictor: information type within the abstract sound condition (aggregated-information toaster vs individualized-information toaster)
sample_definition: Participants assigned to the abstract sound condition and retained in the paper's analysis filter (filter=1), with nonmissing toaster evaluation means; N=16.
model_specification: paired-samples t-test comparing the two within-participant toaster evaluation means in the abstract sound group
operationalization_notes: The quoted claim is specifically about participants hearing the abstract sound favoring the aggregated-information toaster over the individualized-information toaster, so I tested the within-subject evaluation difference in that condition using the paper's five-item toaster evaluation composites.
reasoning: Among the included participants in the abstract-sound condition, the mean evaluation of the toaster favored by aggregated information exceeded the evaluation of the toaster favored by individualized information by 2.16 scale points. A paired-samples t test showed this difference was statistically reliable, t(15)=7.86, p=1.07e-6.

dependent_variable: GDP per capita / national affluence (GDPcapita, in thousands of dollars)
main_predictor: One-year lagged imports from the South (totalimport, scaled to trillions of USD)
sample_definition: Country-year observations for the 18 OECD countries from 1970-2003; observations with missing model variables were dropped; the paper-identified outliers Norway 1999-2003 and Belgium 1998-1999 were excluded.
model_specification: OLS panel regression with country fixed effects and five-year period fixed effects; standard errors clustered by country; test is the coefficient t-test for lagged imports from the South.
controls: One-year lagged exports to the South, one-year lagged unemployment rate, country fixed effects, and five-year period indicators.
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's indirect-effects model for national affluence as the outcome, using lagged explanatory variables and the same country-year window and outlier exclusions. The available replication file provides South import/export values in dollars, so I used the level of imports scaled to trillions rather than imports as a percentage of GDP.
reasoning: In a two-way fixed-effects panel regression for 18 OECD countries, the coefficient for lagged imports from the South was positive, b = 27.36 thousand dollars of GDP per capita per trillion USD of imports, with a cluster-robust t(17) = 3.78, p = 0.0015. This supports the claimed positive relationship between imports from the South and national affluence.

dependent_variable: Average benefit-minus-symbolism difference score across symbolic products (college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards)
main_predictor: Branding level: branded product/brand condition versus unbranded category-level condition
sample_definition: Participants in the combined dataset with valid condition assignment; included Cond 1/2 as category-level and Cond 3/4 as branded; excluded incomplete responses, failed attention checks, participants reporting prior participation, and cases missing the symbolic-product difference score.
model_specification: Independent-samples equal-variance t-test comparing branded versus category-level conditions on the participant-level average symbolic-product benefit-minus-symbolism score.
operationalization_notes: Following Study 1B's method, I used the Shavitt-style utilitarian and symbolic ratings and computed benefit minus symbolism so that higher values indicate more utilitarian/less symbolic attitudes; the focal test is the simple branding effect among products classified as symbolic.
reasoning: For the four symbolic categories, the average benefit-minus-symbolism score was higher in the branded conditions (M = -2.100, n = 268) than in the category-level conditions (M = -2.645, n = 277), t(543) = 3.879, p = 0.000118. Because higher scores indicate relatively more utilitarian and less symbolic attitudes, this supports the claim that branding makes symbolic product categories less symbolic and more utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic self-discipline (ASD; used as the self-regulation measure per the data dictionary)
sample_definition: All observations represented in the supplied aggregate correlation/mean/SD matrix from Jung et al.; N = 366.
model_specification: Multiple linear regression reconstructed from the supplied correlation matrix: Semester GPA regressed on Academic self-discipline and Self-discipline facet; the reported test is the t test for the Academic self-discipline coefficient.
operationalization_notes: The original paper tested whether a self-regulation latent factor predicted GPA while accounting for self-discipline. Because the available dataset is an aggregate correlation matrix rather than raw item-level data, I used the provided self-regulation proxy (Academic self-discipline) to predict GPA while controlling for the provided self-discipline proxy, yielding the path/regression coefficient test most directly tied to the claim.
reasoning: Using the supplied summary correlation matrix (N = 366), academic self-discipline, used here as the available self-regulation measure, positively predicted semester GPA when controlling for the self-discipline facet: standardized beta = 0.336, t(363) = 4.855, p = 1.79e-6. This supports a positive association between self-regulation and GPA.

dependent_variable: Mean belief in four COVID-19 conspiracy theories
main_predictor: Mean national/collective narcissism score from three items
sample_definition: Participants in the provided COVID_finaldata.csv with complete data on all national narcissism items, four COVID-19 conspiracy belief items, national identification items, individual narcissism items, and CRT reflection items; N = 1501.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression predicting COVID-19 conspiracy belief from national narcissism and covariates; the reported statistic is the t test for the national narcissism coefficient.
controls: National identification, individual narcissism, and cognitive reflection (CRT correct responses scaled as in the paper).
operationalization_notes: The paper states that Study 3 did not measure intentions to disseminate COVID-19 conspiracy theories. Because the provided dataset corresponds to Study 3 and lacks a sharing/dissemination outcome, I used COVID-19 conspiracy belief as the closest available construct tied to potential dissemination while treating the direct sharing claim as not directly testable.
reasoning: In the provided German Study 3 dataset, no variable measured intentions to share or disseminate COVID-19 conspiracy theories, so I analyzed the closest available construct: mean belief in four COVID-19 conspiracy theories. National narcissism was strongly positively associated with this belief measure after controls, t(1496) = 23.18, p = 8.68e-102, but the specific sharing claim remains inconclusive because sharing was not measured.

dependent_variable: Participant-level proportion of fWHR trials on which the higher-fWHR face was chosen as more aggressive
main_predictor: Higher versus lower facial width-to-height ratio (fWHR) face within each forced-choice pair
sample_definition: Participants in Processed_Data_2.csv who answered 'Yes' to the data-quality/use question; first 24 face-choice trials treated as the fWHR trials, yielding N=288 participants and 6,912 choices
model_specification: One-sample t-test of each participant's proportion of higher-fWHR choices against chance level 0.50
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 procedure used 24 fWHR pairs and 12 masculinity pairs in a two-alternative forced-choice aggression judgment task; I therefore tested whether the higher-fWHR option was selected above chance using participant-level proportions, matching the paper's primary fWHR analysis. The supplied data files contain this 36-trial Study-1-style task rather than the Study 2 male/female 54-trial task, so the analysis targets the directly available fWHR component.
reasoning: Participants chose the higher-fWHR face as more aggressive on 53.04% of the 24 fWHR trials, which was significantly above chance, t(287)=4.21, p=3.46e-05. This positive above-chance choice rate supports the claim that increased fWHR is perceived as more aggressive in the available fWHR-face data.

dependent_variable: money: amount of bribe demanded by the public official or amount proposed to keep by Participant B, in USD, including zero demands
main_predictor: Game frame / treatment: harassment bribery game versus neutral ultimatum game
sample_definition: Public Official / Participant B observations in the bribery-game and ultimatum-game conditions with non-missing money values; citizen/Participant A observations and missing amount decisions were excluded.
model_specification: Independent-samples Welch t-test comparing the mean money amount in BG to the mean money amount in UG, using the directional alternative that BG is lower than UG.
operationalization_notes: The abstract claim concerns the average bribe/transfer amount being lower in the bribery frame than in the strategically identical ultimatum frame. I therefore used the paper's core BG-versus-UG comparison on the decision-maker amount variable and retained zero demands because they are part of the average extent of the demanded bribe/transfer.
reasoning: Among decision-makers with a recorded bribe/transfer amount, the mean amount demanded/kept was lower in the bribery game (M = 0.578, n = 199) than in the neutral ultimatum game (M = 0.910, n = 195). A one-sided Welch two-sample t-test of BG < UG gave t(344.68) = -5.37, p = 7.10e-8, supporting the claim that average demands were lower in the bribery frame.

dependent_variable: Estimated total number of taxicabs, divided by the largest observed serial number at that point
main_predictor: Number of observed examples/serial numbers provided (1, 3, or 10)
sample_definition: Taxicab-condition records only; participants/files with any nonnumeric estimate or any estimate below the currently largest observed serial number were excluded, and participants with any normalized response more than 3 SD from the cell mean were excluded, leaving 575 complete participants.
model_specification: One-way repeated-measures ANOVA on normalized estimates with within-subject factor values_seen (1, 3, 10)
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed the taxicab scenario with a within-subjects ANOVA after excluding implausible responses and transforming responses to t/t_part, where t_part is the largest example. I followed that approach, using the available taxicab data and normalizing by each trial's current maximum serial number because the observed serial numbers varied across participants.
reasoning: In the taxicab condition, normalized estimates of the total fleet size decreased as the number of observed cab serial numbers increased: M=1.85 with 1 observation, M=1.33 with 3 observations, and M=1.15 with 10 observations. A repeated-measures ANOVA showed a strong effect of number of observations, F(2, 1148)=127.92, p=6.99e-51, supporting the claim that additional examples led to smaller relative predictions.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that the district-level Beber-Scacco last-digit chi-square test for total vote counts was significant at the 5% level (fraudchi2_total).
main_predictor: Insurgent attacks around election day per 1,000 population and its squared term; the reported test is for the squared violence term.
sample_definition: Afghan districts in the replication dataset with non-missing fraud, election-day violence, closed-station, electrification, expenditure, distance-to-Kabul, elevation, and regional-command variables; N = 375.
model_specification: Logistic regression with regional-command clustered standard errors, matching the paper's district-level Model 1 specification.
controls: Number of closed polling stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure in 1,000 AFs, distance from Kabul, and elevation.
operationalization_notes: The paper operationalizes the inverted-U claim by regressing the binary last-digit fraud measure on violence and violence squared with controls. I used the election-day SIGACT violence specification because it is the first and most direct test of the hypothesis in the paper.
reasoning: In a district-level logit model of last-digit-test fraud, the election-day violence term was positive (b = 8.477) and its squared term was negative and statistically significant (b = -13.748, cluster-robust z = -2.913, p = 0.0036). The fitted turning point is within the observed violence range, supporting an inverted-U relationship rather than a purely monotone increase.

dependent_variable: Social undermining, operationalized as reverse-coded willingness to be matched with the potential partner (8 - Undermin), so higher values indicate greater undermining
main_predictor: Temporal social comparison condition (0 = favorable, 1 = unfavorable) interacted with competition condition (0 = low, 1 = high)
sample_definition: All observations in the provided analytical data file: 574 participants, each contributing two TSC-condition ratings, for 1,148 person-target observations clustered by participant id
model_specification: Ordinal cumulative logit GEE model for social undermining predicted by TSC, competition, and their interaction, with participant id as the clustering variable and a global odds-ratio working dependence structure
operationalization_notes: This follows Study 1a's behavioral operationalization: competition was experimentally manipulated between participants, TSC was manipulated within participant, current/static comparison was held constant by design, and the focal test of the claim is the TSC × competition interaction.
reasoning: I reverse-coded the original matching-preference item so that higher scores indicated greater social undermining, then tested the TSC × competition interaction in a clustered ordinal cumulative-logit model. The interaction was positive and statistically significant, z = 3.192, p = 0.00141, indicating that unfavorable temporal social comparison related more strongly to undermining under high competition than low competition.

dependent_variable: Mean coronavirus-specific conspiracy theory belief endorsement across SpecCTs_1, SpecCTs_2, SpecCTs_3r, SpecCTs_4, SpecCTs_5, and SpecCTs_6r
main_predictor: Mean COVID worry/threat score from COVID1 and COVID3
sample_definition: All 806 observations in the cleaned replication dataset with complete observed values on the conspiracy-belief items, COVID worry/threat items, and sample identifier
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression: mean coronavirus-specific conspiracy beliefs ~ mean COVID worry/threat + categorical sample fixed effects; reported statistic is the t test for the COVID worry/threat coefficient
operationalization_notes: The supplied dataset did not contain the paper's trust-in-institutions, lack-of-control, demographic, or full risk-perception variables. I therefore tested the portion of the claim directly represented in the data by using the available COVID worry and threat items as the pandemic anxiety/risk predictor and the available coronavirus-specific conspiracy items as the outcome, adjusting for the three sample sources.
reasoning: Using the available dataset, the mean COVID-specific conspiracy-belief score was regressed on mean COVID worry/threat while controlling for sample. The main coefficient for COVID worry/threat was negative and statistically significant, t(802) = -4.69, p = 3.18e-06, indicating that higher worry/threat was associated with lower, not higher, conspiracy-belief endorsement in these data.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time in milliseconds
main_predictor: Central face valence, comparing angry vs neutral faces within the GAD group
sample_definition: Participants coded Group = 1 (GAD/likely GAD) with complete AngryM and NeutralM values; all 63 such participants were included.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing participant-level mean RT for angry-face trials with participant-level mean RT for neutral-face trials.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim as a within-GAD follow-up contrast of reaction times by face valence after excluding incorrect and outlier trials; the available dataset provides participant-level condition means, so I used the directly corresponding within-subject angry-versus-neutral comparison.
reasoning: Within the GAD/likely-GAD group, mean RT was 486.81 ms for angry faces and 485.36 ms for neutral faces. The paired comparison did not support faster responses to angry faces, t(62)=0.471, p=0.639; the observed mean difference was slightly in the opposite direction (angry slower by 1.45 ms).

dependent_variable: Change in brand personality impression, computed as post-scenario mean sophistication rating (Q5_1-Q5_4) minus pre-scenario mean sophistication rating (Q2_1-Q2_4)
main_predictor: Employee behavior consistency × pseudorelevant information disclosure, restricted to high outcome dependency
sample_definition: All complete observations in Wentzel_et_aldataStage2.csv with Outcome Dependency = 1; the first Qualtrics label row was excluded
model_specification: Two-way between-subjects OLS/ANOVA: change in sophistication ~ Consistency * Pseudorelevant Information; reported the interaction F test
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim in Study 2 using change scores for brand personality impressions and factorial ANOVA. I used brand personality impressions as the primary outcome and tested whether, under high dependency, the effect of pseudorelevant information differed in opposite directions for consistent versus inconsistent employee behavior.
reasoning: Among participants in the high outcome-dependency condition, the behavior × pseudorelevant-information interaction on change in brand sophistication was not significant, F(1,421)=0.671, p=.413. The cell means were only weakly in the predicted direction: inconsistent behavior produced similar changes with information vs no information (-0.683 vs -0.723), and consistent behavior was slightly more positive with no information (-0.021 vs 0.132).

dependent_variable: Aversiveness/disturbing rating rescaled from 1-7 to 0-6 and averaged within participant and humor type
main_predictor: Humor type: Covid Verbal versus Non-Covid Verbal
sample_definition: Participants from completed deidentified survey rows with complete aversiveness ratings for all 12 assumed Non-Covid Verbal items (pic1-pic12) and all 12 assumed Covid Verbal items (pic13-pic24); N = 832 paired participant means.
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test of participant-level mean aversiveness difference, Covid Verbal minus Non-Covid Verbal
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies aversiveness as the outcome for this claim and highlights the a-priori contrast between Covid Verbal and Non-Covid Verbal humor; I operationalized that contrast using the first 24 stimulus IDs as the two 12-item verbal sets and analyzed within-participant means.
reasoning: Using participant-level mean aversiveness ratings, Covid Verbal items were rated as more aversive (M = 0.863 on the 0-6 rescaled scale) than Non-Covid Verbal items (M = 0.750). The paired-samples t-test showed a positive difference, t(831) = 7.55, p = 1.16e-13, supporting the claim that Covid-19 humor carries greater aversiveness than non-pandemic humor.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for adopting at least one avoidance behavior in the last month, defined from prep selections: avoiding social events, avoiding public transport, eating out less, shopping for groceries less, or staying home from work.
main_predictor: Trust in coronavirus/COVID-19 information from government or official sources in the country of residence (govtrustQ1, 1 = did not trust at all to 7 = completely trusted).
sample_definition: Australian respondents in replication_data.csv with nonmissing avoidance-behavior outcome, government/official-source trust, age quota category, gender, education, and COVID-19 worry; doctorate education was combined with masters/higher, yielding N = 561.
model_specification: Logistic regression of the binary avoidance-behavior indicator on continuous government/official-source trust, reporting the Wald z test for the trust coefficient.
controls: Age quota category, gender, education category, and worry about coronavirus/COVID-19 (FinitePool_2).
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed adoption of any avoidance-related behavior using logistic regression adjusted for demographics and worry. The available dataset did not contain the paper's exact two-item trust-in-government/authorities scale, so I used the directly relevant government/official-source trust item and constructed an analogous any-avoidance outcome from the survey's preparation behaviors.
reasoning: In an adjusted logistic regression, greater trust in information from government/official sources predicted higher odds of having adopted at least one avoidance behavior (z = 2.44, p = 0.0147; OR = 1.28 per 1-point increase on the 1-7 trust scale). Thus the data support the directional claim that higher government/authority trust is associated with more avoidance behavior.

dependent_variable: CMMSRC: reverse-coded average current money management stress scale score, with higher values indicating lower current money management stress/more positive responses
main_predictor: Group: writing prompt valence, comparing success/positive frame (Group = 2) versus failure/negative frame (Group = 1)

model_specification: Independent-samples equal-variance t test comparing mean CMMSRC between success and failure frame groups.
operationalization_notes: The paper describes Study 3a as manipulating recent current-finance thoughts via success versus failure frames and testing the manipulation on reverse-scored current money management stress; therefore I used the provided reverse-coded CMMS average and compared the two randomized frame groups among included participants.
reasoning: Among included participants, the success/positive writing-prompt group had higher reverse-coded current money management stress scores (M = 3.003) than the failure/negative prompt group (M = 2.559), where higher scores indicate lower stress/more positive financial well-being. An independent-samples equal-variance t test showed this difference was significant, t(260) = 3.65, p = 0.00032, supporting the claimed directional effect.

dependent_variable: Situational attributions scale constructed from bidirectional items
main_predictor: Dispositional attributions scale constructed from bidirectional items
sample_definition: Respondents in the processed Qualtrics dataset assigned to the bidirectional-question condition (Bal_Group = 1) with complete data on the outcome, predictor, and covariates.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of situational attributions on dispositional attributions and covariates, using HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors; the reported statistic is the coefficient test for dispositional attributions.
controls: Perceived victimization risk, perceived crime trend, news consumption, conservatism, religiosity, family victimization, education, female, White, and age.
operationalization_notes: I followed the paper's Table 4-style operationalization for the target attribution claim: within the bidirectional condition, predict situational attribution style from dispositional attribution style while adjusting for the demographic and attitudinal controls listed in the methods.
reasoning: In the bidirectional-question group, dispositional attributions significantly predicted lower situational attributions in the adjusted OLS model (b = -0.223, robust SE = 0.045), t(630) = -4.94, p = 9.96e-7. This supports the claim that the relationship is highly significant when the attribution items are formulated bidirectionally.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 SCORE
main_predictor: MONTHLY INCOME
sample_definition: Overall dataset; participants with non-missing gender coding were included, excluding 18 participants coded as other/missing on BE MALE, yielding N = 2035.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of PSS-10 SCORE on MONTHLY INCOME and sociodemographic covariates; the reported statistic is the t test for the MONTHLY INCOME coefficient.
controls: AGE, BE MALE, EDUCATION, FAMILY MEMBERS
operationalization_notes: The paper's sociodemographic analysis tested perceived stress using PSS-10 score and monthly household income as a predictor; I used the final sociodemographic regression specification corresponding to that analysis.

dependent_variable: Mean of the four behavioral inclination items: chips, casual sex partners, social-network friends, and wanting a newer phone

controls: Actor's own warmth/trustworthiness ideal-standard match rating for the partner, and participant sex (men = 1, women = -1).
operationalization_notes: The paper tests this claim as the APIM partner effect of ideal discrepancies on relationship satisfaction; I used the warmth/trustworthiness dimension because it is the central ideal-standard dimension emphasized in the paper and directly maps to whether the actor matches the partner's ideals.
reasoning: In a dyadic mixed-effects APIM, the partner's report that the actor more closely matched the partner's warmth/trustworthiness ideals positively predicted the actor's relationship quality, b = 0.2233, SE = 0.0283, z = 7.891, p = 3.00e-15. Because higher scores mean closer matching of the partner's ideal standards, this supports the claim that individuals are less satisfied when they fail to match those standards.

dependent_variable: Stroop interference score: mean log response time on correct incongruent trials minus mean log response time on correct congruent trials

operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 operationalized immediate cognitive control as Stroop interference after excluding errors and very fast responses and analyzed log-transformed response times; I followed that approach and tested the condition effect on participant-level interference scores.
reasoning: Using log-transformed Stroop interference (mean log RT on incongruent trials minus mean log RT on congruent trials), the coded stereotype-threat group had slightly lower interference than the control group (0.128 vs. 0.134), but the independent-samples test was not significant, t(302) = -0.416, p = .678. Thus, this analysis does not provide clear evidence that stereotype threat facilitated immediate cognitive control capacity.

dependent_variable: Future Health Behavior: Hygiene composite (mean of Q28_7, Q28_8, Q28_10, Q28_11, reverse-scored so higher = stronger intended hygiene endorsement)

The negative coefficient is consistent with the claim that dark traits predict lower health-behavior endorsement.

dependent_variable: Creativity (study-level correlation with intrinsic motivation, Fisher z-transformed for analysis)

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the overall positive intrinsic motivation-creativity relationship, so I analyzed the study-level correlations for intrinsic motivation and creativity following the paper's meta-analytic focus, without adding moderators or covariates.
reasoning: Using the 68 independent study-level intrinsic motivation-creativity correlations (total N = 19,695), a random-effects meta-analysis of Fisher z-transformed correlations produced a positive pooled association, r = 0.282. The test of the pooled Fisher-z effect was z = 10.31, p = 6.20e-25, supporting a positive relationship between intrinsic motivation and creativity.

Because the provided dataset lacks White-target observations, I used the closest estimable test of the claimed low-IMS Black-target positivity-to-increased-prejudice relation, but the central race comparison remains untestable.

In a within-Black-target regression of pre-to-post change in anti-Black attitudes, the simple slope of communication positivity at low IMS (-1 SD) was negative and non-significant, t(25) = -0.92, p = .366, so this dataset does not support the claimed increase.

dependent_variable: Supervisor-rated organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) composite: average of sportsmanship, civic virtue, courtesy, and altruism facet scores, with negatively worded sportsmanship items reverse-coded.

controls: Trust in leader, tenure with supervisor in years, and organizational level; trust is the mediator being adjusted for in the direct-effect test.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested full mediation with employee-reported leadership and trust predicting supervisor-rated OCB while controlling for organizational level and tenure with the direct leader. I used scale composites from the provided item-level data rather than a latent SEM, using the five trust items specified in the methods and the four OCB facet averages described in the paper.

Because adding the direct leadership terms substantially improved prediction beyond trust, this analysis does not support full mediation by trust.

The independent-samples t-test for mortality minus control was t(191)=0.558, p=.578, so the data do not support significantly more negative attitudes in the mortality-salience condition.

dependent_variable: Natural logarithm of country-level mean mortality rate (mean daily increase in COVID-19 deaths during the ascending phase)

operationalization_notes: Following the paper's ecological regression approach, I used the provided country-level derived mean mortality outcome and adjusted for available demographic, environmental, health-system and economic predictors most closely corresponding to the multivariable model described in the methods. dependent_variable: points contributed to the shared account (cont)

operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 tested the claim with within-subject contribution decisions and a contrast comparing losses-and-gains prospects to no-variance plus gains-only prospects. dependent_variable: HP-filtered cyclical component of the intercounty migration rate (HPmigration)

operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's aggregate CPS time-series specification in which detrended national migration is related to national business-cycle conditions while controlling for dispersion in state economic conditions; the employment-gap dispersion measure is the local-conditions dispersion variable most directly tied to the claim.

The coefficient test for state-gap dispersion was not statistically significant, t(50)=1.56, p=0.125, so this analysis does not find a reliable relationship between dispersion in local conditions and migration.

dependent_variable: Subject-level composite anger-bias latency score in seconds: for White faces, young-minus-old latency for anger-onset transitions plus old-minus-young latency for anger-offset transitions, averaged across happy-to-angry, neutral-to-angry, angry-to-happy, and angry-to-neutral transitions.

I combined the four anger-relevant White-face transitions into one directional score so that positive values uniformly represent anger appearing sooner or lasting longer on old than young White faces.

dependent_variable: Not following social distancing: coded 1 for responses 1-4 and 0 for responses 5-7 to 'I keep my distance from other people as much as possible.'
main_predictor: Male respondent, coded 1 for male and 0 for female.
sample_definition: Respondents aged 20-64 with complete data on the outcome, sex, survey round, demographic controls, smoking, household income, employment, education, marital/children variables, and Big Five personality items.
model_specification: Binary logistic regression; the reported statistic is the Wald z test for the male coefficient.
controls: Survey round; age category; marital status; no children under 18 in household; low education; employment category; household income category; smoking indicator; extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, neuroticism, and openness TIPI scores.
operationalization_notes: The paper used a logit model for non-adherence to social distancing with individual-characteristic controls. The available dataset measured social distancing on a 1-7 scale, so I dichotomized the directly relevant item on keeping distance from others into non-adherence (1-4) versus adherence (5-7) and fit a comparable adjusted logit model.
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting not following social distancing, the coefficient for male was positive and highly significant (z = 6.38, p = 1.82e-10; OR = 2.48). Men also had a higher adjusted likelihood of non-adherence, supporting the claim that men are less likely to follow social distancing.

dependent_variable: Prefs_1: criticality/preference for part-time work (1 = doesn't matter to 5 = must have)
main_predictor: Three-profile cluster membership derived from the 24 work-desire items (interpreted as satisficer/free-agent/maximizer-type profiles)
sample_definition: Participants who finished the survey, consented, reported being age 40 or older, and reported currently seeking employment; all had complete data for the 24 desire items and Prefs_1 (N = 771).
model_specification: Two-stage clustering following the paper's approach: Ward hierarchical clustering on the 24 Desire items to obtain three initial clusters, followed by k-means refinement with k = 3; then one-way ANOVA of Prefs_1 on cluster membership.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim with a one-way ANOVA comparing the three clusters on the part-time work characteristic, so I used the same outcome and an analogous cluster-then-ANOVA approach on the provided data rather than using covariates.
reasoning: Using a three-cluster solution derived from the 24 work-desire items, part-time work preference did not differ across the profiles, F(2, 768) = 0.046, p = 0.955. The cluster means were essentially identical (approximately 2.74 to 2.77 on the 1-5 part-time criticality scale), so this analysis does not support the original claim of variation in part-time preference.

dependent_variable: Perceived stress score (PSQ average score)

Thus, individuals with higher optimism scores reported substantially lower perceived stress, matching the original claim.

dependent_variable: Negative affect at T2, computed as the sum of the 10 negative PANAS items (negative1-negative10)
main_predictor: Realistic threat at T1, computed as the mean of the five COVID realistic threat items (covid_real1-covid_real5)

model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of T2 negative affect on T1 realistic threat and T1 symbolic threat; the reported statistic is the t test for the realistic threat coefficient.
controls: T1 symbolic threat, computed as the mean of the five symbolic threat items.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 tested whether T1 realistic and symbolic COVID-19 threats predicted criterion outcomes one week later, with both threat dimensions included simultaneously. I therefore used the longitudinal Study 3-style sample and the direct composite-score analogue of that simultaneous model for the negative affect outcome.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting subsequent-week negative affect from T1 realistic and symbolic threat, the coefficient for realistic threat was positive (b = 1.85) but not statistically significant, t(189) = 1.63, p = .105. Thus, this reanalysis does not provide clear evidence for the claimed positive unique association.

dependent_variable: Whether the participant chose to work together / cooperate in the coordination task (Cooperate = 1 vs 0)
main_predictor: Knowledge condition dichotomized as common knowledge (Knowledge = 4; public/loudspeaker) versus non-common knowledge (Knowledge = 1-3; private, secondary, or tertiary/shared messenger knowledge)

model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on a 2 x 2 contingency table comparing cooperation rates between common-knowledge and private/shared-knowledge conditions.
operationalization_notes: The paper's method excluded participants who did not understand the payoff structure, so I applied the same type of exclusion. I combined private, secondary, and tertiary knowledge as the comparison group because the target claim contrasts common knowledge with shared or private knowledge in general.
reasoning: Among participants who passed the payoff comprehension checks, 47/67 (70.1%) in the common-knowledge condition chose risky coordination, compared with 83/180 (46.1%) in the private/shared-knowledge conditions. A Pearson chi-square test for common versus non-common knowledge was significant, chi-square(1, N = 247) = 11.32, p = 0.00077, supporting the claim that common knowledge increased attempts at risky coordination.

dependent_variable: Intention to support the nonprofit, computed as the mean of ITS1_1, ITS2_1, and ITS3_1
main_predictor: Mean-centered relationship fit × mean-centered sponsor–nonprofit similarity interaction, tested as an indirect effect via clarity of positioning
sample_definition: Completed sponsorship-condition responses with non-missing fit, similarity, clarity of positioning, attitude toward sponsorship, intention-to-support, trustworthiness, and condition variables (N = 907)
model_specification: Observed-variable path analysis using OLS composite scales: clarity of positioning was regressed on mean-centered fit, mean-centered similarity, their interaction, sponsor trustworthiness, and nonprofit brand; intention to support was regressed on clarity of positioning and attitude toward sponsorship. controls: Sponsor trustworthiness and nonprofit brand in the mediator model; attitude toward sponsorship in the intention model
operationalization_notes: The paper tested H2b as a moderated-mediated effect of relationship fit and similarity on intention to support via clarity of positioning, with trustworthiness and nonprofit brand considered as covariates. I mirrored that specification with mean composite scales rather than latent SEM variables.
reasoning: Using composite scales, the fit-by-similarity term positively predicted clarity of nonprofit positioning, and clarity positively predicted intention to support. The resulting Sobel test for the indirect fit × similarity effect through clarity was significant, z = 2.05, p = .040, indicating a positive joint indirect effect on intention to support the nonprofit.

dependent_variable: Self-reported physical distancing: b7, 'Because of coronavirus (COVID-19), I am massively curtailing social contact (so-called social distancing)'

dependent_variable: Additive scale of traditionalism in attitudes to mothering and gender divisions of labor

sample_definition: Intended: respondents aged 18-50 in waves with attitude measures; actual: no analyzable respondent-level data file available
model_specification: Intended fixed-effects linear panel regression; not estimated because original data file was absent
controls: Intended controls from paper: marital status, education, religiosity/missing flag, age, years since first birth; not estimated

dependent_variable: Subject-level SNARC slope: regression coefficient of dRT (median RT for right responses minus median RT for left responses) on digit magnitude.
main_predictor: Task condition within the verbal working-memory group: baseline parity judgment versus parity judgment during verbal memory load.
sample_definition: Participants assigned to verbal working-memory load who self-approved data use, recalled at least 25% of load memory blocks, were not overall RT outliers using the paper's median-plus-4-SD criterion, and had sufficient correct parity trials to estimate both baseline and load SNARC slopes; correct parity trials only were used for RT medians.
model_specification: For each subject and phase, median RTs on correct parity trials were computed for each digit separately for left- and right-key responses; dRT=right minus left was regressed on digit magnitude, and the resulting baseline and load slopes were compared with a paired-samples t-test.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's regression approach to quantify the SNARC effect and tests the central claim as a within-subject reduction of the SNARC slope under verbal memory load in the parity task.

A paired t-test on subject-level SNARC slopes showed no evidence that the verbal memory-load phase reduced/abolished the SNARC effect relative to baseline, t(88)=0.20, p=.841.

dependent_variable: Participant-level signal-detection d' for grammaticality judgments across all test trials
main_predictor: Training condition / Version: starting small (small) versus random

dependent_variable: Monthly indicator for arrest, coded 1 if the NLSY97 monthly arrest status reported one or more arrests in that month and 0 otherwise.
main_predictor: Within-individual divorce status: monthly divorced indicator group-mean centered within respondent, with married months as the reference state after including single and legal-separation states.
