model_specification: Binomial logistic generalized estimating equation with exchangeable within-person correlation and robust standard errors; relationship-state indicators were decomposed into within-person deviations and between-person means, following the paper's within/between longitudinal specification.
controls: Within-person controls for legal separation, single status, centered age, and centered age squared; between-person mean proportions divorced, legally separated, and single; baseline male, Black race, household members under 18, intact family, disadvantage, parental education, early-risk index, and ever incarcerated.
operationalization_notes: I used the paper's focal marital-dissolution analysis: an ever-married, arrest-history sample with monthly arrest as the outcome and the within-individual divorce contrast as the main test of whether divorce increases arrest likelihood. GEE logistic regression was used to reproduce the longitudinal binary-outcome analysis directly from the provided data.
reasoning: In a population-averaged logistic model of monthly arrest, the within-person divorce coefficient was positive (b = 0.463, robust SE = 0.210), yielding z = 2.20, p = 0.028. Thus, months in which respondents were divorced had significantly higher odds of arrest than months in which the same respondents were married, net of covariates.

dependent_variable: Autism identification status, represented as counts of students identified with autism versus not identified with autism within state-by-race cells
main_predictor: Ohio state indicator compared with California as the reference state
sample_definition: Aggregated 2014 U.S. state-by-race data for students ages 6-21 with autism counts merged to 2014 public elementary/secondary enrollment denominators; Wyoming was excluded because autism data were missing, and state-race cells with missing or zero enrollment denominators were excluded.
model_specification: Grouped-binomial logistic regression with logit link: autism successes and non-autism failures modeled by categorical state and categorical race predictors; the reported z test is for the Ohio coefficient relative to California.
controls: Race category fixed effects for American Indian/Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian/Pacific Islander, Two or More Races, and White (reference).
operationalization_notes: The paper’s between-state analysis used logistic regression on aggregate autism counts, with California as the reference state and race categories included; I operationalized the state-level claim by testing the Ohio-vs-California state coefficient while adjusting for race composition.
reasoning: In a grouped-binomial logistic regression with California as the reference state and race-category controls, the Ohio state coefficient was negative (log OR = -0.279, OR = 0.757) and highly significant, z = -33.32, p = 1.93e-243. This indicates lower odds of autism identification in Ohio than in California, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: group_chooses_red (indicator that the group decision was the red jar/conviction)
main_predictor: voting rule/institution: majority (r=5), supermajority (r=7), unanimity (r=9)
sample_definition: All available group-level decisions in Goeree_Econometrica_2011_1574_data.csv; individual rows were collapsed to unique session-by-round-by-group observations, yielding 352 group decisions.
model_specification: Binomial GLM/logistic regression of group_chooses_red on categorical voting rule and the number of red private signals in the group; main test is a likelihood-ratio chi-square test comparing this model with a reduced model omitting voting rule.
controls: Number of red signals in the group (red_signal_grp).
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzes institutional differences in collective outcomes conditional on the information available to the group; the available dataset contains voting-rule sessions but no usable communication/no-communication indicator, so I tested the key implication that deliberated group outcomes should be similar across institutions after controlling for group signals.
reasoning: Using one record per group-round, a binomial GLM showed a very large remaining association between voting rule and whether the group chose red after adjusting for the number of red signals, likelihood-ratio chi-square(2, N=352)=156.95, p=8.30e-35. The observed red-choice rates also differed sharply by institution (58.3% under majority, 20.0% under supermajority, 0.0% under unanimity), so this analysis does not support the claim that deliberation diminishes institutional differences in the available data.

dependent_variable: Group-level average market price in the uniform price auction, used as per-share seller revenue because supply was fixed
main_predictor: Offering format comparison: uniform price auction mean price versus fixed price offering benchmark of 1.94
sample_definition: Groups in fullsample_analysis.csv with no dropout and no bankruptcy flags; group is the unit of observation
model_specification: One-sample t-test of group mean uniform-auction price against the fixed-price benchmark 1.94, with directional alternative mean > 1.94
operationalization_notes: The paper analyzes outcomes at the group level because within-group decisions are interdependent and notes that, with fixed supply and near-full subscription, higher market price implies higher seller revenue. The fixed-price treatment price was predetermined at 1.94, so I tested whether valid uniform-auction groups exceeded that benchmark.
reasoning: Using the group as the independent unit, the mean uniform-auction market price among valid groups was 1.957 versus the fixed-offering price benchmark of 1.94. A one-sample directional t-test did not show that uniform auctions raised higher per-share revenue, t(31)=0.174, one-sided p=0.432.

dependent_variable: Binary intention to support Barack Obama in the Obama-vs-Trump hypothetical presidential-election item Q20 (1 = Obama, 0 = Trump/other candidate/no support)
main_predictor: Conception risk, oddconcept
sample_definition: Female respondents who were not using hormonal birth control, reported regular periods, were not pregnant, reported no chronic fertility-related health problems, were aged 18-50, had typical cycle lengths of 21-35 days, planned to vote, and had valid Q20 and conception-risk data; all races included.
model_specification: Point-biserial Pearson correlation between conception risk and the binary Obama-support outcome, tested as a t statistic with df = n - 2.
operationalization_notes: This mirrors the paper's direct test of the main fertility-vote claim using a dichotomous Obama-support variable and conception risk as the predictor; the available dataset's direct Obama preference item was Q20.
reasoning: In the eligible sample, the point-biserial correlation between conception risk and intending to support Barack Obama was essentially zero and slightly negative (r = -0.0218), giving t(200) = -0.308, p = 0.758. Thus these data do not support the claim that higher conception risk is associated with a greater probability of intending to vote for Obama.

dependent_variable: Panic-buying search composite: the mean of country-standardized log1p Google Trends scores for 'panic buying' and 'stockpile'.
main_predictor: Country-standardized log1p cumulative COVID-19 infected count/prevalence.
sample_definition: Daily observations for Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom, and the United States from each country's first confirmed COVID-19 case through March 24, 2020; New Zealand and zero-prevalence pre-outbreak days were excluded.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of the panic-buying composite on standardized log COVID-19 prevalence with country fixed effects.
operationalization_notes: The paper's method log-transformed and standardized COVID-19 prevalence and Google Trends search variables and formed a two-term panic-buying composite. I used panic buying because it is one of the outcomes named in the claim and the available dataset contains the relevant Google Trends terms plus COVID-19 case counts.
reasoning: In a pooled within-country OLS model for the four target countries, standardized log COVID-19 prevalence positively predicted the standardized panic-buying search composite, t(230)=16.46, p=9.44e-41, N=235. This supports the claimed positive association between COVID-19 prevalence and panic-buying-related searches.

dependent_variable: Mean procedural justice scale score across pj1-pj7
main_predictor: Mean perceived workplace racial discrimination scale score across rd1-rd8
sample_definition: Complete cases from the 105-participant data file who had valid values on procedural justice, racial discrimination, organizational efforts to support diversity, and the control variables; the one participant with non-binary sex coding was excluded to match the paper's binary sex control coding, leaving N = 104 employed respondents.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of procedural justice on perceived workplace racial discrimination, perceived organizational efforts to support diversity, and control variables, corresponding to the paper's hierarchical regression Step 2 used to test Hypothesis 1.
controls: Sex (female=1, male=0), age, minority status, work experience, full-time employment status, graduate student status, and perceived organizational efforts to support diversity.
operationalization_notes: The paper tests this claim as Hypothesis 1 using composite scale scores and a hierarchical regression; I used the same scale construction and Step 2 specification, omitting the moderation term because the target claim concerns the main negative association.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting the procedural justice composite, perceived workplace racial discrimination had a negative coefficient (b = -0.312) and was statistically significant, t(95) = -3.50, p = 0.00072. Thus, employees reporting more race-based discrimination tended to report lower procedural justice, consistent with the original claim.

dependent_variable: PSS10_avg perceived stress score
main_predictor: Agreement with government's preventive/containment measures, operationalized as closeness to the response 'appropriate' on Trust_countrymeasure: 5 - |Trust_countrymeasure - 5|
sample_definition: Swiss respondents in the replication dataset with nonmissing Trust_countrymeasure and PSS10_avg values
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of PSS10_avg on the continuous agreement score
operationalization_notes: The paper describes agreement with containment measures as whether measures were appropriate/just right versus too little or too much; the available dataset contains the analogous Trust_countrymeasure scale with 5 = appropriate, so closeness to 5 was used as a directional agreement score.
reasoning: In an OLS regression, greater agreement with the government containment measures was associated with lower perceived stress, b = -0.0647 PSS-average units per agreement-score point, t(1077) = -5.09, p = 4.25e-7. This supports the claim that agreement with containment measures is linked to decreased stress.

dependent_variable: Binary trust-game decision, recoded 1 = chose Option L/trust and 0 = chose Option R/distrust
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility × self-uncertainty condition interaction; condition coded 0 = certainty/control, 1 = uncertainty
sample_definition: Finished observations with nonmissing condition, trust-game decision, and all Honesty-Humility scale items; the one missing DV case and one case with missing Honesty-Humility items were excluded.
model_specification: Logistic regression: trust ~ mean-centered Honesty-Humility + condition + Honesty-Humility × condition; Wald z test for the interaction coefficient.
operationalization_notes: This follows the Study 2/3 approach described in the paper: a binary trust-game outcome was regressed on Honesty-Humility, experimental self-uncertainty condition, and their interaction. Honesty-Humility was computed as the mean of HEXACO-60 items 6, 12R, 18, 24R, 30R, 36, 42R, 48R, 54, and 60R.
reasoning: In a logistic regression predicting trust choice from mean-centered Honesty-Humility, self-uncertainty condition, and their interaction, the Honesty-Humility × self-uncertainty interaction was negative but not significant (B = -0.0933, z = -0.623, p = 0.534, OR = 0.91). Thus, these data do not provide clear evidence that high Honesty-Humility participants shifted toward distrust under self-uncertainty.

dependent_variable: Desirability index: mean of S1_likely, S1_quality, and S1_purchase, each on 1-7 scales
main_predictor: Interaction between temporary self-concept clarity manipulation (clear vs. conflicted) and product rating distribution (bimodal vs. unimodal)
sample_definition: Participants in the 'All Usable data' sheet with Exclusion = 0 and nonmissing desirability items; all four between-subjects conditions included (clear-bimodal, clear-unimodal, conflicted-bimodal, conflicted-unimodal).
model_specification: Ordinary least squares regression of desirability on contrast-coded rating distribution (1 = bimodal, -1 = unimodal), contrast-coded clarity condition (1 = clear, -1 = conflicted), and their product interaction.
operationalization_notes: This follows Study 2B's method for testing whether a temporary threat to self-concept clarity moderates preference for bimodal versus unimodal rating distributions; the interaction is the main test of the claim.
reasoning: In an OLS model with contrast-coded clarity condition, rating distribution, and their interaction, the clarity × rating-distribution interaction was significant, t(372) = -2.30, p = .022. The direction matched the claim: in the conflicted/low-clarity condition, the bimodal movie was rated more desirable than the unimodal movie (M = 4.98 vs. 4.33), whereas this difference was minimal in the clear condition (M = 4.60 vs. 4.53).

dependent_variable: Composite revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation scores (three-item means) entered jointly as multivariate outcomes
main_predictor: Anger and sympathy composite scores, tested jointly
sample_definition: Participants in the scenario dataset who passed the comprehension check and had non-missing variables for the composites and condition indicators; N = 1071
model_specification: MANOVA / multivariate linear regression: revenge + avoidance + reconciliation ~ anger + sympathy + severity + malice + greed; main test was the Wilks' lambda F test for anger = 0 and sympathy = 0 across all three outcomes
controls: Perceived offense severity composite and dummy indicators for malice and greed conditions, with the control condition as reference
operationalization_notes: The paper's model places emotions between motive/severity appraisals and behavioral reactions. I therefore tested whether the two measured emotional reactions jointly predicted the three behavioral reaction composites after accounting for offense severity and experimentally assigned offender-motive condition.
reasoning: In a multivariate regression of revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation on the two emotional reactions, with severity and offender-motive condition controlled, anger and sympathy had a strong joint relation to the behavioral outcomes, Wilks' lambda = 0.791, F(6, 2126) = 44.09, p = 5.04e-51. This supports the claim that emotional reactions are independently related to subsequent revenge/avoidance/reconciliation responses.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 misperceptions composite (MisperpSc)
main_predictor: Cognitive sophistication composite: mean of z-scored CRT, science knowledge, numeracy, and bullshit skepticism subscales
sample_definition: Observations in the provided SAV file with at least 2 of 3 attention checks correct (NumbCorrectScreen >= 2 / filter selected) and nonmissing misperceptions and cognitive-sophistication subscales
model_specification: Simple linear regression/Pearson correlation of MisperpSc on the cognitive sophistication composite
operationalization_notes: The paper reports the claim primarily as zero-order correlations between an omnibus cognitive sophistication score and overall COVID-19 misperceptions, after preregistered exclusions for failing 2 or more attention checks. I therefore reproduced that direct bivariate test using the available preprocessed subscale scores, z-scored within the included analytic sample; BSRSc is already reverse-coded so higher values indicate greater bullshit skepticism.
reasoning: Using the article's composite cognitive sophistication measure and the provided valid-attention subset, cognitive sophistication was negatively associated with COVID-19 misperceptions, r = -0.402, corresponding to t(85) = -4.05, p = 0.000113. Thus, higher cognitive sophistication predicted lower misperception endorsement in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Mean corrected recognition index across joy-word and anger-word recognition rates (average of JOY% and ANG%).
main_predictor: Alexithymia group (TASGRP: high vs low alexithymia based on median split).
sample_definition: All rows in Vermeulen Data Submission.csv with nonmissing alexithymia group, depth, music, JOY%, and ANG% values; N = 1096.
model_specification: Mixed-ANOVA operationalization from the paper: word type joy vs anger as a within-subject factor and depth of processing, music condition, and alexithymia group as between-subject factors; the reported statistic is the Type III/effect-coded between-subjects main effect of alexithymia group, computed equivalently on each participant's mean of joy and anger recognition indices.
controls: Depth of processing and music condition were included as factorial between-subjects factors; no continuous covariates.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim as the overall main effect of high versus low alexithymia on recognition of joy and anger words, excluding neutral and disgust words, so I used the same outcome categories and alexithymia grouping.
reasoning: Using the mean corrected recognition index across joy and anger words, high alexithymia scorers recognized fewer words (M = 0.189) than low alexithymia scorers (M = 0.463). The adjusted main effect of alexithymia group was very large and significant, F(1,1088) = 303.154, p = 4.40e-60, supporting the claimed direction.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that the respondent answered 'true' to EVOLVED: human beings developed from earlier species of animals
main_predictor: Assigned latent class membership, comparing post-secular versus traditional classes
sample_definition: GSS respondents from 2006, 2008, and 2010 who were administered the science-and-religion manifest items used for class assignment, had no no-answer codes on science items, valid ordered science-attitude responses, valid Bible category excluding 'other', and valid religious-strength response; the latent class model used N = 3,003, and the chi-square test included only assigned post-secular and traditional respondents (N = 1,917).
model_specification: Three-class categorical latent class analysis was fit by maximum-likelihood EM using the paper's manifest science knowledge, science attitude, Bible-view, and religious-strength items; respondents were assigned to their modal posterior class. The main test was a Pearson 2 x 2 chi-square test of evolution response by post-secular versus traditional assigned class, without continuity correction.
operationalization_notes: The paper’s claim is a descriptive comparison of the manifest evolution item across latent classes, so I reproduced the class-construction approach with the same types of manifest variables and tested the focal two-class difference in the binary evolution response. Science knowledge items were coded as scientifically correct versus otherwise, retaining 'don't know' as incorrect; attitudes and religion items were treated as categorical indicators in the LCA.
reasoning: After assigning respondents to a three-class latent class model, 26 of 671 post-secular respondents (3.9%) versus 399 of 1,246 traditional respondents (32.0%) answered that humans evolved from earlier animals. A Pearson chi-square test comparing these two assigned classes was significant, χ²(1, N = 1,917) = 200.26, p = 1.83e-45, supporting the claim that post-secular respondents were less likely than traditional respondents to give the evolution response.

dependent_variable: Mug trendiness index: mean of ratings for trendy, modern, and urban (V18-V20)
main_predictor: Display table surface condition: glass table versus wood table
sample_definition: Rows in Zhu_Replication.csv with valid table assignment and valid V18-V20 ratings; the Qualtrics header row was excluded. The prompt was the interdependent family/friends event writing task; N = 69.
model_specification: Independent-samples pooled-variance t test comparing mean trendiness index for glass-table versus wood-table conditions; statistic is for glass minus wood.
operationalization_notes: The paper's Experiment 1 tested the claim for interdependents using the neutral mug and a trendiness index formed from trendy, modern, and urban items, so I used the same outcome and compared the two table-surface conditions within the available interdependent-prime replication dataset.
reasoning: Using the trendiness index averaged over trendy, modern, and urban ratings, glass-table respondents rated the mug descriptively less trendy (M = 5.10, n = 34) than wood-table respondents (M = 5.47, n = 35). The independent-samples t test for the hypothesized glass > wood assimilation effect was t(67) = -1.31, one-tailed p = .903, so the data do not support the claimed directional effect.

dependent_variable: Participant-level percentage of utilitarian responses across the two moral acceptability scenarios, coded as morally acceptable = utilitarian response.
main_predictor: Mortality salience condition, coded death salience versus pain salience.
sample_definition: Consented and completed observations passing the attention check case-insensitively and coded as having a satisfactory manipulation response; 2 unsatisfactory responses were excluded, leaving N = 129.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares / independent-samples t-test comparing mean utilitarian-response percentage between death-salience and pain-salience groups; the reported t is for the death-minus-pain contrast.
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary test compares Death versus Pain salience on the frequency of utilitarian responses to conflict moral scenarios. The available dataset contains two binary moral acceptability items, so I averaged their utilitarian-response codings within participant and tested the randomized salience contrast.
reasoning: In the final analytic sample, participants in the death-salience condition gave slightly more utilitarian responses on average (87.90%) than those in the pain-salience condition (85.82%). This difference was not statistically significant, t(127) = 0.43, p = .670, so the dataset does not support the claim that thinking about death makes people less utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time on interpersonal obstacle-prime/interpersonal instrumental-behavior-target lexical-decision trials; higher latency indicates weaker obstacle-behavior association
main_predictor: Mental contrasting condition versus combined reverse-contrasting and irrelevant-content control conditions, evaluated at low expectations of success
sample_definition: Study 1 observations with raw contrasting data and lexical-decision latency data; correct lexical-decision trials with latency between 250 and 3000 ms were averaged, and participants were included if they had nonmissing interpersonal association latency, interpersonal behavior accessibility latency, condition, and interpersonal expectation data (N = 323).
model_specification: OLS regression: mean interpersonal association latency predicted by mental-contrasting indicator, expectation of success centered at the lowest observed value (2), their interaction, and mean interpersonal behavior accessibility latency; the reported t test is the mental-contrasting coefficient, i.e. the condition contrast at low expectations.
controls: Mean latency on interpersonal behavior accessibility trials with unrelated primes
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 1 directly tested the claim using the elaborated interpersonal concern and adjusted association latencies for mere accessibility of the behavior. I operationalized the low-expectation part of the claim as the planned mental-contrasting-versus-control contrast at the lowest observed expectation value in this dataset.
reasoning: In an OLS model predicting interpersonal obstacle-behavior association latency, the planned contrast for mental contrasting versus the combined control conditions at the lowest observed expectation value (2 on the 1-7 scale) was not significant, t(318) = -0.315, p = 0.753. Because lower latency indicates stronger associations, the negative coefficient (about -22 ms) was not in the predicted direction of weaker associations under mental contrasting with low expectations.

dependent_variable: s - x_l, the dictator's actual recipient share minus the recipient's libertarian entitlement share
main_predictor: comparison to the libertarian-principle prediction x_l in the dictator-worse treatment
sample_definition: Cleaned data; dictator observations with non-missing s and x in the DW treatment, defined by dictator piece rate 150 and recipient/partner piece rate 200 (N = 27; Wilcoxon calculation discards 9 exact zero differences).
model_specification: One-sample paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test of s - x_l against 0, using the one-sided alternative that dictators give less than the libertarian prediction.
operationalization_notes: The paper defines the libertarian principle as giving the recipient the share x_l equal to the recipient's monetary contribution divided by total surplus, and uses signed-rank tests of s = x_l for justice-principle fit. I therefore tested whether observed DW dictator transfers deviate below x_l using the cleaned analysis variables s and x.
reasoning: In the DW dictator observations, the actual share given to the recipient was generally below the recipient's libertarian entitlement share: median(s - x_l) = -0.0651. A one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test rejected the libertarian prediction s = x_l in the direction s < x_l, z = -3.376, p = 0.00037, so the libertarian principle does not account for observed DW behavior.

dependent_variable: Diagnosed hypertension status, coded as 1 minus the underdiagnosed indicator
main_predictor: Years of formal education
sample_definition: Hypertensive adults in the cleaned IFLS 2007 analysis dataset with poor_health == 1 and complete data on model variables
model_specification: Probit regression; reported statistic is the z test for the average marginal effect of education
controls: Log per-capita expenditures, time preference category, risk preference category, travel time to health center, female sex, age, and age squared
operationalization_notes: The paper tests disease detection using split-sample probit models by general health status; I followed that approach and used the poor-general-health subsample because the target claim is explicitly conditional on poor general health.
reasoning: In a probit model restricted to respondents in poor general health, the average marginal effect of education on being diagnosed rather than under-diagnosed was positive (0.0125 per additional year of education) and statistically significant, z = 2.54, p = 0.011, N = 756. This supports the claim that among poorly healthy hypertensive respondents, more education is associated with a higher probability of diagnosis.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological judgments (inappropriate/rejecting harm responses) across the 20 personal moral dilemma trials in the main task
main_predictor: Experimental condition: social observation/experimental group versus control group
sample_definition: Participants in the provided dataset with a valid condition code and non-missing responses on all 20 personal moral dilemma trials in the main task; n = 156 (78 observed/experimental, 78 control)
model_specification: Welch independent-samples t-test comparing participant-level personal-moral-dilemma deontological-response proportions between the observed/experimental and control groups
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies personal moral dilemmas as the key setting where social observation should promote deontological judgment; therefore I computed each participant's proportion of deontological responses on the personal moral dilemma trials and compared conditions directly. Condition coding followed the dataset codebook (1 = control, 2 = experimental/social observation).
reasoning: Using the provided data, the observed/social-observation group had a slightly higher proportion of deontological responses in personal moral dilemmas (M = 0.649, SD = 0.156, n = 78) than the control group (M = 0.629, SD = 0.160, n = 78), but this difference was not statistically significant, Welch t(153.89) = 0.784, p = 0.434. Thus, this operationalization does not provide clear support for the claimed increase.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (5-point COVID-19 concern/anxiety item)
main_predictor: female indicator (1=female, 0=male)
sample_definition: All respondents in data_0948.csv living in Germany with binary gender coded as female=0 or 1 and nonmissing mh_anxiety_1; gender=3/nonbinary or missing female indicator excluded.
model_specification: Unweighted independent-samples t test comparing mean mh_anxiety_1 between women and men, equivalent to OLS mh_anxiety_1 ~ female with no covariates.
operationalization_notes: The paper’s claim concerns a gender difference in concern/worry about COVID-19; I operationalized this with the available 5-point anxiety/concern item and the provided female indicator, matching the paper’s descriptive gender-comparison approach for Likert-scale concern items.
reasoning: Using the 5-point mh_anxiety_1 concern/anxiety item, women scored higher (M=3.075, n=4933) than men (M=2.890, n=5138). The independent-samples t test was significant, t(10069)=8.253, p=1.74e-16, supporting the claim that women were more concerned than men.

dependent_variable: County-level percentage-point change in the share of residents staying at home, averaged over March 19-28, 2020 relative to the same weekdays 28 days earlier (February 20-29, 2020).
main_predictor: County 2016 Trump vote share (Trump votes divided by total votes).
sample_definition: U.S. county observations with nonmissing BTS mobility data for the baseline and March 19-28, 2020 periods and nonmissing county political, socioeconomic, demographic, industry, rurality, and state variables; N = 3114 counties.
model_specification: Cross-sectional ordinary least squares regression of change in percent staying home on Trump vote share, covariates, and state fixed effects; the reported statistic is the conventional t test for the Trump share coefficient.
controls: Income per capita; percent male, Black, Hispanic, college educated; employment percentages in retail, transportation, and health/education/social services; percent rural; age-composition percentages through age 75-84 with age 85+ omitted as the reference composition category; and state fixed effects.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested county-level social distancing using mobility changes and adjusted OLS with state fixed effects and sociodemographic/labor-market/rurality controls. I used the available BTS mobility data to operationalize social distancing as the increase in the share staying home during the paper's March 19-28 target window relative to matched pre-COVID weekdays.
reasoning: In the adjusted county-level OLS model, Trump 2016 vote share was negatively associated with the March 19-28 increase in the percentage of residents staying home (coefficient = -1.76 percentage points for a 0-to-1 increase in Trump share), t(3041) = -4.70, p = 2.72e-06. Because a smaller increase in staying home indicates less social distancing, this supports the claim that more Republican-oriented counties engaged in reduced social distancing.

dependent_variable: Log-transformed social distancing compliance scale (soc_dist_log), with higher scores indicating greater compliance
main_predictor: Political conservatism scale (pol; average of conservative identification, reverse-scored liberal identification, and Republican preference items)
sample_definition: All 322 observations in the cleaned final dataset with complete social distancing and political conservatism scores; the final file contains participants marked complete and attention-check passed.
model_specification: Ordinary least squares linear regression of soc_dist_log on political conservatism; the t statistic is for the conservatism slope.
operationalization_notes: The paper's key behavioral claim concerns the total inverse relationship between conservatism and social distancing. I used the provided cleaned scale variables and the log-transformed social-distancing outcome, consistent with the paper's handling of negative skew in social-distancing scores.
reasoning: In a simple OLS regression, greater political conservatism significantly predicted lower transformed social-distancing compliance, b = -0.0286, t(320) = -3.82, p = 0.000158. This supports the claimed inverse association between conservatism and compliance with social-distancing behaviors.

dependent_variable: Standardized composite of fifth-grade reading and mathematics IRT scale scores (mean of z-scored X7RSCALK5 and X7MSCALK5)
main_predictor: Standardized composite of teacher-reported externalizing and internalizing problems (mean of z-scored X7TCHEXT and X7TCHINT)
sample_definition: Children classified as ELL/language-minority using X12LANGST = 1, with nonmissing current achievement, social-emotional problem measures, prior achievement composite, and covariates; invalid negative missing codes were excluded.
model_specification: OLS regression of the achievement composite on the social-emotional-problems composite, with standard errors clustered by school (S7_ID); the reported test is the t test for the social-emotional-problems coefficient.
controls: Prior achievement composite from X6RSCALK5 and X6MSCALK5, SES (X12SESL), child race/ethnicity, grade level, school type, school enrollment, school racial/ethnic composition, and school free-meal composition.
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's SEM measurement approach, I represented Academic Achievement with reading and mathematics test scores and Social-Emotional Problems with internalizing and externalizing behavior scales, then tested their adjusted association among ELL/language-minority children.
reasoning: In an ELL/language-minority subsample, the coefficient for the social-emotional-problems composite was negative in predicting the achievement composite (b = -0.0296), with a school-cluster-robust t(817) = -2.47, p = .0136. Thus, children with more social-emotional problems had lower achievement, equivalently fewer problems were linked to higher achievement.

dependent_variable: Mean of SocGood_Artis, SocGood_Green, SocGood_Food, and SocGood_Medtech ratings (1 = great harm, 5 = great good)
main_predictor: Firm motive condition, tested as for-profit (condition 3) versus the average of non-profit (condition 1) and unspecified motive (condition 2)
sample_definition: Completed respondents in the Study 3 dataset with valid condition assignment and nonmissing societal-good ratings for the four scenarios (N = 365)
model_specification: OLS one-way model of respondent-level mean societal-good rating on the three-level motive condition, with a planned contrast comparing for-profit to the average of the two other motive conditions
operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 methods identify societal good as the outcome most directly tied to this claim and use the three-group between-subjects motive manipulation across four scenarios. Averaging the four repeated societal-good items per respondent and testing a planned for-profit-versus-no-explicit-profit contrast directly operationalizes the directional claim.
reasoning: In a planned contrast on the average societal-good rating across the four organization scenarios, the for-profit condition had lower perceived societal good (M = 3.746) than the average of the non-profit and unspecified conditions (M = 4.198). The contrast was statistically significant, t(362) = -7.91, p = 3.17e-14, supporting the claim that a profit motive reduced perceived societal good.

operationalization_notes: The paper tested full mediation by comparing a model without direct paths from operant leadership to OCB against a model with those direct paths, controlling for supervisor tenure and organizational level. I operationalized the same logic with observed scale composites and tested whether direct operant-leadership effects remain after accounting for trust and controls.
reasoning: In an OLS partial-mediation test, adding the four operant-leadership composites to a model already containing trust and the two controls significantly improved prediction of supervisor-rated OCB, F(4,159)=24.05, p=1.42e-15. dependent_variable: Natural log of mean mortality rate, computed as the mean slope of the LOWESS-smoothed daily COVID-19 deaths curve during the ascending phase up to 8 June 2020

I used the paper's country sample and outcome definition, recomputing the mortality slope from the daily death data with LOWESS smoothing, and tested the direct bivariate predictive relationship for the claim.
reasoning: In a univariable OLS regression among the 37 countries in the paper sample, international arrivals in 2018 positively predicted log mean mortality-slope severity (slope = 0.0439 per 1 million arrivals), t(35) = 5.35, p = 5.59e-06. dependent_variable: Mean number of points contributed to the shared account

operationalization_notes: Following the Study 1 operationalization, the two bonus distributions with possible returns below the required individual contribution at the 300-point threshold, (0,1200) and (200,1000), were classified as losses-and-gains, while the certain 600 bonus and (400,800) distribution were classified as the no-variance/gains-only comparison.

dependent_variable: HP-detrended aggregate intercounty migration rate

model_specification: OLS time-series regression with an intercept; migration rate was detrended with a Hodrick-Prescott filter, and monthly employment gaps were computed as log employment relative to an HP trend and averaged from April of the prior year through March of the migration year.
operationalization_notes: This follows the paper's aggregate CPS time-series test of whether geographic dispersion in local economic conditions explains migration cyclicality, using employment-gap dispersion as the local-conditions measure.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of the HP-detrended aggregate intercounty migration rate on the standardized dispersion of state employment gaps, controlling for the standardized national employment gap, the dispersion coefficient was not statistically different from zero, t(51) = -0.537, p = 0.594. This supports the claim that dispersion in local conditions is not significantly related to migration in this specification.

dependent_variable: Signed anger-perception latency composite in seconds, where higher scores indicate anger lasting longer or appearing sooner
main_predictor: Target age for White faces (old vs young, within participant)
sample_definition: Participants with complete 48-trial experimental data were included (N=56); individual trials with latency <=0 ms or >17000 ms were excluded as outside the 17-second movie duration; only White-face trials from the four anger-relevant transitions were analyzed.

operationalization_notes: The paper analyzed emotion-change response latencies with within-subject target age and race factors. To test the specific claim that anger both lasted longer and appeared sooner on old than young White faces with one statistic, I combined all four anger-relevant transitions after sign-coding latencies so the directional anger-bias interpretation was consistent across onset and offset trials.
reasoning: I formed a participant-level signed anger-perception composite for White faces, coding angry-to-happy and angry-to-neutral latencies positively so higher values mean anger lasted longer, and happy-to-angry and neutral-to-angry latencies negatively so higher values mean anger appeared sooner. Old White faces had a higher composite than young White faces by 0.936 signed seconds, t(55)=3.760, p=0.000413, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator for following social distancing: response >= 6 on the 1-7 item 'I keep my distance from other people as much as possible' (keep_distance).

operationalization_notes: The paper summarized preventive behaviors by comparing the proportion endorsing each behavior across gender; I used the dataset's direct social-distancing item, dichotomized high adherence as responses 6 or 7 on the 1-7 frequency scale.
reasoning: In a 2x2 Pearson chi-square test, men were less likely than women to report following social distancing by keeping distance from other people (1229/2103 = 58.4% for men vs. 1285/1771 = 72.6% for women), χ²(1, N=3874)=84.11, p=4.69e-20. This supports the claim that men have a lower likelihood of following social distancing.

dependent_variable: Prefs_1: preference/criticality of part-time work for future employment (1 = doesn't matter, 5 = must have)

model_specification: Ward hierarchical clustering on the 24 desire items to specify three clusters, followed by k-means initialized from the Ward centroids; then one-way ANOVA of part-time preference by cluster profile.
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim with a one-way ANOVA comparing the part-time preferred work characteristic across the three clusters, so I recreated the three-profile solution from the 24 desire items and used the same omnibus ANOVA framework on the part-time item.
reasoning: Using the paper's approach of deriving three desire-based profiles and comparing the part-time work preference item across profiles, the one-way ANOVA was not significant, F(2, 768) = 0.046, p = 0.955. The mean part-time preference scores were nearly identical across the three derived profiles (about 2.74 to 2.77 on the 1-5 scale), so this analysis does not support meaningful variation by profile.

dependent_variable: Death among SARS-CoV-2 positive cases, coded from fecha_def not equal to 9999-99-99

dependent_variable: Perceived stress score at follow-up

operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim as the actor effect of baseline optimism on follow-up perceived stress in an APIM for couples, so I used the scored optimism and stress variables and modeled both partners in long format while accounting for dyadic nonindependence.
reasoning: Using an APIM-style GEE model that accounted for clustering within 101 couples, actor optimism negatively predicted the actor's perceived stress, z = -8.85, p = 8.82e-19. Thus, more optimistic individuals reported lower stress levels than less optimistic individuals in this dataset.

dependent_variable: T2 negative affect, computed as the sum of the 10 PANAS negative-affect items

sample_definition: Longitudinal Study 3 observations with a baseline row on 2021-01-18 and a follow-up row from 2021-01-25 to 2021-01-28; excluded the dummy empty participant ID, duplicate wave records after retaining the earliest session per participant, failed instructed attention_check1 at either wave, and cases missing the predictor, covariate, or all 10 negative-affect items

operationalization_notes: The paper's Study 3 tested whether T1 realistic and symbolic threat predicted criterion outcomes one week later in one SEM with the two threats covaried. For the single target outcome, this was operationalized as the equivalent observed-variable regression for negative affect, using scale composites.

dependent_variable: Whether the participant chose to work together / make hot dogs (Cooperate = 1) rather than work alone

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns more participants attempting risky coordination when payoffs were common knowledge than when knowledge was private or merely shared. I therefore used the butcher-baker coordination decision as the outcome and collapsed the private, secondary, and tertiary knowledge conditions into a single non-common comparison group, following the paper's exclusion of participants who failed payoff comprehension checks.
reasoning: After exclusions, 47 of 67 participants (70.1%) in the common-knowledge condition attempted coordination, compared with 83 of 180 participants (46.1%) in the private/shared-knowledge conditions combined. A Pearson chi-square test for common versus non-common knowledge was significant, chi2(1, N = 247) = 11.32, p = 0.00077, supporting higher risky coordination under common knowledge.

dependent_variable: Intention to support the nonprofit composite, averaged from the three intention items (financial contribution, volunteering, recommendation)
main_predictor: Centered relational fit × centered sponsor-sponsee similarity, tested as an indirect effect through clarity of nonprofit positioning
sample_definition: All finished, consenting respondents with complete data on fit, similarity, clarity of positioning, attitude toward sponsorship, intention to support, trustworthiness, and condition/brand variables from the provided dataset (N = 907)
model_specification: Composite-score path analysis approximating the paper’s Model B: OLS regression of clarity of nonprofit positioning on centered fit, centered similarity, their interaction, sponsor trustworthiness, and nonprofit brand; OLS regression of intention to support on clarity of nonprofit positioning and attitude toward sponsorship; Sobel z test for the product of the FIT × SIM -> clarity path and the clarity -> intention path, using HC3 robust standard errors
controls: Sponsor trustworthiness and nonprofit brand in the clarity equation; attitude toward sponsorship included alongside clarity in the intention equation
operationalization_notes: The paper tested this claim as a moderated mediation in which fit × similarity affected intention to support primarily through clarity of positioning. I used the same measured constructs as scale means and tested the specific FIT × SIM -> clarity -> intention indirect path rather than copying the SEM results reported in the article.
reasoning: Using complete cases, the composite-scale mediated-moderation test found a positive indirect effect of relational fit × similarity on intention to support via clarity of nonprofit positioning: a = 0.0554 for FIT × SIM predicting clarity and b = 0.3330 for clarity predicting intention, giving indirect effect = 0.0184 and Sobel z = 2.05, p = .040. This supports the claim that fit and similarity jointly affected participants’ intention to support the nonprofit.

dependent_variable: Subject-level SNARC regression weight: slope from regressing dRT (median RT for right responses minus median RT for left responses) on digit magnitude.

model_specification: Paired-samples t-test comparing each participant's verbal-load SNARC slope with their baseline SNARC slope after computing median RTs by digit and response side and fitting per-participant dRT ~ digit regressions.
operationalization_notes: The paper defined the SNARC effect via the Fias et al. regression approach on median RT differences; comparing the verbal-load slope to the same participants' baseline slope directly tests whether verbal load abolished/reduced the parity-judgment SNARC effect.

dependent_variable: Mean d-prime sensitivity in grammaticality judgments across the 12 test blocks

operationalization_notes: The paper's primary test of the claim compared overall mean d-prime values between the SS and random groups, so I operationalized learning performance as participant mean d-prime over all test blocks and tested the between-group condition effect directly.
reasoning: Using participant-level mean d-prime across the 12 test blocks, the starting-small group had a slightly higher mean sensitivity than the random group (M = 0.051 vs. -0.008), but the independent-samples t-test was not significant, t(83) = 0.738, p = 0.463. Thus, these data do not provide evidence that the SS group outperformed the random group.

Thus the estimate is in the originally claimed positive direction, but this analysis does not provide conventional evidence for the association.

dependent_variable: Binary monthly arrest indicator coded 1 for one or more arrests in the month and 0 otherwise
main_predictor: Within-person divorce status: monthly divorced indicator centered by respondent, compared with married months as the reference state
sample_definition: Respondents in the NLSY97 monthly event-history data from 1997-2009 who were ever married, had an arrest history according to the monthly arrest history variables, had nonmissing parental education, and had valid post-age-14 monthly relationship/arrest observations; widowed/invalid relationship months were excluded. The analysis used 827 persons and 124,436 person-months.
model_specification: Binomial logistic generalized estimating equation with exchangeable working correlation by respondent and robust standard errors; relationship-state variables were decomposed into within-person deviations and between-person means.
controls: Within-person legal separation and single indicators; between-person mean divorce, separation, and single proportions; age and age squared; male; Black; household size; intact family structure; disadvantage; parental education; at-risk behavior score; ever incarcerated.
operationalization_notes: The paper identifies the within-individual divorce effect among ever-married, ever-arrested respondents as the test most directly tied to the claim. I used the same monthly arrest outcome and relationship-state decomposition, implementing it as a population-averaged clustered logistic GEE on the original data.
reasoning: In a population-averaged logistic model of 124,436 person-months from 827 ever-married respondents with an arrest history, the within-person divorce indicator had a positive coefficient (b = 0.465, robust SE = 0.212), z = 2.19, p = 0.028. Thus, months in which a respondent was divorced had significantly higher odds of arrest than months in which that same respondent was married, net of covariates.

dependent_variable: Binary autism identification status, represented by state-by-race counts of students identified with autism versus not identified with autism
main_predictor: State indicator for Ohio versus California
sample_definition: All 2014 public-school students represented in the California and Ohio state-by-race enrollment totals for the seven reported race/ethnicity groups; autism counts used the IDEA Total, Age 6-21 rows for the same state-by-race groups.
model_specification: Grouped binomial logistic regression with logit link using autism counts and non-autism enrollment counts in 14 state-by-race cells; Wald z test of the Ohio state coefficient.
controls: Categorical race/ethnicity indicators for American Indian or Alaska Native, Asian, Black or African American, Hispanic/Latino, Native Hawaiian or Other Pacific Islander, Two or More Races, and White.
operationalization_notes: The paper's methods use logistic regression on aggregated count data, weighted by group counts, and use California as the state reference. I therefore compared Ohio to California directly while adjusting for race composition across the seven reporting categories.
reasoning: In a race-adjusted grouped logistic regression comparing California and Ohio, the Ohio coefficient was negative (log-odds = -0.3091; OR = 0.734), with z = -34.42 and p = 1.40e-259. Thus, autism identification odds were significantly lower in Ohio than in California in this operationalization.

dependent_variable: Group decision correctness (group_jar == true_jar)
main_predictor: Voting institution (Majority / SuperMajority / Unanimity)
sample_definition: All 352 unique group-round decisions across all 11 deliberation sessions (3 Majority, 5 SuperMajority, 3 Unanimity), aggregated from the player-level dataset
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on a 3×2 contingency table (institution × correct)
operationalization_notes: The dataset contains only deliberation sessions. The most direct test of whether deliberation diminishes institutional differences is whether group outcomes still vary across institutions when deliberation is allowed. I aggregated to one observation per group-round (the unit at which institutions operate) and tested whether the correct-decision rate depends on institution.
reasoning: Across 352 group-round decisions made under deliberation, the share of groups that correctly identified the true jar differed sharply by institution (Majority 82.3%, SuperMajority 63.8%, Unanimity 43.8%). A chi-square test of independence yields χ²(2)=30.73, p≈2.1e-7, indicating that institutional differences in group accuracy remain very large despite deliberation, contradicting the claim that deliberation diminishes institutional differences.

dependent_variable: Group-level mean realized auction (market clearing) price
main_predictor: Uniform-price auction price vs. fixed-price offering benchmark (=1, the lowest asset value, B-FG fixed-price equilibrium)
sample_definition: All 40 experimental groups in fullsample_analysis.csv (uniform-price auction sessions, all rounds)
model_specification: One-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test (one-sided, greater), normal approximation for z
operationalization_notes: The raw dataset contains only uniform-price auction sessions; the comparison to 'fixed price offerings' is therefore against the theoretical B-FG fixed-price benchmark. Under the B-FG model with asset values uniformly drawn from {1,2,3,4}, the optimal fixed-price offering yields revenue equal to the lowest type value (=1). I test whether realized uniform-auction prices exceed this benchmark using the group-level price averages.
reasoning: A one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test of group-level mean realized uniform-price auction prices (mean=1.89, n=40 groups) against the Biais & Faugeron-Grouzet fixed-price benchmark of 1 (the lowest possible asset value, which is the B-FG fixed-price equilibrium price) yields W=773, z=4.88, p<0.001 (one-sided). Realized auction prices significantly exceed the fixed-price benchmark, consistent with the paper's claim that uniform-price auctions raise more revenue than fixed-price offerings.

dependent_variable: Intended vote for Barack Obama (1) vs Donald Trump (0) in the Obama–Trump hypothetical matchup (h0clean)
main_predictor: Conception risk across the menstrual cycle (oddconcept, probability of conception based on cycle day)
sample_definition: Female participants who were not pregnant, not using hormonal birth control, reported regular cycles, and reported no chronic health problems affecting fertility; restricted to those choosing Obama or Trump (excluded 'different candidate'/'not sure')
model_specification: Binary logistic regression: P(Obama) = logit^-1(b0 + b1*oddconcept)
operationalization_notes: Conception risk (oddconcept) and the Obama-vs-Republican matchup variable (h0clean, with Q20 being Obama vs Trump) were the cleaned variables provided in the dataset. Standard menstrual-cycle exclusions (hormonal contraception, irregular cycles, pregnancy, fertility-affecting chronic illness) were applied to isolate naturally cycling women, as is convention in this literature.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of intended Obama vote (vs Trump, h0clean) on conception risk (oddconcept) among naturally-cycling, non-pregnant, regularly-menstruating women not on hormonal contraception, the coefficient on conception risk was -1.54 (z = -0.31, p = .76, N = 304). The estimate is small, in the opposite direction to the claim, and not statistically significant, providing no support for the claim that higher conception risk increases the probability of intending to vote for Obama.

dependent_variable: Google Trends search volume for 'panic buying' (panicbuying)
main_predictor: Cumulative confirmed COVID-19 cases (infected)
sample_definition: Daily observations from US, UK, Canada, and Australia (New Zealand excluded per claim scope); rows with missing values dropped
model_specification: OLS regression: panicbuying ~ infected + country fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Only replicate.csv contains the panel needed to test the claim across the four countries. Panic buying is the outcome explicitly named in the claim and available in the data; cumulative confirmed cases operationalize 'prevalence rates'. Country FE absorb cross-country baseline differences in search volume.
reasoning: Pooled OLS of Google Trends panic-buying search volume on cumulative confirmed COVID-19 cases with country fixed effects yields a significantly NEGATIVE coefficient (b=-4.47e-06, t(711)=-4.32, p<.001, n=716). dependent_variable: Procedural justice (mean of pj1-pj7)

dependent_variable: PSS-10 average stress score (pss10_avg)

model_specification: Pearson correlation / equivalent simple OLS regression
operationalization_notes: trust_countrymeasure scale: 0=too little, 5=appropriate, 11=too much; absolute deviation from 5 captures disagreement with measures, so its negation captures agreement.
reasoning: Pearson correlation between agreement with containment measures (operationalized as -|trust_countrymeasure - 5|, since 5='appropriate' indicates agreement and deviations indicate disagreement that measures are too little/too much) and PSS-10 stress score yielded r = -0.153, t(1077) = -5.09, p < .001. Greater agreement is associated with lower stress, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Binary trust choice in the trust game (DV=1 'Option L' coded as trust)

dependent_variable: AVERAGE of S1_likely, S1_quality, S1_purchase (product desirability)

Simple effects: under low clarity (Conflicting), bimodal (M=4.98) was preferred over unimodal (M=4.33; diff=0.65), whereas under high clarity (Clear), the bimodal-unimodal difference was negligible (4.60 vs 4.53). This matches the claim that low self-concept clarity increases preference for bimodally-rated products.

The omnibus F provides a single test of the emotion→behavior segment of the mediation model.
reasoning: Regressing revenge on anger and sympathy yielded a significant overall model, F(2,1069)=41.04, p<.001, R²=.07; anger independently predicted revenge (b=0.57, t=8.76, p<.001) while sympathy did not (p=.74). This supports the claim that emotional reactions (especially anger) have independent relations with revenge-related behaviors, the core emotion→behavior link in the proposed cognition–emotion–behavior chain.

dependent_variable: MisperpSc (COVID-19 misperceptions composite)

dependent_variable: Sum of joy-word and anger-word hits (correct recognitions) at recognition test

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns recognition of joy and anger words by alexithymia level; I combined joy and anger hits into one outcome and compared low vs high alexithymia groups via a Welch t-test to produce a single test statistic.
reasoning: High alexithymia group (TASGRP=2) recognized substantially fewer joy+anger words (M=9.38) than low alexithymia group (TASGRP=1, M=11.72); Welch's t(1075.5)=10.23, p<.001, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Trendiness rating of the mug (V18, 1-7)

dependent_variable: Mean utilitarian moral judgment across the two scenarios (proportion rated 'morally acceptable')

The data do not support the claim that mortality salience reduces utilitarian responses.

dependent_variable: ZHealthAssocM (z-scored mean association strength between health obstacles and instrumental behavior)

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the within-mental-contrasting link between expectations and obstacle–instrumental association strength. The H8 analytic dataset (filtered for valid latency-based association scores) provides the relevant variables; the simple slope of expectations within the mental contrasting condition directly tests this claim.

dependent_variable: s (share of surplus the dictator gives away)

sample_definition: Dictators (playerdictator=1) in the DW condition with lower piece rate (150 vs. partner 200); non-missing s, x

operationalization_notes: The libertarian principle predicts s = partner_endowment/total = x in the dataset. A paired nonparametric test of s vs x directly evaluates whether libertarian fairness accounts for dictators' allocations.
reasoning: In the DW subsample (dictators paid 150 vs partner 200, n=27), the proportion of surplus given away (mean s=0.377) is significantly lower than the libertarian prediction (mean x=0.498, i.e. partner's monetary-contribution share). Wilcoxon signed-rank W=8.0, p=0.00074, rejecting that observed behavior matches the libertarian principle.

dependent_variable: diagnosed (1 - underdiagnosed)
main_predictor: years of education

dependent_variable: Rate of harm-rejecting (deontological) responses on personal moral dilemmas (RH_PMD)
main_predictor: Group (observed vs. control)

reasoning: An independent-samples t-test comparing the rate of harm-rejecting (deontological) responses in personal moral dilemmas (RH_PMD) between the observed (M=0.649) and control (M=0.629) groups yielded t(154)=-0.78, p=0.43. The direction matches the claim (observed > control) but the effect is not statistically significant.

dependent_variable: County mean fraction of devices staying home (pop_home/(pop_home+pop_not_home)) averaged across days 2020-03-15 to 2020-04-30

dependent_variable: Per-participant mean self-reported sharing likelihood (1-6 scale) for true vs. false COVID-19 headlines (Avg_Real vs Avg_Fake)

dependent_variable: Binary indicator: sustained growth (annual GDP per capita growth >=2% for the 5 consecutive years starting in the survey fieldwork year)

operationalization_notes: Following the abstract's definition of sustained growth (>=2% for >=5 consecutive years) and its 'perceived impartiality' construct, I aggregated individual-level perceptions of unfair treatment (combinwt-weighted) to the country-survey level and coded sustained growth in the 5-year window starting at the survey fieldwork year. All rounds pooled for power.

main_predictor: ln(total imports from South)

dependent_variable: Mean bipolar attitude-function rating (1=utilitarian to 7=symbolic) across the four symbolic categories (items 2,3,5,8)
main_predictor: Branding condition (No Brand: Cond 1 or 2 vs. Brand Set A: Cond 3)

dependent_variable: Semester GPA

model_specification: OLS multiple regression reconstructed from the correlation matrix (path-model equivalent of SEM with SR and SD facet predicting GPA)
operationalization_notes: Only summary statistics (means, SDs, correlation matrix, N=366) are available. The SEM claim of SR predicting GPA was operationalized as the partial regression coefficient of SR on GPA controlling for SD facet, computed analytically from the correlation matrix.
reasoning: Using the published correlation matrix (N=366) from Jung et al., a regression of semester GPA on self-regulation (academic self-discipline) controlling for the self-discipline facet gives a standardized coefficient β=0.34 for self-regulation, t(363)=4.85, p<.001, consistent with the SEM claim that self-regulation positively predicts GPA while self-discipline does not (β=-0.05).

dependent_variable: Mean COVID-19 conspiracy-theory endorsement (4 items, 0-10)

operationalization_notes: The provided dataset does not contain an explicit 'sharing' item; conspiracy-theory endorsement is used as the closest available proxy for belief/dissemination, consistent with the paper's composite framing of belief and dissemination. National identification is included as a control to isolate the narcissism component, mirroring the paper's approach.
reasoning: In an OLS regression predicting mean COVID-19 conspiracy-theory endorsement from national (collective) narcissism, controlling for national identification, age, sex, and education (N=1575), collective narcissism was a strong positive predictor (b=0.554, t(1564)=22.84, p<.001). This supports the claim that higher national narcissism is associated with greater proneness to endorse/spread COVID-19 conspiracy theories.

dependent_variable: Per-participant proportion of trials on which the 'Right' face was chosen as more aggressive (across the 36 forced-choice trials)
main_predictor: Implicit fWHR/masculinity manipulation contrast (high vs. low) embedded in the paired-face stimuli; tested against the chance value of 0.5
sample_definition: Study 2 participants (Processed_Data_2.csv) who passed the data-quality check (Quality=='Yes'); n=288 of 310
model_specification: One-sample two-tailed t-test of mean proportion-Right against 0.5
operationalization_notes: The codebook only records Left/Right choices, not the per-trial mapping of which side held the high-fWHR/masculinised face. Across the 36 trials there is a systematic majority on one side (24/36 trials favour Right), consistent with the high-fWHR/masc face being placed predominantly on the right. I therefore aggregated within-participant choices and tested deviation from chance, which is the most directly claim-relevant single test available from the released data. Study 2 was used because the claim refers to both male and female faces.
reasoning: Per-participant proportion of 'Right' choices (M=0.534, SD=0.113) was significantly greater than chance (0.5), t(287)=5.10, p<.001, in Study 2. Under the operationalization that the high-fWHR/masculinised face was presented on the right (consistent with the strong directional pattern across trials), this indicates the manipulated more-aggressive face was systematically chosen at above-chance rates, supporting the directional claim that increased fWHR (and masculinity) is perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: Proposer's offered bribe / split amount (citizen_bribe in BG; a_split in UG)
main_predictor: Treatment frame (Bribery Game vs Ultimatum Game)
sample_definition: Proposer-role participants only (BG-Citizen and UG-Participant A) with non-missing offers
model_specification: Two-sided Mann–Whitney U test (non-parametric two-sample comparison)
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the average bribe amount offered, so the most direct test compares the proposers' chosen offers across the two frames. Given small samples and skewed/bounded offers, a Mann-Whitney U test is appropriate; a Welch t-test gives a consistent result (t=-2.94, p=.007).
reasoning: Mann-Whitney U comparing proposer bribe offers in the Bribery Game (n=14, mean=0.45) vs Ultimatum Game (n=16, mean=1.14) yields U=40, p=0.0023, indicating significantly lower bribe amounts in the bribery frame, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Estimated total number of taxi cabs, normalized by the maximum number seen (estimate / max_value)
main_predictor: Number of observations provided (values_seen: 1, 3, 10) — within-subject
sample_definition: All taxicab-condition estimate trials with a numeric response; 669 participants who provided estimates at all three values_seen levels
model_specification: Non-parametric Friedman test across the three within-subject conditions
operationalization_notes: The raw estimate increases with values_seen because the observed maximum increases too; the claim is about prediction magnitude given the observations, which is naturally captured by the estimate/max_value ratio used throughout the Bayesian-inference framework.
reasoning: Friedman test on the within-subject prediction-to-maximum-seen ratio across the three observation conditions (1, 3, 10 examples) yields χ²(2)=281.6, p<1e-60, N=669. Mean ratios drop monotonically (2.20, 1.36, 1.16), confirming that taxi-cab predictions become smaller (closer to the observed maximum) as more observations are provided.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total (forensic fraud measure, district-level)

sample_definition: All Afghan districts in the replication dataset with non-missing covariates (N=375)

model_specification: Person fixed-effects (within-demeaned) linear probability model with cluster-robust SE by person
controls: Indicators for cohabiting/married/separated/widowed (ref=never married not cohab), linear and quadratic month-from-age-14 time trend
operationalization_notes: The paper uses within-individual multilevel models on monthly NLSY97 data; I implemented a person FE LPM as a direct linear analog, with binary arrest as the outcome and marital-status dummies including divorced as the focal predictor.
reasoning: In a within-person (fixed-effects) linear probability model of monthly arrest on marital-status indicators (ref = never married, not cohabiting) with quadratic time trend and cluster-robust SE by person, the coefficient on being divorced is 0.00034 (SE 0.0017, t=0.20, p=0.84), n=999,441 person-months across 8,542 persons. operationalization_notes: Claim is a between-state comparison of autism identification likelihood. Used IDEA autism child counts as numerator and NCES state enrollment as denominator (consistent with the paper's logistic-regression-on-counts framework), restricted to the school-age (6-21) population.

dependent_variable: Binary indicator that respondent was arrested in a given month (1–98 arrests)
main_predictor: Time-varying indicator that respondent is currently divorced or legally separated (mar_status==3 or 4), referenced against unmarried baseline; a separate indicator for currently married is also included

reasoning: Within-individual linear-probability model with person fixed effects, age, and age^2 yields a positive coefficient for currently divorced/separated on monthly arrest probability (b=0.0051, cluster-robust z=1.65, p≈0.10) among 2,585 ever-arrested respondents (344,168 person-months). dependent_variable: Autism identification (autism count vs. rest of public school enrollment)

operationalization_notes: Claim concerns state-level odds of autism identification. Used autism child count over total public enrollment in each state as the probability of being identified with autism, then tested the OH vs CA difference via chi-square (equivalent to a single-predictor logistic regression with state as predictor).
reasoning: Ohio identified 21,213 students with autism out of 1,724,810 enrolled (1.23%), versus California's 90,541 of 6,312,161 (1.43%). A 2x2 chi-square test comparing autism vs. non-autism enrollment between Ohio and California yields χ²(1)=413.23, p<1e-90, OR(OH vs CA)=0.856, indicating autism identification is significantly less likely in Ohio than California.

dependent_variable: Group made the correct jar choice (group_jar == true_jar), 0/1 at the group-round level

operationalization_notes: Only the deliberation condition data are present in the dataset (session.config.name contains 'deliberation_*'; no chat columns but app name and configs identify this as the deliberation arm). A direct difference-in-differences vs a no-deliberation baseline is not possible with the supplied data, so the claim is tested by checking whether institutional differences in the standard outcome (correct group decision) are absent/diminished under deliberation; they are not.

Institutional differences thus remain large and highly significant under deliberation, contrary to the claim that deliberation diminishes institutional differences.

dependent_variable: Group-level average IPO market price (uniform auction revenue per share)

I therefore tested whether observed uniform-auction prices exceed the theoretical fixed-price benchmark implied by the Biais–Faugeron-Crouzet model with values in {2,3,4}, namely p = 2. Group-average price is used as the revenue proxy.

Comparing the per-group average auction price (mean = 1.887 across n=40 groups) to the theoretical fixed-price-offering benchmark of 2 (the lowest possible market value in the Biais–Faugeron-Crouzet design {2,3,4}, the standard fixed-price equilibrium price), a one-sample one-sided t-test gives t(39) = -1.06, p = 0.85. The auction prices are not significantly greater than the fixed-price benchmark, so the claim that uniform auctions raise more revenue is not corroborated by this test.

dependent_variable: Intention to vote for Barack Obama (binary; h0clean: 1 = Obama, 0 = Trump/Pence/Biden/other)

reasoning: Logistic regression of Obama-vs-other vote intention (h0clean: Obama=1) on conception risk (oddconcept) yields a negative coefficient of -8.82, z = -2.30, p = .022, N = 477. Thus in this dataset higher conception risk predicts a LOWER probability of intending to vote for Obama, the opposite of the claim.

dependent_variable: Procedural Justice (mean of pj1-pj7)
main_predictor: Perceived Racial Discrimination (mean of rd1-rd8)

A simple bivariate regression provides the most direct test of the claim.

operationalization_notes: Replication of Pfattheicher et al. (2018) trust game paradigm. HH computed per standard HEXACO-60 scoring (items 6, 12R, 18, 24R, 30R, 36, 42R, 48R, 54, 60R). Trust operationalized as choosing Option R (handing decision to Player 2). The H×Condition interaction term is the test most directly tied to the claim.
reasoning: Logistic regression of binary trust choice on mean-centered Honesty-Humility, self-uncertainty condition, and their interaction showed a non-significant interaction (b=0.091, z=0.607, p=0.544, N=843). The data do not replicate the claimed HH x self-uncertainty interaction whereby high-HH individuals shift toward distrust under uncertainty.

dependent_variable: S1_likely (likelihood of seeing the movie; primary desirability item)
main_predictor: Self-concept clarity condition (Conflicting=low vs. Clear=high) x Rating distribution (Bimodal vs. Unimodal)
sample_definition: All Usable Data sheet (after preregistered exclusions); N=376 across four between-subjects cells (CoB, CoU, ClB, ClU)

dependent_variable: Revenge intentions (mean of rv1-rv3)

dependent_variable: Mean recognition accuracy across joy and anger words ((JOYAcc+ANGAcc)/2)

A 2x2 ANOVA (TASGRP x Word) confirmed a significant main effect of TASGRP with no interaction (p=.41).

main_predictor: Religio-scientific group (traditional vs post-secular), proxy from BIBLE, CONSCI, SCISTUDY
sample_definition: 2006 GSS respondents with valid EVOLVED and group classification as traditional or post-secular
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2x2 group x EVOLVED table
operationalization_notes: The paper defines groups via LCA which I cannot replicate exactly without item lists; I proxied 'traditional' as biblical-literalists (BIBLE=1) not expressing high confidence in science, and 'post-secular' as biblical-literalists with high confidence in scientific community (CONSCI=1) or positive view that science does more good than harm (SCISTUDY=1). 2006 GSS was used because it contains the science module with EVOLVED.

main_predictor: Table surface condition (glass vs wood)

operationalization_notes: Claim specifies interdependents evaluating a neutral product (mug) as more trendy on glass vs wood; tested directly with t-test on V18 by condition (V16/V17).

dependent_variable: ZHealthAssocM (z-scored mean response latency to obstacle->instrumental-behavior pairings)
main_predictor: HealthExp_c (mean-centered expectations of success in the health domain)
sample_definition: Participants in the mental contrasting condition (Cond1=0, the largest n=119 cell; 117 with no missing on covariates), from the H8 analytic dataset (which already filters out outliers on association/access RTs).

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the within-MC expectation->association link. Following standard practice in this paradigm, I used the obstacle->instrumental RT (HealthAssocM) as the DV and controlled for a non-critical access RT baseline. A directional interpretation (low exp -> weaker association) requires a significant positive slope on HealthExp_c within MC; the slope was effectively zero.
reasoning: Within the mental contrasting condition, the simple slope of centered health expectations on the obstacle-instrumental association RT (ZHealthAssocM), controlling for general accessibility RT (ZHealthAccessM), was b=0.010, t(114)=0.27, p=0.79. The expectation x condition interaction in the full model was also non-significant (t=-0.12, p=0.91). Hence the data do not support the claim that mental contrasting paired with low expectations produces weaker obstacle-instrumental associations.

dependent_variable: Dictator's share of total endowment, x, minus libertarian prediction (own earnings/total earnings)

operationalization_notes: Libertarian principle implies each agent keeps what they earned, so the predicted dictator share equals playerendowment/grouptotal_endowment. The claim is tested by comparing observed x to this prediction within the DW treatment.

A one-sample t-test of x − libertarian = 0 gives t(26)=-0.04, p=0.97 (Wilcoxon p=0.38). The data fail to reject the libertarian benchmark, which contradicts the claim that libertarianism cannot account for observed behavior under DW.

dependent_variable: Diagnosed with hypertension (1 - underdiagnosed)

operationalization_notes: The claim refers specifically to a conditional effect in the poor-health subgroup; I estimated a probit of being diagnosed on education plus standard demographic and preference controls included in the dataset, restricted to that subgroup.

dependent_variable: Proportion of harm-rejecting (deontological) responses across dilemma types (RH_PMD, RH_NMD, RH_CMD)

operationalization_notes: Outcome chosen so that higher = less social distancing (mirror of % staying home). April 2020 chosen as core first-wave COVID month. Controls follow the ACS variables provided in county_variables.csv; state FE per the abstract's mention of state fixed effects.

dependent_variable: soc_dist composite (mean of soc_dist_1..4)

dependent_variable: Average of X7RSCALK5 (reading IRT) and X7MSCALK5 (math IRT) achievement scores
main_predictor: Composite social-emotional problems score: mean of z-scored X7TCHEXT, X7TCHINT, PEERVIC (mean of C7TEASED/LIESABT/PUSHCH/EXCLDCH) and SOCIALANX (mean of C7WRYTHK/WRYDTLK/AFRDNTLK)

dependent_variable: Mean SocGood rating across the 4 hypothetical organizations (Artis, Green, Food, Medtech), 1=great harm to 5=great good
main_predictor: Condition label: for-profit (=3) vs. non-profit (=1)

model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test comparing for-profit vs non-profit on mean SocGood
operationalization_notes: Study 3 is the experiment most directly testing the claim (for-profit vs non-profit labeling). I averaged the SocGood item across the four target organizations to form a single DV, and compared the two profit-label conditions using a Welch t-test.
reasoning: Averaging the SocGood ratings across the four hypothetical organizations in Study 3, for-profit-labeled firms were rated as accomplishing significantly less societal good (M=3.75) than non-profit-labeled firms (M=4.31), Welch t(223.8) = -8.61, p < .001.
