operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the simple within-condition contrast for the abstract-sound group reported in the paper as part of the Sound x Information Type interaction follow-up. Using the included-cases filter matches the paper's reported cell means (5.14 vs. 2.98).
reasoning: Within the abstract-sound condition (group 5, filter==1, n=16), a paired-samples t-test comparing the 4.5-star toaster (positive aggregated info; M=5.14) vs. the 2.5-star toaster (positive individualized info; M=2.98) yields t(15)=7.86, p<.001. This strongly supports the claim that participants who listened to the abstract sound favored the toaster with positive aggregated information.

dependent_variable: GDP per capita (national affluence)
main_predictor: Imports from the South (totalimport, scaled to USD billions)
sample_definition: 18 OECD countries, 1970-2003, excluding observations with missing values; N = 468 country-years
model_specification: OLS with two-way fixed effects (country dummies and 5-year period dummies), cluster-robust standard errors by country
controls: Exports to the South, unemployment rate, country fixed effects, 5-year period fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's indirect-effects equation (Model 4 in Table 2) where national affluence is regressed on the trade variables and unemployment with country and period fixed effects. The 'totalimport' variable in northsouth_NoNA.xlsx corresponds to imports from the global South per the dataset's north/south categorization.
reasoning: In a two-way fixed-effects regression of GDP per capita (national affluence, in $000s) on imports from the South (in $billions), the coefficient is positive (0.0274) and highly significant (t = 4.53, p < .001), consistent with the paper's claim that imports from the South have a positive effect on national affluence (paper Model 4: coef = .910, SE = .104).

dependent_variable: Average benefit (Util) minus symbolism (Symbol) difference score across the 4 symbolic product categories per participant
main_predictor: Branding condition (No-Brand: Cond 1/2 vs Brand: Cond 3/4)
sample_definition: All 10 datasets concatenated (n=637); retained participants passing Attention1 (=7), Attention2 (=1), and screenQ (=2), leaving N=499
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test (equal-variance) comparing brand vs no-brand on symbolic-product difference score
operationalization_notes: Claim relates to Study 1's symbolic-product effect on p.351. Combined three response blocks (one per condition assignment) into single per-item Util/Symbol scores, computed Util-Symbol difference per symbolic item, then averaged across the 4 symbolic items per participant, and compared by branding factor.
reasoning: Across symbolic product categories (College T-shirts, American Flags, Class Rings, Greeting Cards), the benefit-minus-symbolism difference score was significantly higher (less symbolic / more utilitarian) in the Brand conditions (M=-2.06) than in the No-Brand conditions (M=-2.66), t(497)=4.04, p<.001, confirming the claim.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic self-regulation (academic self-discipline scale)
sample_definition: All 366 students in Jung et al. (2017) aggregate summary data
model_specification: Bivariate regression / correlation test (t = r*sqrt(n-2)/sqrt(1-r^2)); equivalent to a single-path SEM regressing GPA on self-regulation using the provided correlation matrix
operationalization_notes: Only summary statistics (means, SDs, correlations, N) are available, so the SEM path from self-regulation to GPA reduces to the standardized regression coefficient = correlation r=.30, tested via t.
reasoning: Using the summary correlation matrix from Jung et al. (the only data available), the zero-order correlation between academic self-regulation and semester GPA is r=.30 with n=366, yielding t(364)=6.00, p<.001. This supports the claim that self-regulation positively predicts GPA.

main_predictor: National (collective) narcissism

model_specification: Intended: OLS linear regression of sharing intentions on national narcissism (per paper's Studies 1 & 2). Could not be executed.

dependent_variable: Proportion of trials on which the high-fWHR face was chosen as more aggressive (cannot be constructed from data)
main_predictor: fWHR level of the face (high vs low) — encoded only via the stimulus key, which is missing
sample_definition: Would have been all participants passing the quality check in Processed_Data_2 (Study 2, including male and female faces)
model_specification: Intended: one-sample t-test of per-participant proportion of high-fWHR-face choices against chance (0.5).
operationalization_notes: The Codebook references a stimulus-key file ('Questionnaire Development') that is not included in /workspace/data; without it the Right/Left responses cannot be translated into the high- vs low-fWHR choice variable required by the claim, so no valid test statistic can be produced.
reasoning: The provided data files (Raw/Processed Data 1 & 2 and Codebook) record each of the 36 trial responses only as 'Right' or 'Left' indicating the spatial position of the chosen face. The Codebook explicitly states that the mapping of each trial number to a specific stimulus pair (and thus which side displayed the high-fWHR/high-masculinity face, and whether the face was male or female) is contained in a separate 'Questionnaire Development' file that is NOT present in the supplied data directory. Per-trial proportions of 'Right' responses vary from 0.38 to 0.83, confirming sides were counterbalanced across trials, so a naive Right=high assumption is invalid (and indeed does not reproduce the per-condition means reported in Table 1 of the paper). I therefore cannot legitimately compute the targeted test statistic from the supplied data.

dependent_variable: Amount offered (po_bribe in BG; b_split in UG), in monetary units
main_predictor: Game frame (Bribery Game vs Ultimatum Game)
sample_definition: Proposers in each game who made an offer: BG Public Officials (n=199) and UG Participant Bs (n=195)
model_specification: Mann–Whitney/Wilcoxon rank-sum test (one-sided, BG<UG); z derived from U
operationalization_notes: The proposer in the harassment bribery game is the Public Official (po_bribe); the strategically identical proposer in the neutral ultimatum game is Participant B (b_split). Offer amounts are non-normal/ordinal so a rank-sum test is appropriate. The reported z is computed from the normal approximation U=12390.5 with n1=199, n2=195.

dependent_variable: Correct recognition index (mean of JOY% and ANG%, hits minus false alarms)

operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the main effect of alexithymia on recognition of anger and joy words. I averaged JOY% and ANG% per participant (the recognition indices defined by hits−false alarms) and tested the main effect of alexithymia group from a 2×2×2 between-subjects ANOVA mirroring the design described in the paper.
reasoning: Mixed/between-subjects ANOVA on average recognition rate (mean of JOY% and ANG%) with Alexithymia group, Depth and Music as between-subject factors showed a strong main effect of alexithymia group, F(1,1088)=126.62, p<.001. High alexithymia scorers recognized far fewer joy/anger words (M=.19) than low alexithymia scorers (M=.46), matching the original directional claim.

dependent_variable: EVOLVED (GSS item: 'Human beings developed from earlier species of animals' True/False)
main_predictor: Latent class membership (post-secular vs. traditional)
sample_definition: GSS 2006, 2008, 2010 respondents with complete data on the LCA manifest indicators (n=1542 total LCA sample; analysis restricted to the 785 respondents in the post-secular or traditional classes)

operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's two-stage approach: 3-class LCA on manifest items (BIBLE, EVOLVED, BIGBANG, SCIBNFTS, plus CONSCI and the 2006/2008/2010 science-knowledge items EARTHSUN, CONDRIFT, ODDS2 to stabilize the solution), then labeled classes by their EVOLVED/BIBLE/SCIBNFTS profiles. The recovered classes have the same qualitative structure as the paper (traditional: literal Bible, low science attitudes; modern: liberal Bible, high evolution acceptance; post-secular: literal Bible but favorable science attitudes and rejection of evolution).
reasoning: In a 3-class LCA of GSS 2006/2008/2010 respondents using science knowledge and attitude items plus BIBLE, EVOLVED, BIGBANG, and SCIBNFTS as manifest indicators, the post-secular class (favorable science attitudes, literal-Bible) had only 2.2% (11/494) endorsing 'humans developed from earlier animals' (EVOLVED=True), versus 36.8% (107/291) in the traditional class. The 2x2 chi-square = 168.39 (df=1, p ~ 1.7e-38), in the direction predicted by the paper.

dependent_variable: Trendiness rating of the mug (V18, 7-point scale)
main_predictor: Display fixture condition (glass table V17=1 vs. wood table V16=1)

operationalization_notes: Claim targets the simple interdependent-prime glass-vs-wood contrast on trendiness. Dataset is the replication of Study 1 with only interdependent prime, so the contrast directly maps to a two-group t-test on V18.
reasoning: Among interdependent-primed participants, mean trendiness was 4.85 (SD=1.64, n=34) for the glass table and 5.29 (SD=1.41, n=35) for the wood table. An independent-samples t-test gave t(67)=-1.18, p=.24 — non-significant and numerically in the opposite direction of the predicted assimilation effect.

dependent_variable: Utilitarian (morally acceptable = 2) response on the conflict moral scenario (moral_accept)
main_predictor: Salience condition (death vs pain)

operationalization_notes: Of the two moral acceptability items, moral_accept showed clear variability (consistent with the 'conflict' problem in the original Footbridge-type design) whereas moral_accept1 was near-ceiling (consistent with a 'no-conflict/control' scenario). The claim is about conflict problems, so chi-square was run on moral_accept by salience condition.
reasoning: In the conflict-scenario item (moral_accept), 82.3% of death-salience participants gave the utilitarian ('morally acceptable') response vs 73.9% in the pain condition — a non-significant difference in the OPPOSITE direction to the original claim (χ²(1)=1.32, p=.25, N=131). The data do not replicate the predicted decrease in utilitarian responding under mortality salience.

dependent_variable: Mean interpersonal obstacle->behavior lexical-decision reaction time (IntAssocM, mean of IntAssoc1-4); lower RT = stronger association
main_predictor: Mean-centered expectation of success in the interpersonal domain (IntExp_c) within the mental contrasting condition
sample_definition: Participants in the H8 analytic dataset (interpersonal-association outlier filter applied: IntAssocObs=0 & IntAccessObs=0) with non-missing IntAssocM and IntExp; N=317 across three conditions (MC n=90, reverse n=108, irrelevant n=119).

controls: None beyond condition dummies and their interactions with expectation
operationalization_notes: The claim is most directly tested by the simple slope of expectation on obstacle-behavior association strength within the MC condition. Study 1 elaborated the interpersonal concern, so I used the interpersonal association RT as the DV, following the original Study 1 analysis. Coding mapping (raw group 1 = MC) was verified by merging with the raw data.
reasoning: Within the mental contrasting condition, the simple slope of expectation of success predicting the interpersonal obstacle-behavior association strength (mean lexical-decision RT, lower = stronger association) was b = +11.14, t(311) = 0.42, p = .68. The slope is in the opposite direction of the prediction and far from significant; the claim that MC+low expectations yields weak (slow) associations does not replicate.

dependent_variable: share of surplus given to recipient (s) vs libertarian benchmark (xl = partner_endowment/total endowment)
main_predictor: libertarian principle benchmark xl

operationalization_notes: The claim that the libertarian principle does not account for DW behavior corresponds to rejecting H0: s = xl. Used the nonparametric Wilcoxon signed-rank test (one of the tests reported by the paper). The dataset variable x equals partner_endowment/(own+partner endowment), which is the libertarian share the dictator should pass on.
reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of s vs xl (libertarian share) among DW dictators yields W=8, p<0.001 (n=27), so the libertarian principle (s=xl) is significantly rejected — dictators systematically deviate from the libertarian allocation in DW, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: underdiagnosed (1 = hypertensive but undiagnosed)
main_predictor: years of education
sample_definition: Hypertensive respondents reporting poor general health (poor_health==1), with non-missing covariates

controls: log per-capita expenditures, time preference, risk preference, distance/travel time to health center, sex
operationalization_notes: Replicates the Table-equivalent disease-detection probit (underdiagnosis) on the poor-health subsample; the directional claim (education raises diagnosis probability conditional on poor health) corresponds to a negative coefficient on education in this probit.
reasoning: Probit of under-diagnosis on years of education and controls, restricted to respondents in poor general health, yields a significantly negative education coefficient (b=-0.0297, z=-2.49, p=0.013, N=756). Lower probability of being under-diagnosed = higher probability of being diagnosed for more-educated respondents in poor health, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological (harm-rejecting) responses in personal moral dilemmas (RH_PMD)
main_predictor: Experimental condition (1=Control, 2=Observed)
sample_definition: All participants in SCORE_all data.sav with non-missing RH_PMD and Condition (N=156, 78 per group)

operationalization_notes: The claim singles out personal moral dilemmas, so I focused the test on RH_PMD, the dataset's pre-computed deontological-response rate for personal moral dilemmas. Rather than the omnibus 2x3 mixed ANOVA interaction, I report the direct between-group comparison within personal dilemmas, which is the specific contrast the verbal claim refers to.
reasoning: An independent-samples Welch t-test comparing the observed (M=64.87%, SD=15.62) vs. control group (M=62.88%, SD=16.05) on the proportion of deontological (harm-rejecting) judgments in personal moral dilemmas yielded t(153.89)=0.78, p=.434. The direction is consistent with the claim (more deontological responses under observation), but the difference is far from significant in the available dataset (N=156), so the claim does not reproduce as a statistically reliable effect.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1 (worry about COVID-19, 5-point Likert)
main_predictor: gender (1=men, 2=women)
sample_definition: Respondents in data_0948.csv with gender coded male (1) or female (2); 'other' (3) excluded
model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test comparing women vs men
operationalization_notes: The mh_anxiety_1 item corresponds most directly to general COVID-19 concern/worry highlighted in the paper's claim. Independent-samples t-test on the 5-point Likert response, comparing the two genders.
reasoning: Women report significantly higher COVID-19 worry (mh_anxiety_1) than men (M=3.07 vs M=2.89 on a 5-point scale), Welch's t(10067.5)=8.26, p<1e-15, supporting the claim that women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men.

dependent_variable: Percentage-point change in mean county-day mobility (share of population not at home) during March 19-28, 2020 relative to March 19-28, 2019 (matched-days reference)
main_predictor: County Trump vote share in the 2016 presidential election
sample_definition: All U.S. counties with non-missing trips data for both 2020 and 2019 reference windows and complete covariates (N=3,102)
model_specification: OLS regression with state fixed effects
controls: Per-capita income, % college, % male, % black, % hispanic, age-decade shares (under 5 through 75-84), state fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Paper used proprietary Unacast distancing data (unavailable); I proxied with BTS Trips_by_Distance pop_not_home share, comparing March 19-28 2020 to the matched calendar window in 2019 as a pre-COVID reference, and replicated the multivariable specification described in Table 1.
reasoning: In an OLS regression with state fixed effects and socio-demographic controls, higher Trump 2016 vote share predicts a less-negative change in county mobility (March 19-28, 2020 vs same dates in 2019), i.e. less social distancing (β=1.33 pp per unit, t=3.04, p=0.0024, N=3102). Sign and significance match the original claim.

dependent_variable: Social distancing compliance composite (soc_dist; mean of 4 items)
main_predictor: Political conservatism composite (pol)
sample_definition: All respondents in the provided final dataset with non-missing values on both measures (N=322)
model_specification: Bivariate Pearson correlation / equivalent simple linear regression t-test
operationalization_notes: The claim is about a direct inverse association; the most direct test is the bivariate correlation between the two composite scales as constructed in the dataset.
reasoning: Zero-order Pearson correlation between political conservatism (pol) and social distancing compliance (soc_dist) is r = -.179, t(320) = -3.26, p = .001, indicating conservatism inversely predicts social-distancing compliance, consistent with the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Mean z-score of third-grade reading (X6RSCALK5) and mathematics (X6MSCALK5) IRT scale scores
main_predictor: Mean z-score of teacher-reported third-grade externalizing (X6TCHEXT) and internalizing (X6TCHINT) problems

model_specification: Pearson correlation between social-emotional problems composite and academic achievement composite
operationalization_notes: The claim asserts a bivariate negative association between social-emotional problems and achievement among ELLs. I built simple composites of the two indicators of social-emotional problems (SDQ externalizing and internalizing, here proxied by X6TCHEXT/X6TCHINT) and the two main achievement outcomes (reading and math scale scores) reported in Table 3, and tested their correlation in the ELL subsample defined by non-English home-language status.
reasoning: Among ECLS-K children whose home language was non-English (X12LANGST==1), a composite of teacher-rated third-grade externalizing and internalizing problems was significantly and negatively correlated with a composite of third-grade reading and mathematics IRT scale scores (r = -0.098, t(2159) = -4.57, p < .001, n = 2161). Higher social-emotional problems are linked to lower achievement, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Mean perceived societal good (SocGood_Artis, _Green, _Food, _Medtech; 1=great harm to 5=great good) averaged across the four organizations
main_predictor: Firm motive condition (For-Profit vs. Non-Profit)
sample_definition: Participants with non-missing condition and all four SocGood ratings; restricted to For-Profit (condition=3, n=123) and Non-Profit (condition=2, n=120) conditions
model_specification: Independent-samples (Welch-equivalent two-sample) t-test on subject-level mean of the four SocGood items
operationalization_notes: Methods section was redacted; based on data dictionary, condition 1=Unspecified, 2=Non-Profit, 3=For-Profit. The claim specifically references the pairwise Profit vs Non-Profit comparison of mean perceived societal good averaged across the four organization scenarios, so I implemented exactly that test.
reasoning: Averaging perceived societal good ratings across the four organization scenarios, participants in the For-Profit condition (M=3.75) rated societal good significantly lower than those in the Non-Profit condition (M=4.09), t(241)=-4.82, p<.001, d≈-0.62. This replicates the directional pairwise effect reported on p. 680 that a profit motive reduces perceived societal good.

dependent_variable: Participant-level mean sharing intention (1–6) across 15 headlines per veracity type
main_predictor: Headline veracity (true vs. false)
sample_definition: Participants assigned to the treatment (accuracy nudge) condition of Study 2 who provided complete sharing ratings (N = 440)
model_specification: Paired-samples t-test (true vs. false within subject)
operationalization_notes: Claim concerns within-treatment true vs. false sharing intentions. The simplest, most direct test is a paired t-test on participant-level means; results closely match a mixed-effects model (b = -0.031, p = .30).
reasoning: Within the treatment condition, a paired t-test comparing each participant's mean sharing intention for the 15 true vs. 15 false COVID-19 headlines (6-point Likert recoded 1–6) yielded t(439) = -1.12, p = .27. The means were almost identical (true M = 3.49, false M = 3.52), failing to replicate the claim that true headlines were shared significantly more than false ones; the small numerical difference actually runs in the opposite direction.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth dummy = 1 if GDP per capita growth ≥ 2% in each of the 5 years starting at the survey year
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index (from Afrobarometer, Q on whether respondent's group is 'never' treated unfairly by government)
sample_definition: Country-survey-year observations from the 20 sub-Saharan African countries listed in the paper's Appendix Table 5 (Afrobarometer waves 1-4, 1999-2009); 63 observations (one dropped because Polity2 missing)
model_specification: Pooled OLS: sustained = a + b1·log(Impartiality) + b2·Polity2
operationalization_notes: Chose the simplest specification reported in the paper (Table 2 column 1), constructing the sustained-growth indicator from WDI GDP per capita growth using a forward 5-year window starting at the survey year and the 2.0% per-year threshold described in the abstract.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's pooled OLS specification (Table 2 col 1) — a country-survey observation regression of a sustained-growth dummy (1 if GDP-per-capita growth ≥ 2% in each of the next 5 years following the Afrobarometer survey year) on log Impartiality index and Polity2 — yields a small, statistically insignificant (and even slightly negative) coefficient on log impartiality (b = -0.026, t = -0.247, p = 0.81, N = 63). On this operationalization the data do not support the claim that more impartial governments are more likely to experience sustained growth.

dependent_variable: Mean evaluation of toaster (average of 5 evaluation items) for the 4.5-star vs the 2.5-star toaster (within-subjects)
main_predictor: Information type (aggregated 4.5-star vs individualized 2.5-star), within abstract-sound condition

model_specification: Paired-samples t-test on toaster evaluation means
operationalization_notes: The claim concerns the within-condition simple effect for the abstract sound, which the paper tests as a planned contrast within the 5x2 mixed ANOVA. A paired t-test on the two evaluation means within the abstract-sound subgroup is the most direct test of this specific within-cell contrast; filter==1 applied to match paper's reported descriptives.
reasoning: Within the abstract-sound condition (group 5, valid filter), a paired t-test comparing evaluations of the 4.5-star (positive aggregated) vs. 2.5-star (positive individualized) toaster yielded t(15)=7.86, p<.001, with means 5.14 vs 2.98, replicating the paper's reported simple contrast.

dependent_variable: GDP per capita (national affluence)
main_predictor: Imports from the South (totalimport, USD billions)
sample_definition: 18 OECD countries, 1966-2003 yearly observations with no missing values (northsouth_NoNA.xlsx, N=755)
model_specification: OLS with country and 5-year period fixed effects
controls: Exports to the South, unemployment rate, country FE, 5-year period FE
operationalization_notes: Methods section was redacted; chose the analysis most directly tied to the indirect-effect claim that imports from South raise national affluence (Table 2, Model 4). Used the cleaned panel file (northsouth_NoNA) at annual frequency with country and period fixed effects.
reasoning: In a panel OLS regression of GDP per capita (national affluence, in $1000) on imports from the South (in $billion) with exports to the South, unemployment, and country and 5-year period fixed effects, the coefficient on imports from the South is positive and highly significant (b=0.024, t(727)=4.29, p<0.001, N=755), consistent with the paper's reported positive indirect effect of southern imports on national affluence.

dependent_variable: Mean difference score (Util rating minus Symbol rating) averaged over the four symbolic product categories (T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards)
main_predictor: Branded vs Unbranded condition (Cond 3/4 vs Cond 1/2)
sample_definition: All participants across the 10 replication datasets who passed both attention checks (Attention1=7 and Attention2=1); n=593
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test comparing branded vs unbranded conditions on the participant-level mean symbolic-product difference score
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Study 1 operationalization: subtracted symbolism rating from benefits rating per item, then averaged across the four symbolic product categories. Higher values indicate more utilitarian / less symbolic attitudes. Compared branded conditions (Brand Sets A and B) against unbranded conditions.
reasoning: Among the four symbolic product categories (T-shirts, flags, class rings, greeting cards), the average benefits-minus-symbols difference score was significantly higher (less negative, i.e., less symbolic / more utilitarian) when products were branded (M=-2.11) than when unbranded (M=-2.64), t(591)=3.91, p<.001. This replicates the paper's reported finding that branding shifts symbolic product attitudes toward the utilitarian end.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Self-regulation (Academic Self-Discipline composite from Jung et al., the IV in the replication)
sample_definition: All 366 college students from Jung et al. (2017) summary statistics provided for the Zimmerman & Kitsantas replication
model_specification: Single-predictor structural regression (SEM with observed variables) using the supplied correlation matrix; equivalent to test of bivariate correlation
operationalization_notes: The data file is a 5x5 correlation/SD/mean matrix from Jung et al. (2017) provided with n=366 for replicating the SR→GPA SEM path. With only summary statistics, the SEM path coefficient for SR→GPA equals the bivariate r; significance is computed via t = r*sqrt((n-2)/(1-r^2)).
reasoning: Using the Jung et al. (2017) summary correlation matrix supplied for the replication (n=366), the zero-order correlation between the self-regulation indicator (Academic Self-Discipline composite per Jung et al.) and semester GPA is r=.30, giving t(364)=6.00, p<.001. This is equivalent to the regression slope of GPA on self-regulation in a just-identified SEM with one predictor, and confirms a significant positive effect of self-regulation on GPA, in line with the original claim.

dependent_variable: Intentions to share/disseminate COVID-19 conspiracy theories — NOT AVAILABLE in provided data

The dissemination analyses reported in the paper come from Study 1 (US, N≈293) and Study 2 (UK, N≈637), whose raw item-level data are not included in this data release, so the dissemination claim cannot be directly tested from these data.

dependent_variable: Per-participant proportion of trials on which the high-fWHR/high-masculinity face (right-side image) was chosen as more aggressive (out of 36 trials)
main_predictor: High vs. low transform face (tested against chance = 0.5)
sample_definition: Study 2 dataset (Processed_Data_2.csv), restricted to participants flagged Quality='Yes' (n=288); all three transform conditions (25%, 37.5%, 50%) and both face sexes pooled.
model_specification: One-sample t-test of mean per-participant proportion against chance (0.5)
operationalization_notes: The codebook records responses as Left/Right and Figure 1 indicates the high-fWHR/masculinity face was always on the right. Without a per-trial mapping of fWHR vs masculinity trials, I tested the broader compatible operationalization: choosing the high-transform face above chance in the dataset that includes both male and female face stimuli, matching the claim's 'both male and female faces' scope.
reasoning: Across 36 forced-choice trials in which the high-transform face (high fWHR or high masculinity) was presented on the right and the low-transform face on the left, participants in Study 2 (which included both male and female face stimuli) chose the high-transform face on 53.4% of trials, significantly above the 50% chance level (one-sample t(287) = 5.10, p < .001). This supports the directional claim that faces with increased fWHR (and masculinity) are perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: Amount demanded/kept by player B (po_bribe in BG, b_split in UG), 0-$2
main_predictor: Treatment frame: bribery game (briberygame=1) vs ultimatum game (briberygame=0)
sample_definition: All participants assigned to BG or UG treatments who made a B-side decision (n=394; excludes BG-neutral language treatment and missing responses)
model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test (unequal variances), two-sided
operationalization_notes: The claim compares the average bribe demanded (BG) with the strategically identical proposal to keep for oneself (UG). I used the two B-player decision variables po_bribe and b_split and compared their means across the two treatment groups.
reasoning: Mean bribe demanded by public officials in the bribery game (M=0.578, n=199) is significantly lower than the amount B proposed to keep in the ultimatum game (M=0.910, n=195); Welch's t(344.68)=-5.37, p<.001, consistent with the claim that average bribe is lesser in BG than in UG.

dependent_variable: Ratio of participant's total-cab estimate to the maximum cab number seen so far
main_predictor: Number of observations seen (values_seen: 1, 3, 10)
sample_definition: Taxicab condition, estimate trials only; 669 subjects with non-missing estimates at all three observation counts.
model_specification: Friedman non-parametric repeated-measures test across the three observation-count levels
controls: none (within-subject design; dependent variable normalised by observed max)
operationalization_notes: Raw estimates rise with sample count because the maximum observed value also rises; the theoretically relevant 'smaller prediction' is the multiplicative gap between estimate and observed max, hence I used the estimate/max ratio. Friedman test is appropriate for repeated measures with skewed responses.
reasoning: Within-subject Friedman test on the ratio of estimated fleet size to the maximum cab number observed shows the ratio decreases monotonically with the number of observations (2.20 at 1 sample → 1.36 at 3 → 1.16 at 10), χ²(2)=281.6, p<1e-60, with N=669 subjects each contributing all three conditions. This supports the original claim that participants' predictions shrink toward the observed maximum as more observations are provided.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total (binary indicator of last-digit fraud from chi-squared test of vote totals)
main_predictor: Election-day violence per capita (v.elday.pc) and its square (v.elday.pc.2)
sample_definition: All 375 Afghan districts with non-missing covariates (2009 presidential election)
model_specification: Logistic regression of fraud indicator on violence, violence^2, and controls; z-test on quadratic term
controls: Number of closed polling stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure, distance from Kabul, elevation
operationalization_notes: Replicates Model 1 from Table 1, which is the specification most directly tied to the inverted-U claim. The z-test on the squared violence term directly tests for curvature.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of district-level last-digit fraud indicator on election-day violence per capita, its square, and controls (closed stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure, distance from Kabul, elevation), the linear violence term is positive (b=8.48, z=2.55) and the squared term is negative and significant (b=-13.75, z=-2.14, p=0.032), consistent with an inverted U-shape between violence and fraud.

dependent_variable: Social undermining (Undermin; 1-7, lower = more undermining)
main_predictor: TSC × ConditionCompetition interaction (unfavorable vs favorable temporal comparison × high vs low competition)
sample_definition: All 574 participants with both TSC observations each (1148 observations)
model_specification: Linear mixed-effects model: Undermin ~ TSC * ConditionCompetition + (1|id)
operationalization_notes: TSC was manipulated within-subjects and competition between-subjects; random intercepts capture within-person dependence. The claim corresponds to the interaction term.
reasoning: A linear mixed model (random intercept per participant) regressing Undermin on TSC, ConditionCompetition, and their interaction yielded a significant TSC×Competition interaction (b = -0.578, z = -3.38, p = .001). Because Undermin is reverse-coded (lower = more undermining), the negative interaction means that the unfavorable-TSC vs favorable-TSC increase in undermining is stronger under high competition, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Mean of six SpecCTs items (COVID-19-specific conspiracy belief endorsement; SpecCTs_3r and _6r reverse-coded)
main_predictor: Mean of COVID1 (worry about COVID spread) and COVID3 (feeling threatened by COVID) — proxy for the paper's anxiety / risk-perception construct
sample_definition: All 806 respondents in the released replication file (pooled across Survey 1 USA, 2a USA, 2b UK); no exclusions because no missing data.
model_specification: OLS regression: CT_mean ~ worry_mean (t-test on slope)
controls: None — age, gender, education and trust/lack-of-control variables are not present in the released dataset
operationalization_notes: The provided replication file only contains the six COVID conspiracy items and two COVID worry/threat items. With no anxiety, lack-of-control, trust, or demographic variables available, the most direct testable element of the causal chain is whether higher COVID-related worry/threat predicts higher COVID conspiracy belief endorsement.
reasoning: Using the only COVID-related affect/risk items provided in the data (COVID1 worry and COVID3 threat) as a proxy for the anxiety/risk-perception construct in the paper's mediation chain, and the six SpecCTs items (with reverse coding applied) as COVID-19 conspiracy belief endorsement, the bivariate OLS shows worry/threat is a significant but NEGATIVE predictor of conspiracy beliefs (b = -.146, t(804) = -4.83, p < .001, r = -.17, N = 806). This is the opposite of the claim that COVID worry/anxiety predicts higher conspiracy belief. Note: the dataset does not contain the separate anxiety, lack-of-control, trust-in-institutions, or demographic variables used in the published path model, so the full mediation could not be reproduced.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) per participant for angry vs neutral central face
main_predictor: Central face emotion (angry vs neutral), within-subjects
sample_definition: Participants in the GAD group (Group==1)

My attempts to reproduce the paper's three-class LCA in stepmix did not recover a distinct post-secular class (the EM converged to traditional/modern/middle solutions across many seeds), so a proxy was needed; this proxy does not capture the paper's defining feature of the post-secular class (extreme evolution rejection combined with literal Bible belief and high science knowledge), which is largely tautological with the EVOLVED item being one of the LCA's manifest indicators.

dependent_variable: Trendiness composite (mean of trendy, modern, urban; V18-V20)

operationalization_notes: Trendiness operationalized as the average of the three trendy/modern/urban items per the codebook; glass vs wood coded from V17/V16 indicators. The dataset is restricted to interdependents (no independent-prime condition present), matching the claim's focal subsample.

The predicted assimilation effect (glass > wood) does not replicate and is non-significant.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time for interpersonal obstacle-prime → instrumental-behavior-target lexical decision trials (IntAssocM); lower RT = stronger obstacle-behavior association
main_predictor: Expectations of success for the interpersonal concern (IntExp, mean-centered), with MC as reference condition in a hierarchical regression including two condition dummies and their interactions with expectations

controls: Mere accessibility of the interpersonal instrumental behavior (IntAccessM)
operationalization_notes: The claim is most directly tested by the simple slope of expectations on obstacle-behavior associations within the mental-contrasting condition: a positive (in association strength) / negative (in RT) slope would mean that lower expectations under MC yield weaker associations. Following the paper's Study 1 analytic strategy, I used hierarchical regression on the elaborated (interpersonal) concern with the MC condition as the reference category, controlling for mere accessibility, on the pre-registered H8 analytic dataset.
reasoning: The simple slope of expectations of success on interpersonal obstacle-behavior associations within the mental-contrasting condition was in the predicted direction (negative coefficient on RT-based association strength, b = -13.31, indicating that lower expectations were associated with slower RTs/weaker associations), but the effect was far from significant, t(300) = -0.86, p = .39. Thus, while the direction is consistent with the original claim that MC + low expectations weakens obstacle-behavior associations, the replication does not provide reliable evidence for it.

dependent_variable: Deviation of dictator's share offered from libertarian benchmark, s - x_l

Mean s - x_l = -0.12, indicating dictators systematically gave less than the libertarian benchmark, so the libertarian principle does not account for dictators' behavior in DW — matching the paper's conclusion.

dependent_variable: mh_anxiety_1: worry/concern about COVID-19 in general (5-point Likert scale)

The most direct test is the zero-order association between the conservatism composite and the social distancing composite in Study 1 (Study 2 data not present in the provided dataset).

dependent_variable: Academic achievement composite (mean of standardized 3rd-grade reading and math IRT scale scores, X7RSCALK5 + X7MSCALK5)

As a direct, simple test I correlated the standard composites for these two latent constructs (averages of z-scored indicators) at the 3rd-grade wave on the ELL subsample. Fewer social-emotional problems were associated with higher achievement, consistent with the paper's claim (paper reported r = -.388, p < .001).

dependent_variable: Mean perceived societal good across 4 firm scenarios (SocGood_Artis, _Green, _Food, _Medtech; 1=great harm, 5=great good)

Means were ordered Profit (cond3, M=3.75) < Unspecified/NonProfit (cond2, M=4.09; cond1, M=4.31), replicating the original direction that profit motive reduced perceived societal good.

dependent_variable: Per-participant average sharing intention (1-6 Likert) for true headlines vs. false headlines

sample_definition: Participants assigned to the Treatment (accuracy-nudge) condition (Condition==2) with valid Avg_Fake and Avg_Real, using the available Roozenbeek et al. replication dataset (the test/mock CSVs in the data folder contained lorem-ipsum placeholders and could not be used for a real test).

Aggregating to the participant level (Avg_Real, Avg_Fake) avoids the rating-level non-independence the paper handled via clustered SEs while still testing the same simple effect.

A paired-samples t-test yielded t(789)=9.33, p<.001 (Cohen's d_z≈0.33), supporting the original claim that sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines in the treatment condition.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth indicator (=1 if annual GDP-per-capita growth >= 2% in every year of the 5-year window starting the year after the Afrobarometer survey, 0 otherwise)
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index (country-level weighted share of Afrobarometer respondents answering 'Never' to: 'How often is your ethnic group treated unfairly by the government?'), at the survey year (lagged one year relative to the dependent variable)

operationalization_notes: Most direct test of the claim is the baseline Pooled OLS specification (Table 2, col. 1). Impartiality index reproduced from the Afrobarometer question on unfair treatment using within-country weights, producing values that closely match Table 5 of the paper. Sustained growth defined exactly as in the paper using World Bank GDP-per-capita growth data; differences from the paper's results likely reflect data-vintage revisions to WB GDP series.
reasoning: Replicating Table 2 column 1 (Pooled OLS regression of Sustained Growth on lagged Log Impartiality index and lagged Polity2), I obtain a coefficient on log impartiality of -0.049 (SE 0.101, t=-0.486, p=0.63) with N=62. The coefficient is in the opposite direction from the paper's reported +0.18 and is far from significant, so the most direct test of the claim does not reproduce on the current (revised) World Bank GDP data — providing no evidence that perceived government impartiality is associated with greater likelihood of sustained growth.

dependent_variable: Evaluation score (mean of 5 items) for the aggregated-favored (4.5-star) vs individualized-favored (2.5-star) toaster

dependent_variable: National affluence (GDP per capita, in $1000s PPP, 2000 prices)
main_predictor: Imports from the South (total imports from Southern countries, in $billions)

controls: Exports to the South, Unemployment, country fixed effects, period (1975-79, 1980-84, 1985-89, 1990-94, 1995-99, 2000-03; 1970-74 baseline)
operationalization_notes: Mirrors the paper's Model 4: regresses national affluence on North-South trade plus unemployment with country FE and period dummies. reasoning: In an FE regression of GDP per capita on Imports from the South, Exports to the South, Unemployment, country fixed effects, and period dummies (1970-2003), imports from the South have a positive and highly significant effect (b=0.0274, t=4.77, p<.001, N=468), consistent with the paper's Model 4 finding that North-to-South imports raise the affluence of Northern economies.

dependent_variable: Composite attitude-function score (Util rating - Symbol rating), averaged across the four symbolic products

operationalization_notes: Claim specifically concerns symbolic categories; followed paper's Study 1 operationalization of attitude function as Util - Symbol composite, and most directly tested branding's effect on symbolic products via the brand-vs-category contrast (paper reports t(204)=3.54 in Study 1b for this comparison).
reasoning: Among the four symbolic product categories (college T-shirts, American flags, class rings, greeting cards), the mean utilitarian-minus-symbolic difference score was higher (less symbolic, more utilitarian) in the branded condition (M = -2.09) than in the unbranded condition (M = -2.66), t(555) = 4.07, p < .0001. This replicates the original finding that branding makes attitudes toward symbolic categories less symbolic and more utilitarian.

dependent_variable: Semester GPA
main_predictor: Academic self-regulation (academic self-discipline scale per Jung et al.)
sample_definition: All 366 students from the Jung et al. (2017) aggregate summary data (replication dataset)
model_specification: OLS multiple regression derived from the correlation matrix; GPA regressed on self-regulation with self-discipline facet as a control (equivalent to the SEM structural path from SR to GPA available with this summary dataset)
operationalization_notes: Only summary statistics (means, SDs, correlations) are available, so SEM with multiple indicators is not identified; the most direct test of the SR→GPA structural path is a regression on the correlation matrix controlling for the self-discipline facet, matching the paper's framework of separating SR from SD.
reasoning: Using the Jung et al. summary correlation matrix (N=366), regressing semester GPA on academic self-regulation while controlling for the self-discipline facet yields a standardized partial coefficient of β=0.336 for self-regulation, t(363)=4.85, p<.001. Self-regulation is a significant positive predictor of GPA, consistent with the original SEM claim.

Only belief in COVID-19 conspiracy theories was measured (conspiracy_theories__1..4), along with collective narcissism, national identification, and perceived truthfulness/familiarity of news claims. dependent_variable: Proportion of trials per participant on which the high-fWHR/masculinity face (right-side image, per Figure 1 convention) was chosen as more aggressive
main_predictor: High vs low fWHR/masculinity face (within-trial choice; test against chance = 0.5)
sample_definition: Processed_Data_2.csv (Study 2 replication with both male and female faces); participants who indicated their data should be used (Quality = Yes); N = 288.
model_specification: One-sample t-test comparing per-participant proportion of high-fWHR/masc choices against 0.5
operationalization_notes: The provided codebook does not include the per-trial mapping of which side held the high-fWHR face. Following the original paper's stimulus description (low feature on left, high feature on right; Figure 1), 'Right' responses were coded as choosing the high-feature face. Because the trial mapping for fWHR vs. masculinity is unavailable, all 36 trials are aggregated; this is the most charitable defensible test of the directional claim that high-fWHR faces (across male and female stimuli) are judged more aggressive.
reasoning: Across 288 quality-approved participants viewing 36 face-pair trials (male and female faces), the mean proportion of trials in which the high-fWHR/masculinity face (presented on the right per the paper's stimulus convention) was selected as more aggressive was 0.534 (SD = 0.113), significantly above the 0.5 chance level, t(287) = 5.10, p < .001. This replicates the original directional claim that higher-fWHR faces are perceived as more aggressive.

dependent_variable: Amount demanded by the public official (po_bribe) in BG vs. proposer split (b_split) in UG
main_predictor: Treatment (briberygame: 1=BG, 0=UG)
sample_definition: All participants in BG and UG treatments with non-missing demanded amount (briberygame in {0,1})
model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test on the amount demanded across the two frames
operationalization_notes: Most direct test of the claim: compare the average bribe/transfer amount demanded between BG and UG conditions using a two-sample t-test, mirroring the comparison reported in Table 1 of the paper.
reasoning: Mean amount demanded by the proposer in the bribery game (M=0.578, n=199) is significantly lower than in the strategically identical ultimatum game (M=0.910, n=195); Welch's t = -5.37, p < 0.001. This matches the original claim that average bribe is lower than the ultimatum transfer.

dependent_variable: Estimate divided by the largest example seen (t/t_part)

operationalization_notes: Mirrors the original paper's analysis: exclusion of misunderstanding responses and >3SD outliers, transformation to t/t_part, then a within-subjects ANOVA on the number-of-examples factor for the taxicab scenario.
reasoning: In the taxicab scenario, the within-subjects ANOVA on response/max-value ratios across the three observation-count conditions (1, 3, 10) yielded F(2,1166)=84.71, p<.001. Mean ratios decreased monotonically (1.76, 1.38, 1.21), confirming smaller predictions with more observations.

dependent_variable: fraudchi2_total (last-digit-test fraud indicator at district level)

controls: Number of closed stations, electrification, per-capita expenditure, distance from Kabul, elevation
operationalization_notes: Replicated the paper's Model 1 directly. The most direct single test of the inverted-U claim is the z-statistic on the squared violence term (expected negative); the linear term is positive but not individually significant under clustered SEs.
reasoning: Logit of last-digit fraud indicator on election-day violence and its square (with controls and regional-command-clustered SEs) yields a positive linear term (b=8.48) and a negative, statistically significant squared term (b=-13.75, z=-2.50, p=0.012), confirming the inverted U-shaped relationship between violence and fraud.

dependent_variable: Undermin (matching preference; lower values = more social undermining)
main_predictor: TSC × ConditionCompetition interaction (temporal social comparison crossed with competition condition)
sample_definition: All 574 participants in the analytical data file (Study 1a/b sample), each contributing 2 observations (favorable and unfavorable TSC); N=1148 observations.

reasoning: In a mixed-effects model with TSC (within-subjects: favorable=0 / unfavorable=1) × Competition (between-subjects: low=0 / high=1) predicting matching preference (lower = more undermining), the interaction was significant (b = -0.578, z = -3.384, p = .001). dependent_variable: COVID-19 conspiracy belief composite (mean of SpecCTs_1..6r)

A multiple regression including COVID3 (threat/risk perception) confirms the negative anxiety coefficient (b=-0.34, t=-7.69) while the overall model is significant F(2,803)=32.83.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) on angry vs. neutral central-face trials (AngryM, NeutralM)

sample_definition: Participants coded as likely GAD (Group=1) in the OSF dataset (n=63)

operationalization_notes: The paper's claim arises from a follow-up paired contrast on Valence of Face within the GAD group; the OSF dataset provides only one mean RT per emotion per participant, so the most direct test is a within-subjects paired contrast of AngryM vs. NeutralM restricted to Group=1 (likely GAD).
reasoning: In the GAD group (Group=1, n=63) the mean RT for angry central faces (486.8 ms) was essentially identical to neutral central faces (485.4 ms). operationalization_notes: Followed Table 3 Level-1 specification. TAS computed per paper: indirect = 1 - mean(checked) over 3 items (charting, reviewing diagnostic test results, patient history reviews); direct = 1 - mean(checked) over 6 items (oral hygiene, skin care, teaching, comforting, care plans, discharge prep). The claim about magnitude was operationalized as a linear contrast of fixed effects from the multilevel model.

operationalization_notes: The claim emphasizes that emotional reactions (anger, sympathy) bear independent relations with the three behavioral outcomes. Sympathy and severity also showed independent multivariate effects, supporting that emotional reactions (shaped by attributions of malice/greed) bear independent relations with revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: EVOLVED (binary: 'Human beings developed from earlier species of animals' True/False)

operationalization_notes: Since the paper's primary comparison of EVOLVED by class is descriptive (Table 1), I operationalized the test as a chi-square comparing the two classes named in the claim. A Pearson chi-square test of the EVOLVED response across these two classes yields χ²(1, N=593) = 169.8, p ≈ 8e-39, supporting the claim that post-seculars are significantly less likely than traditionalists to say humans evolved from other animals.
