dependent_variable: Identified with autism (yes/no) among students ages 6–21
main_predictor: State (Ohio vs California, reference = California)
sample_definition: All ages 6–21 public-school students in California and Ohio in 2014 (autism count from IDEA Section 618 Child Count; denominator = total fall 2014 public K-12 enrollment from NCES table 203.20)
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on a 2×2 contingency table (autism vs not autism × CA vs OH); equivalent to a logistic regression of autism on state
operationalization_notes: The claim is a direct state-vs-state comparison of overall autism identification, so I collapsed across race and used the simplest 2×2 test. Autism counts come from the IDEA 2014 Child Count file (Total, Age 6-21), and total enrollment denominators come from NCES tabn203.20 (Fall 2014), matching the population basis used in the paper for between-state comparisons.
reasoning: In a 2×2 chi-square comparing autism identification (ages 6–21) versus the rest of the public K-12 enrollment in California vs Ohio, Ohio's odds of autism identification were lower than California's (OR_Ohio/CA = 0.946; χ²(1)=46.49, p<.001).

dependent_variable: group_chooses_red (group-level decision, 1=red)
main_predictor: voting rule (Majority r=5 / SuperMajority r=7 / Unanimity r=9)
sample_definition: All unique group decisions in the no-communication replication dataset (one row per session×round×group)
model_specification: Pearson chi-squared test of independence on a 3 (rule) x 2 (group decision red/blue) contingency table
operationalization_notes: The replication dataset only includes the no-communication arm, so the direct interaction (rule x deliberation) cannot be estimated. Following the paper's approach (Fisher/KS tests of group decisions across rules), I tested whether voting rule alone produces different group outcomes in the absence of deliberation, which is the necessary condition for deliberation to 'diminish' institutional differences.
reasoning: Using the only condition available in the replication data (no communication), group decisions (red vs. blue) differ massively across the three voting rules: 58% red under Majority, 20% under SuperMajority, 0% under Unanimity (chi2(2)=91.02, p<1e-19, n=352 group decisions). Large institutional differences are present without deliberation, consistent with the premise the paper invokes when it argues deliberation diminishes those differences. The data only contain the no-deliberation arm, so the 'diminishing' effect itself cannot be tested directly here — but the institutional gap that deliberation would attenuate is clearly present.

dependent_variable: Group-level average market price (proxy for revenue, since supply is fixed and demand exceeds supply in both treatments)
main_predictor: Auction mechanism (UNIFORM vs FIXED, where FIXED price = 1.94 is a constant set by BF model)
sample_definition: All 40 UNIFORM groups in fullsample_analysis.csv, restricted to the 34 groups without a dropout (dropout==0)
model_specification: One-sided one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test of group-level mean price against the constant fixed price 1.94, alternative = greater
operationalization_notes: Because demand exceeds supply in both treatments, revenue ranking reduces to a price comparison. The FIXED treatment by design produces a constant price of 1.94, so the comparison is operationalized as a one-sample test of UNIFORM group prices against 1.94. Groups with a dropout were excluded as their price observations are not valid auction outcomes; this is the most defensible operationalization given the data's structure.
reasoning: Excluding the 6 groups with dropouts, a one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test of the 34 group-level UNIFORM average market prices against the predetermined FIXED price of 1.94 yielded W=341.5 (normal-approximation z=0.75, p=0.226). The point estimate goes in the predicted direction (mean diff = +0.045) but does not reach significance, so the data do not support the claim that uniform-price auctions raise significantly higher revenues than fixed-price offerings.

dependent_variable: Binary preference for Obama vs. Donald Trump (h0clean: 1=Trump, 2=Obama)
main_predictor: Conception risk (oddconcept; calculated odds of conception for a single sex act based on cycle position)
sample_definition: Female participants who reported regular cycles, were not on hormonal birth control, not pregnant, and had no chronic health issues affecting fertility, with non-missing conception risk and Obama-vs-Trump preference (n=304)
model_specification: Point-biserial (Pearson) correlation between conception risk and binary Obama preference, with t-test on r
operationalization_notes: The paper's most direct test for the main claim was a point-biserial correlation between conception risk and Obama voting preference among normally cycling women (Study 2 in the paper). I mirrored that test here, using oddconcept as conception risk and h0clean (Trump-vs-Obama binary, the cleanest analog to the original McCain-vs-Obama outcome) as the dependent variable. Note: the supplied dataset is from a 2020 hypothetical-election study and not the original 2008 election survey, so this is the closest possible replication on the provided data.
reasoning: Among normally cycling women (female, not on hormonal birth control, regular cycle, not pregnant, no chronic health issues affecting fertility), the point-biserial correlation between conception risk (oddconcept) and choosing Obama over Trump (h0clean) was essentially zero, r = -0.018, t(302) = -0.31, p = .76. This does not replicate the originally claimed positive association between conception risk and Obama voting preference.

dependent_variable: Panic-buying composite: mean of standardized log(panicbuying+1) and standardized log(stockpile+1) Google Trends scores
main_predictor: Standardized log(infected+1) COVID-19 cumulative cases
sample_definition: US daily observations from first confirmed case through March 24, 2020 (matches paper's window)
model_specification: OLS linear regression (single predictor)
operationalization_notes: Only the panic-buying outcome is available in the replication data (protective behaviors and health knowledge keyword series are not provided), so the most direct testable piece of the claim is the COVID-prevalence -> panic-buying link. Followed the paper's preprocessing: log-transform, standardize, restrict to the country's epidemic period through March 24, 2020. Chose US as the largest/primary country.
reasoning: Regressing the standardized log-transformed composite of panic buying (avg of panicbuying & stockpile Google Trends) on standardized log-transformed COVID-19 cumulative infections for the United States from the date of first confirmed case through March 24, 2020 yields B=0.80, SE=0.07, t(61)=11.16, p<1e-15. This replicates the paper's finding that COVID-19 prevalence positively predicts panic-buying searches.

dependent_variable: Procedural justice scale (mean of pj1-pj7)
main_predictor: Perceived workplace racial discrimination (mean of rd1-rd8, rd7/rd8 reverse-scored)
sample_definition: 82 participants who completed both Phase 1 and Phase 2 of the survey
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS regression (Step 2 of the paper's analysis): PJ regressed on controls + perceived discrimination + perceived organizational efforts to support diversity
controls: sex, age, minority status (poc), full-time work experience, full-time employment status, graduate student status
operationalization_notes: Mirrors the paper's Step 2 regression supporting H1. Report t-test on the discrimination coefficient with controls as the most demanding direct test of the directional claim.
reasoning: In an OLS regression of procedural justice on perceived racial discrimination and perceived organizational efforts to support diversity, controlling for sex, age, minority status (poc), work experience, employment status, and graduate status, the coefficient on perceived racial discrimination was significantly negative (b=-0.33, t(73)=-2.45, p=.017). This supports the claim that perceiving racial discrimination is associated with lower procedural justice.

dependent_variable: PSS-10 perceived stress (mean across 10 items)
main_predictor: Agreement with containment measures (3 levels)
sample_definition: All respondents in the replication dataset (Swiss residents) with non-missing PSS-10 and trust_countrymeasure (n=1079)
model_specification: One-way ANOVA (OLS) of stress on the 3-level agreement factor
operationalization_notes: Replicated Table 1's grouping: trust_countrymeasure (0=too little – 10=too much, 5=appropriate) was recoded into 'agreement' (5), 'no agreement' (1-4, 6-9), and 'no agreement at all' (0, 10), matching the paper's collapsing of the five-point response into three categories.
reasoning: A one-way ANOVA comparing PSS-10 stress across three groups defined by agreement with containment measures (agree = trust_countrymeasure = 5; partial agreement = 1–4 or 6–9; no agreement at all = 0 or 10) yielded F(2,1076) = 17.99, p ≈ 2e-8. Mean stress was lowest among those who agreed (M=2.27), higher for partial agreement (M=2.42), and highest for no-agreement-at-all (M=2.73), consistent with the claim that agreement decreases stress.

dependent_variable: Binary trust decision in the trust game (1 = Option L / trust, 0 = Option R / distrust)
main_predictor: Honesty-Humility × Self-uncertainty condition interaction
sample_definition: All 844 participants in the replication dataset with complete data on DV, HEXACO Honesty-Humility, and Condition
model_specification: Logistic regression: trust ~ Hc * Condition, where Hc is mean-centered Honesty-Humility (10 HEXACO-60 items with items 12, 24, 30, 42, 48, 60 reverse-coded) and Condition is 0=control, 1=self-uncertainty
controls: none (same specification as Studies 2 and 3 in the original paper)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Studies 2/3 model exactly (logistic regression of binary trust on H, condition, and their interaction with H mean-centered). The interaction coefficient is the test most directly tied to the claim.
reasoning: In a logistic regression of the binary trust choice on mean-centered Honesty-Humility, self-uncertainty condition (0=control, 1=uncertainty), and their interaction, the Honesty-Humility × Condition interaction was not significant (b = -0.088, z = -0.59, p = .56), though directionally negative as the original paper predicted. The main effect of Honesty-Humility on trust was positive and significant (z = 2.95, p = .003); the condition main effect was null.

dependent_variable: Mean of three 7-point desirability items (S1_likely, S1_quality, S1_purchase)
main_predictor: Self-concept clarity manipulation (Clear vs Conflicted) x rating-distribution condition (Unimodal vs Bimodal) interaction
sample_definition: All 376 usable participants from the 'All Usable data' sheet (Exclusion=0); 4 cells: ClB=83, ClU=95, CoB=112, CoU=86
model_specification: OLS regression of desirability on contrast-coded clarity (-1=Conflicted, +1=Clear), contrast-coded distribution (-1=Unimodal, +1=Bimodal), and their interaction
operationalization_notes: Study 2b operationalization (manipulated/temporary low SCC). Desirability index per paper. Interaction term is the test most directly tied to the moderation claim.
reasoning: In a 2 (self-concept clarity manipulation: Clear vs Conflicted) x 2 (rating distribution: Unimodal vs Bimodal) OLS regression on the 3-item desirability index, the clarity x distribution interaction was significant, t(372) = -2.30, p = .022. Cell means show that under the Conflicted (low SCC) condition, the bimodal product was rated more desirable than the unimodal one (4.98 vs 4.33), while in the Clear condition the two were nearly equal, supporting the claim.

dependent_variable: Composite scores for Severity, Anger, Sympathy, Revenge, Avoidance, Reconciliation modeled jointly in a path analysis
main_predictor: Manipulated offender motive (Malice dummy, Greed dummy; Control as reference) and the intervening severity/emotion variables
sample_definition: All Finished=1 participants assigned to one of the three motive conditions (Malice, Greed, Control) with complete responses on all composite indicators (N=1117)
model_specification: Path analysis (SEM via semopy) testing the hypothesized fully-mediated model: Severity ~ MaliceD + GreedD; Anger ~ Severity; Sympathy ~ Severity; Revenge/Avoidance/Reconciliation ~ Anger + Sympathy. Reported statistic is the model chi-square goodness-of-fit.
operationalization_notes: Selected the omnibus SEM chi-square because the claim spans the entire mediational chain (attributions distinguished, shape emotions, which independently relate to three behavioral outcomes); manipulated condition dummies operationalize malice vs. greed attributions. This is the most demanding single test of the joint claim.
reasoning: The hypothesized fully-mediated path model (Malice/Greed -> Severity -> Anger/Sympathy -> Revenge/Avoidance/Reconciliation) yielded a significant overall model chi-square (chi2(20)=328.81, p<.001, N=1117), mirroring the significant chi-square obtained in the original paper. All emotion->behavior paths emerged in the expected directions (Anger positively predicted revenge and avoidance and negatively predicted reconciliation; Sympathy positively predicted reconciliation and negatively predicted avoidance), supporting the claim that attribution-shaped emotions independently relate to revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation.

dependent_variable: MisperpSc (COVID-19 misperceptions composite)
main_predictor: Cognitive sophistication composite (mean of ZCRTSc, ZNumerSc, ZBSRSc, ZSciKnowSc)
sample_definition: All respondents in the provided replication dataset with complete data on the four cognitive-sophistication subscales and the misperceptions measure (N=87 of 161).
model_specification: Pearson correlation between the cognitive-sophistication composite and the misperceptions score (equivalently a bivariate OLS regression).
operationalization_notes: The paper defines cognitive sophistication as the bundle of analytic thinking (CRT), numeracy, basic science knowledge, and bullshit skepticism; the dataset provides standardized versions of each plus the misperceptions composite, so I averaged them and correlated with misperceptions to test the simple claim of a negative bivariate relationship.
reasoning: A cognitive sophistication composite (mean of z-scored CRT, numeracy, basic science knowledge, and bullshit-skepticism scores) correlated r = -0.40 with the misperceptions scale, t(85) = -4.05, p < .001, indicating that more cognitively sophisticated respondents held fewer COVID-19 misperceptions, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: Average correct recognition index for emotion words ((JOY% + ANG%)/2, i.e. hits minus false alarms divided by max)
main_predictor: Alexithymia group via TAS-20 median split (TASGRP: 1=low, 2=high)
sample_definition: All participants in the submitted dataset (n=1096), collapsing across music condition and depth-of-processing condition
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test comparing mean emotion-word recognition between low and high alexithymia groups (equivalent to the between-subjects main effect of alexithymia from a 2x2 mixed ANOVA with word type as a within factor)
operationalization_notes: Claim concerns the main effect of alexithymia level on recognition of joy and anger words. Used the paper's median-split TASGRP and the recognition index already provided in the data, averaged across the two emotion word types to capture the joint claim in a single test.
reasoning: High-alexithymia scorers (TASGRP=2) recognized fewer joy and anger words than low scorers: mean emotion-word recognition index = .19 vs .46; independent-samples t(1094)=16.85, p<.001. Both joy (.19 vs .46) and anger (.18 vs .46) recognition are lower in high-alex, supporting the directional claim.

dependent_variable: EVOLVED (binary: agree humans developed from earlier species of animals)
main_predictor: Latent class membership (traditional vs. post-secular)
sample_definition: GSS 2006/2008/2010 respondents with science module data; complete-case LCA assignments restricted to those classified as traditional or post-secular with non-missing EVOLVED (n=2,292)
model_specification: Pearson chi-square test of independence on 2x2 table (class x EVOLVED) following latent class assignment from 3-class categorical LCA over 14 knowledge items, 4 science-attitude items, and 2 religion items
operationalization_notes: Used stepmix (3-class categorical LCA with NaN handling). Classes labeled by their conditional means on EVOLVED/BIGBANG and overall knowledge: traditional=low knowledge & low evolution acceptance; modern=high knowledge & high evolution acceptance; post-secular=high knowledge but near-zero evolution acceptance. The chi-square compares the two relevant classes named in the claim.
reasoning: After replicating the three-class LCA with stepmix on the 2006/2008/2010 GSS science/religion indicators, the post-secular class endorsed 'humans developed from earlier animals' at only 2.7% versus 42.9% in the traditional class (chi2(1)=465.12, p<.001, n=2,292), strongly confirming the paper's directional claim.

dependent_variable: Trendiness index = mean of V18 (trendy), V19 (modern), V20 (urban) on 1-7 scales
main_predictor: Table surface condition (glass vs. wood)
sample_definition: All 69 participants in the replication dataset (all under interdependent self-view prime; 34 glass, 35 wood)
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test (equal variance) comparing glass vs wood
operationalization_notes: Replication data contains only interdependent prime condition with glass vs wood manipulation, matching the focal subgroup of H1. Trendiness composite defined as in the paper's pretest (trendy+modern+urban).
reasoning: Among interdependent-primed participants, the trendiness index (avg of trendy, modern, urban) was actually slightly lower for the glass table (M=5.10, n=34) than for the wood table (M=5.47, n=35). The independent-samples t-test yielded t(67) = -1.31, p = .19, failing to support and trending opposite to the claimed assimilation effect.

dependent_variable: Mean percentage of utilitarian (morally acceptable) responses across the two moral scenarios per participant
main_predictor: Mortality salience condition (death vs. pain)
sample_definition: All 131 participants in the provided generalizability dataset (no exclusions; consent and attention-check fields not used to drop cases because no participant failed)
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test comparing mean per-subject utilitarian response rate between the death and pain conditions
operationalization_notes: The data file contains two moral_accept items per subject, coded 1=not acceptable, 2=acceptable (utilitarian). I averaged the two items into a per-subject utilitarian rate and contrasted the two salience conditions, mirroring the paper's between-subjects test of the death-vs-pain effect on utilitarian responding.
reasoning: Mean utilitarian response rate was 87.9% in the death condition (n=62) vs 84.8% in the pain condition (n=69); the difference is in the opposite direction to the prediction and is far from significant, t(129)=-0.64, p=.52. The dataset thus does not reproduce the claim that mortality salience reduces utilitarian responses.

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time (ms) on the 4 interpersonal obstacle-prime / instrumental-behavior-target lexical decision trials (lower = stronger association)
main_predictor: Expectations of success × Condition (mental contrasting vs. reverse contrasting vs. irrelevant control)
sample_definition: All filter_$=1 participants in the H8 analytic dataset with complete data on expectations, association RT, and accessibility RT (n=307)
model_specification: Hierarchical OLS: Step1 IntAssocM ~ IntExp_c + IntAccessM + D_RC + D_IC; Step2 adds IntExp_c×D_RC and IntExp_c×D_IC; F-change tests the joint interaction.
controls: Mere accessibility of the instrumental behavior (mean RT of neutral-prime/behavior-target trials)
operationalization_notes: Followed the paper's Study 1 interpersonal-domain hierarchical regression. The F-change test of the two expectation×condition interactions is the most direct overall test of whether MC produces expectancy-dependent (high→strong, low→weak) obstacle–behavior associations relative to control conditions.
reasoning: Hierarchical regression on the interpersonal obstacle–behavior associations (mean RT of 4 prime-target trials), controlling for mere accessibility, with expectations and two condition dummies (MC reference) in step 1 and two expectation×condition interactions in step 2, yielded R²_change with F(2,300)=1.17, p=.31. The simple slope of expectations within the mental contrasting condition was b=-13.31, t(300)=-0.86, p=.39, providing no support that MC paired with low expectations yields weaker obstacle–behavior associations.

dependent_variable: s - xl: difference between share given to recipient (s) and recipient's libertarian fair share (partner_endowment / total endowment)
main_predictor: Libertarian benchmark (xl) compared to actual transfer s
sample_definition: All dictators in the DW (150:200) treatment (n=27); cleaned_data.dta contains only DW dictators
model_specification: Wilcoxon signed-rank test (normal approximation) of H0: median(s - xl) = 0
operationalization_notes: Following Table 1 of the paper, the libertarian principle is tested via a Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing dictators' transfers to the libertarian benchmark. xl computed as partner_endowment/(player_endowment+partner_endowment) since s is the share given away.
reasoning: Wilcoxon signed-rank test of (s - xl) for DW dictators yields z = -3.53 (p < 0.001, n=27, 23 non-zero differences). Dictators' shares given away differ significantly from the libertarian benchmark (mean s-xl = -0.12), so the libertarian principle does not account for observed behavior in DW.

dependent_variable: Under-diagnosed (=1 if hypertensive but not previously diagnosed)
main_predictor: Years of education
sample_definition: Hypertensive adults in poor general health (poor_health==1) from the provided analytic data.Rds (n=756 of 3131)
model_specification: Probit regression of underdiagnosed on education, log per-capita expenditure, time preference, risk preference, travel time to health center, and female indicator
controls: log PCE, time preference, risk preference, travel time to health center, female
operationalization_notes: Column 3 of Table 2 (under-diagnosis probit, poor-health subsample) is the analysis most directly tied to the claim. Sample size differs from the paper's 1064 because data.Rds appears to contain a complete-case analytic subset (3131 obs vs 4209), but the specification and conclusion replicate.
reasoning: In the poor-health subsample, a probit of under-diagnosis on education plus the paper's controls yields a negative, significant education coefficient (β=-0.0297, z=-2.485, p=0.013, marginal effect ≈ -1.16 percentage points per year of schooling). More education thus lowers the probability of being under-diagnosed (i.e., raises the probability of being diagnosed) conditional on poor general health, matching the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Proportion of deontological responses per participant (RH_PMD, RH_CMD, RH_NMD)
main_predictor: Group (Observed vs. Control) x Dilemma type (Personal/Impersonal/Non-moral) interaction
sample_definition: All participants in SCORE_all data.sav with non-missing Condition and RH scores (N=156; 78 per group)
model_specification: 2 (Group, between) x 3 (Dilemma type, within) mixed ANOVA; primary test is the interaction term
operationalization_notes: Operationalization follows the methods section, which specifies a 2x3 mixed ANOVA on the proportion of deontological responses with the interaction effect as the key test of the claim. The full dataset (N=156) was used rather than a 48-participant subset because no filter variable in the provided data identifies the paper's reported n=48 sample.
reasoning: A 2 (Group: Observed vs. Control) x 3 (Dilemma type: personal/impersonal/non-moral) mixed ANOVA on the proportion of deontological responses (RH_PMD, RH_CMD, RH_NMD) yielded no significant Group x Dilemma interaction, F(2,308)=0.24, p=.79, eta_p^2=.002, and no main effect of Group (F(1,154)=1.00, p=.32). The direct between-group comparison for personal moral dilemmas was also non-significant (Welch's t(153.9)=0.78, p=.43). The data therefore do not reproduce the claim that social observation selectively increased deontological judgments for personal moral dilemmas.

dependent_variable: Worry about coronavirus (worrycovid19, 7-point Likert)
main_predictor: sex (1=female, 2=male)
sample_definition: All survey respondents with non-missing values on sex and worrycovid19 (n=696)
model_specification: Welch's two-sample t-test (unequal variances)
operationalization_notes: Selected the single variable most directly indexing concern about COVID-19 (worrycovid19); compared means between gender groups with a Welch t-test, matching the paper's bivariate gender comparison on the same worry item.
reasoning: Women (n=345, M=5.81, SD=1.44) reported significantly higher worry about COVID-19 on the 7-point item than men (n=351, M=5.51, SD=1.52); Welch's t(693.1)=2.61, p=.009. This supports the paper's claim that women are more concerned about COVID-19 than men.

dependent_variable: Percent change in distance traveled per capita (March 19-28, 2020 relative to weekday-matched reference week Jan 23-Feb 1, 2020), computed from BTS Trips_by_Distance using bin midpoints
main_predictor: County Trump vote share in 2016 (trump_share)
sample_definition: U.S. counties with non-missing BTS trip data for both periods and complete covariates (n=3114)
model_specification: OLS with state fixed effects
controls: Per capita income (in $1000s), percent male, percent Black, percent Hispanic, percent with college degree, percent employed in retail, transportation, and health/education/social services, percent rural; state fixed effects
operationalization_notes: Original paper used Unacast distance data unavailable in the replication archive; BTS trips data is the provided substitute. Distance per capita computed by weighting trip-count bins by their midpoints (cap at 500 mi). Reference period chosen 8 weeks earlier to match weekdays.
reasoning: OLS regression of the percent change in distance-per-capita (March 19-28, 2020 vs. weekday-matched reference Jan 23-Feb 1, 2020) on Trump's 2016 county vote share with state fixed effects and sociodemographic/industry/rurality controls yields a positive coefficient of 23.5 (t=5.39, p<0.001, n=3114). Higher Trump vote share predicts a smaller decline (i.e., less social distancing), confirming the claim.

dependent_variable: Social distancing composite (soc_dist; mean of 4 items)
main_predictor: Political conservatism composite (pol; mean of 3 ideology items)
sample_definition: All respondents in the provided final (cleaned) data file (N=322).
model_specification: Bivariate OLS regression: soc_dist ~ pol (equivalent to Pearson correlation)
operationalization_notes: The claim is a direct directional statement about conservatism predicting social-distancing compliance, so the most direct test is the simple bivariate regression of the social-distancing composite on the conservatism composite as constructed by the authors. Only one of the two studies' datasets appears to be present in the data folder, so the analysis is restricted to that sample.
reasoning: OLS regression of composite social distancing on composite conservatism yields B=-0.135, t(320)=-3.26, p=.001 (Pearson r=-0.18), confirming that more conservative respondents report significantly less compliance with social-distancing behaviors.

dependent_variable: Third-grade reading IRT scale score (X7RSCALK5)
main_predictor: Social-emotional problems composite: mean of teacher-reported externalizing (X7TCHEXT) and internalizing (X7TCHINT) problems
sample_definition: ELL children identified by X12LANGST=1 (non-English home language / limited English proficient at K) with non-missing values on all variables
model_specification: Bivariate Pearson correlation between SE-problem composite and reading IRT score
operationalization_notes: Provided dataset is ECLS-K:2011, which lacks the SDQ child-report SE scales used by the original ECLS-K:1998-99 paper; the closest available analogues are teacher-reported externalizing/internalizing problems and the X7 (spring 3rd grade) reading IRT scale score. The single most direct bivariate test of the claim was a Pearson correlation on the ELL subsample.
reasoning: Among third-grade ELL children (X12LANGST=1), a composite of teacher-reported externalizing and internalizing problems was significantly negatively correlated with third-grade reading IRT scale score (r=-.259, t(2075)=-12.23, p<.001, N=2077). Fewer social-emotional problems are associated with higher reading achievement, replicating the direction reported by the authors.

dependent_variable: Mean of SocGood ratings across the four organizations (Artisanal, Green tech, Healthy food, Medical tech), 1=great harm to 5=great good
main_predictor: Firm motive condition (Non-profit / Unspecified / For-profit; the between-subjects 'condition' variable with 3 levels)
sample_definition: All participants who passed the embedded attention check (Socimpact_Green_6 == 1); N = 347
model_specification: One-way between-subjects ANOVA on per-subject mean societal-good rating across the 4 organizations
operationalization_notes: Paper used a repeated-measures ANOVA combining across the four organizations with motive condition as the between-subjects factor; a one-way ANOVA on the per-subject across-organization mean is the most direct equivalent test of the main effect of motive condition.
reasoning: Between-subjects one-way ANOVA on each subject's mean perceived societal good across the four organizations yielded F(2, 344) = 36.77, p < .001. Condition means (4.31, 4.09, 3.74) show the profit-motive condition produced the lowest perceived societal good, replicating the directional claim.

dependent_variable: Sharing intention rescaled to [0,1] (Likert 1-6 -> 0-1)
main_predictor: Headline veracity (1=true, 0=false)
sample_definition: Treatment condition participants only (Condition==2); all rating observations after dropping missing responses
model_specification: OLS regression at the rating level with two-way cluster-robust SEs (clustered on participant and headline), as specified in the paper's methods
operationalization_notes: Only the replication file ('Pennycook et al (2020) - replication - final.csv') contained real data; the two 'test data' files contained lorem-ipsum dummy responses. Used Roozenbeek et al. (2021) replication data, which is the closest direct test of the original claim available.
reasoning: Within the treatment condition only, an OLS regression of rescaled sharing intentions (0-1) on headline veracity with two-way clustered SEs by participant and headline yields a positive veracity coefficient of 0.052 (z=2.31, p=0.021, n=23,700 ratings from 790 participants). Sharing intentions for true headlines are significantly higher than for false headlines, consistent with the paper's claim, though the effect size is smaller than originally reported.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth indicator (1 if annual real GDP per capita growth ≥2% in each of the 5 years beginning with the Afrobarometer survey year)
main_predictor: Log of country-level Impartiality index (weighted share of respondents saying their group is 'never' treated unfairly by government), built from Afrobarometer rounds 1-4
sample_definition: All 64 country-survey-years from Afrobarometer rounds 1-4 (20 sub-Saharan African countries, 1999-2009) for which the impartiality index can be computed and 5 subsequent years of WDI growth data exist
model_specification: Pooled OLS linear probability model: SG = b0 + b1*log(Impartiality) + b2*Polity2 + e, with country-clustered robust standard errors
operationalization_notes: Mirrors paper's column-1 pooled OLS specification (Table 3) using only the impartiality index and Polity2 as controls. Sustained growth is operationalized forward from the survey year as the most direct reading of the verbal definition; impartiality index is rebuilt from raw Afrobarometer microdata using survey weights as described in Appendix A and matches Table 5 values.
reasoning: In a pooled OLS regressing the sustained-growth indicator (=1 if real GDP-per-capita growth was ≥2% for each of the 5 years starting in the survey year) on log impartiality and Polity2 with country-clustered SEs, the coefficient on log impartiality is -0.023 (cluster-robust z = -0.24, p ≈ 0.81). The data do not support the claim that more impartial governments are more likely to experience sustained growth under this direct operationalization.

dependent_variable: Mean toaster evaluation (toaster45_mean vs toaster25_mean, averaged across 5 evaluation items)

model_specification: MANCOVA: cbind(Revenge, Avoidance, Reconciliation) ~ Anger + Sympathy + Malice_dummy + Greed_dummy; Wilks' lambda for Anger's joint effect on the three outcomes.
controls: Sympathy and dummy-coded Malice and Greed conditions (Control = reference).
operationalization_notes: The claim is a chain (motive attributions → emotions → behaviors). The most direct single test of the final, independence-of-emotions link is a multivariate test of Anger's effect on the three behavioral outcomes after partialing out the motive manipulations and the other emotion (sympathy). The lab/experimental dataset (only data provided) was used; condition dummies serve as controls for the motive attribution stage.
reasoning: In a MANCOVA with Revenge, Avoidance, and Reconciliation as dependent variables and Anger, Sympathy, and dummy-coded Malice and Greed conditions as predictors, Anger had a strong independent multivariate effect on the three behavioral reactions (Wilks' λ = 0.816, F(3,1111) = 83.55, p < .001). Sympathy also showed an independent multivariate effect (F(3,1111) = 41.88, p < .001), supporting the claim that emotional reactions are independently related to revenge, avoidance, and reconciliation.

dependent_variable: COVID-19 misperceptions composite (MisperpSc)

This supports the claim that cognitive sophistication negatively predicts COVID-19 misperceptions.

dependent_variable: Mean recognition rate (correct recognition index) averaged over joy and anger words (JOY% and ANG%)
main_predictor: Alexithymia group (TASGRP: low vs high based on median split TAS-20)

model_specification: Between-subjects ANOVA on subject-mean recognition rate with factors DEPTH x MUSIC x TASGRP (Type III SS); equivalent to the between-subjects main effect of alexithymia in a 2x2x2x2 mixed ANOVA with word type as within-subject factor
controls: Depth of processing and music condition included as factors in the factorial ANOVA
operationalization_notes: Following the paper's mixed ANOVA on recognition rates (level of processing x music x alexithymia x word type), the claim of fewer joy/anger words in high alexithymia maps to the between-subjects main effect of alexithymia, which is identical to a between-subjects ANOVA on the subject-mean of joy and anger recognition. reasoning: Mixed ANOVA on recognition rate (joy & anger words averaged within subject) with between-subjects factors Depth, Music, and Alexithymia group yields a significant main effect of alexithymia, F(1,1088)=126.62, p<.001. Low-alex scorers recognized 46.3% of joy/anger words vs. 18.9% for high-alex scorers, matching the directional claim that high alexithymia scorers recognize fewer anger and joy words.

dependent_variable: EVOLVED (human beings developed from earlier species of animals; 1=true, 0=false)
main_predictor: Latent class membership (traditional vs. post-secular) from a 3-class LCA
sample_definition: GSS 2006/2008/2010 respondents with non-missing BIBLE and RELITEN and at least one response on the science module (n=4129 for LCA); test restricted to traditional+post-secular cases with observed EVOLVED (n=2246).
model_specification: Pearson chi-squared test of independence on a 2x2 table (class x EVOLVED), with class assignments obtained by modal posterior probability from a 3-class LCA fit with stepmix (categorical_nan emissions, n_init=5, max_iter=1000).
controls: none (LCA is unconditional; chi-square is bivariate)
operationalization_notes: Most direct test of the claim is the bivariate comparison of EVOLVED endorsement between paper-defined classes. I had to re-fit the LCA in stepmix; coding BIBLE as a single multinomial indicator (rather than 3 mutually exclusive dummies) was essential to recover classes matching the paper's profiles. The recovered post-secular class proportion (25.7%) is somewhat larger than the paper's 21%, but its profile (very low EVOLVED, high RELITEN, no BIBLE-as-fable) cleanly matches.
reasoning: After fitting a 3-class LCA on the science-knowledge, science-attitude, and religion manifest variables (BIBLE coded as a single 4-category indicator to avoid double-counting; RELITEN ordinal), classes recovered closely match the paper's profiles: a post-secular class (n=1063, EVOLVED=2.8%), a traditional class (n=1540, EVOLVED=42.2%), and a modern class (n=1526, EVOLVED=93.6%). Comparing the proportion endorsing 'humans evolved from earlier species of animals' between the traditional and post-secular classes yields χ²(1, N=2246)=446.57, p<.001. Post-seculars are dramatically less likely than traditionals to affirm human evolution, matching the paper's claim.

dependent_variable: Mean trendiness index of mug (V18 trendy, V19 modern, V20 urban; 1–7 scale)
main_predictor: Display table surface: glass (V17=1) vs wood (V16=1)
sample_definition: All 69 participants in Zhu_Replication.csv; codebook/data indicate all received the interdependent self-view writing prime (the only writing task variable, V11, is the interdependent prompt)
model_specification: Independent-samples t-test (equal variances) comparing glass vs wood on the trendiness index
operationalization_notes: Closest available analogue to the paper's planned contrast for interdependents on the trendiness dimension. The replication dataset does not include an independence condition, so the analysis collapses to a single 2-level comparison of table surface within interdependent priming.
reasoning: On the replication data (which uses only the interdependent priming task, V11), a between-subjects t-test of the 3-item trendiness index (trendy/modern/urban) showed mug trendiness was numerically lower in the glass-table condition (M=5.10, n=34) than the wood-table condition (M=5.47, n=35), t(67) = -1.31, p = .19. The direction is opposite to the predicted assimilation effect and is not statistically significant, failing to replicate the claim.

dependent_variable: Utilitarian (morally acceptable) response on the two moral scenarios, coded 1 = acceptable, 0 = not
main_predictor: Salience condition (death vs. pain) × problem type (conflict moral_accept vs. control moral_accept1)
sample_definition: Participants who gave consent (Q1=2), passed the attention check (attn='c'), and whose manipulation response was rated satisfactory (satisfactory_manipulation_response1=1); N=129 (62 death, 67 pain)
model_specification: Mixed 2×2 ANOVA on binary utilitarian response, implemented as an independent-samples t-test on the within-subject (control − conflict) difference between salience groups (algebraically equivalent to the interaction F; F = t²)
operationalization_notes: The paper's primary support for the claim is the problem-type × salience interaction showing the salience effect is concentrated on conflict items. I therefore tested that interaction directly. Standard exclusions (consent, attention check, manipulation-quality coding) were applied as defined in the codebook.
reasoning: The 2 (problem: conflict vs control, within) × 2 (salience: death vs pain, between) mixed ANOVA interaction—the analog to the paper's headline F(1,83)=6.89—is non-significant in the replication data, F(1,127)=1.61, p=.21. In fact, on conflict items the death group endorsed the utilitarian option slightly MORE (82.3%) than the pain group (76.1%), the opposite of the original direction, though this simple-effect difference is also non-significant (t=0.85, p=.40).

dependent_variable: Mean reaction time on 4 interpersonal obstacle->behavior priming trials (IntAssocM); lower RT = stronger association
main_predictor: Condition (MC vs RC dummy) × Expectations of success interaction; key test = simple effect of MC vs RC at low expectations (Exp=1)
sample_definition: Participants in H8 analytic dataset passing the latency filter (filter_$=1) with complete data on key variables; reverse contrasting set as reference category, mental contrasting vs reverse contrasting contrast tested
model_specification: OLS hierarchical regression: IntAssocM ~ IntExp + IntAccessM + Dummy1(MC) + Dummy2(Control) + Dummy1:IntExp + Dummy2:IntExp, with IntExp centered at 1 so the Dummy1 coefficient = MC vs RC effect at low expectations
controls: Mere accessibility of interpersonal behavior (IntAccessM); irrelevant-content control dummy
operationalization_notes: Followed Study 1 analytic template from the original paper (the replicated study). The most direct test of 'MC + low expectations -> weak associations' is the simple effect of MC vs RC at the low end of expectations, computed by centering expectations at 1 within the full interaction model.
reasoning: In a hierarchical regression of obstacle-behavior priming RTs (IntAssocM) on expectations, accessibility, and condition dummies (MC vs RC reference; Control vs RC) plus expectation×condition interactions, the simple effect of MC vs RC at low expectations (IntExp = 1) was b = 27.40, t(300) = 0.32, p = .75. Although the direction (positive, meaning slower RT = weaker associations under MC) is consistent with the claim, the effect is far from significant and the overall expectation×condition interaction is also non-significant (F(2,300) = 1.17, p = .31), so the replication does not support the claim.

dependent_variable: Dictator's deviation from libertarian benchmark (s - x_l)

operationalization_notes: Paper explicitly tests the libertarian principle in DW via a Wilcoxon signed-rank test of s = x_l; the dataset's x variable corresponds to x_l (recipient's monetary contribution share). Test statistic reported as the z from the normal approximation derived from W=8, n=27.
reasoning: A Wilcoxon signed-rank test of H0: s = x_l on the 27 DW dictators yields W=8 and a normal-approximation z ≈ -3.38 (p ≈ 0.00074), with mean (s - x_l) = -0.12. Dictators give significantly less than the recipient's monetary contribution share, so the libertarian principle does not account for behavior in the DW treatment — matching the original paper's conclusion.

Although the direction is consistent with the claim (OBS M = 0.649 vs. CON M = 0.629), the difference is small and far from statistical significance, so the claim that social observation promoted deontological judgments in personal moral dilemmas does not reproduce on this dataset.

The effect is significant but in the opposite direction to the claim that women are more concerned than men.

dependent_variable: Percent change in num_trips per capita, mean over March 19-28, 2020 vs. mean over matched calendar dates (March 19-28, 2019), constructed from BTS Trips_by_Distance (used as a proxy for the Unacast measure unavailable in the replication data)

model_specification: Cross-sectional OLS regression with state fixed effects
controls: income_per_capita, percent_college, percent_male, percent_black, percent_hispanic, percent_retail, percent_transportation, percent_hes, percent_rural, single-year age-group shares (under 5 through 75-84), and state fixed effects

Positive sign indicates higher Republican vote share is associated with a smaller decline in mobility, i.e. less social distancing, reproducing the paper's claim.

Cell means (Profit M=3.75 < Non-Profit/Unspecified M≈4.09 and 4.31) match the paper's direction: a profit motive reduced perceived societal good.

dependent_variable: Sharing intention for a headline (1=Extremely unlikely to 6=Extremely likely), averaged within participant across the 15 true and 15 false COVID-19 headlines

A rating-level OLS with veracity (-0.5/0.5) and SEs clustered on participant gave an equivalent result (Wald z = -1.12, p = .27, n_ratings = 13,200).
reasoning: In the treatment (accuracy nudge) condition of Study 2, a paired t-test comparing each participant's mean sharing intention for true vs. false headlines yielded t(439) = -1.12, p = .27 (M_true = 3.49 vs. M_false = 3.52 on the 1-6 likelihood scale). The direction is opposite to that claimed (false slightly higher than true) and the difference is not significant, so the claim that sharing intentions for true headlines were significantly higher than for false headlines in the treatment condition does not reproduce in this dataset.

dependent_variable: Sustained growth dummy (=1 if WB GDP/capita growth ≥2% in each of years t+1..t+5, where t is the Afrobarometer survey year)
main_predictor: Log Impartiality index (country-survey share of respondents answering 'Never' to whether their ethnic/identity group is treated unfairly by the government, sample-weighted)
sample_definition: 20 sub-Saharan African countries, Afrobarometer rounds 1-4 (survey years 1999-2009); two 2009 surveys (Zambia, Zimbabwe) dropped because the 5-year forward growth window exceeds available WB GDP data (capped at 2013, matching the paper's data window), yielding 62 country-year observations.
model_specification: Pooled OLS linear probability model with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors: sustained_growth = a + γ·log(Impartiality) + β·Polity2 + e.
operationalization_notes: Mirrors the most direct test corresponding to Table 3, column 1 of the paper. Impartiality index built from Afrobarometer question on how often the respondent's ethnic group is treated unfairly (=1 if 'Never', else 0), using combined sample weights. Sustained growth follows the paper's main definition (≥2% for ≥5 consecutive years) using the lagged-impartiality timing described in §4. The WB GDP series used was the one shipped with the replication archive, restricted to ≤2013 to mimic data available when the paper was written.
reasoning: Replicating the paper's main pooled-OLS LPM (Table 3, col. 1)—regressing a sustained-growth dummy (=1 if real GDP/capita growth ≥2% for five consecutive years starting the year after the survey) on log Impartiality index and Polity2 across 62 Afrobarometer country-survey observations (1999-2008, rounds 1-4)—the coefficient on log Impartiality is -0.049 (HC1 SE 0.10; t=-0.49, p=0.63). The estimate is wrong-signed and far from statistically significant, providing no evidence for the paper's claim that more impartial governments are more likely to experience sustained growth.

dependent_variable: Choice of toaster (aggregated-positive vs. individualized-positive)

Direct test of the claim is the omnibus chi-square across all five sound conditions on the dichotomous toaster choice; descriptive percentages confirm the abstract group's strong preference for the aggregated-information toaster.
reasoning: Chi-square test of independence on choice of toaster across the 5 sound conditions (filter-selected sample, N=95) yields χ²(4)=12.47, p=.014. In the abstract-sound group, 15/16 (93.8%) chose the aggregated-information toaster vs. 8/20 (40%) in concrete sound, consistent with the claim.

dependent_variable: GDP per capita PPP (national affluence)
main_predictor: Imports from the South (USD, scaled to billions)
sample_definition: 18 OECD countries, 1970–2003, observations with non-missing GDPcapita, unemployment, totalimport, totalexport (N=468)

controls: Exports to the South, unemployment rate, country fixed effects, 5-year period fixed effects (1970–74 baseline)
operationalization_notes: Mirrors paper's Model 4 (national affluence on North–South trade with country & period FE). reasoning: In a two-way fixed-effects regression of GDP per capita (national affluence) on imports-from-the-South (and exports-to-the-South, unemployment, country and 5-year period dummies), the coefficient on imports from the South is positive (b≈27.4 per $1B of imports) and highly significant (t=4.53, cluster-robust SE on 18 countries; p<0.001), confirming the paper's claim that North–South imports raise national affluence in OECD countries.

The branded score is significantly less symbolic / more utilitarian, t(608)=4.20, p<.001, supporting the claim.
